gustavklimt.blurb: The Vienna Secession's golden founding father.
gustavklimt.bio: Gustav Klimt, born in 1862, was an Austrian symbolist painter whose work gave Art Nouveau its most opulent European face. In 1897 he helped found the Vienna Secession alongside the architect and designer Josef Hoffmann, breaking with the academy on the way. Klimt painted allegories, portraits, murals and landscapes, but the female body was his lasting subject, treated with a frankness that unsettled Vienna; The Kiss and the Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I, both from 1907, remain the works everyone knows. Of the Secession artists he absorbed Japanese art most deeply, flattening space and letting pattern carry the meaning. His Beethoven Frieze of 1901 pushed painting into architecture. From 1907 he mentored the young Egon Schiele, trading drawings with him and steering patrons his way. Klimt died in 1918.

kolomanmoser.blurb: Vienna's graphic designer before the term existed.
kolomanmoser.bio: Koloman Moser, born in 1868, was an Austrian artist and designer whose flat, geometric graphic work shaped twentieth-century design far beyond Vienna. He was among the foremost figures of the Vienna Secession, and in 1903 he co-founded the Wiener Werkstätte with the architect Josef Hoffmann, a workshop that carried Secession ideas into furniture, metalwork and everyday objects. Moser moved easily between disciplines, working as painter, designer, architect and even designer of postage stamps, and treated each with the same rigour. His 1902 image of the dancer Loïe Fuller as The Archangel shows how completely he could turn a body into pattern. In later years he returned to painting, producing Marigolds in 1909, a cloud study in 1913 and The Wayfarer in 1914. He died in 1918.

josefhoffmann.blurb: The architect who built the Secession's ideas.
josefhoffmann.bio: Josef Hoffmann, born in 1870, was an Austrian-Moravian architect and designer who turned Vienna's new ideas into buildings and objects. He was among the founders of the Vienna Secession in 1897, alongside Gustav Klimt, and in 1903 he co-established the Wiener Werkstätte with Koloman Moser, giving the movement a workshop where architecture, furniture and tableware were designed as a single whole. His most famous building is the Stoclet Palace in Brussels, built between 1905 and 1911, a pioneering work of modern architecture, part Art Deco and the high point of Secession building. Hoffmann designed at every scale, from the Otto Wagner memorial at the Academy in 1929 down to a tablecloth. A teacher as well as a practitioner, he worked on for decades and died in 1956.

alphonsemucha.blurb: The poster artist Paris could not escape.
alphonsemucha.bio: Alphonse Mucha, born in 1860, was a Czech painter, illustrator and graphic artist who lived in Paris through the Art Nouveau years and gave the style its most recognisable look. His life changed with the Gismonda poster of 1894, designed for the actress Sarah Bernhardt; she signed him to a six-year contract, and his stylised, decorative theatrical posters became the images people still associate with the period. He worked as a lithographer, photographer and designer, producing advertisements, decorative panels and illustration alongside the posters, with sets such as Zodiac in 1896 and the Byzantine Heads. Later he turned to something very different, the vast cycle of Slav Epic canvases begun in 1910. Mucha died in 1939, his commercial work long since absorbed into the language of modern design.

hectorguimard.blurb: He gave the Métro its iron curves.
hectorguimard.bio: Hector Guimard, born in 1867, was a French architect and designer whose name is inseparable from Art Nouveau in Paris. He made his reputation with the Castel Béranger, Paris's first Art Nouveau apartment building, which an 1899 competition picked out as one of the city's best new facades. He is best remembered for something far more public: the glass and iron canopies and edicules, all ornamental curves, that he designed to shelter the entrances of the first Paris Métro stations. Guimard worked as a sculptor and designer as well as an architect, and applied the same whiplash line to the furniture made for Madame Guimard in 1909, to a paper knife, and to the grave of Ernest Caillat. He died in 1942.

antonigaudi.bio: Antoni Gaudí i Cornet, born in 1852, was a Catalan architect and designer, widely regarded as the greatest exponent of Catalan Modernisme. His work belongs to no school but his own: a sui generis style that bent structure, tile and stone into forms drawn from nature and from faith. Almost all of it stands in Barcelona, where his buildings became the city's signature, and his magnum opus is the Sagrada Família church, a project that outlived him. Gaudí was a designer and draftsman too, and thought at every scale, from the Font d'Hèrcules of 1884 to the confidant seat made for the Batlló house in 1904 and the Primer Misteri de Glòria of 1916. He died in 1926, leaving work that later architects found easier to admire than to imitate.

aubreybeardsley.blurb: Black ink, decadence, and an early death.
aubreybeardsley.bio: Aubrey Vincent Beardsley, born in 1872, was an English illustrator and author whose black ink drawings gave the 1890s their most disquieting images. Influenced by Japanese woodcuts, he worked in flat, stark contrasts and drew the grotesque, the decadent and the erotic with a line that made even his admirers uneasy. He was a leading figure in the aesthetic movement that also gathered Oscar Wilde and James McNeill Whistler, and his covers for The Yellow Book in 1894 fixed his reputation. He wrote as well as drew, and produced oddities such as A Large Christmas Card of 1895 and the 1894 Caprice with its masked woman and white mouse. Tuberculosis killed him in 1898, yet his contribution to Art Nouveau and to poster design was already significant.

roberthenri.blurb: The teacher who sent painters into the street.
roberthenri.bio: Robert Henri, born in 1865, was an American painter and, by common consent, one of the most consequential teachers his country produced. From 1891 he gathered a circle of Philadelphia newspaper illustrators around his Walnut Street studio, among them John Sloan, and pushed them towards the unpolished life of the modern city. At the New York School of Art his students included Edward Hopper, who studied with him from 1900 to 1906, and George Bellows. In 1908 he assembled the exhibition of The Eight at the Macbeth Galleries, with Sloan, George Luks and Everett Shinn among them, a show that loosened the academy's grip on what American painting could look like. His own canvases, among them The Irish Girl of 1900 and Snow in New York of 1902, are direct and warmly handled. He died in 1929.

johnsloan.blurb: Ashcan life, watched from a Chelsea window.
johnsloan.bio: John French Sloan, born in 1871, was an American painter and etcher and one of the founders of the Ashcan School. He came to painting through newspaper illustration in Philadelphia, where from 1891 he belonged to the circle Robert Henri drew around his Walnut Street studio, and he exhibited with Henri as one of The Eight. Sloan is best known for urban genre scenes that catch the texture of New York neighbourhood life, much of it observed from his Chelsea studio window: Red Kimono on the Roof and Renganeschi's Saturday Night, both 1912, and The City from Greenwich Village of 1922. He is sometimes named the school's premier artist. A committed socialist, he nonetheless insisted his politics and his painting be kept apart. He died in 1951.

georgebellows.blurb: Boxing, tenements, and a very short career.
georgebellows.bio: George Wesley Bellows, born in 1882, was an American realist painter who took the crowded life of New York City as his subject and rendered it boldly. He studied with Robert Henri at the New York School of Art and took from him the instruction to paint the city as it was; the results include Stag at Sharkey's of 1909, a boxing match rendered as a blur of lit flesh, and Cliff Dwellers of 1913, a tenement street in high summer. He also worked as a lithographer and draughtsman and taught at university level, and The Barricade of 1918 pushed the same directness further still. The Columbus Museum of Art has called him the most acclaimed American artist of his generation. He died in 1925.

georgeluks.blurb: The Ashcan School's loudest, roughest brush.
georgeluks.bio: George Benjamin Luks, born in 1867, was an American painter who belongs with the roughest and most aggressive wing of the Ashcan School. He came out of illustration and comics work and never lost the appetite for a broad, fast, unflattering figure. In 1908 he showed with The Eight at the Macbeth Galleries, the exhibition Robert Henri assembled to force American realism into view. Luks painted the people around him without deference or sentimentality, in pictures such as The Wrestlers and The Old Duchess, both 1905, and later Fishermen of 1920 and Boy with Baseball of 1925. His handling was thick and quick, closer to a caricaturist's shorthand than to academic finish, and it is exactly that roughness his admirers value. He died in 1933.

everettshinn.blurb: An Ashcan realist with theatrical instincts.
everettshinn.bio: Everett Shinn, born in 1876, was an American painter and draughtsman and a member of the urban realist Ashcan School. He exhibited as one of The Eight, the group Robert Henri gathered in order to show American life without academic polish. Shinn's own subjects leaned towards the stage and the street: Girl on Stage and Frederique Follows Her Husband, both 1906, then Fifth Avenue and Girl in Bathtub, both 1910. He brought a designer's sense of lighting and gesture to scenes his colleagues treated more bluntly, and that theatrical instinct set him slightly apart from the rest of the Ashcan circle without ever taking him out of it. He kept working for decades after the group had scattered, and died in 1953.

alfredstieglitz.blurb: Photographer, gallerist, importer of European modernism.
alfredstieglitz.bio: Alfred Stieglitz, born in 1864, was an American photographer and, across a fifty-year career, the person most responsible for photography being accepted as an art form. His own pictures, among them The Terminal of 1892 and the Spring Showers images made around the turn of the century, argued the case in practice. He argued it in print as publisher and critic, and above all through the New York galleries he ran in the early twentieth century, where he introduced avant-garde Europeans to American audiences and built American careers: he showed John Marin from 1909, backed Arthur Dove for decades, and funded Marsden Hartley's Berlin years through the 291 gallery. He met the painter Georgia O'Keeffe in 1916 and married her in 1924. Stieglitz died in 1946.

marsdenhartley.blurb: Made modern in Berlin, grounded in landscape.
marsdenhartley.bio: Marsden Hartley, born in 1877, was an American modernist painter, poet and essayist. He built his painting by observing the Cubists at close range in Paris and Berlin, and the German years produced his most charged work, including Portrait of a German Officer of 1914, an image assembled almost entirely from insignia and emblems. Those years were made possible by Alfred Stieglitz, who showed him at the 291 gallery and funded his time in Berlin. Hartley wrote as well as painted and worked as a journalist and draughtsman, but the through-line is landscape: The Dark Mountain of 1909, the Provincetown houses of 1916, and finally the Mount Katahdin paintings of 1939, in which he turned to the mountains of Maine and rendered them as blunt, weighted form. He died in 1943.

arthurdove.blurb: Probably the first American abstract painter.
arthurdove.bio: Arthur Garfield Dove, born in 1880, was an American artist and early modernist, often considered the first American abstract painter. He worked outward from landscape rather than away from it, so his abstractions keep the weather and light of a real place; Silver Sun and Silver Tanks, both 1929, and Reflections of 1935 show the method. Dove used an unusually wide range of media, sometimes in unconventional combinations, made a series of experimental collages in the 1920s, and laid hand-mixed oil or tempera over a wax emulsion in later works such as the 1938 painting Tanks, now in Boston. Me and the Moon of 1937 has been called one of the culminating works of his career. Alfred Stieglitz supported him for decades. He died in 1946.

johnmarin.blurb: Watercolour used as structure, not decoration.
johnmarin.bio: John Marin, born in 1870, was an early American modernist known for abstract landscape paintings and for watercolours that treat the medium as a structural rather than a decorative tool. An architect as well as a painter, he built pictures out of leaning planes and interrupted edges, and his Maine sea paintings of the early 1920s, among them The Sea, Maine and the untitled Blue Sea of 1921, keep the force of a place while giving up its description. The Tree of 1917 shows the same instinct inland. Alfred Stieglitz showed him from 1909 and went on doing so, which put Marin in front of the American public earlier than most of his abstract contemporaries. He also worked as a draughtsman and photographer. Marin died in 1953.

georgiaokeeffe.bio: Georgia Totto O'Keeffe, born in 1887, painted and drew for seven decades as an American modernist who stayed largely clear of the movements forming around her. Called the mother of American modernism, she won international recognition for paintings of natural form, particularly flowers, hills and desert landscapes drawn from the places she lived, alongside city work such as Radiator Building at night, painted in New York in 1927. Her Blue abstractions of 1916 already show the sureness of the mature work; Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills of 1935 shows where the desert took it. She met the photographer and gallerist Alfred Stieglitz in 1916 and married him in 1924. Though claimed by feminist readings, she resisted being called a woman artist and asked only to be seen as an artist. She died in 1986.

maxweber.bio: Max Weber, born in 1881, was a Jewish-American painter and one of the first artists to bring Cubism into American painting. Raised in the United States after an early childhood in Poland, he absorbed the new European languages of form at first hand and returned to apply them to American subjects. Chinese Restaurant of 1915 is the work he is best known for today, held by the Whitney Museum of American Art and described by the art historian Avis Berman as the finest canvas of his Cubist phase. Russian Ballet followed in 1916, and earlier canvases such as Summer of 1909 and a 1907 portrait of Abraham Walkowitz record the company he kept. He also worked as a sculptor, draughtsman and writer. In later life he turned away from abstraction towards more figurative Jewish themes. Weber died in 1961.

henrimatisse.blurb: The twentieth century's great advocate for colour.
henrimatisse.bio: Henri Émile Benoît Matisse, born in 1869, was a French artist known equally for his handling of colour and for a fluid, wholly original draughtsmanship. He trained under Gustave Moreau at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris between 1892 and 1898, a teacher who told his students to go out and paint in the street. In the summer of 1905 he painted beside André Derain at Collioure, and the canvases they brought back caused the Salon d'Automne scandal that named Fauvism; Gertrude Stein and her family bought Woman with a Hat from that show, a year after Ambroise Vollard gave him his first solo exhibition. He met Picasso at the Steins' salon in 1906 and the two circled each other for fifty years. Sergei Shchukin commissioned Dance and Music in 1909. Matisse died in 1954.

andrederain.blurb: Fauvism's co-founder, later a strict classicist.
andrederain.bio: André Derain, born in 1880, was a French painter, sculptor and engraver, and with Henri Matisse the co-founder of Fauvism. He studied at the Académie Carrière under Eugène Carrière between 1898 and 1900, where he met Matisse, and in 1900 he met Maurice de Vlaminck after a train derailment; the two went on to share a studio at Chatou. His paintings of 1905 and 1906, made partly beside Matisse at Collioure, are riots of colour, from Mountains at Collioure to the Pont de Charing Cross of 1906. By 1910 the riot had subsided: study of Cézanne and the old masters pushed him towards something far more austere. After the First World War he became a leader of the new classicism known as the return to order. He died in 1954.

mauricedevlaminck.blurb: A Fauve of intense, unmixed colour.
mauricedevlaminck.bio: Maurice de Vlaminck, born in 1876, was a French painter and, with André Derain and Henri Matisse, one of the principal figures of the Fauve movement, the group held together between 1904 and 1908 by its use of intense colour. He met Derain in 1900 after a train derailment, and the two shared a studio at Chatou, working side by side at a pitch of colour nobody had attempted before. Vlaminck was among the Fauves at the controversial Salon d'Automne of 1905, the exhibition that made the movement notorious. He wrote poetry and novels and worked as a printmaker too, and painted on for decades after Fauvism dissolved, producing Snowy Landscape and The Two Haystacks in 1950. He died in 1958.

raouldufy.blurb: Fauve colour turned light and sociable.
raouldufy.bio: Raoul Dufy, born in 1877, was a French painter who came out of Fauvism and kept its colour longer and more cheerfully than anyone. He gained recognition for a vibrant, decorative style that travelled easily out of the gallery and into textile design and the decoration of public buildings, most spectacularly in La Fée Électricité of 1937. His paintings favour outdoor social gatherings, along with landscapes such as the view near Vence in Provence of 1920 and the bullfight picture Corrida course de taureaux of 1949. Dufy also drew, made prints, illustrated books, designed stage sets and furniture and planned public spaces, moving between them without much regard for hierarchy. That range once counted against him; it now looks like the point. He died in 1953.

albertmarquet.blurb: Matisse's lifelong friend, painting quiet water.
albertmarquet.bio: Albert Marquet, born in 1875, was a French painter who began among the Fauves and then, quietly, went his own way. He trained in Gustave Moreau's studio at the same time as Henri Matisse; the two shared lodgings, painted the same motifs and stayed friends for life. Marquet soon moved towards something closer to Impressionism and made his name with landscapes and river views handled in flat, low-keyed tones: the port at Fécamp in 1906, the Seine at the Pont-Neuf in fog in 1907, the Pont Saint-Michel in 1908 and again in winter. He also painted portraits, and between 1910 and 1914 a series of female nudes. His restraint has often been read as modesty; it was closer to precision. He died in 1947.

keesvandongen.blurb: The Fauve who painted Paris nightlife.
keesvandongen.bio: Cornelis Theodorus Maria van Dongen, known as Kees, was born in 1877 and became a Dutch-French painter and one of the leading Fauves. His early work owed something to the Hague School and to symbolism before shifting into a rough pointillist style, and from 1905, when he took part in the controversial Salon d'Automne, his use of form and colour turned steadily more radical. The paintings of 1905 to 1910 are held by some to be his most important, and their subject is almost always nightlife: dancers, singers, masquerades, theatre. Van Dongen also made prints and sculpture, and built a reputation on sensuous and at times garish portraits, particularly of women. He lodged in the Bateau-Lavoir alongside Pablo Picasso. He died in 1968.

othonfriesz.blurb: A Fauve from the Le Havre coast.
othonfriesz.bio: Achille-Émile Othon Friesz, who later called himself simply Othon Friesz, was born in Le Havre in 1879 and became a French artist of the Fauvist movement. His subjects stayed close to landscape and still life: Spring of 1913, The Cliff at Sainte Marguerite and The Peaches, both 1914, pictures in which the Fauve appetite for colour has been brought under control. He worked as a printmaker as well as a painter, and he taught, passing on a version of Fauvism that had already cooled into something more structured. Friesz remains one of the less discussed members of a movement whose noisier figures took most of the attention, though he was there for its brief and decisive years. He died in 1949.

georgesbraque.bio: Georges Braque, born in 1882, was a French painter, collagist, draughtsman, printmaker and sculptor whose two great contributions were an early alliance with Fauvism from 1905 and, more consequentially, the development of Cubism. Guillaume Apollinaire introduced him to Pablo Picasso at the Bateau-Lavoir in 1907, and between 1908 and 1912 the two worked so closely that their canvases were long held to be indistinguishable; Braque described the pair as roped together like mountaineers. Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler bought the Cubist output of both men, which kept the experiment funded. Braque's quiet nature left him partly eclipsed by Picasso's fame, though pictures such as Trees at l'Estaque of 1908 show the new language already taking shape. He worked on for decades, including on the church at Assy in 1946, and died in 1963.

charlescamoin.blurb: A gentler Fauve of saturated colour.
charlescamoin.bio: Charles Camoin, born in 1879, was a French painter associated with the Fauves and usually described as an expressionist landscapist. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in the 1890s under Gustave Moreau, the teacher whose studio produced several of the movement's founders, and he shared their appetite for saturated colour without ever pushing it to the point of provocation. A picture such as Pont Royal in Grey Weather of 1905 shows him applying Fauve means to an unshowy subject: a bridge under low cloud. He worked as a draughtsman, lithographer and printmaker as well as a painter, and he kept going long after Fauvism itself had dispersed, dying in 1965 as one of the last survivors of the group.

ernstludwigkirchner.blurb: Die Brücke's driving force and street painter.
ernstludwigkirchner.bio: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, born in 1880, was a German expressionist painter and printmaker, and the central figure of Die Brücke, the artists' group founded in Dresden in 1905 that led towards Expressionism in twentieth-century art. He and Erich Heckel were architecture students when they started it, with Fritz Bleyl and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff, who supplied the group's name; Emil Nolde and Max Pechstein joined in 1906 and Otto Mueller in 1910. Kirchner's Berlin street scenes of 1913, all spiked angles and electric colour, are the pictures the movement is now known by. He volunteered for army service in the First World War, suffered a breakdown and was discharged. The Nazis branded his work degenerate in 1933, and in 1937 more than six hundred of his works were sold or destroyed. He died in 1938.

erichheckel.blurb: Die Brücke's co-founder and steadiest printmaker.
erichheckel.bio: Erich Heckel, born in 1883, painted and made prints in Germany and was one of the founders of Die Brücke, the Dresden group that ran from 1905 to 1913. He and Ernst Ludwig Kirchner were both architecture students when they started it, and Heckel became one of its most productive graphic artists; printmaking was his natural medium, and the girl's head he made for the magazine Genius in 1913 shows how far he could simplify a face. He painted landscape too, including a snow landscape of 1915. His work featured in the art competitions at the 1928 and 1932 Summer Olympics, a reminder of how differently the art world once organised itself. He later taught at university level, and he died in 1970, having outlived every one of his fellow founders but one.

karlschmidtrottluff.blurb: He gave Die Brücke its name.
karlschmidtrottluff.bio: Karl Schmidt-Rottluff, born in 1884, was a German expressionist painter and printmaker and one of the four founders of Die Brücke. It was he who supplied the group's name, and he worked alongside Ernst Ludwig Kirchner from the group's beginnings. His handling was the heaviest of the group: broad slabs of colour and forms cut down to a few blunt planes, an approach that carried naturally into printmaking and into sculpture, which he practised as well. A picture such as the Untitled Portrait of 1922 shows the manner at full strength. He taught at university level and kept working for decades after the group dissolved, outliving his fellow founders by many years and going on making prints and paintings in a Germany quite unlike the one Die Brücke had set out to shake. He died in 1976, the last survivor of the four.

maxpechstein.blurb: The Brücke painter his friends expelled.
maxpechstein.bio: Hermann Max Pechstein, born in 1881, was a German expressionist painter and printmaker who joined Die Brücke in 1906, a year after Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and his fellow students founded it. In 1912 he was expelled from it for exhibiting with the Secession. His nudes and interiors of 1909 and 1910, among them Two Girls, Two Female Nudes in a Room and Girl on a Green Sofa, carry Brücke colour into a slightly more accommodating register. Pechstein fought on the Western Front during the First World War. Under the Nazis his art was classified as degenerate and more than three hundred paintings were removed from German museums. He worked as a designer and draughtsman as well, and died in 1955.

emilnolde.blurb: Expressionism's colourist of storms and flowers.
emilnolde.bio: Emil Nolde, born in 1867, was a German painter and printmaker and one of the first Expressionists. He joined Die Brücke in 1906, the year after its founding, but left again after eighteen months. What he took from those years was licence with colour, and he became one of the earliest painters of the century to explore it systematically in both oil and watercolour. The palette is unmistakable: golden yellow and deep red keep surfacing, and where they meet darker tones the whole picture seems lit from inside. His watercolours range from brooding storm-scapes to brilliant florals, and his brushwork stayed loose and his colour expressive to the end. An early sheet such as Abschied, or Parting, of 1906 dates from the Brücke months. Nolde, who held both German and Danish nationality, died in 1956.

ottomueller.blurb: Die Brücke's painter of figures in landscape.
ottomueller.bio: Otto Mueller, born in 1874, was a German painter and printmaker who belonged to the Die Brücke circle of Expressionists, joining in 1910, some years after Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and his fellow students founded the group. Where the other Brücke painters went to the city, Mueller kept returning to one motif: slender nude figures set in landscape, painted in soft, chalky colour that runs against the group's usual harshness. Landscape with Yellow Nudes of 1919, the two nudes in a landscape of 1926 and the half-length portrait of two women from 1919 all work that vein. He was also a graphic artist and illustrator and taught at university level. His self-portrait of 1918 is among the few pictures in which he turned the same gaze on himself. He died in 1930.

fritzbleyl.blurb: The Brücke founder who quietly left.
fritzbleyl.bio: Fritz Bleyl, born Hilmar Friedrich Wilhelm Bleyl in 1880, was a German Expressionist artist and one of the four who founded Die Brücke, the group started in 1905 with Ernst Ludwig Kirchner. Bleyl designed graphics for the group, including the poster for its first show, which the police banned. He left after only two years, in 1907, when he married and decided to support his family as an architect, and he did not exhibit publicly again. It is an unglamorous ending, and it is why his is the least familiar of the four names; the group he helped start went on to reshape German art without him, and he lived quietly alongside that history until his death in 1966, nearly sixty years after he walked away.

wassilykandinsky.blurb: Abstraction's pioneer and its first theorist.
wassilykandinsky.bio: Wassily Kandinsky, born in Moscow in 1866, was a Russian painter and art theorist who worked mainly in Germany and is generally counted among the pioneers of abstraction in Western art. He took up the study of painting only at thirty. In Munich he ran the Phalanx school, where in 1902 he taught Gabriele Münter; she became his partner until 1916, and her house at Murnau served as the Blaue Reiter's base and later as the hiding place that saved the group's work through both wars. He founded the Neue Künstlervereinigung with Alexej von Jawlensky in 1909, then resigned from it with Franz Marc to co-edit the Blaue Reiter almanac in 1911. Paul Klee was a Munich neighbour and later a Bauhaus colleague. Walter Gropius appointed him to the Bauhaus in 1922. He died in 1944.

franzmarc.blurb: He painted animals as pure colour.
franzmarc.bio: Franz Marc, born in 1880, was a German painter and printmaker and one of the key figures of German Expressionism. With Wassily Kandinsky he resigned from the Neue Künstlervereinigung and co-edited the Blaue Reiter almanac of 1911 and 1912, whose name came to stand for the whole circle of artists gathered around it. Marc's subject was almost always the animal, painted in colour used symbolically rather than descriptively: Blue Horse I and Fox, both 1911, The Tower of Blue Horses of 1913 and, in the same year, the darkening Fate of the Animals. Herwarth Walden showed the Blaue Reiter at his Der Sturm gallery. Marc and August Macke were close friends from 1910 until both were killed in the war; Marc died in 1916.

augustmacke.blurb: Der Blaue Reiter's brightest, briefest talent.
augustmacke.bio: August Robert Ludwig Macke, born in 1887, was a German Expressionist painter and one of the leading members of Der Blaue Reiter. He lived through an unusually active time for German art, watching the main Expressionist movements form while successive avant-gardes arrived from elsewhere in Europe, and he had a gift for taking exactly what he needed from each without losing his own light, sociable touch. His last year produced Girls under Trees, Gartentor and the Landscape with Cows and Camel, all 1914, in colour that stays luminous rather than turning symbolic. Macke was a close friend of Franz Marc from 1910 and worked as a draughtsman and sculptor as well. Marc, Otto Soltau and Macke himself all belong to the roll of young German artists killed in the First World War; Macke died in 1914.

gabrielemunter.blurb: She hid the Blaue Reiter's paintings.
gabrielemunter.bio: Gabriele Münter, born in 1877, was a German expressionist painter who helped found Der Blaue Reiter and stood in the front rank of Munich's avant-garde in the century's first decades. She met Wassily Kandinsky as his student at the Phalanx school in Munich in 1902; they studied and lived together until 1916, and her house at Murnau became the group's base, the place where the arguments and the almanac took shape. Her own painting is flatter and blunter than his, built from heavy contour and unbroken colour. Her greatest single act on the movement's behalf was practical: she kept the group's work hidden through both world wars, when its destruction was a real possibility, so much of what survives of the Blaue Reiter survives because of her. She died in 1962.

paulklee.blurb: A private language of line and colour.
paulklee.bio: Paul Klee, born in 1879, was a Swiss-born German artist whose highly individual style drew on expressionism, cubism and surrealism without ever settling inside any of them. He was part of Der Blaue Reiter in Munich, where he and Wassily Kandinsky were neighbours; the two later became colleagues at the Bauhaus, where Walter Gropius appointed Klee master of form in 1921. He worked as painter, graphic artist and lithographer and taught for years, producing along the way a body of teaching as considered as his pictures. The works are small, dense and often funny: Sumpflegende and Villa R, both 1919, Angelus Novus of 1920, and the Twittering Machine of 1922, in which mechanism and birdsong are drawn as one contraption. He died in 1940.

alexejvonjawlensky.blurb: Faces reduced to icon and colour.
alexejvonjawlensky.bio: Alexej von Jawlensky, born in 1864, was a Russian expressionist painter who spent his working life in Germany. He trained in St Petersburg in the 1890s under Ilya Repin before moving to Munich, where he became a key member of the New Munich Artists' Association, founded with Wassily Kandinsky in 1909, and then of Der Blaue Reiter; in 1924 he and Kandinsky formed Die Blaue Vier. His subject was the human head, pursued for decades from vividly coloured portraits such as Head of a Woman of 1911 towards the Abstract Head series of the 1920s, in which a face becomes a few weighted lines. He was the partner of Marianne von Werefkin for nearly thirty years, and she gave up painting for a decade to support his career. He died in 1941.

mariannevonwerefkin.blurb: The Russian Rembrandt who paused a decade.
mariannevonwerefkin.bio: Marianne von Werefkin, born Mariamna Vladimirovna Veryovkina in 1860, left Russia to work in Germany and Switzerland, and it is her Expressionist painting that is remembered. She studied under Ilya Repin, who called her the Russian Rembrandt, and arrived in Germany with a reputation already made. She then stopped painting for around a decade in order to support the career of her partner Alexej von Jawlensky, with whom she spent nearly thirty years. When she returned to the easel the work had changed entirely: The Factory, Women in Black, The Red Tree and a self-portrait, all around 1910, are built from heightened colour and a strong sense of unease. She died in 1938, that long interruption still shaping how her career is read.

egonschiele.blurb: Raw line, raw bodies, twenty-eight years.
egonschiele.bio: Egon Schiele, born in 1890, was an Austrian Expressionist painter whose work is known for its intensity, its raw sexuality and the sheer number of self-portraits it contains, a good many of them nude. Bodies come out twisted and the line is left exposed and nervous, the qualities that make him an early exponent of Expressionism and the reason his drawings still unsettle. Gustav Klimt mentored him from 1907, traded drawings with him and steered patrons his way. Wally Neuzil was his model and companion between 1911 and 1915, appearing in pictures such as Wally Neuzil in Black Stockings of 1912, before he left her to marry Edith Harms, whom he painted in a striped dress in 1915. Seated Woman with Bent Knees of 1917 shows a steadier hand. He died in 1918.

oskarkokoschka.blurb: Portraits that look straight through the sitter.
oskarkokoschka.bio: Oskar Kokoschka, born in 1886, was an Austrian painter, poet and playwright whose expressionistic portraits and landscapes, and whose theories of vision, shaped the Viennese Expressionist movement. He treated a sitter as something to be excavated rather than described, and the series of variations he painted on Kamilla Swoboda in 1920 shows how far he would push a single face. Between 1912 and 1915 he had an affair with Alma Mahler; after it ended he commissioned a life-size doll made in her likeness, an episode that has attached itself permanently to his biography. He taught for much of his life and never stopped writing alongside the painting. He worked into old age, dying in 1980, by then among the last living links to pre-war Vienna.

richardgerstl.blurb: The painter who taught Schoenberg to paint.
richardgerstl.bio: Richard Gerstl, born in 1883, was an Austrian painter and draughtsman known for expressive, psychologically searching portraits and for the almost complete absence of critical acclaim during his lifetime. Between 1906 and 1908 he taught the composer Arnold Schoenberg to paint, and the friendship pulled him into the Schoenberg household; his portrait of the family dates from 1907. He then began an affair with Mathilde Schoenberg, the composer's wife, and its ending led to his suicide in 1908. The work he left behind is startling for its date: the Semi-Nude Self-Portrait of 1904, the portrait of Professor Ernst Diez from 1906, and the Self-Portrait, Laughing of his final year, in which the face dissolves into loaded, hectic paint. None of it won him critical acclaim while he lived.

pablopicasso.bio: Pablo Ruiz Picasso, born in Spain in 1881, spent most of his adult life in France and became one of the most influential artists of the twentieth century. He co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque between 1908 and 1914, invented constructed sculpture, co-invented collage, and helped develop a range of styles that would have filled several careers. The proto-Cubist Les Demoiselles d'Avignon of 1907 opened the door; Guernica of 1937 answered the Spanish Civil War bombing of the town by German and Italian air forces. He lived in the Bateau-Lavoir in Montmartre alongside Juan Gris and Kees van Dongen, met Matisse at the Steins' salon in 1906, and let Vladimir Tatlin into his studio in 1914. Vollard, Kahnweiler and Gertrude Stein carried him commercially. He worked over seventy-six years and died in 1973.

juangris.bio: Juan Gris, born José Victoriano González-Pérez in Madrid in 1887, was a Spanish painter who spent nearly the whole of his working life in France and made some of the most distinctive pictures in all of Cubism. He arrived in Paris in time to become a neighbour of Pablo Picasso at the Bateau-Lavoir in Montmartre from 1906, and he took the new language from its inventors and made it more deliberate: clean divisions, calculated colour, a structure you can follow. His Portrait of Pablo Picasso of 1912 is both homage and argument. Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler contracted him from 1912, which gave him a living. Later works such as Carafe and Book of 1920 and The Blue Carpet of 1925 show the style relaxing without losing its rigour. He died in 1927.

fernandleger.blurb: Cubism rebuilt out of machine parts.
fernandleger.bio: Fernand Léger, born in 1881, was a French painter, sculptor and filmmaker who created a personal form of Cubism and then gradually bent it back towards the figure. His early work breaks bodies and objects into tubes and cylinders; Les Fumeurs of 1911 and The Alarm Clock of 1914 belong to that phase, and by Man and Woman of 1921 the forms have settled into a boldly simplified treatment of modern subject matter that later made him look like a forerunner of pop art. He belonged to the Puteaux Group with Albert Gleizes and shared in the room 41 scandal at the 1911 Salon des Indépendants. He made films, worked on the church at Assy in 1946, and taught the artist Lygia Clark in his Paris studio from 1950 to 1952. He died in 1955.

albertgleizes.bio: Albert Gleizes, born in 1881, was a French painter, theoretician and philosopher who called himself a founder of Cubism and did as much as anyone to explain it. With Jean Metzinger he wrote Du Cubisme in 1912, the first major treatise on the movement. He was a founding member of the Section d'Or and of the Puteaux Group, which met at Jacques Villon's studio and drew in Marcel Duchamp, František Kupka and Fernand Léger; the room 41 scandal at the 1911 Salon des Indépendants was their doing. His paintings of 1912, among them Harvest Threshing and Football Players, put the theory to work. A member of Der Sturm, most closely read in Germany and at the Bauhaus, he also spent four crucial years in New York arguing for modern art. He died in 1953.

jeanmetzinger.bio: Jean Dominique Antony Metzinger, born in 1883, was a French painter, theorist, writer, critic and poet who, with Albert Gleizes, produced the first theoretical work on Cubism, Du Cubisme, in 1912. His route there ran through the styles of the previous generation: the neo-Impressionism of Georges Seurat and Henri-Edmond Cross shaped his earliest work from 1900 to 1904, after which he painted in Divisionist and Fauvist manners with a strong Cézannian component, arriving at some of the first proto-Cubist pictures. By 1912 he was working in the mature idiom, in canvases such as Danseuse au café and L'Oiseau bleu. Much of the movement's reputation for being explicable rests on the book he co-wrote rather than on the paintings that provoked it. He died in 1956.

louismarcoussis.blurb: A Polish Cubist among the Montparnasse cafés.
louismarcoussis.bio: Louis Marcoussis, born in 1878, was a Polish-French avant-garde painter who worked mainly in Paris. He read law in Warsaw before enrolling at the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts, then moved to France and trained under Jules Lefebvre at the Académie Julian; his work reached a major exhibition for the first time at the Salon d'Automne of 1905. In the cafés of Montmartre and Montparnasse he came to know the artists and writers of the School of Paris, and his painting turned towards Cubism: The Musician of 1914, Composition of 1921, the portrait of Guillaume Apollinaire made the same year, and Night Café of 1923. He worked as an illustrator and graphic artist as well as a painter. He died in 1941.

marielaurencin.blurb: A singular painter among the Cubists.
marielaurencin.bio: Marie Laurencin, born in 1883, was a French painter and printmaker who counted among the Cubists gathered under the Section d'Or and became a figure of consequence in the Parisian avant-garde. She was a poet, an illustrator and a designer for the stage as well, moving between painting and theatre with unusual ease. Her pictures keep their distance from the analytic severity of the men around her, favouring a pale, particular palette and a cast of women entirely her own; a late portrait such as Jeanne Charrier of 1948 shows the manner still intact after four decades. She worked on into the 1950s and died in 1956, one of the few women named as part of the Cubist circle in its own day rather than recovered long afterwards.

alexanderarchipenko.blurb: Cubism translated into sculpture and space.
alexanderarchipenko.bio: Alexander Porfyrovych Archipenko, born in 1887, was a Ukrainian-American sculptor and graphic artist of the avant-garde, working first in France and later in the United States. He was among the earliest artists to carry Cubist principles into sculpture and into architecture, analysing the human figure into geometrical forms rather than smoothing it into a likeness; Woman Combing Her Hair of 1914 is the best-known result, and Médrano II belongs to the same experimental run. He painted as well, and worked as a graphic designer and illustrator, including a Figurative Composition made for the journal Genius in 1921. He kept inventing long after the movement that formed him had passed, producing pieces such as the Queen of Sheba in 1961. He died in 1964.

jacqueslipchitz.blurb: He made Cubism stand up in bronze.
jacqueslipchitz.bio: Jacques Lipchitz, born in 1891, was a Lithuanian-born French-American sculptor and one of the few to make Cubism work fully in three dimensions. His pieces up to about 1915 keep highly figurative and legible components; after that the naturalistic and descriptive elements are muted and the work moves into the tight, faceted manner known as Crystal Cubism. His first solo exhibition came in 1920, at Léonce Rosenberg's Galerie L'Effort Moderne, which placed him firmly among the School of Paris. Le chant des voyelles dates from 1931. Fleeing the Nazis, he settled in New York and later Hastings-on-Hudson, and made several of his best-known works in America, including the John F. Kennedy Memorial of 1965, Birth of the Muses and Bellerophon Taming Pegasus, completed after his death in 1973.

henrilaurens.blurb: Cubism carried into carved and modelled volume.
henrilaurens.bio: Henri Laurens, born in France in 1885, was a sculptor and illustrator who carried Cubism's fractured geometry off the canvas and into three dimensions. He worked as a painter, designer and printmaker too, but sculpture was where his thinking settled: form broken into planes and then reassembled with a builder's patience. Over four decades the hard faceting of his early work gave way to rounded, swelling volumes, and 'Océanide' of 1933 and 'Femme accroupie (le torse)' of 1935 sit at that turn. 'The Great Musician' followed in 1938, and 'L'Amphion', one of his last major pieces, in 1953. Laurens died in 1954, having spent a career proving that a movement usually explained through paintings had just as much to say about weight, mass and the space a body occupies.

raymondduchampvillon.blurb: Cubist sculptor, lost to the war.
raymondduchampvillon.bio: Raymond Duchamp-Villon, born in France in 1876, was a sculptor who brought Cubism's restless geometry into solid form. He trained as a painter as well, and the two disciplines stayed close in his work. The portrait head 'Maggy' of 1912 pushed a human face towards abstraction, and 'The Horse' of 1914, also known as 'Le Cheval', compressed an animal into a coiled knot of machine-like curves and became one of the most quoted sculptures of its moment. He belonged to an extraordinary artistic family: his younger brother was Marcel Duchamp. The war cut the career short. Serving at the front, he contracted typhoid fever and died in 1918, leaving a body of work that reads as a beginning rather than a summing-up, and a handful of pieces that shaped how sculptors thought about the machine for a generation afterwards.

ftmarinetti.bio: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, born in 1876, was an Italian poet, editor and art theorist who did not so much join a movement as declare one into existence. Between 1907 and 1908 he moved in the orbit of the Symbolist community at the Abbaye de Créteil; a year later he published the Manifesto of Futurism, a call for speed, machinery and the demolition of the past that handed a generation its vocabulary. Painters gathered fast. Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Luigi Russolo, Gino Severini and the elder Giacomo Balla signed the Manifesto of Futurist Painters in 1910, each carrying the programme somewhere different, Russolo into noise machines and Severini into Paris and Cubism. Marinetti's politics followed the same appetite for rupture: in 1919 he co-authored the Fascist Manifesto. He died in 1944.

umbertoboccioni.bio: Umberto Boccioni, born in 1882, gave Futurism its visual force. In Rome around 1900 and 1901 he studied under Giacomo Balla, who taught him the Divisionist technique of broken colour; a decade later he was signing the Manifesto of Futurist Painters with Marinetti and pushing far past his teacher's example. 'The City Rises' of 1910 turned building work into a surge of light and muscle, and 'The Street Enters the House' of 1911 let a city pour in through a window. In sculpture he went furthest: 'Unique Forms of Continuity in Space', made in 1913, is a striding figure dissolved into its own momentum. He died in 1916, yet his handling of dynamism and dissolving mass guided artists for decades afterwards, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art gathered a hundred works for a retrospective in 1988.

giacomoballa.blurb: Futurism's elder, teacher of its firebrands.
giacomoballa.bio: Giacomo Balla, born in 1871, was the oldest of the Futurist painters and, in a real sense, their teacher. In Rome in 1900 and 1901 he passed the Divisionist method of broken colour to Umberto Boccioni and Gino Severini, both of whom would sign the Futurist manifesto beside him. Balla was after movement above all: the way light travels, the way speed smears a shape across the eye. Where his younger colleagues were drawn to machinery and violence, his work kept a lighter temperament, witty and often whimsical, closer to play than to war. 'Mercury Passing Before the Sun' takes an astronomical event and handles it as pure pattern and light. He taught, and wrote poetry, and lived long enough to see Futurism become history, dying in 1958.

ginoseverini.bio: Gino Severini, born in Italy in 1883, learned the Divisionist technique in Rome from Giacomo Balla, alongside Umberto Boccioni, then moved to Paris, a decision that made him the most useful member of the group. Living among the Cubists, he became Futurism's link to what was happening in France, and when he signed the Futurist manifesto he brought a Parisian sense of structure with him. 'Dancer = Propeller = Sea' of 1915 is his equation of a body, a machine and the ocean in one shimmering surface. After the First World War he turned towards neo-classicism and the wider return to order, and for the rest of his life he worked between Paris and Rome, working in mosaic and fresco as readily as in oil. His 'Stations of the Cross' dates from 1947. He died in 1966.

carlocarra.blurb: Futurist who turned to metaphysical stillness.
carlocarra.bio: Carlo Carrà, born in Italy in 1881, was one of the leading figures of Futurism and among the painters who signed its manifesto with Marinetti in 1910. What makes his career unusual is where it went next. In 1917, convalescing in a military hospital in Ferrara, he met Giorgio de Chirico, and out of that meeting came Pittura Metafisica, an art of silent squares, mannequins and long shadows that was the opposite of Futurism's noise in almost every respect. Carrà was a writer as well as a painter, publishing a number of books about art, and Milan kept him teaching for many years, generations of students passing through his classes. He died in 1966, his reputation resting on two movements he helped shape rather than one, which is more than most of his colleagues managed.

luigirussolo.blurb: Futurist painter who built noise machines.
luigirussolo.bio: Luigi Russolo, born in 1885, finished his schooling at the seminary in Portogruaro in 1901, moved to Milan and fell in with the artists there, signing the Futurist painters' manifesto with Marinetti in 1910 and producing canvases such as 'Lightning' of 1910 and 'Racing car' of 1912 that chase energy across the surface. Then he did something no other Futurist did: he built the sound. His 1913 manifesto 'The Art of Noises' argued that the modern ear had outgrown orchestral music, and he designed and constructed a family of noise-generating machines, the intonarumori, to prove it. He gave noise concerts in 1913 and 1914 and again after the war, notably in Paris in 1921. He is now regarded as one of the first experimental composers of noise music. He died in 1947.

antoniosantelia.bio: Antonio Sant'Elia, born in Italy in 1888, was the architect of Futurism, a movement that reached him mostly as an idea about speed and machinery and that he answered with drawings of a city nobody had built. He completed almost no architecture at all. What survives is a body of bold sketches, and their influence on modern architecture has far outrun the scale of the work itself, which is why he is remembered at all. He died in 1916, still in his twenties, with the drawings standing in for everything he never got to build. The gap between what he imagined and what he lived to make is, in the end, the point of him: a designer whose entire argument had to be carried by paper.

benedettacappa.bio: Benedetta Cappa, born in Italy in 1897, was a painter and writer whose work belongs to the second phase of Italian Futurism, the movement's later and less chronicled stretch. She worked in words and in paint, and her reputation has grown considerably since her death: the Walker Art Center and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum have both given her retrospectives, exhibitions that helped restore a figure long treated as a footnote to a movement told through its men. She died in 1977. Much of the recent interest in Futurism's women runs through her example, and she now reads less as a late arrival than as evidence that the movement kept developing, and kept finding new practitioners, long after its noisy beginning.

robertdelaunay.blurb: Orphism's co-founder, half a colour partnership.
robertdelaunay.bio: Robert Delaunay, born in France in 1885, was a painter of the School of Paris who decided that colour itself could carry a picture. With his wife Sonia Delaunay, whom he married in 1910, and a small circle around them, he co-founded Orphism: strong colour and geometric form used not to describe things but to generate light and movement on the canvas. The two developed Simultanism together, a genuine partnership rather than a shared signature. 'Eiffel Tower with Trees' of 1910 shatters the great structure into overlapping planes, while 'L'Équipe de Cardiff' of 1913 and 'Hommage to Blériot' of 1914 take modern sport and modern flight as occasions for the same investigation. His later work moved further into abstraction, the disc paintings reducing the argument to bands of pure colour. He died in 1941.

soniadelaunay.blurb: Orphist colour, from canvas to cloth.
soniadelaunay.bio: Sonia Delaunay, born in the Russian Empire in 1885 to Jewish parents, trained in Russia and Germany before settling in Paris, where she spent her working life. Her first marriage, to the dealer Wilhelm Uhde in 1908, was an arrangement of convenience; it ended in 1910, the year she married Robert Delaunay. With him she co-founded Orphism and developed Simultanism, and unlike most of her contemporaries she refused to keep painting separate from the rest of life. The 'Simultaneous Dress' of 1914 puts the same colour theory on a body that 'Electric Prisms' puts on canvas. Textiles, fashion and set design were not sidelines but the argument extended. In 1964 she became the first living woman artist given a retrospective at the Louvre, and in 1975 an officer of the Legion of Honour. She died in 1979.

frantisekkupka.blurb: Walked from realism into pure abstraction.
frantisekkupka.bio: František Kupka, the Czech painter and illustrator, was born in 1871 and began as a realist, then went somewhere no painter had been before him. Working in France, he belonged to the Puteaux Group, the circle that gathered around Jacques Villon's studio next door to his own and that included Albert Gleizes, and out of those conversations came Orphism, which he helped to pioneer. 'The Yellow Scale' of 1907 still holds a figure; by 1912 he had let it go, and 'Disks of Newton' and 'Localization of Graphic Motifs II' treat colour and form as ends in themselves, borrowing from music and optics rather than from description. He taught as well as painted, and kept refining the vocabulary for decades, with 'Divertimento I' dating from 1935. He died in 1957.

francispicabia.bio: Francis Picabia, born in France in 1879, moved through the avant-garde faster than most of it could keep up. Filed with the Orphists for his early abstract work, he was closest in temperament to Dada, and with Marcel Duchamp he carried the movement between New York and Paris, keeping the two cities in conversation when little else did. His magazine 391 became Dada's journal of record, a shifting and deliberately unstable publication that reads now like the movement's nervous system. He was a painter, poet, writer, filmmaker and typographer, and restlessness was his method rather than his failing: he changed manner whenever one threatened to settle into a career, which cost him a stable reputation and gave the work an unusual freedom. 'Egoïsme' dates from 1948. He died in 1953.

mikhaillarionov.bio: Mikhail Larionov, born in the Russian Empire in 1881, was among the first Russian artists to push painting towards abstraction. He founded two of the crucial exhibiting groups of the Moscow avant-garde, the Knave of Diamonds and then the more radical Donkey's Tail, where Kazimir Malevich showed in 1912, and with Natalia Goncharova he invented Rayonism, an art built from intersecting rays of light rather than solid objects. 'Red and Blue Rayonism (Beach)' of 1911 and 'Glass' of 1912 show the method taking hold. Goncharova was his partner from 1900; they finally married in 1955, fifty-five years on. Together they left Russia for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, designing for the company in France and Switzerland, and he spent the rest of his life in France, dying in 1964.

nataliagoncharova.bio: Natalia Goncharova, born in the Russian Empire in 1881, was a painter, illustrator, writer and designer at the centre of the Moscow avant-garde. She was a founding member of the Jack of Diamonds, the city's first radical independent exhibiting group, and then of the more confrontational Donkey's Tail. With Mikhail Larionov, her partner from 1900 and eventually her husband in 1955, she invented Rayonism between 1912 and 1914, painting built from beams of light rather than solid form; 'Rayonist Lilies' and 'Cats' both date from 1913. She also belonged to the German group Der Blaue Reiter, and worked extensively for the stage, designing the ballet 'Liturgie' in 1915. Paris became her home from 1921 onwards, and she stayed until her death in 1962.

kazimirmalevich.blurb: Painting reduced to a black square.
kazimirmalevich.bio: Kazimir Malevich, a Russian avant-garde artist and theorist of Polish ancestry, took painting further from description than anyone before him. He showed with Mikhail Larionov's Donkey's Tail group in 1912, still working figuratively, and 'The Knife Grinder' comes from that moment. In 1915 he introduced Suprematism, a radically non-objective painting whose founding statement, 'Black Square', offers the eye nothing to recognise; 'Suprematist Composition: White on White' of 1918 pushed the reduction to its limit. He was also a formidable organiser: the Supremus group and journal of 1916 and 1917 drew in Lyubov Popova, Olga Rozanova, its secretary until her death in 1918, his old Moscow friend Ivan Kliun, and Nadezhda Udaltsova. Invited into the Vitebsk school Marc Chagall had founded, he took it over, Chagall left in 1920, and through UNOVIS he turned El Lissitzky to abstraction. He died in 1935.

davidburliuk.bio: David Burliuk, born in the Russian Empire in 1882 to a Ukrainian family, was a poet and painter as much as a publicist, and it was the last of those roles that mattered most. The father of Russian Futurism is the description that has stuck to him, a title earned less by any single painting than by his talent for gathering people, staging provocations and arguing the new art into public existence. His own work moved between Futurism and Neo-Primitivism, drawing on folk sources as readily as on the machine; 'The Cossack Mamay' of 1911 reaches straight back into Ukrainian tradition. He eventually settled in the United States, where he painted for decades more, producing 'Portrait Study (The Artist's Wife)' in 1920 and 'Decorative Study' in 1924. He died in 1967.

wyndhamlewis.blurb: Vorticism's founder, editor and chief antagonist.
wyndhamlewis.bio: Wyndham Lewis, born in Canada in 1882 and British by adoption, was a painter, novelist and critic who ran England's only home-grown avant-garde. In 1913 he joined Roger Fry's Omega Workshops and walked out months later after a furious row over a commission, a departure that produced the Rebel Art Centre and, in 1914, the magazine BLAST, which he edited. Ezra Pound supplied the name Vorticism; Lewis supplied the aggression, a hard angular manner built for machinery and confrontation. The signatories around him included the sculptors Henri Gaudier-Brzeska, killed at Neuville-Saint-Vaast in 1915, and Jacob Epstein, and the painters Helen Saunders and Jessica Dismorr, the movement's two women. The war ended Vorticism; Lewis served, and 'A Canadian Gun-pit' of 1918 came out of it. He died in 1957.

davidbomberg.blurb: Vorticist geometry, then a teacher's legacy.
davidbomberg.bio: David Bomberg, born in 1890, was one of the Whitechapel Boys, a name that has attached itself to him ever since and that says more about where he started than about the painting. 'In the Hold' of 1913 breaks a ship's hold into a grid of shattered colour and pushes English painting about as far towards abstraction as it went in that decade. The war changed the work: 'Sappers at Work: A Canadian Tunnelling Company', finished in 1919, is a very different picture. His deepest influence came through teaching. From 1947 to 1953 he ran evening classes at the Borough Polytechnic in London, where Frank Auerbach and Leon Kossoff were among his students, two painters who carried his sense of mass and touch into the second half of the century. He died in 1957.

henrigaudierbrzeska.blurb: Direct carving, cut short by war.
henrigaudierbrzeska.bio: Henri Gaudier-Brzeska, born in France in 1891, made sculpture by cutting straight into the block. Direct carving gave his work its rough-hewn, deliberately primitive character, and it put him at the centre of the small English avant-garde: he signed the Vorticist manifesto alongside Wyndham Lewis. The hyphenated name was his own invention. He took the surname of Sophie Brzeska, his partner, the two of them living and presenting themselves to the world as brother and sister. His output is compressed into a handful of years. The 'Self-portrait' and the head of Alfred Wolmark date from 1913, 'Birds Erect' from 1914 and 'Portrait of a Whitechapel Jew' from 1915. That same year he was killed at Neuville-Saint-Vaast, still in his twenties, one of the war's most conspicuous losses to modern sculpture.

jacobepstein.bio: Jacob Epstein, born in the United States in 1880, moved to Europe in 1902 and became a British subject in 1910, by which point he was already among the figures dragging sculpture out of the nineteenth century. He worked in Wyndham Lewis's orbit around the Rebel Art Centre and the BLAST circle, and the work from those years remains his most famous: 'Rock Drill' of 1913, and the related 'Torso in Metal from Rock Drill' of 1914, are the sharpest sculptural statements the English machine age produced. Public commissions followed and kept him in the public eye for the rest of a long career, among them the W. H. Hudson Memorial of 1925 and, in the year of his death, 'Rush of Green'. He died in 1959, by then knighted and thoroughly established.

crwnevinson.blurb: The First World War's sharpest eye.
crwnevinson.bio: C. R. W. Nevinson, born in England in 1889, became one of the First World War's most famous war artists, and he got there by driving an ambulance. What he saw at the front he brought back into a hard, faceted manner that suited mechanised warfare better than any inherited pictorial language. 'La Mitrailleuse' dates from 1915 and 'The Strafing' from 1916; 'Banking at 4,000 Feet' of 1917 took the subject into the air, and 'Paths of Glory', from the same year, is among the bleakest images to come out of the conflict. He was a figure and landscape painter as well, and worked as an etcher and lithographer, and was also known simply as Richard. It is the war pictures that have held. He died in 1946.

helensaunders.bio: Helen Saunders, born in England in 1885, was one of only two women to sign the Vorticist manifesto, and one of the painters who pushed English art towards abstraction in the years before the First World War. She worked closely with Wyndham Lewis in the period around BLAST, and her painting and drawing take up the movement's hard diagonals and clashing planes as fully as anything by its louder members. The story of Vorticism was written afterwards around Lewis, and the signatories who were neither its editor nor its theorist have been recovered slowly, which is the usual fate of a movement's quieter half. Saunders died in 1963, having outlived by nearly half a century the movement she helped to make.

jessicadismorr.bio: Jessica Dismorr, born in England in 1885, turns up in almost every avant-garde group active in London between 1912 and 1937, a career of continuous participation rather than a single allegiance. Early landscapes such as 'Sunlight, Martigues' and 'Landscape with Cottages', both of 1911, gave way to Vorticism, where she was one of only two women members, contributing poems and illustrations to BLAST as well as paintings; 'Abstract Composition' dates from 1915. She was the only woman in Group X, and her work appeared with the Allied Artists Association, the Seven and Five Society and the London Group. In the 1930s she was among the very few English painters working in a completely abstract manner, and 'Related Forms' of 1937 belongs to that phase. She died in 1939.

stantonmacdonaldwright.blurb: Colour as music, made in America.
stantonmacdonaldwright.bio: Stanton Macdonald-Wright, born in the United States in 1890, went to Paris and found a teacher and a collaborator in the same room. In Percyval Tudor-Hart's studio he met Morgan Russell, and between 1912 and 1913, working in Munich and Paris, the two of them founded Synchromism: abstract painting organised by colour on the analogy of musical composition. It was the first American avant-garde movement to attract serious international attention. 'Arm Organization' of 1914 keeps a trace of the body inside the colour, while the 'Synchromy' canvases of 1917 let it go entirely. He returned to the United States and worked there for the rest of a long career, taking on public commissions including a mural for the Santa Monica Library in 1934. He died in 1973.

morganrussell.blurb: Synchromism's other founder, colour as music.
morganrussell.bio: Morgan Russell, born in the United States in 1886, was painting a fairly conventional self-portrait in 1907 and inventing an abstract idiom five years later. The turn happened in Paris. In Percyval Tudor-Hart's studio in 1911 he met Stanton Macdonald-Wright, and between 1912 and 1913, moving between Munich and Paris, the two founded Synchromism, a deliberately provocative kind of abstract painting that treated colour the way a composer treats sound, arranged in chords and rhythms rather than used to describe things. 'Cosmic Synchromy' of 1913 and 'Four Part Synchromy, Number 7' of 1914 are the argument at full strength. The style ran on into the 1920s, one of the first American contributions to modernism as it took hold. He died in 1953.

hugoball.blurb: Opened the cabaret where Dada began.
hugoball.bio: Hugo Ball, born in Germany in 1886, was a writer, poet, dramatist and journalist before he was anything else, and Dada began as a room he rented. In February 1916, with the cabaret performer Emmy Hennings, his partner and later his wife, he opened the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich, and the group that formed around it included Tristan Tzara, Jean Arp, Marcel Janco, who made the masks for the performances, and Richard Huelsenbeck, who would carry Dada to Berlin the following year. Ball's own contribution was to take language apart: his sound poems abandoned meaning for pure phonetic material, and he counts as a pioneer of the form. He was one of the principal founders of a movement that quickly outgrew him. He died in 1927.

tristantzara.bio: Tristan Tzara, born in Romania in 1896, was a poet before he was a provocateur. As an adolescent, drawn to Symbolism under the influence of Adrian Maniu, he started the magazine Simbolul with Ion Vinea and the painter Marcel Janco, a partnership that would matter later. In 1916 he was at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich with Hugo Ball, and he became one of Dada's founders and its most conspicuous public voice, arguing the anti-establishment case in print with more energy than anyone, and the movement would not have travelled as far without him. He worked as a journalist, playwright, critic, composer, film director and performance artist, collected art as well as making it, and later took French nationality and a diplomatic role. He died in 1963.

jeanhansarp.blurb: Dada's poet of soft organic shapes.
jeanhansarp.bio: Jean Arp, Hans in German and he answered to both, was born in Alsace in 1886 and spent his life moving between French and German identity. He was in Zurich in 1916 for the founding of Dada at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire, and he wrote poetry throughout, treating words and forms as the same problem. He met Sophie Taeuber in 1915 and married her in 1922; they made duo-collages together and collaborated on the Aubette in Strasbourg, a partnership of equals unusual for its moment. As a sculptor he arrived at the shapes he is now known for, smooth swelling volumes that suggest bodies, clouds or seeds without settling into any of them. 'Schalenboom' dates from 1947, 'Evocation of a Form: Human, Lunar, Spectral' from 1950 and 'Berger des Nuages' from 1954. He died in 1966.

sophietaeuberarp.bio: Sophie Taeuber-Arp, born in Switzerland in 1889, worked across more disciplines than almost anyone of her generation and treated none of them as secondary. She painted and made sculpture; she designed textiles, furniture and interiors; she was a dancer; she worked as an architect. 'Composition with Diagonals and Cross' of 1916 is geometric abstraction arrived at early and without fuss, and it came out of a practice rooted in weaving and applied design rather than in easel painting. She moved in the Zurich Dada circle, and 'Composition Dada' dates from 1920. She met Jean Arp in 1915 and married him in 1922, and the two collaborated closely, on duo-collages and on the interiors of the Aubette in Strasbourg. She died in 1943, her reputation only later catching up with the range of the work.

marcelduchamp.blurb: Turned choosing into an artistic act.
marcelduchamp.bio: Marcel Duchamp, born in France in 1887, came from one of the century's most remarkable artistic families: his brothers Jacques Villon and Raymond Duchamp-Villon and his sister Suzanne all made art, and Villon's studio at Puteaux hosted the Section d'Or circle where Duchamp met Albert Gleizes. His early painting ran from 'Sad Young Man on a Train' in 1911 to 'The Bride' in 1912, and then he changed the question entirely: 'Bicycle Wheel' of 1913 proposed that selecting an object could itself be the artistic act. In New York from 1915 he met Man Ray, beginning a collaboration that lasted fifty years, and in 1920 the two of them founded the Société Anonyme with Katherine Dreier, America's first museum of modern art. He spent his last twenty-five years in New York and died in 1968.

manray.blurb: Dada's camera, Surrealism's photographer of record.
manray.bio: Man Ray, born in the United States in 1890, spent most of his career in Paris and became a French citizen, but insisted to the end that he was a painter first. The world knows him mainly through the camera. He met Marcel Duchamp in New York in 1915 and worked with him for fifty years; in Paris he made photograms he called rayographs, after himself, and served as the photographer of record for André Breton's Surrealist circle while keeping a parallel career in fashion and portraiture. His partners were collaborators. Kiki de Montparnasse, with him from 1921 to 1929, was the model for 'Le Violon d'Ingres'; Lee Miller arrived as his assistant in 1929 and left in 1932 as a partner, the solarisation technique having come out of their shared darkroom. He died in 1976.

raoulhausmann.blurb: Berlin Dada's photomontage and sound poems.
raoulhausmann.bio: Raoul Hausmann, born in Austria in 1886, was one of the central figures of Berlin Dada, the harder and more political wing of the movement. With John Heartfield he founded Club Dada in 1918, and with George Grosz he organised the First International Dada Fair in 1920. Photographic collage, sound poetry and a running attack on the institutions of art were his instruments, and their mark on the European avant-garde after the First World War was deep. He was with Hannah Höch from 1915 to 1922; his portrait of her dates from that first year, and the competing claims the two of them made to have invented photomontage belong to the same period, a dispute that says as much about how the movement treated its women as about the technique. He died in 1971.

hannahhoch.blurb: Cut the Weimar Republic into collage.
hannahhoch.bio: Hannah Höch, born in Germany in 1889, was one of the originators of photomontage, collage built from actual photographs and images pulled from the illustrated press, the visual junk of a society talking to itself. Her best-known work comes from the Weimar years: 'Dancing into the Dark' of 1919, 'Man and Machine' of 1921, 'Creatures' of 1927 and 'Resignation' of 1928. She was with Raoul Hausmann from 1915 to 1922, the period in which both of them claimed the invention of the technique. Working with the mass media's own material let her turn its images back on it, an argument made entirely out of the thing it was arguing with. She died in 1978, by which point the medium she helped invent was everywhere.

johnheartfield.bio: John Heartfield was born in Germany in 1891 under a German name and gave it up, anglicising it in protest at the nationalism running through the country. In 1916 he founded the publishing house Malik-Verlag with his brother Wieland Herzfelde and George Grosz, and in 1918 he was one of the founders of Club Dada in Berlin with Raoul Hausmann. He turned art into a political weapon before anyone else had thought to, and his anti-Nazi and anti-fascist photomontages, printed and distributed for a mass readership rather than hung in a gallery, are among the sharpest political images of the century. He also designed book jackets for authors including Upton Sinclair, and stage sets for Bertolt Brecht and Erwin Piscator. He died in 1968.

georgegrosz.bio: George Grosz, born in Germany in 1893, drew Berlin in the 1920s in a caricatural line that has fixed the period's image ever since. He was a prominent member of Berlin Dada, organising the First International Dada Fair of 1920 with Raoul Hausmann, and later of New Objectivity, and he worked alongside John Heartfield at Wieland Herzfelde's Malik Verlag, where much of that work reached print. In 1933 he emigrated to the United States and became a naturalised citizen in 1938. There he abandoned both the style and the subject matter that had made him, showing steadily instead and holding a long teaching post at the Art Students League of New York. He returned to Berlin in 1959 and died shortly after arriving, having outlived the city he had drawn.

kurtschwitters.blurb: Built a one-man movement called Merz.
kurtschwitters.bio: Kurt Schwitters, born in Hanover in 1887, was refused entry to Berlin's Club Dada, blackballed by Richard Huelsenbeck, and responded by founding a movement of one. He called it Merz and used the name for collages, assemblages, poems and eventually architecture. Herwarth Walden's gallery Der Sturm began showing the work in 1919, the year of 'Merzbild 1A (The Psychiatrist)', and he found allies elsewhere: in 1923 he toured the Netherlands with Theo van Doesburg on the Dada Veldtocht. Smaller pieces such as 'Entrance Ticket (Mz 456)' of 1922 and 'Merz 1925, 1. Relief in the Blue Square' kept the method going, while the 'Merzbau', under way by 1933, turned Merz into a growing interior structure. From 1937 he lived in exile. He died in 1948.

maxernst.blurb: Invented frottage; lived through every rupture.
maxernst.bio: Max Ernst, born in Germany in 1891, had no formal artistic training, which may explain his freedom. Four years as a soldier in the First World War left him permanently sceptical of the modern world, and in 1920 he and Johannes Baargeld founded Cologne Dada and staged the Dada-Vorfrühling exhibition. His technical inventions followed: frottage, taking rubbings from textured surfaces, and grattage, scraping paint across canvas over objects placed beneath, along with collage novels. He became the first major painter of André Breton's Surrealist group and was expelled from it in the 1950s. His life ran through the century's dislocations: a household shared with Paul Éluard and Gala at Eaubonne from 1922, years with Leonora Carrington until his internment separated them, a marriage to Peggy Guggenheim that got him into the United States, and finally Dorothea Tanning, his wife from 1946 until his death in 1976.

johannesbaargeld.blurb: Cologne Dada's co-founder under an alias.
johannesbaargeld.bio: Johannes Baargeld was the name Alfred Emanuel Ferdinand Grünwald used for his art. Born in Germany in 1892, he was a painter and poet who, with Max Ernst, founded the Cologne Dada group and mounted the Dada-Vorfrühling exhibition of 1920. He sometimes signed himself Zentrodada instead. The invented names were part of the work rather than a convenience: Dada set out to dismantle the idea of the artist as an author with a fixed identity, and Baargeld took the joke seriously enough to live inside it. He wrote as much as he painted, and the two activities were not kept apart. He died in 1927, young enough that his part in Cologne Dada is usually told as an episode in Ernst's career rather than as a chapter of his own.

beatricewood.blurb: The Mama of Dada, later a potter.
beatricewood.bio: Beatrice Wood, born in the United States in 1893, studied art and theatre in Paris and was working as an actress in New York when she fell in with Marcel Duchamp and the writer Henri-Pierre Roché. In 1917 the three of them founded and edited 'The Blind Man' and 'Rongwrong', the small magazines at the centre of New York Dada, and the friendship among them later became the basis for 'Jules et Jim'. She was called the Mama of Dada, and she outlasted everyone who gave her the title. Turning from painting to sculpture and then to clay, she built a long second career as a studio potter, working almost to the end of a life that ran from 1893 to 1998.

baronesselsavonfreytagloringhoven.blurb: Wore Dada as a living costume.
baronesselsavonfreytagloringhoven.bio: Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven, born in Germany in 1874, made herself the artwork. Active in Greenwich Village between 1913 and 1923, she was a sculptor, poet and model whose most radical medium was her own appearance: assembled costumes and self-displays that turned her passage through New York into a living piece of Dada, and no artist of the period drew more controversy. The assemblage titled 'God' is among the works that survive. Much of what she did was ephemeral by design, which is why her reputation rested for so long on the accounts of people who had seen her rather than on objects in collections. She died in 1927, and has since moved from anecdote back towards the centre of the story of New York Dada.

ellissitzky.blurb: Suprematism turned into design and propaganda.
ellissitzky.bio: El Lissitzky, born in the Russian Empire in 1890, worked as an architect as well as a painter and never stopped thinking like one. At Vitebsk in 1919 he met Kazimir Malevich, joined UNOVIS and abandoned figurative work under his mentor's influence, and began the Proun compositions that occupy the ground between painting and architecture: 'Proun 4 B' dates from 1919 and 'Proun 19D' from 1920. From there he carried Suprematist geometry out of the gallery and into typography, book design, photomontage and exhibition display, much of it propaganda made for the Soviet state, and he became one of the most influential figures of the avant-garde. 'The Constructor' of 1924 is his best-known photographic self-image. He died in 1941, after a career spent translating abstraction into things people used.

lyubovpopova.blurb: Built paintings like pieces of architecture.
lyubovpopova.bio: Lyubov Popova, born in the Russian Empire in 1889, made some of the most rigorously constructed abstract paintings of the Russian avant-garde.
