She joined Kazimir Malevich's Supremus group and its journal in 1916 and 1917, and the 'Painterly Architectonic' canvases of 1917 do exactly what their title claims, stacking and tilting planes of colour into something with structural weight rather than decorative effect. Earlier work such as 'Birsk' of 1916 shows her arriving at that language. She taught at VKhUTEMAS in Moscow, where Alexander Rodchenko was a colleague, and like many in that circle she moved from easel painting towards design in the service of the new state. Her career was short. She died in 1924, leaving a body of work whose influence is far out of proportion to its size.

olgarozanova.bio: Olga Rozanova, born in the Russian Empire in 1886, moved through Neo-Primitivism and Cubo-Futurism into Suprematism in barely a decade, and was a poet and book illustrator alongside her painting. 'Red House' of 1910 and the harder, faceted 'Factory and the Bridge' and 'Man on the Street (Analysis of Volumes)' of 1913 track the change. She served as secretary of Kazimir Malevich's Supremus group, keeping the practical business of a circle of manifesto-writers in order. Her late work went further than his in one direction: 'Green Line' of 1917 hands the whole picture over to a single band of colour on a bare ground, an act of reduction that later painters would take decades to catch up with. She died in 1918, still in her early thirties.

ivankliun.bio: Ivan Kliun, born in the Russian Empire in 1873, was the senior figure in the Suprematist circle and one of Kazimir Malevich's earliest friends; the two met as students in Moscow, long before either had a movement to belong to. That friendship carried into the Supremus group, where Kliun was among the founding participants. His own work moved quickly. 'Landscape Rushing By' of 1910 is already interested in motion and dissolution, 'The Clockmaker' of 1914 still holds a subject, and by 1916 he was painting pure Suprematist compositions, followed by the 'Composition' of 1917. He worked as a sculptor and wrote as an art theorist as well, thinking the new abstraction through on paper as much as on canvas. He died in 1943.

nadezhdaudaltsova.bio: Nadezhda Udaltsova, born in the Russian Empire in 1885, was a painter and teacher who worked through the three positions the Russian avant-garde argued over, Cubism, Cubo-Futurism and Suprematism, and took each seriously in turn. Her canvases of the mid-1910s, among them 'At the Piano', 'Kitchen' and 'Blue jug', all of 1915, apply Cubist analysis to ordinary domestic subjects with a firmness that owes nothing to Parisian charm; a painting of 1914 is titled simply 'Cubism'. She joined Kazimir Malevich's Supremus group, the circle formed around his non-objective painting, and pushed her own work towards pure form. What holds the phases together is a draughtsman's precision that never deserts her, even at the most abstract. Teaching occupied much of her later working life, and she outlived almost everyone she had started out with, dying in 1961.

vladimirtatlin.bio: Vladimir Tatlin, born in the Russian Empire in 1885, began as a painter, with 'Sailor' of 1911 and 'Female Model' of 1913, and changed course after talking his way into Pablo Picasso's studio in 1914. The constructions he saw there led directly to his counter-reliefs, works assembled from real materials that came off the wall and into the corner of the room; 'Corner Counter-Relief' dates from that same year. In 1919 he began the Monument to the Third International, better known as Tatlin's Tower, the design that made his name and became the emblem of Constructivism. He worked as an architect and stage designer too, and alongside Kazimir Malevich he stood at the centre of the Soviet avant-garde of the 1920s. He died in 1953.

alexanderrodchenko.blurb: Founder of Constructivism and Russian design.
alexanderrodchenko.bio: Alexander Rodchenko, born in the Russian Empire in 1891, stood among the founders of Constructivism and, with it, of Russian design. He painted and sculpted, then largely gave both up for work he considered more useful: photography, graphic design and stage sets, made for a mass audience rather than a gallery wall. He taught at VKhUTEMAS in Moscow, where Lyubov Popova was a colleague, and from 1921 he and his wife Varvara Stepanova worked as a design partnership, one of the most productive of the century. 'The Bedbug' dates from 1928. His photography, as much as anything he painted, carried Constructivist thinking to a wide public, and the visual language he assembled still turns up wherever design wants to look modern and urgent.

varvarastepanova.blurb: Constructivism applied to cloth and stage.
varvarastepanova.bio: Varvara Stepanova, born in the Russian Empire in 1894, belonged to the Constructivist wing of the Russian avant-garde, the part of it that threw out aesthetic values altogether and put revolutionary ones in their place. Art, on that argument, was not something to be contemplated but something to be used. With her husband Alexander Rodchenko she worked as a design partnership from 1921, and her own output ran across propaganda, poetry, stage scenery and textile design, patterns printed on cloth that ordinary people would actually wear, which was precisely the point. Clothing and fabric were where the theory met daily life, and she pursued them with more conviction than most of the theorists around her. She died in 1958, remembered as much for what she designed as for what she painted.

naumgabo.blurb: Sculpture made of space, not mass.
naumgabo.bio: Naum Gabo, born in the Russian Empire in 1890, spent his career arguing that sculpture should be made of space rather than mass. With his brother Antoine Pevsner he co-signed the Realistic Manifesto in Moscow in 1920, a founding document of Constructivism, and his 'Kinetic Construction' of 1919 is among the earliest works of kinetic art. Leaving Russia, he moved through Europe and spent years in England, co-editing the journal 'Circle' with Ben Nicholson in 1937 and joining the artists who regrouped in St Ives from 1939. Later he worked in the United States, and the transparent, open constructions of his maturity resolved the argument of his youth. 'Revolving Torsion' dates from 1972. He was a theorist as much as a maker, and a key figure in twentieth-century sculpture. He died in 1977.

antoinepevsner.blurb: The elder brother of Constructivist sculpture.
antoinepevsner.bio: Antoine Pevsner, born in the Russian Empire in 1884, was the elder brother of Naum Gabo, and the two of them are counted among the originators of Constructivism and the pioneers of twentieth-century sculpture. They co-signed the Realistic Manifesto in Moscow in 1920, the document on which the movement rests. Pevsner later settled in France and became a French citizen, working in metal on constructions that treat a sculpture as a diagram of movement rather than a solid body: 'Élan' and '30-Degree Dynamic Projection', both of 1953, and the 'Construction in the Third and Fourth Dimension' whose title he used more than once. His widely known 'The Flight of the Bird' stands at the General Motors Technical Center in Warren, Michigan. He died in 1962.

gustavklutsis.blurb: Photomontage in service of the state.
gustavklutsis.bio: Gustav Klutsis, a Latvian artist born in 1895, was a pioneering photographer and a leading member of the Constructivist avant-garde. He worked almost entirely in the service of the state, producing Soviet revolutionary and later Stalinist propaganda with his wife Valentina Kulagina, and in the process pushed the techniques of photomontage a long way forward. The mass-produced political poster, rather than the gallery, was his medium. His 'Propaganda Stand (Workers of the World Unite)' of 1922 is a design for exactly the kind of public apparatus he believed art should become: a structure to be used in the street by people who would never think of themselves as an audience. He died in 1938, his career one of the clearest cases of an avant-garde given wholly to a political programme.

alexandervesnin.bio: Alexander Vesnin, born in the Russian Empire in 1883, trained as an architect and worked equally as a painter, draftsman and lecturer. With his brothers Leonid and Viktor he formed the leading family of Constructivist architecture, the three of them usually spoken of as a single design mind. His reputation rests above all on drawing: the meticulous perspectival studies he produced, of which the Leningrad Pravda project of 1924 is the best known, made the Constructivist argument more persuasively on paper than most built work of the period managed in brick. Like others in the movement he moved from easel painting towards the design of useful things, the shift that carried Constructivism into Productivism. Teaching mattered to him as much as building, and he passed the method on to a younger Soviet generation before his death in 1959.

vladimirandgeorgiistenberg.bio: Vladimir and Georgii Stenberg worked as a pair at the centre of the Russian avant-garde, beginning as sculptors before moving through theatre design, architecture and drafting. They are remembered above all for the film posters they made for Sergei Eisenstein's features, Dziga Vertov's documentaries and a flood of imported pictures. Working in a Constructivist and later Productivist idiom, they treated the film still as raw material, cutting and reassembling it into compositions that owed nothing to narrative illustration. Proportion was theirs to break: figures were enlarged, tipped, turned upside down, whatever it took to stop a busy passer-by in the street, and Vladimir was frank that the posters were designed to shock. Their design work ran well beyond cinema to clothing, shoes and railway carriages, holding to the Productivist conviction that an artist's job was to shape the everyday world.

pietmondrian.blurb: De Stijl's co-founder, who resigned over a diagonal.
pietmondrian.bio: Piet Mondrian, born in the Netherlands in 1872, was a painter and art theoretician regarded as one of the pivotal figures of twentieth-century art. He began in figurative painting and moved away from it by degrees, paring his vocabulary down until nothing remained but simple geometric elements. In 1917 he co-founded De Stijl with Theo van Doesburg and gave the movement its most uncompromising account of what abstraction was for; he resigned in 1924 when van Doesburg introduced the diagonal, ending a seven-year alliance over the tilt of a line. In 1929 he joined Joaquín Torres-García and Michel Seuphor in founding Cercle et Carré in Paris, bringing geometric abstraction there under one banner. His late canvases Broadway Boogie Woogie and Victory Boogie Woogie, both dated 1942, close a career that had begun in figurative painting. He died in 1944.

theovandoesburg.blurb: De Stijl's founder, agitator and organiser.
theovandoesburg.bio: Theo van Doesburg, born in the Netherlands in 1883, was a painter, poet, writer and architect, and the founder and driving force of De Stijl. He launched the movement in 1917 with Piet Mondrian, Bart van der Leck and the sculptor Georges Vantongerloo, and drew in Gerrit Rietveld, whose Red-Blue Chair and Schröder House gave the group's flat geometry three dimensions. Van der Leck's flat planes helped push Mondrian towards pure abstraction; van Doesburg's own Contra-Compositions of 1924 and 1928 carry the diagonal that cost him Mondrian, who resigned from De Stijl in 1924. He was a propagandist as much as a painter: in 1922 he set up a rival De Stijl course beside the Bauhaus in Weimar and was never offered a post there, and in 1923 he toured the Netherlands with Kurt Schwitters on the Dada Veldtocht. He died in 1931.

bartvanderleck.blurb: The flat planes behind Mondrian's turn.
bartvanderleck.bio: Bart van der Leck, born in the Netherlands in 1876, was a painter, designer, graphic artist and ceramicist who, with Theo van Doesburg and Piet Mondrian, founded De Stijl. His contribution to the group came close to being its starting point: the flat, unmodelled planes of colour he had arrived at in his own work shaped Mondrian's turn towards pure abstraction. Unlike his co-founders he never treated painting as a separate calling, moving between canvas, ceramics, graphic work and design without ranking them, and the commissions continued long after De Stijl itself had dispersed; a project for the Rijksluchtvaartschool dates from 1957. His name is less recognised than Mondrian's or van Doesburg's, but the vocabulary of clean colour laid flat on a white ground, which became the movement's signature, passed through his hands first. He died in 1958.

vilmoshuszar.bio: Vilmos Huszár, born in Hungary in 1884, was a painter and designer who settled in the Netherlands and became one of the founding members of De Stijl. Graphic design occupied him as fully as painting did, and the Dada-tournee work of 1923 shows how readily he moved from the canvas to the printed sheet. That range was typical of the group, which refused to treat fine art and applied design as separate problems, but Huszár moved between them more freely than most, working as painter, graphic designer and designer across three decades of Dutch modernism. The records of his life also list him as a resistance fighter. He died in 1960, his part in De Stijl less discussed than that of its better-remembered members but present from the beginning.

georgesvantongerloo.blurb: De Stijl's sculptor, working in three dimensions.
georgesvantongerloo.bio: Georges Vantongerloo, born in Belgium in 1886, was a sculptor, painter and designer of furniture and buildings, and a founding member of De Stijl. He was the group's sculptor: while Theo van Doesburg and his fellow painters argued over the picture plane, Vantongerloo took the same geometry into three dimensions, where a composition has to hold from every side rather than one. His listed occupations, running from sculpture and painting to illustration and architecture, are typical of a movement that refused to treat art and use as separate problems, and he moved among them without changing his principles. He stayed with a constructed, mathematical kind of abstraction long after De Stijl itself had scattered, and went on working until his death in 1965, one of the movement's most consistent and least publicised members.

gerritrietveld.blurb: The furniture designer who built De Stijl.
gerritrietveld.bio: Gerrit Rietveld, born in the Netherlands in 1888, was a furniture designer and architect, and the member of De Stijl who moved the movement's flat geometry off the canvas and into the room. He joined the group around Theo van Doesburg, and the Red and Blue chair and the Berlin Chair, both dated 1923, translated its intersecting planes and clear colour into objects you could sit in. The Schröder House carried the same thinking into a whole building, argued through walls and openings rather than paint. His practice was unusually broad even by De Stijl standards, taking in furniture, graphic design, photography and architecture; an early building at Buerweg 19 in Bergen dates from 1921. He kept designing for the rest of his life and died in 1964, the objects long since outliving the movement that produced them.

waltergropius.blurb: The Bauhaus's founder and talent scout.
waltergropius.bio: Walter Gropius, born in Germany in 1883, founded the Bauhaus in Weimar and ran it as much by hiring as by teaching. Lyonel Feininger was his first appointment and cut the woodcut that fronted the 1919 manifesto; Johannes Itten was brought in that same year to build the preliminary course, then forced out in 1923 and replaced by László Moholy-Nagy. Gropius made Paul Klee a master of form in 1921, appointed Wassily Kandinsky in 1922 after his return from Russia, and gave Oskar Schlemmer the theatre workshop. Not everyone got in: Theo van Doesburg set up a rival De Stijl course beside the school in 1922 and was never offered a post. Married to Alma Mahler between 1915 and 1920, Gropius left for England in 1934 and the United States in 1937, teaching at Harvard, working with Marcel Breuer, and winning the AIA Gold Medal in 1959.

johannesitten.bio: Johannes Itten, born in Switzerland in 1888, was an expressionist painter, designer, writer and theorist whose real medium turned out to be teaching. Walter Gropius hired him in 1919 to build the Bauhaus preliminary course, and with the painter Lyonel Feininger and the sculptor Gerhard Marcks he formed the core of the Weimar school under Gropius's direction. That foundation course was his invention as much as anyone's, the year every student passed through before entering a workshop, and it has been imitated by art schools ever since. Josef Albers arrived as one of its students in 1920 and stayed on to become a master himself. Itten was forced out in 1923, four years after Gropius had brought him in, an abrupt end to the arrangement that had shaped the school's first phase. He died in 1967.

laszlomoholynagy.bio: László Moholy-Nagy, born in Hungary in 1895, was a painter, photographer, sculptor and designer, and one of the Bauhaus's most restless minds. Walter Gropius hired him in 1923 to replace Johannes Itten, a change that swung the school towards technology and industry, causes Moholy-Nagy argued for all his life. The critic Peter Schjeldahl called him relentlessly experimental, and the range bears it out: painting, drawing, photography, collage, sculpture, film, theatre and writing, from the constructed abstractions of LIS and E IV (Construction VII), both 1922, through Construction of 1924 to Z VII of 1926. Constructivism shaped his thinking throughout. He was married to the photographer Lucia Moholy, whose images are the reason we know what the Bauhaus looked like. He later settled in the United States, where he died in 1946, still working across more media than most artists attempt in one.

josefalbers.bio: Josef Albers, born in Bottrop in Westphalia in 1888, came to art through craft, learning glass engraving, plumbing and wiring as a boy in a family of tradespeople and working as a schoolteacher from 1908 to 1913. He received his first public commission in 1918, moved to Munich in 1919, and arrived at the Bauhaus in 1920 as a student in Johannes Itten's preliminary course, staying on to become a master. He met Anni there, a fellow student, in 1922; they married in 1925 and taught at the school together. Emigration made him one of the most influential art teachers in the United States: at Black Mountain College he taught Ruth Asawa and Kenneth Noland in the late 1940s and, in 1948 and 1949, Robert Rauschenberg, who called him the most important teacher he ever had. He died in 1976.

annialbers.bio: Anni Albers, born in Berlin in 1899, became the leading textile artist of the twentieth century and is credited with dissolving the line between craft and fine art. She studied first with the impressionist painter Martin Brandenburg between 1916 and 1919, attended the Kunstgewerbeschule in Hamburg briefly in 1919, and in 1922 enrolled at the Bauhaus, the school Walter Gropius had founded in Weimar. The loom was not entirely her own choice: women there were kept out of other disciplines, and she took up weaving because the other doors were closed. She met Josef Albers at the school the same year, married him in 1925, and the two taught there together. A printmaker as well as a weaver, she spent the rest of a long life insisting that woven cloth could carry ideas as seriously as paint. She died in 1994.

oskarschlemmer.blurb: The Bauhaus's painter of the stage.
oskarschlemmer.bio: Oskar Schlemmer, born in Germany in 1888, was a painter, sculptor, designer and choreographer, and the Bauhaus figure who took the school's ideas onto a stage. Walter Gropius put him in charge of the theatre workshop, where the human body was treated as a form to be measured, costumed and moved through space with the same rigour the other workshops brought to metal or cloth. The same preoccupation runs through his painting: Danceress (The Gesture) of 1922, Concentric Group of 1925 and, best known of all, Bauhaus Stairway of 1932, in which anonymous figures climb through architecture like notation across a page. An early view of the Jagdschloss Grunewald dated 1912 shows how far he had travelled. He also worked as a sculptor, a librettist and a maker of marionettes. He died in 1943.

guntastolzl.bio: Gunta Stölzl, born in Germany in 1897, was the textile artist who turned the Bauhaus weaving workshop into one of the school's most productive departments. She took the workshop over from Georg Muche and steered it away from one-off pictorial hangings towards designs made for industrial production, fabrics that could be woven in quantity rather than admired singly. In doing so she became one of a very small number of women teaching at the Bauhaus and the first to hold the title of Master, a distinction that says as much about the school's limits as about her standing inside it. She held German and Swiss nationality and went on designing, weaving and writing for decades after the school closed. She died in 1983, by which time the industrial approach to textile design she had argued for at the loom had become ordinary practice.

marcelbreuer.blurb: Bauhaus furniture designer turned American architect.
marcelbreuer.bio: Marcel Breuer, born in Hungary in 1902, was a furniture designer and architect who carried the Bauhaus outlook into American practice. The furniture came first and made his name: the Lattenstuhl, the Wassily Chair of 1927 and the Isokon Long Chair of 1930, pieces assembled from a small number of standard elements and meant for production rather than the drawing room. Emigration took him to the United States in 1937, and naturalisation followed in 1944; he taught and built there for the rest of his career, an American architect by then as much as a Hungarian one. Architecture gradually took over from furniture design, though the two shared a method: reduce the parts, standardise them, and let the assembly do the expressive work. He died in 1981, furniture and buildings equally identified with modernism.

mariannebrandt.bio: Marianne Brandt, born in Germany in 1893, trained first as a painter, at a private art school and then the Grand Ducal College of Art in Weimar between 1911 and 1917, where she produced work in an Expressionist manner and studied sculpture. The Bauhaus redirected her entirely. She studied at the school and in 1928 became head of the metal workshop in Dessau, one of very few women to run a Bauhaus department. The household objects she designed there, lamps and ashtrays among them, are now treated as models of modern industrial design: sleek, unornamented, made to be manufactured. She worked seriously in photography too, favouring unusual angles and using glass and metal surfaces to distort and multiply her subjects, herself included. She later headed the design department of a manufacturing company, and died in 1983.

amedeeozenfant.bio: Amédée Ozenfant, born in France in 1886, was a Cubist painter, writer and art theorist who then set about defining what should come next. With Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, later known as Le Corbusier, he wrote Après le cubisme in 1918, the text that launched Purism and argued its case directly from its title. The two ran the movement together as painters and writers, though it is Le Corbusier's later architectural career that has kept the Purist name in circulation. Ozenfant was the more consistent theorist of the pair, working as an illustrator and photographer alongside his painting and continuing to write about art long after the movement's moment had passed. He died in 1966, remembered less for his own canvases than for the argument he made about what painting after Cubism should look like.

lecorbusier.bio: Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, known as Le Corbusier, was born in Switzerland in 1887 to French-speaking parents and acquired French nationality in 1930. Painter, writer, urban planner and above all architect, he is one of the figures modern architecture is usually said to begin with, and across five decades he designed buildings in Europe, Japan, India and the Americas. His entry into the avant-garde was as a painter and theorist: in 1918 he and Amédée Ozenfant published Après le cubisme, the manifesto that launched Purism, and he kept painting alongside building for the rest of his life. Furniture and sculpture followed, from the LC4 of 1928 to the Open Hand Monument of 1964. His office sent people in unexpected directions, Roberto Matta working there as an architect before turning to painting. He named Viollet-le-Duc as modern architecture's root, and died in 1965.

giorgiodechirico.blurb: Empty squares, long shadows, waiting mannequins.
giorgiodechirico.bio: Giorgio de Chirico, born in Volos, Greece, in 1888, invented an art of empty city squares in the years before the First World War. The scuola metafisica he founded gave twentieth-century painting its arcades, long shadows, faceless mannequins, distant trains and perspectives that refuse to resolve; The Song of Love and The Child's Brain, both of 1914, and The Disquieting Muses of 1916 are its central images. Schopenhauer and Nietzsche shaped the mood, as did the mythology of his birthplace. In 1917, in a military hospital in Ferrara, he met Carlo Carrà, and Pittura Metafisica took shape as a shared project. His brother, who wrote, composed and painted under the name Alberto Savinio, worked the same seam in words and music. The Surrealists claimed him as an ancestor and he outlived them, dying in 1978.

giorgiomorandi.blurb: A lifetime of bottles, quietly observed.
giorgiomorandi.bio: Giorgio Morandi, born in Italy in 1890, spent a career painting a small number of vessels over and over. His still lifes of ceramic jars and bottles, occasional flowers and the odd landscape are held in a subtly muted range of colour, and their quietness is the point: variation inside severe limits, the same objects rearranged until the arrangement itself becomes the subject. He was an etcher as well as a painter, and printmaking's discipline of line and tone suited him; he also taught at university level and had served in the military. Grouped here with Pittura Metafisica, he shared that movement's stillness and its sense of ordinary things turned strange, but arrived at it without arcades or mannequins, using only what stood on the table in front of him. He died in 1964.

albertosavinio.blurb: De Chirico's brother, and everything at once.
albertosavinio.bio: Alberto Savinio was born Andrea Francesco Alberto de Chirico in 1891, the younger brother of the metaphysical painter Giorgio de Chirico, and worked under a pseudonym across an improbable number of forms. He was a writer, composer, musician, journalist, essayist, playwright, set designer and painter, and no one of those descriptions can be treated as the main one; music and literature occupied him as fully as canvas did. His work circled philosophical and psychological questions, and he wrote at length on the philosophy of art itself, supplying the theoretical half of a family partnership in which his brother supplied the images. The painting belongs to the same metaphysical world, and Orpheus and Eurydice of 1951 shows him still working classical myth late on. He died in 1952, leaving a body of work that has to be read across literature, music and painting at once.

ottodix.blurb: Painted the war without looking away.
ottodix.bio: Otto Dix, born in Germany in 1891, was a painter and printmaker whose depictions of German society under the Weimar Republic are among the harshest images the period produced. He looked at that society, and at the brutality of war, without softening either; the realism is deliberately merciless rather than merely descriptive. With George Grosz and Max Beckmann he is counted among the essential figures of the Neue Sachlichkeit, the movement that answered Expressionism's inwardness with a cold look outward at the world as it actually was. Printmaking mattered to him as much as painting, the etched line suiting a taste for exact and unforgiving detail, and he later held a university teaching post. He was also an Esperantist, a small detail that hints at his generation's hopes for a rebuilt world. He died in 1969.

maxbeckmann.blurb: Refused every label pinned on him.
maxbeckmann.bio: Max Beckmann, born in Germany in 1884, painted, drew, sculpted, made prints and wrote, and spent much of his life refusing the categories attached to him: he rejected both the term Expressionist and the movement itself. In the 1920s he was associated instead with the New Objectivity, the reaction against Expressionism's introverted emotion, though his own work never lost its undercurrent of unease. Even the light subjects carry it, circus performers included, and so does the Self-Portrait in Tuxedo of 1927. By the 1930s the imagery had turned explicitly horrifying and the forms distorted, brutal realism fused with social criticism, in step with the rise of Nazism in Germany; Departure dates from 1930 and Birds' Hell from 1937. The earlier Self-Portrait with Red Scarf of 1917 shows how long the self-scrutiny ran. He died in 1950.

christianschad.blurb: Painted Vienna and Berlin's cool, glassy decadence.
christianschad.bio: Christian Schad, born in Germany in 1894, was a painter and photographer whose portraits have come to stand for Vienna and Berlin at their most decadent after the First World War. He passed through Dada before arriving at the New Objectivity, and something of Dada's detachment stayed with him: his sitters are set down with a glassy exactness that flatters nobody and explains nothing. He worked as a photographer, graphic artist and collagist alongside the painting, and the photographic habit of looking is visible in the pictures. Cool where his contemporaries were savage, he made a comparable point by opposite means, letting the surfaces of that demi-monde speak for themselves. He lived until 1982, long enough to watch the portraits he made in the 1920s become the standard illustration of the era they describe.

georgschrimpf.bio: Georg Schrimpf, born in Germany in 1889, was a painter and graphic artist counted, alongside Otto Dix, George Grosz and Christian Schad, among the principal representatives of the Neue Sachlichkeit. The movement grew out of Expressionism in Weimar Germany between 1919 and 1933, and Schrimpf occupied its calmer wing: figures and landscapes held very still, as in the child portraits of 1925, one of them made in Sicily, On the balcony of 1927 and Railway Crossing of 1932. Where others in the group used realism as an instrument of attack, he used it for quiet, which did not protect him. In the 1930s the National Socialist government listed him among the producers of Degenerate Art. He died in 1938, before the war that ended the world his paintings had recorded.

alexanderkanoldt.blurb: Magic realism's painter of still things.
alexanderkanoldt.bio: Alexander Kanoldt, born in Germany in 1881, was a painter and printmaker described as a magic realist and grouped with the New Objectivity. Still life was his territory: jugs, cacti and household vessels arranged with an almost architectural firmness, as in the two still lifes of 1922, the cactus still life of 1923 and Still Life I of 1926. The objects are ordinary; the treatment is not, each one placed and lit with a clarity that tips the everyday towards the uncanny. Alongside painting he taught at university level, and unusually for his circle he was also active in politics. He died in 1939. The still lifes remain the argument for him, a demonstration that the New Objectivity's cold precision could be turned on a table of pots as effectively as on the streets of Berlin.

rudolfschlichter.bio: Rudolf Schlichter, born in Germany in 1890, was a painter, engraver and writer, and one of the most important practitioners of verism, the critical-realist wing of the New Objectivity that used exact drawing as a weapon rather than a courtesy. His picture Scala of 1926 belongs to that project. He worked in lithography and printmaking as well as paint, and illustration ran alongside both, giving his line the speed of reportage. He was a writer too, and produced several autobiographical books, an unusual second archive for a painter of his generation and a record of the Weimar art world from inside it. He died in 1955, having lived through the full arc his generation faced: the Republic that gave the verists their subject, the regime that followed it, and the long aftermath.

jeannemammen.bio: Jeanne Mammen, born in Germany in 1890, was a painter, illustrator and printmaker best known for what she recorded of Berlin between the wars. Her pictures of the city's street life and, above all, of its queer women are among the closest observations anyone made of the Weimar capital: watchful, unsensational, and interested in her subjects rather than in the shock they might deliver. Her work touches several movements at once, taking the New Objectivity's cool exactness, an earlier Symbolist strain and, later, elements of Cubism, none of them adopted wholesale. Much of her living came from illustration, which is part of why the pictures read as observation rather than statement. She lived until 1976, and the Weimar-era work is now taken as one of the essential records of that city and that decade.

picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso, born in Spain in 1881, spent most of his adult life in France and shaped twentieth-century art more comprehensively than any of his contemporaries. He co-founded Cubism, invented constructed sculpture, co-invented collage, and then kept moving, working through a run of styles that would have made several separate careers, among them the classicising return to order that this part of the map records. The proto-Cubist Les Demoiselles d'Avignon of 1907 opened one decade; Guernica of 1937, painted in response to the bombing of the town by German and Italian air forces during the Spanish Civil War, remains the century's central anti-war painting. He worked as printmaker, sculptor and even choreographer, and made public sculpture including the Chicago Picasso of 1967. His career ran more than seventy-six years, ending with his death in 1973.

mariosironi.blurb: Novecento's painter of heavy, motionless form.
mariosironi.bio: Mario Sironi, born in Italy in 1885, was a painter, sculptor, illustrator and designer whose work sits at the heavy end of Italian modernism. His pictures are typically sombre, built from massive forms that refuse to move, blocks of architecture and figure that seem to have settled into place and stayed there. That weight is what separates him from his contemporaries: where others chased speed and motion, Sironi painted immobility. He worked in drawing, engraving and graphic art as well as painting, and the graphic sense shows in the flattened, poster-like clarity of his compositions. He belongs to the Novecento Italiano and the wider return to order, the interwar Italian tendency that turned from avant-garde experiment towards mass, structure and classical reference. He died in 1961.

felicecasorati.blurb: Figures held in strange, exact perspective.
felicecasorati.bio: Felice Casorati, born in Italy in 1883, was a painter, sculptor and printmaker whose figure compositions, portraits and still lifes are recognisable for one reason above all: the perspective is never quite ordinary. Rooms tilt, floors rise, and objects sit at distances that do not agree with one another, so that a perfectly calm scene is held in a state of suspension. He worked in all three of the traditional genres and moved between them without changing his temperament, which was cool, deliberate and interested in geometry as a way of organising a face or a bowl. Grouped with the Novecento Italiano and the interwar return to order, he shared that movement's respect for the classical picture while quietly unsettling its stability. He also designed and made graphic work. He died in 1963.

achillefuni.bio: Achille Funi, born in Italy in 1890, painted a modernist version of the Neoclassical, taking the classical vocabulary of figure, drapery and monumental composition and handling it with twentieth-century flatness and clarity. He was a sculptor and a theatre designer as well, and the stage sense shows in pictures composed like tableaux. The titles of his known works trace the direction of Italian art in his lifetime: Glory of 1940, Roman Soldier and Goddess Roma both of 1941, subjects belonging to a period when Rome's imperial past served as official imagery, and then the Madonna of 1956. He belongs to the Novecento Italiano, the interwar Italian movement that answered the avant-garde with order, scale and reference to the past. He worked well beyond that moment, dying in 1972.

margheritasarfatti.blurb: Critic, patron, and Fascism's art adviser.
margheritasarfatti.bio: Margherita Sarfatti, born in Italy in 1880, shaped Italian art between the wars without ever picking up a brush. She was a journalist, art critic, collector, patron and salonnière, and it was through criticism, patronage and the salon that she set the terms on which interwar Italian painting was seen, the territory of the Novecento Italiano and the return to order. Her influence cannot be separated from her politics. She was a prominent propaganda adviser to the National Fascist Party, Benito Mussolini's biographer, and for years his mistress, and that proximity was the source of much of her leverage over which artists were exhibited and bought. She remains one of the clearest cases in twentieth-century art of the critic as power broker, and of what happens when an aesthetic programme is built alongside a political one. She died in 1961.

amedeomodigliani.bio: Amedeo Modigliani, born in Italy in 1884, studied the art of antiquity and the Renaissance at home before moving to Paris in 1906, where he came into contact with Pablo Picasso and Constantin Brâncuși. Brâncuși, his neighbour in Montparnasse, taught him direct carving in stone between 1909 and 1914 and turned him briefly into a sculptor; by 1912 he was showing highly stylised carvings with the Section d'Or Cubists at the Salon d'Automne. The paintings came to define him instead: portraits and nudes with faces, necks and figures drawn out into long surreal curves, poorly received in his lifetime and much sought after since. He shared quarters at La Ruche with Chaïm Soutine and introduced him to Léopold Zborowski, the dealer, landlord and unpaid promoter who kept them both going. He died in 1920; his partner Jeanne Hébuterne died two days later, nine months pregnant.

chaimsoutine.blurb: Expressionism's rawest School of Paris painter.
chaimsoutine.bio: Chaïm Soutine, born in the Russian Empire in 1893 and of Belarusian Jewish origin, made his contribution to Expressionism from inside the School of Paris, where he lived and worked for most of his life. Where his neighbours refined, he attacked: portraits and still lifes built from thick, agitated paint that seems not to have settled, as in Woman in Red Blouse of 1919, Still Life with Fish and Man with Horse of 1920, and the Portrait of Madeleine Castaing of 1929. He shared quarters at La Ruche with Amedeo Modigliani, who introduced him to his own dealer, Léopold Zborowski, and Zborowski then kept Soutine housed and painting through the 1920s, a practical patronage without which the work would not exist. He remained a French painter of Belarusian origin, at ease in neither category. He died in 1943.

marcchagall.bio: Marc Chagall, born in 1887, was a Belarusian and French artist of Jewish ancestry and one of the most widely loved figures of the École de Paris, working in nearly every medium available to him: painting, drawing, book illustration, stained glass, stage sets, ceramics, tapestry and prints. Herwarth Walden gave him his first solo show at the Der Sturm gallery in Berlin in 1914. He married Bella Rosenfeld in 1915, and she is the figure floating through thirty years of his paintings. He founded an art school in Vitebsk and invited Kazimir Malevich to teach there; Malevich took the school over and Chagall left in 1920. I and the Village dates from 1911 and Hommage à Apollinaire from 1913, with the church at Assy in 1946 and the Chagall Windows in 1962 coming much later. He died in 1985.

julespascin.bio: Jules Pascin, born Julius Mordecai Pincas in Bulgaria in 1885, was known around Montparnasse as its prince, the host and centre of a social world as much as a painter within it. He belonged to the School of Paris and later took American citizenship, moving between two countries without quite settling into either. Women were his subject almost to the exclusion of everything else: models nude or partly dressed, caught in casual attitudes rather than arranged, in works such as The Foolish Virgins of 1909, Reclining Girl of 1921 and Seated Model of 1925. He worked as an illustrator, draftsman and printmaker as well, and the drawing underneath the paintings is what holds them together, quick and exact. He also painted individual sitters, among them Pierre Mac Orlan in 1924. He died in 1930.

tsuguharufoujita.bio: Tsuguharu Foujita, born in Japan in 1886, studied Western-style painting at home before travelling to Paris, where he encountered the international modern scene of Montparnasse and became one of its recognisable figures. What he built there was genuinely double: an eclectic style that borrowed from Japanese and European traditions at once, setting the line and surface of one inside the subjects and formats of the other so that neither tradition wins outright. He worked as a printmaker, illustrator and draftsman as well as a painter, and drawing is the common thread, the calligraphic line surviving the change of continent. He became French in later life, and the Foujita Chapel of 1966 stands as the summary work of that second existence. He died in 1968, an artist claimed by two countries and fully explained by neither.

moisekisling.blurb: Polish painter of the School of Paris.
moisekisling.bio: Moïse Kisling was born in Kraków in 1891 to Jewish parents, in a city then part of Austria-Hungary, and studied at the Academy of Fine Arts there before leaving for Paris in 1910 at the age of nineteen. He settled in Montmartre and became a member of the Parisian avant-garde later known as the School of Paris, developing close professional relationships with Amedeo Modigliani and Jules Pascin, the two painters his own work is most often set beside. Recognition came from his treatment of the female form, and he completed a long series of nudes and portraits over his career, among them Kiki de Montparnasse of 1924 and Woman in green skirt of 1928, alongside still lifes such as the Still Life of 1915 and A Bouquet of Cornflowers of 1938. He died in 1953.

constantinbrancusi.blurb: Modern sculpture's patriarch of pure form.
constantinbrancusi.bio: Constantin Brâncuși, born in Romania in 1876, carved wooden farm tools as a child and ended as the figure usually called the patriarch of modern sculpture. He studied in Bucharest, then Munich, then at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris from 1905 to 1907, and worked in Auguste Rodin's studio for a month in 1907 before leaving with the remark that nothing grows under big trees. What followed was a lifetime of reduction: The Kiss of 1907, Sleeping Muse of 1910, Bird in Space of 1923 and The Endless Column of 1938, forms cut back until material and idea arrive at the same place. Romanian folk art and non-European sources fed the work as much as anything in Paris did. He taught Amedeo Modigliani direct carving between 1909 and 1914, the two being neighbours in Montparnasse. He died in 1957.

charlessheeler.blurb: Painted America with a camera's eye.
charlessheeler.bio: Charles Sheeler, born in the United States in 1883, was among the earliest American artists to adopt modernism, and he did it in two media at once. His Precisionist paintings, Church Street El of 1920, Pertaining to Yachts and Yachting of 1922, Connecticut Barns of 1934 and American Interior of 1935, take American structures, industrial and domestic alike, and render them with a flat clarity that is unsurprising in an artist who worked throughout as a commercial photographer. In 1921 he and Paul Strand co-directed Manhatta, an avant-garde film that stands among the first American experiments in the form. Camera and brush informed each other continuously in his hands: the photographs are composed like paintings and the paintings framed like photographs. He also drew and made sculpture. He died in 1965.

charlesdemuth.bio: Charles Demuth, born in the United States in 1883, was a watercolourist first and one of the finest of his generation, turning to oils only late in his career. Out of that shift came Precisionism, the style he did as much as anyone to define: American industrial subjects, chimneys, water towers and machinery, reduced to clean planes and ruled lines, as in Machinery of 1920 and Chimney and Water Tower of 1931. He also worked in a looser register, and In Vaudeville of 1918 belongs to a run of pictures about performance and the stage. His best-known painting, I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold of 1928, functions as picture, poster and street sign at once, which is a fair summary of what Precisionism was after. He also photographed and drew. He died in 1935.

ralstoncrawford.blurb: Industry abstracted into flat, hard shapes.
ralstoncrawford.bio: Ralston Crawford, born in Canada in 1906 and long resident in the United States, painted urban life and industry as arrangements of flat shape and hard edge, pushing Precisionism further towards abstraction than most of the artists grouped with it. The structures of the industrial city became, in his hands, compositions of plane and line in which the subject stays legible but stops being the point. He worked as a lithographer and a photographer alongside the painting, and the three practices circled the same material from different angles. Teaching occupied much of his life; he was on the staff of the Cincinnati Art Academy for many years, and a long succession of students passed through his classes there. He kept working until his death in 1978, by which time the industrial landscape he had spent a career abstracting was itself beginning to disappear.

elsiedriggs.blurb: The only woman among the Precisionists.
elsiedriggs.bio: Elsie Driggs, born in the United States in 1898, was the only woman to take part in Precisionism, the one indigenous modern movement America produced before Abstract Expressionism, which through the 1920s and 1930s applied a Cubist-inspired vocabulary to the skyscrapers and factories that were remaking the national landscape. Her industrial pictures belong squarely to that project, and her work is held today by the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Columbus Museum of Art, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, the Houston Museum of Fine Arts and the James A. Michener Art Museum in Pennsylvania. Her career did not end with the movement: she turned later to floral and figurative subjects in watercolour, pastel and oil, a body of work quite unlike the steel and smoke that made her name. She was married to the abstract painter Lee Gatch, and died in 1992.

georgeault.blurb: Painted the same crossroads at night.
georgeault.bio: George Ault, born in the United States in 1891, is loosely grouped with the Precisionists, though the label sits a little awkwardly on him. Cubism and Surrealism both left marks on his work, but what has lasted is essentially realist: buildings, interiors and roads set down with an exactness that turns quiet into unease. The Mill Room dates from 1923 and Studio Interior from 1938. His most concentrated achievement is the series he made at a crossroads called Russell's Corners, returning to the same few buildings at night again and again, among them Black Night: Russell's Corners of 1943 and Bright Light at Russell's Corners of 1946. Painting one place repeatedly was his method for reaching something no single version could hold. He died in 1948.

aarondouglas.blurb: Gave the Harlem Renaissance its images.
aarondouglas.bio: Aaron Douglas, born in the United States in 1899, gave the Harlem Renaissance much of its visual language. Winold Reiss encouraged him, in New York in 1925, to draw on African sources, and the African-centred imagery that followed became recognisable as the look of the movement. That same year Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro appeared with Douglas's illustrations, putting the style in front of a national readership; like several Harlem figures he also relied on Charlotte Osgood Mason, a white patron whose support came on controlling terms. He painted murals addressing race and segregation, and through his involvement with the Harlem Artists Guild he opened the field of public art to younger Black artists. In 1944 he founded the art department at Fisk University in Nashville, where he taught until retiring in 1966. He died in 1979.

archibaldmotley.blurb: Chicago's Black experience in saturated colour.
archibaldmotley.bio: Archibald Motley, born in New Orleans in 1891 and raised in Chicago, trained through the 1910s at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, graduating in 1918. From there he spent decades chronicling African American life in Chicago, from the 1920s to the 1940s, in colour-saturated, crowded compositions that catch a city's social life rather than posed individuals. He is counted among the major contributors to the Harlem Renaissance, also called the New Negro Movement, though his own version of it took place in Chicago, in what is now known as the Chicago Black Renaissance, which is the proof that the flowering was national rather than confined to one neighbourhood of New York. The Self-Portrait of 1920 dates from the start of that long project. He died in 1981.

palmerhayden.blurb: Painted Black life and open water.
palmerhayden.bio: Palmer Hayden, born in the United States in 1890, was a prolific painter of the Harlem Renaissance whose work covered more ground than that label usually implies. Scenes of African American life sit alongside landscapes and seascapes, and African imagery and influence run through the pictures, part of the same turn towards African sources that shaped the movement's visual thinking as a whole. He sketched constantly and painted in both oils and watercolours, moving between the two across a long working life and producing a great deal in an era when few Black American artists found the means to. Water recurs often enough in the subjects to count as a preoccupation. He also worked as a draftsman. He died in 1973.

williamhjohnson.blurb: From French modernism to folk directness.
williamhjohnson.bio: William H. Johnson, born in Florence, South Carolina, in 1901, enrolled at the National Academy of Design in New York and worked there with Charles Webster Hawthorne, then went to France and was exposed to modernism at first hand. He married the Danish textile artist Holcha Krake, and the couple lived for some time in Scandinavia, where a strong folk-art tradition changed his painting fundamentally; Vieille Maison at Porte of 1927 belongs to the European years before that shift took hold. They moved to the United States in 1938, and he eventually found work through the Federal Art Project teaching at the Harlem Community Art Center. The later paintings, Sowing of 1941, Fright of 1942 and the Self-Portrait of 1950, carry the flattened directness that folk art gave him. He died in 1970.

augustasavage.bio: Augusta Savage, born in the United States in 1892, was a sculptor of the Harlem Renaissance whose studio came to matter as much as her own work. Gamin of 1929 is her best-known piece, but her lasting influence ran through teaching: Gwendolyn Knight studied with her at the Harlem studio, and at the Harlem Community Art Center she taught Norman Lewis and Jacob Lawrence, whom she also got onto the WPA payroll, a piece of practical help that made a career possible. Equal rights for African Americans in the arts was her cause, and she treated access to training, commissions and exhibition as inseparable from the art itself. A generation of nationally known artists came out of rooms she ran. She died in 1962, her importance measured as much in other people's work as in her own.

metawarrickfuller.blurb: Afrocentric sculptor who made her name in Paris.
metawarrickfuller.bio: Meta Vaux Warrick Fuller, born in the United States in 1877, was a sculptor, painter, poet and theatre designer whose subject was the Black American experience and whose imagery drew consistently on Africa. She built her reputation in Paris, where she was a well-known sculptor at the turn of the twentieth century, before returning to the United States as the first Black woman to establish herself as a sculptor at that level. That standing placed her at the fore of the Harlem Renaissance while many of its figures were still children; she was a generation older than the painters and writers who made the movement famous, and her Afrocentric themes anticipated theirs by years. She worked across forms all her life, in verse and design as well as sculpture. She died in 1968.

loismailoujones.bio: Loïs Mailou Jones, born in the United States in 1905, was a painter and an educator, and the two careers reinforced each other for the better part of a century. She taught at Howard University for forty-seven years, and her students there included Elizabeth Catlett and David Driskell, two artists who would go on to define the field. Her own painting, usually associated with the Harlem Renaissance, is held today by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the Brooklyn Museum, the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, the National Museum of Women in the Arts, the Phillips Collection and the Muscarelle Museum of Art. She kept working and exhibiting into old age, dying in 1998, by which time both halves of her working life had been properly recognised.

jamesvanderzee.bio: James Van Der Zee, born in 1886, was an American photographer whose portraits of Black New Yorkers made him a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. His sitters included Marcus Garvey, Bill Bojangles Robinson and Countee Cullen, but the weight of his life's work rests on the ordinary residents of Harlem, whom he photographed with exactly the same care he gave the famous. Aside from the artistic merit of any single picture, what accumulated over the decades was a record of Harlem more complete than anyone else assembled: a portrait of a whole community rather than a handful of celebrated individuals. He went on working long after the Renaissance had passed into history, and the pictures together amount to the fullest documentation the period received. Van Der Zee died in 1983.

richmondbarthe.blurb: Sculptor of the spirit in man.
richmondbarthe.bio: Richmond Barthé, born in 1901, was an African-American sculptor whose name belongs with the Harlem Renaissance and who is best known for his portrayals of Black subjects. He described his ambition plainly enough: what he wanted, he said, was to catch the spiritual quality he found in people, and he held that no better vehicle for it existed than the human figure itself. His work therefore turns on the diversity and the inner life of the people he modelled rather than on argument or protest. He painted as well as sculpted, and there is a painter's attention to surface and light in the modelling. Barthé went on working into old age and died in 1989, leaving a body of figures grounded in reverence for the human form.

diegorivera.blurb: The muralist who painted a nation.
diegorivera.bio: Diego Rivera, born in Mexico in 1886, was the painter who made the wall the central form of modern Mexican art. His large frescoes established the mural movement at home and then abroad: The History of Mexico in 1929, the Detroit Industry Murals in 1933, and in 1947 the panoramic Sueño de una Tarde Dominical en la Alameda Central. The opening had come from José Vasconcelos, who as Minister of Education commissioned the first murals in 1921, and in 1922 Rivera helped found the Syndicate of Technical Workers, Painters and Sculptors in Mexico City alongside José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros. With Siqueiros the alliance later curdled into bitter political rivalry. He married Frida Kahlo in 1929, divorced her in 1939 and remarried her the following year. An early Portrait of Ramón Gómez de la Serna survives from 1915. Rivera died in 1957.

joseclementeorozco.blurb: Muralism's darkest and least doctrinaire voice.
joseclementeorozco.bio: José Clemente Orozco, born in 1883, stands as the most complex and least doctrinaire of the Mexican muralists. With Diego Rivera and David Alfaro Siqueiros he established the Mexican mural renaissance, and in 1922 he joined Rivera in founding the Syndicate of Technical Workers, Painters and Sculptors; it was José Vasconcelos who commissioned the cycle at the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria. His politics leaned left but never settled into the Marxism of his two colleagues, and his imagery owes as much to Symbolism as to any programme. Between 1922 and 1948 he painted murals in Mexico City, Orizaba, Guadalajara and Jiquilpan, and in the United States at Claremont, New York City and Hanover, New Hampshire. Among the works that carry his name are The Subway of 1928, The Epic of American Civilization of 1930, Barricade of 1931 and The Demagogue of 1946. He was a lithographer too, and died in 1949.

davidalfarosiqueiros.blurb: The muralist with the spray gun.
davidalfarosiqueiros.bio: David Alfaro Siqueiros was the technician among the great Mexican muralists. A social realist painter, printmaker, teacher and soldier, he built enormous public murals while reaching for the newest equipment, materials and technique available to him, so that the method was as much the argument as the subject. He co-founded the Syndicate with Diego Rivera, the two of them later becoming bitter political rivals as thoroughly as they had once been allies. América Tropical: Oprimida y Destrozada por los Imperialismos of 1932, Patricians and Patricides of 1944 and the 1956 mural addressed to the university and the people mark out his range. In 1936 he ran an Experimental Workshop in New York where a young Jackson Pollock poured and sprayed enamel, an episode whose consequences ran far beyond Mexican art. Siqueiros went on working until his death in 1974.

rufinotamayo.bio: Rufino Tamayo, born in 1899 in Oaxaca de Juárez and of Zapotec heritage, is grouped with the Mexican muralists but painted an entirely different kind of picture. Working in Mexico and in New York through the middle decades of the century, he made figurative abstraction touched by Surrealism, in which colour and simplified form carry the weight rather than narrative or political programme. He was a printmaker and a sculptor as well as a painter, and the work moves easily between those disciplines; La Espiga is among the pieces recorded under his name. His Oaxacan background stayed present in the painting without ever hardening into folklore. Across a long career he offered Mexican art a quieter alternative to the public rhetoric of the mural movement, and a route out to the wider world.

jeancharlot.blurb: French-born painter of the Mexican years.
jeancharlot.bio: Jean Charlot, born in France in 1898, was a painter, illustrator and printmaker who worked mainly in Mexico and the United States and held American as well as French nationality. The record gathered here is slim, but its outline is clear: he belongs with the Mexican muralists, in whose orbit much of his career was spent, and he moved between painting, illustration and printmaking rather than settling into a single medium. Teaching mattered to him too, and he held a university post alongside the studio work. Working across two countries and two languages made him one of the connective figures of the period, at home in the Mexican art world and in the American one, and useful to both. He went on working for more than fifty years and died in 1979.

murayamatomoyoshi.bio: Murayama Tomoyoshi, born in 1901, was the driving figure of Mavo, the group he founded in Tokyo in 1923 with Yanase Masamu and Okada Tatsuo. Mavo belonged to the Japanese avant-garde, and its founding put Japan squarely inside the anti-art moment then running through Europe, at much the same time and largely on its own terms. Murayama's own energies ran the same way. He was an artist, but also a writer, a playwright and a novelist, and a producer of drama besides, and much of his later working life through the Shōwa period was given to the theatre rather than to the gallery. That refusal to stay inside a single discipline is the shape of his whole career, and Mavo was its most concentrated expression. He died in 1977.

yanasemasamu.bio: Yanase Masamu, born in 1900, was a Japanese visual artist who in 1923 helped Murayama Tomoyoshi found Mavo, the Tokyo group that pushed the country's avant-garde into performance, design and print. Yanase's own ground was graphic rather than painterly: he worked as a mangaka and as a graphic designer, which placed him on the side of the movement that wanted its art printed and passed around rather than hung on a wall. A work of his titled Twilight is dated 1938. He died in 1945, in the final year of the war, and the summary record he leaves is brief. What survives is enough to place him at the centre of one of the most inventive episodes in modern Japanese art, at the point where the avant-garde met mass printing.

okadatatsuo.bio: Okada Tatsuo, born in 1900, was a Japanese avant-garde artist and a member of Mavo, the radical performance group he helped Murayama Tomoyoshi establish. His work sat where the visual arts met the printed page: he was an illustrator, a graphic designer, a typographer and an editor as well as an artist, and in a group that treated exhibitions, publications and staged events as equivalent forms of action, that combination was central rather than peripheral. Mavo's short life coincided with the anti-art energy then running through Europe and Japan, and Okada was one of the people who gave the Japanese version of it a look on paper. His career was cut short in 1937, and only a scattered record of the work remains.

andrebreton.bio: André Breton, born in 1896, was the theorist, organiser and gatekeeper of Surrealism. A poet and writer first, he produced the Surrealist Manifesto of 1924, which defined the movement as pure psychic automatism, and with Philippe Soupault he had already written the first automatic text, Les Champs magnétiques, in 1919. That year he founded the review Littérature with Louis Aragon, who broke with him over Communism in 1932; Paul Éluard was close to the review and to the manifesto circle. Around the 1924 group Breton gathered the painters who gave Surrealism its images: Max Ernst, its first major painter; André Masson, who invented automatism in drawing and left in 1929; Joan Miró, who signed on but stayed clear of the politics; Yves Tanguy, converted by a de Chirico seen in a shop window; and Salvador Dalí, tried by the group in 1934 and expelled in 1939. Breton died in 1966.

joanmiro.blurb: The Catalan who kept his distance.
joanmiro.bio: Joan Miró, born in Catalonia in 1893, was a painter, sculptor and ceramicist who moved through Surrealism without ever quite belonging to it. From 1922 he worked in a studio at 45 rue Blomet in Paris, next door to André Masson, and the traffic between those two rooms is one of the small hinges of the period. He signed on with André Breton's group in 1924 but kept a careful distance from its politics and its quarrels, which is part of why he was still working, and still recognisably himself, long after the movement had split apart. His late work reached out into public space and monumental form: The Caress of a Bird in 1967, the Miró Wall of 1979, Femme in 1981 and Dona i Ocell, dated 1983, the year of his death.

andremasson.bio: André Masson, born in 1896, brought automatism into drawing and so gave Surrealism one of its working methods. Wounded in battle, he was discharged from the French Army in 1915 after a year in uniform. From 1922 his studio at 45 rue Blomet in Paris adjoined Joan Miró's, and the two fed each other's inventions. He was central to André Breton's group and broke with him in 1929, one of the earliest of the movement's many ruptures. Exiled to the United States during the Second World War, Masson became a conduit: young American painters, Jackson Pollock and Arshile Gorky above all, took the automatic line from him, and through them it passed into the New York School. He kept working into old age and died in 1987.

yvestanguy.bio: Yves Tanguy, born in France in 1900, painted what are usually called abstract landscapes: deep, level, thinly populated spaces in which the forms resemble nothing that can be named. His conversion was sudden. In 1923 he saw a painting by de Chirico in a shop window and decided to become a painter, and he joined André Breton's Surrealist group soon after. Mama, Papa Is Wounded! of 1927, Promontory Palace of 1931, The Sun in Its Jewel Case of 1937 and There, Motion Has Not Yet Ceased of 1945 chart the slow refinement of that single world across two continents; he settled in the United States and held American as well as French nationality. He drew, illustrated and made sculpture besides. Tanguy died in 1955.

renemagritte.blurb: Belgium's painter of unsettled ordinary things.
renemagritte.bio: René Magritte, born in Belgium in 1898, built a career out of placing familiar objects in unfamiliar and unexpected contexts. He painted them plainly, in a deliberately unremarkable hand, and then set them in relations that quietly refuse to work, so that the pictures raise questions about the nature and the boundaries of reality and representation rather than simply reporting a dream. The Human Condition of 1933 and Les barricades mystérieuses of 1961 are among the titles that carry his name. His influence travelled a long way past Surrealism, into pop art, minimal art and conceptual art. In 1964 he gave the young Marcel Broodthaers a copy of Mallarmé, a gift that prompted Broodthaers to abandon poetry for art. Magritte went on painting until his death in 1967.

salvadordali.bio: Salvador Dalí, born in Spain in 1904, married an academic's technical skill to imagery no academy would have recognised, and it is the precision of the draughtsmanship that makes the strangeness land. At the Residencia de Estudiantes in Madrid between 1922 and 1926 he formed the two attachments that shaped his youth: an intense bond with Federico García Lorca, and a friendship with Luis Buñuel, whose portrait he painted in 1924 and with whom he wrote Un Chien andalou in six days at Figueres in January 1929. That same year he joined André Breton's Surrealists and met Gala, formerly Éluard's wife, who became his model, his manager and half his signature. The group put him on trial in 1934 and expelled him in 1939. He died in 1989.

pauldelvaux.blurb: Dream stations, architecture and quiet skeletons.
pauldelvaux.bio: Paul Delvaux, born in Belgium in 1897, spent a long career painting a single dream and refining it. Women, classical architecture, trains and railway stations, skeletons: the same cast returns, combined and recombined, in scenes lit like a stage after the audience has gone home. He is usually filed under Surrealism, though he identified with the movement only briefly. What he took from Giorgio de Chirico and René Magritte he pushed towards something of his own, keeping the polished detail of academic painting and letting the bizarre juxtapositions do the rest. Gildehuizen op de Grote Markt dates from 1953, The Beautiful Night from 1962 and Nos vieux trams bruxellois from 1978. He was also an illustrator, draughtsman and printmaker. Delvaux died in 1994, after a working life of extraordinary length.

hansbellmer.blurb: The maker of the unsettling dolls.
hansbellmer.bio: Hans Bellmer, born in Germany in 1902, is best known for the female dolls, made at life size, that he produced in the middle of the 1930s. Historians of photography claim him as a Surrealist photographer, and historians of art as a maker of objects; both claims hold, and the dolls sit exactly at the point where the two meet. He was a formidable printmaker and draughtsman too, and his etchings appear in the 1940 edition of Histoire de l'œil. He spent much of his later life in France and held French as well as German nationality, working across painting, sculpture, photography and print without settling into any one of them. Bellmer died in 1975, leaving one of the most disquieting bodies of work Surrealism ever absorbed.

albertogiacometti.blurb: The sculptor of the human condition.
albertogiacometti.bio: Alberto Giacometti, born in Switzerland in 1901, trained in Paris under Antoine Bourdelle at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière between 1922 and 1927, and absorbed Cubism and then Surrealism before arriving at a subject of his own. He was in André Breton's group from 1930 to 1935 and was expelled for going back to working from a model, a small scandal that turned out to be the making of him. His brother Diego served as his model, studio assistant and furniture-maker for forty years. The thin standing and walking figures of his maturity, L'Homme qui marche I of 1956 among them, carry the questions about the human condition that ran through his work; Jean-Paul Sartre's essays framed him for a generation, and in 1961 he made the tree for the Paris revival of Waiting for Godot. He died in 1966.

meretoppenheim.bio: Meret Oppenheim, born in Germany in 1913 and Swiss by nationality, was among the younger figures taken up by Surrealism. She worked as a painter and a photographer, wrote lyrics, and modelled as well, a role that has often been allowed to overshadow her own production. Her practice was built less around a single medium than around the surprise a familiar thing can deliver when its material is changed, and that instinct for transformation runs through the pictures and the objects alike. Late in life she made work for public space, including the fountain that bears her name, dated 1983. Oppenheim died in 1985, having spent half a century moving between media she saw no reason at all to choose between, and refusing to let any one of them define her.

leonoracarrington.bio: Leonora Carrington, born in Britain in 1917, was a painter and novelist who lived out most of her adulthood in Mexico City and became, by simple longevity, one of the last surviving participants in the Surrealism of the 1930s. She was with Max Ernst from 1937 until 1940, when his internment separated them; she reached Mexico, and stayed. There she found the friendship that mattered most, with Remedios Varo, the two of them working closely alongside the photographer Kati Horna and building a Surrealism of their own out of myth and magic rather than doctrine. Carrington wrote as well as painted and designed for the stage, and during the 1970s she was among the founders of the women's liberation movement in her adopted country. She died in 2011.

remediosvaro.blurb: Painter of science, mysticism and magic.
remediosvaro.bio: Remedios Varo, born in Spain in 1908, painted worlds in which science, mysticism and magic operate as a single system, and figures who go about their obscure work inside them with complete seriousness. She was with the poet Benjamin Péret from 1936, and it was he who got her out of Europe, bringing her to Mexico in 1941. Mexico turned out to be the making of her. There she formed the close friendship and working exchange with Leonora Carrington, and with the photographer Kati Horna, that produced the most distinctive strand of late Surrealism outside Europe. She was a writer and graphic artist as well as a painter, and made objects too, among them Homo rodans of 1959. Varo died in 1963, with the largest part of her reputation still ahead of her.

dorotheatanning.blurb: The surrealist who outlived the movement.
dorotheatanning.bio: Dorothea Tanning, born in the United States in 1910, began under the influence of European Surrealism and then spent the rest of a very long career working past it. She married Max Ernst in 1946 and stayed with him until his death in 1976, a partnership that placed her at the centre of Surrealism's later history without ever settling the question of her own work, which changed repeatedly across painting, sculpture, print and writing. She was a poet and a writer as well as an artist. Tanning died in 2012, having outlasted by more than half a century the movement she is usually filed under, and she is now read less as Ernst's widow than as an artist with one of the longest and least predictable careers of the century.

kaysage.bio: Kay Sage, born in the United States in 1898, worked inside a compressed window: her active years run from 1936 to 1963, and the paintings she is known for were all made within them. Her subjects are architectural in character, structures set out in space rather than figures or landscapes, and the work belongs both to the golden age of Surrealism and to its post-war continuation. She was a poet as well as a painter, and an illustrator, and she kept diaries and wrote an autobiography, so the record of her own thinking is fuller than that of many artists of her generation. That double life, on the page and on the canvas, is part of why she has been steadily reassessed. Sage died in 1963.

toyen.bio: Toyen, born in 1902 in what was then Austria-Hungary and later a citizen of Czechoslovakia, was a painter, draughtsman, illustrator and photographer who belonged to the Surrealist movement. The summary record is brief, but the position it describes matters: Surrealism was never confined to one capital, and Toyen is among the artists who show how far it reached and how deeply it took hold in central Europe, across a career carried through the political upheavals that reshaped the region between the wars and after them. Working across painting, drawing, illustration and photography rather than settling into one medium was characteristic of the group, and Toyen did it as thoroughly as anyone: the paintings, the book illustrations and the photographic work all belong to a single project rather than to separate careers. Toyen died in 1980.

robertomatta.blurb: The Chilean who taught New York automatism.
robertomatta.bio: Roberto Matta, born in Chile in 1911, trained as an architect and worked in Le Corbusier's office before turning to painting, which may be why his canvases read as spaces to be entered rather than surfaces to be looked at. He joined André Breton's Surrealists in 1937. When the war carried the movement to New York, Matta became its most effective teacher: between 1941 and 1944 he showed Arshile Gorky and the young American painters what Surrealist automatism actually involved, and in 1941 he travelled to Mexico with Robert Motherwell, who brought the method back to New York with him. The group expelled Matta in 1948, in the aftermath of Gorky's suicide. He went on painting across the Americas and Europe for another half-century, Verbo América of 1996 among the late works, and died in 2002.

wifredolam.blurb: The painter of the Afro-Cuban spirit.
wifredolam.bio: Wifredo Lam, born in Cuba in 1902, spent his career portraying and reviving the Afro-Cuban spirit and culture he came from. Picasso took him up in Paris in 1938 and introduced him to dealers and to André Breton, and contact with Picasso, Matisse, Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera fed a style that belonged to nobody else: hybrid figures that fit no single order of being. He met Breton again in Marseilles in 1940 and escaped Europe with him on the same ship. In Martinique in 1941 he met Aimé Césaire, and went on to illustrate Cahier d'un retour au pays natal. Predominantly a painter, Lam also worked in sculpture, ceramics and printmaking in later life, and his distinctive visual language influenced many artists in turn. He died in 1982.

oscardominguez.bio: Óscar Domínguez, born in Spain in 1906, was a Surrealist painter who worked in France for most of his career and refused to stay inside painting. The list of what he made is long: pictures, sculpture, illustration, photography, tapestry and textile design, and graphic and commercial work. That range is characteristic of Surrealism, which treated the boundary between fine and applied art as one more convention worth ignoring, and Domínguez pushed at it as hard as anyone. The summary record of his life is thin, and the work is scattered across those disciplines rather than gathered into a single celebrated body, which is part of why his name has stayed quieter than those of his contemporaries. He held French as well as Spanish nationality and made his career in France. Domínguez died in 1957.

leonorfini.bio: Leonor Fini, born in 1907, was an Argentine-Italian painter, illustrator, designer and author who spent her working life in France. She is known above all for her images of women who are powerful and erotic, painted with an authority that leaves the figures in command of the scene rather than on display within it. She belonged to the wider Surrealist milieu and took its freedoms without taking on its programme. Alongside painting she designed costumes and jewellery and illustrated books, moving between the studio, the theatre and the printed page with equal ease, and she wrote as well. That spread is part of the point: she treated design and illustration as the equals of painting rather than as a sideline to it. Fini died in 1996.

michelseuphor.bio: Michel Seuphor was the pen name of Fernand Berckelaers, born in Belgium in 1901, a painter who did as much for abstraction with a printing press as with a brush. With Joaquín Torres-García he founded Cercle et Carré, and its journal with it: an attempt to give the geometric abstraction of the years between the wars an organised public voice at a moment when it badly needed one. He was a poet as well, and a printmaker, and he made his own paintings throughout, but the role that fixed his place was the historian's. He wrote the history of a movement he had helped to organise, which is a rare and slightly compromising position for a writer to occupy, and it gave his account an authority nobody else could match. He held French as well as Belgian nationality, and lived until 1999.

augusteherbin.bio: Auguste Herbin, born in France in 1882, spent his career reducing painting to colour and geometry and then working out what could be built from them. He came up through Cubism, and a Portrait de Madame Herbin dates from 1922; what followed was an abstraction made of flat, brightly coloured geometric figures assembled with the rigour of a system. Herbin was also an organiser. In 1931 he and Jean Hélion founded Abstraction-Création in Paris, the group that gathered the non-figurative artists of the interwar years and gave them a shared platform, and he was a co-founder of the Salon des Réalités Nouvelles as well; both existed to promote abstract art at a moment when it had few champions. He died in 1960, after nearly half a century of argument in paint.

jeanhelion.blurb: Abstraction's leader who returned to figures.
jeanhelion.bio: Jean Hélion, born in France in 1904, was one of the leading abstract painters of the 1930s and then, deliberately, stopped being one.
