The abstract work of that decade made his name, and in 1931 he founded Abstraction-Création in Paris with Auguste Herbin, the group that organised the interwar abstract artists into a common front. Then he turned back to the figure and spent almost five decades painting it, a reversal that he defended in print for the rest of his life. He was a considerable writer: several books and an extensive body of criticism came out of the same career. Hélion died in 1987, and the long figurative half of his work has taken much longer to be looked at properly than the abstraction he walked away from.

jeanarp.blurb: Dada's poet of soft, growing forms.
jeanarp.bio: Jean Arp, born in Alsace in 1886 and known in German as Hans Arp, worked as a sculptor, painter and poet across the whole span of the modern movement. He was a Dadaist and an abstract artist, and the two identities never really separated in him: the Dada instinct for chance and play runs through the sculpture as clearly as through the earlier work. What he arrived at was a vocabulary of rounded, swelling forms that look organic without depicting anything, seeming less carved than cultivated. Schalenboom of 1947, Evocation of a Form: Human, Lunar, Spectral of 1950 and Berger des Nuages of 1954 are typical of that late manner. He wrote poetry all along, and never treated it as secondary to the sculpture. Arp died in 1966, having given abstraction its most persuasive natural form.

bennicholson.bio: Ben Nicholson, born in England in 1894, was the most effective advocate abstract art had in Britain. He made abstract compositions, landscapes and still lifes, and worked as a sculptor too, moving between austerity and warmth throughout his career. From 1931 he was with Barbara Hepworth, whom he married in 1938 and remained with until 1951; the pair, together with Naum Gabo, formed the core of the artists who regrouped at St Ives from 1939 and made it the gathering point for British Modernism through the war. In 1937 he and Gabo co-edited Circle, the volume that set out the international case for constructive abstraction. Nicholson kept a stubborn Englishness inside the geometry, and the still life never quite disappeared from work that is otherwise as severe as anything painted in the country. He died in 1982.

barbarahepworth.blurb: St Ives sculptor of pure form.
barbarahepworth.bio: Barbara Hepworth, born in 1903, entered Leeds School of Art in 1920, a year after Henry Moore, and followed him to the Royal College; the two became the leading British sculptors of their generation, and the critic Herbert Read championed them together, along with Ben Nicholson. Her first husband was the sculptor John Skeaping, with whom she carved side by side in the late 1920s. From 1931 she was with Nicholson, married to him from 1938 until 1951, and with him and Naum Gabo she made St Ives the centre of British Modernism during the Second World War. Her sculpture pursues pure form with a rigour that never becomes cold: Curved Form of 1961, Winged Figure of 1963, Figure for Landscape of 1965, Elegy III of 1966. Hepworth died in 1975.

henrymoore.blurb: The sculptor of Britain's public bronzes.
henrymoore.bio: Henry Moore, born in England in 1898, made the public sculpture of the twentieth century as most people actually encounter it: semi-abstract monumental bronzes, reclining and seated figures, installed in squares and parks around the world. He was at Leeds School of Art from 1919, a year ahead of Barbara Hepworth, and both went on to the Royal College. The critic Herbert Read built his reputation from 1931, and in 1933 he joined Paul Nash in founding Unit One. During the Second World War he drew Londoners sheltering from the Blitz, a series that reached a public far outside the art world. Draped Seated Woman of 1957, Two-Piece Reclining Figure: Points of 1969 and Sheep Piece of 1971 show the reach of the later work. Moore died in 1986.

paulnash.blurb: War artist who modernised English landscape.
paulnash.bio: Paul Nash, born in 1889, was a British war artist twice over and among the most important landscape painters Britain produced in the century's first half. We are Making a New World of 1918 and The Menin Road of 1919 came out of the first war and Totes Meer (Dead Sea) of 1940 out of the second; between them, in pictures such as Berkshire Downs of 1922, he pursued the English countryside as something ancient and strange rather than merely picturesque. He was a Surrealist by temperament and by association, and played a key part in bringing Modernism into English art; in 1933 he founded the group Unit One with Henry Moore. He was a photographer, writer and designer of applied art as well. Nash died in 1946.

joaquintorresgarcia.blurb: Founder of schools on two continents.
joaquintorresgarcia.bio: Joaquín Torres-García, born in 1874 and Spanish Uruguayan by nationality, spent his life founding things. In Barcelona he set up the Escola de Decoració. In Paris in 1929 he founded Cercle et Carré with Michel Seuphor and Piet Mondrian, Europe's first abstract-art group, which put Mondrian and Wassily Kandinsky in the same room. In Madrid came the Grupo de Arte Constructivo, and in Montevideo, from 1943, the Taller Torres-García, where his students included Gonzalo Fonseca and Julio Alpuy. He lived in Spain, the United States, Italy, France and Uruguay, and his América Invertida of 1943 became the emblem of an art made in the south on its own terms. Painter, sculptor, teacher and writer, he died in 1949, one of the most influential artists of the century.

alexandergerasimov.bio: Alexander Gerasimov, born in the Russian Empire in 1881, became the foremost advocate of Socialist Realism in Soviet painting. He painted Joseph Stalin and the other Soviet leaders, producing the official images by which the state wished to be seen, and it is that role, rather than any formal invention, that fixed his place in the century. The early portraits show where the skill came from: Nadezhda Gilyarovskaya of 1912 and Viktor Lobanov of 1913 belong to a thoroughly academic Russian tradition, and it was precisely that training, redirected, that Socialist Realism required — a conservative technique carrying a modern political message. Gerasimov worked through the whole Stalin period and died in 1963, by which time the doctrine he had represented was losing its grip.

isaakbrodsky.bio: Isaak Brodsky was Russian, Jewish by descent, and a painter and draughtsman who worked in St Petersburg across two eras: the Silver Age before the revolution and the Soviet decades that followed. Laundresses of 1901 belongs to the first, Lenin and manifestation of 1919 and Vladimir Lenin in Smolny of 1930 to the second. Those pictures of Vladimir Lenin made his name, and they became the blueprint examples of the Socialist Realist style, the model other painters were expected to follow when they depicted the leadership. He painted Maxim Gorky in 1937. What carries the work throughout is straightforward technical command, a nineteenth-century painter's fluency applied to the iconography of a new state. Brodsky died in 1939, at the height of his official standing.

alexanderdeineka.bio: Alexander Deineka, born in the Russian Empire in 1899, ranks among the most important Russian figurative modernists of his half-century, which makes him an awkward fit for the label of Socialist Realism he usually carries. His subjects were the ones the state wanted, from collective farms to the defence of the country, but the handling stayed modern, closer to the poster art he also made than to academic painting. Collective Farmer on a Bicycle of 1935 is the picture usually cited as the socialist realist exemplar, and Defence of Sebastopol of 1942 is his best-known war picture. He worked as a graphic artist and sculptor as well, and taught for much of his career, at university level. Deineka died in 1969, his reputation resting on pictures the state approved of and modern painting can still use.

veramukhina.bio: Vera Mukhina, born in the Russian Empire in 1889, carried the nickname 'the queen of Soviet sculpture', and one work above all earned her the title: Worker and Kolkhoz Woman of 1937. She also made the Monument to Maxim Gorky at Tverskaya Zastava Square, dated 1939, and a Tchaikovsky monument of 1954. Between 1924 and 1931 she belonged to The Four Arts, the association that ran in Moscow and Leningrad in the years when Soviet art still contained several competing tendencies, and she painted as well as sculpted. Her training in design runs right through the work: she was a costume, fashion and textile designer too, and the monumental sculpture keeps a designer's command of silhouette. Mukhina died in 1953, having given Soviet public art its most recognisable image.

yuripimenov.bio: Yuri Pimenov, born in 1903, was a Soviet Russian painter, graphic artist, set designer, poster artist and teacher whose working life ran through the whole Soviet period. The honours he collected map that career precisely: two Stalin Prizes of the second degree, the Lenin Prize in 1967, a seat as academician in the USSR Academy of Arts, and the title People's Artist of the USSR in 1970. That is the profile of an artist who stayed inside the system and was steadily rewarded by it. The breadth matters as much as the honours, though, since painting, drawing, posters and theatre design were all part of a single practice for him rather than separate trades. Pimenov died in 1977, after some five decades of work.

grantwood.blurb: The Midwest, painted from the inside.
grantwood.bio: Grant Wood, born in 1891, painted the rural American Midwest and became, in the public mind, the representative figure of Regionalism. American Gothic of 1930 is the picture everyone knows, an iconic example of early twentieth-century American art that long ago escaped the museum into general circulation. The rest of the work repays the same attention: Daughters of Revolution of 1932, The Midnight Ride of Paul Revere of 1931 and Dinner for Threshers of 1934 treat American subjects with a mixture of affection and sharp edge that is easy to miss at first glance. Wood taught as well, working as an art educator and at university level, and made prints. He died in 1942, with Regionalism still at the centre of American painting.

thomashartbenton.bio: Thomas Hart Benton, born in 1889, was the muralist of the American Scene, a painter of everyday people in scenes of American life whose fluid, sculpted figures roll across the wall as though the whole picture were being pulled by a current. Grant Wood and John Steuart Curry stood beside him at the forefront of Regionalism. Chilmark Landscape of 1922, Louisiana Rice Fields of 1928 and Achelous and Hercules of 1947 show the range, from observed landscape to myth. He taught at the Art Students League from 1930 to 1933, where his most consequential student was Jackson Pollock, who later described his teacher as the thing he had to react against — which is its own kind of tribute. Benton died in 1975.

johnsteuartcurry.blurb: Kansas weather, painted at full scale.
johnsteuartcurry.bio: John Steuart Curry, born in 1897, painted rural life in his home state of Kansas and was hailed, alongside Thomas Hart Benton and Grant Wood, as one of American Regionalism's three great painters. His career was short, running from 1924 until his death, and unusually varied: paintings, book illustrations, prints and posters, made for audiences well outside the gallery system. Spring Shower (Western Kansas Landscape) of 1931 and Wisconsin Landscape of 1938 are among the pictures that carry his reputation, along with Ajax of 1936. Landscape and weather do as much work in those paintings as the people in them, which is part of what separates him from the other two Regionalists. Curry was also a lithographer. He died in 1946.

benshahn.blurb: Social realism with a designer's line.
benshahn.bio: Ben Shahn, born in 1898, was an American artist of Lithuanian descent, best known for his works of social realism and for the left-wing politics that ran through them. The Passion of Sacco and Vanzetti Mural of 1967 addresses one of the defining injustices of American public life; The Riveter, a mural study of 1938 for the Bronx central postal station, belongs to the public mural work of those years. Shahn worked as a photographer as well as a painter, and as a designer and graphic artist, and a poster-maker's economy of line is visible in nearly everything he made. His lectures, published as The Shape of Content, remain among the clearest statements any American artist has set down about what art is for. He died in 1969.

jacoblawrence.blurb: Harlem's historian in flat, bright colour.
jacoblawrence.bio: Jacob Lawrence, born in 1917, told African-American history in flat, bright, interlocking shapes he called dynamic cubism, a form popularised in Europe that had itself drawn deeply on West African and Meso-American art. He learned in Harlem's own institutions: Charles Alston taught him at the Harlem Art Workshop at 306 West 141st Street, and Augusta Savage, at the Harlem Community Art Center, got him onto the WPA payroll, which is what made a working life possible. In 1941 he married Gwendolyn Knight, who had trained under Savage too. His subjects were African-American historical figures and the everyday life of Harlem, painted in blacks and browns set against vivid colour. He held a professorship at the University of Washington for sixteen years, and died in 2000.

philipevergood.blurb: Social realist of the Depression years.
philipevergood.bio: Philip Evergood, born in 1901, was an American social realist painter whose most active years fell in the Depression and the Second World War, the period when American art turned decisively towards ordinary life and public argument. He was an etcher, lithographer, sculptor, illustrator and writer as well as a painter, and that spread of activity is typical of the social realists, who wanted their work reproduced and read as much as exhibited. The summary record of his life is brief, but his position in the American Scene is not in doubt: he belongs with the painters who took the crisis years as their subject rather than retreating from them. Evergood kept working long after that moment had passed, and died in 1973.

isabelbishop.bio: Isabel Bishop, born in 1902, spent her career watching one small patch of Manhattan and painting what she saw there. Kenneth Hayes Miller was her teacher at the Art Students League of New York; in time she returned there as an instructor herself, and she belonged to the loosely defined Fourteenth Street School, the artists grouped in that precinct of the city. Union Square runs all the way through her work, and the figures in it are mainly women, drawn from the everyday life of the streets around her. She was a graphic artist as well as a painter, with a printmaker's attention to movement and gesture. Among other honours, her paintings took the American Academy of Arts and Letters Award. She died in 1988, after six decades of looking at the same few blocks.

reginaldmarsh.blurb: New York's crowds, drawn and redrawn.
reginaldmarsh.bio: Reginald Marsh, born in Paris in 1898 and American by nationality, drew and painted New York City in the 1920s and 1930s more thoroughly than almost anyone. The same subjects return again and again: the packed beaches of Coney Island, burlesque and vaudeville houses, women, and men out of work on the Bowery, all treated with the same appetite for a crowded, restless composition. Egg tempera and oils were his painting media, and alongside them came quantities of watercolours, ink and ink wash drawings and prints; he worked as an illustrator and comics artist as well, habits that show in the speed of the line. Pursuit dates from 1941. Marsh died in 1954, leaving a record of the city between the wars made from inside the crowd.

dorothealangeandwalkerevans.blurb: The Depression, photographed at eye level.
dorothealangeandwalkerevans.bio: This entry pairs two names, but the documented record gathered here is Dorothea Lange's alone. Born in 1895, she worked as a documentary photographer and photojournalist in the United States, and the pictures that made her name came out of her assignments for the Farm Security Administration during the Depression. Migrant Mother, Nipomo, California of 1936 is the photograph that fixed the era in the public mind; Pea Pickers Line Up on Edge of Field at Weigh Scale, near Calipatria, Imperial Valley, California, from February 1939, shows what the assignment actually involved, which was recording agricultural labour at close range, day after day. Her photographs shaped the development of documentary photography and, beyond that, humanised the consequences of the Great Depression for people who would otherwise only have read about it. She died in 1965.

fridakahlo.blurb: The painter who made herself the subject.
fridakahlo.bio: Frida Kahlo, born in Mexico in 1907, made herself her own subject and turned self-portraiture into an instrument for examining identity, gender, class, race and the aftermath of colonialism. She drew on Mexican popular culture and a naïve folk-art manner to do it, mixing realism with fantasy, and belonged to the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement and its search for a Mexican identity; she has been called a Surrealist and a magical realist, and sits comfortably inside neither label. Her experience of chronic pain was among the recurring subjects. She married Diego Rivera in 1929, divorced him in 1939 and remarried him in 1940, and had an affair with Leon Trotsky in 1937 while he sheltered at the Casa Azul. André Breton, who arranged her Paris show in 1939, described her work as a ribbon around a bomb. She died in 1954.

tarsiladoamaral.bio: Tarsila do Amaral, born in Brazil in 1886, was a painter, draughtswoman and translator, and is considered one of the leading modernist artists of Latin America. She is regarded as the painter who came closest to giving Brazil's search for a national voice a genuinely modern form. She belonged to the Grupo dos Cinco alongside Anita Malfatti, Menotti Del Picchia, Mario de Andrade and Oswald de Andrade, the small circle that carried modern art into Brazilian life. Her role in the Antropofagia movement of 1928 and 1929 was decisive: it was her celebrated painting Abaporu that prompted Oswald de Andrade to write his Manifesto Antropofago, the argument that Brazilian artists should devour foreign influence and make something of their own from it. She worked until her death in 1973, and her example still anchors modern Brazilian painting.

anitamalfatti.blurb: Brought Modernism home to São Paulo.
anitamalfatti.bio: Anita Malfatti, born in Brazil in 1889, is credited as the first Brazilian artist to bring European and American forms of Modernism home. Her solo exhibition in São Paulo across 1917 and 1918 caused a scandal: her expressionist handling and her choice of subjects were revolutionary for an audience that wanted a national art but had no appetite for the influences she carried back with her. The controversy did not stop her. In 1922 she was a conspicuous presence at the Week of Modern Art, and with the Group of Five she helped remake both the structure of modern art in Brazil and the response to it. She went on painting until her death in 1964, and is remembered less for any single canvas than for the door she forced open and then refused to let close.

candidoportinari.blurb: Brazil's muralist of workers and history.
candidoportinari.bio: Candido Portinari, born in Brazil in 1903, is considered one of the country's most important painters and a prominent and influential practitioner of neo-realism in painting. He worked as a painter and a draughtsman, and much of his reputation rests on public work made at scale, murals among it. Among his best-known pictures are Coffee Agricultural Worker of 1934, Tiradentes of 1948 and Civilizacao Mineira of 1959, subjects drawn from the fields, the mines and the founding stories of the country rather than from the studio. That combination, a modern painter's handling applied to ordinary working people, made him influential well beyond his own generation, and his neo-realist example shaped how Brazilian artists thought about painting meant for public walls. He died in 1962, his standing at home never seriously challenged since.

antonioberni.blurb: Argentina's realist of the industrial poor.
antonioberni.bio: Antonio Berni, born in Argentina in 1905, was a figurative artist who worked as a painter, printmaker, sculptor and muralist. He is associated with Nuevo Realismo, the Argentine extension of social realism, a position that committed him to the lives of people usually left out of the picture. His best-known achievement is the body of collages gathered under the name Juanito Laguna, which describe poverty and the effects of industrialisation in Buenos Aires. The series travelled: his work has been exhibited around the world, carrying an Argentine argument about class and the modern city into rooms a long way from either. Moving between painting, printmaking, sculpture and the wall gave him an unusually wide reach, and he kept working across all of it until his death in 1981.

xulsolar.blurb: Invented languages and painted their world.
xulsolar.bio: Xul Solar was the name adopted by Oscar Agustin Alejandro Schulz Solari, born in Argentina in 1887. He was a painter and a sculptor, but also a writer and an inventor of imaginary languages, and the halves of that description are hard to pull apart: the invented tongues and the pictures belong to a single project. He worked as an astrologer as well, and the symbolic systems that interested him run through everything he made. Within Latin American modernism he is an unusual figure, as much a builder of private systems as a painter of pictures, which is why his work has always attracted writers as readily as artists. He died in 1963. The strangeness that kept him slightly apart from his generation is precisely what has kept the work alive for the generations after it.

ameliapelaez.blurb: A founder of Cuba's avant-garde painting.
ameliapelaez.bio: Amelia Pelaez, born in Cuba in 1896, was a painter and draughtswoman, and is counted among the important Cuban artists of the avant-garde generation. Her work belongs to the broader current of Latin American modernism, in which artists across the continent were working out how to absorb modern European form without surrendering what was local to them. Pelaez is remembered as one of the Cuban painters who made that argument on canvas, and her standing in the national story has been steady ever since. She worked until her death in 1968. The finer detail of her career, her teachers, her circle and her exhibitions, lies outside the record assembled here, but her place among the founders of modern Cuban painting has never been in question.

pedrofigari.blurb: Took up painting late, remembered everything.
pedrofigari.bio: Pedro Figari, born in Uruguay in 1861, came to painting by a long route. He was a lawyer, a journalist, a writer and a philosopher, and a politician besides, and he did not begin to paint until his later years. What he made when he did start was a kind of memory work. Rather than chase the international avant-garde he painted the everyday life of his own country, the local customs he had watched as a child, and in doing so became one of the earliest modernist painters of the region. Canvases such as Fiesta en el rancho of 1924, Dama antigua of 1932 and Candombe of 1934 are typical of that impulse. He died in 1938, having built an entire late career out of what he had never stopped remembering.

abanindranathtagore.blurb: Founded the Bengal school of art.
abanindranathtagore.bio: Abanindranath Tagore, born in 1871, was the principal artist behind the Indian Society of Oriental Art, founded in 1907, and the creator of the Bengal school, the movement out of which modern Indian painting grew. He was the first major exponent of Swadeshi values in art, arguing for indigenous sources at a time when official training looked only to Europe. With Ernest Binfield Havell he turned the Calcutta School of Art away from European academic teaching, and in Calcutta he taught Nandalal Bose, his leading pupil and the man who carried the school forward. Works such as Bharat Mata of 1905 and The Victory of Buddha of 1914 became touchstones. A nephew of Rabindranath Tagore and popularly known as Aban Thakur, he was also a landmark writer for children. He died in 1951.

nandalalbose.blurb: Santiniketan's teacher of a whole generation.
nandalalbose.bio: Nandalal Bose, born in 1882, helped pioneer modern Indian art and stands as a key figure in the current since named Contextual Modernism. He trained in Calcutta under Abanindranath Tagore, whose leading pupil he became, and in 1922 Rabindranath Tagore brought him to Santiniketan to head Kala Bhavana. That appointment turned him into the most consequential art teacher of his generation: at Kala Bhavana he taught Ramkinkar Baij and Benode Behari Mukherjee, among many others, and built a way of working rooted in its own place rather than in European models. His own subjects ranged from scenes of Vedic and Buddhist life to the well-known 1945 image of Gandhi at prayer. He worked and taught until his death in 1966, and the long line of influence running out of Santiniketan is largely his.

asitkumarhaldar.blurb: Bengal school painter, Tagore's Santiniketan assistant.
asitkumarhaldar.bio: Asit Kumar Haldar, born in 1890, was a painter of the Bengal school and one of the major artists of the Bengal Renaissance. He worked as an assistant to Rabindranath Tagore at Shantiniketan, the experimental centre where much of modern Indian art and education was worked out, and he was a teacher and a writer as well as a painter, a combination typical of that circle, where making pictures and building institutions amounted to the same job. Among the works attributed to him is a bronze portrait of Tagore himself. He belongs to the generation that carried the Bengal school's principles out of the studio and into the classroom, where they did their longest work. Haldar died in 1964, his reputation resting on the pictures and on the students in roughly equal measure.

amritashergil.blurb: Brought Paris training to Indian subjects.
amritashergil.bio: Amrita Sher-Gil, born in 1913, was a Hungarian-Indian painter ranked among the finest avant-garde women artists working anywhere in the early twentieth century, and a pioneer of modern Indian art. Drawn to painting early, she began formal lessons at eight, and between 1930 and 1934 she studied under Lucien Simon at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris. Recognition came at nineteen, for the 1932 oil Young Girls. What distinguishes her is where she took that European training: back to the everyday life of ordinary people in India, in paintings such as Three Girls of 1935. She died in 1941, leaving a body of work small enough to know and large enough to have redirected Indian art. Her nephew, the artist Vivan Sundaram, later made her archive his own subject.

jaminiroy.blurb: Traded the academy for bazaar painting.
jaminiroy.bio: Jamini Roy, born in 1887, was among the most famous pupils of Abanindranath Tagore, and one of the few to walk away from what he had been taught. His mature manner is radically simplified and flattened, and its source was not the academy but the cheap bazaar pictures sold at Indian temples as talismans, a popular tradition he treated as serious material. The results struck viewers as reminiscent of European modern art while drawing on sources that owed it nothing, which is much of the reason they mattered. Works such as Boating of 1920 sit near the start of that long transformation. The Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan in 1954. Roy died in 1972, having demonstrated that a modern Indian art could be built out of Indian popular sources.

gaganendranathtagore.blurb: The Bengal school's painter and satirist.
gaganendranathtagore.bio: Gaganendranath Tagore, born in 1867, was a painter and cartoonist of the Bengal school and, along with his brother Abanindranath, is counted among the earliest modern artists in India. The cartooning matters. Alongside the paintings he produced satire, and he wrote short stories as well, which gave his art a sharper and more worldly edge than the movement is usually credited with. Works such as River View of 1900 and Meeting at the Staircase of 1920 span the two decades in which his painting changed most. He was a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore and part of an extraordinary family whose members between them remade Bengali literature, music and painting within a single household. He died in 1938, the least imitated and perhaps the most independent of that group.

rabindranathtagore.blurb: The poet who also picked up brushes.
rabindranathtagore.bio: Rabindranath Tagore, born in 1861, was a poet, playwright, composer, philosopher and social reformer, one of the foremost figures of the Bengal Renaissance, and a painter as well. In 1913 he became the first Indian, and the first non-European in any category at all, to be awarded a Nobel Prize, and the first lyricist given it in literature. He wrote and composed the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh. His importance to modern Indian painting is partly familial and partly institutional: he was the uncle of Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, the two painters standing at the beginning of modern art in India, and in 1922 he brought Nandalal Bose to Santiniketan to head Kala Bhavana, the school that trained the generation after them. He died in 1941, having shaped Bengali culture in nearly every form it takes.

fnsouza.blurb: The Bombay Progressives' fiercest founding voice.
fnsouza.bio: F. N. Souza, born Francisco Victor Newton de Souza in 1924, was a founding member of the Progressive Artists' Group, formed in Bombay in 1947 with S. H. Raza, M. F. Husain, K. H. Ara and others, the circle around which modern Indian painting reorganised itself. His style has been described as combining decadence and primitivism, a deliberately unlovely manner that made him the group's most confrontational figure and its most quotable one. The Progressives did not work in a vacuum: the Berlin-born emigre critic Rudolf von Leyden backed them in Bombay when few others would, and his advocacy helped turn a handful of young painters into a movement with an argument. Souza died in 2002, by which time the group he helped start had become the founding chapter of modern Indian art.

shraza.blurb: Left Bombay for France, returned home.
shraza.bio: S. H. Raza, born Sayed Haider Raza in 1922, co-founded the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay in 1947 with F. N. Souza, the moment at which modern Indian painting acquired an organised centre. Early work such as Bombay in Rain of 1948 belongs to those first years. In 1950 he moved to France, and it was there that he spent most of his working life; in 1959 he married the French artist Janine Mongillat. His career therefore sits across two art worlds at once, an Indian painter formed in Bombay and sustained by decades in Europe. After Mongillat's death from cancer in 2002 he returned to India in 2010 and lived there until he died in 2016. That long arc, out from Bombay and back again, is inseparable from what the paintings became.

mfhusain.blurb: India's storyteller in modified Cubist form.
mfhusain.bio: M. F. Husain, born Maqbool Fida Husain in 1915, was a painter and film director and one of the founding members of the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay, alongside F. N. Souza. His narrative paintings, made in a modified Cubist style, could be caustic and funny or serious and sombre depending on the subject, and the subjects were deliberately vast: Gandhi, Mother Teresa, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, the British Raj, and the ordinary life of Indian towns and villages, often worked through in series. The Progressives had crucial help early on from Walter Langhammer, art director of the Times of India, who found them their first buyers. Husain died in 2011. In September 2020 his painting Voices sold at auction for a record 2.5 million dollars.

khara.blurb: The Progressives' painter of the nude.
khara.bio: K. H. Ara, born Krishnaji Howlaji Ara in 1914, was part of the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay, the circle founded with F. N. Souza that reshaped Indian painting after independence, and he later founded the Artists' Centre in Mumbai. He is seen as the first contemporary Indian painter to take up the female nude as a sustained and meticulous subject rather than an occasional one. Opinion about the results has always been divided: his critics have argued that the pictures lack finish and were not referenced from life, a charge that has followed his reputation for decades. Interest has persisted regardless, and in 2017 a Mumbai exhibition called Privately Ara brought together twenty-two of his works. Ara died in 1985, an awkward and necessary figure in the Progressives' story.

tyebmehta.blurb: Broke with Bengal, embraced brusque Modernism.
tyebmehta.bio: Tyeb Mehta, born in 1925, was a painter, sculptor and filmmaker, and part of the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay. He belonged to the first post-colonial generation of Indian artists, the painters who broke with the nationalist Bengal school and took up Modernism in its place: Post-Impressionist colour, Cubist form, and a brusque, expressionistic attack. Working across painting, sculpture and film gave him an unusually wide sense of what a single figure could be made to do, and the figure stayed his subject even as the means for describing it grew harsher. He died in 2009, remembered as one of the defining artists of the Bombay group and of the generation that decided modern Indian art would answer to nobody's idea of a national style.

linfengmian.blurb: Hangzhou's teacher of modern Chinese painting.
linfengmian.bio: Lin Fengmian, born in 1900, was among the earliest Chinese painters to study in Europe, and he spent the rest of his life joining what he found there to Chinese painting, a synthesis that made him a pioneer of modern Chinese art. He was equally an innovator in art education, one of the group honoured as the Four Great Academy Presidents, and it is through teaching that his influence is most visible. At the Hangzhou National Academy of Art he taught Zao Wou-Ki, who arrived in 1935, along with Chu Teh-Chun and Wu Guanzhong, three of the most consequential Chinese painters of the century, all formed in the same classroom. He worked as a journalist and university teacher as well. Lin died in 1991, having changed both how modern Chinese painting looked and how it was taught.

xubeihong.blurb: The academy head who canonised Qi Baishi.
xubeihong.bio: Xu Beihong, born in 1895 and also known as Ju Peon, was a Chinese painter and teacher whose career ran through the years in which Chinese art was being rebuilt around new academies. The teaching was not incidental to the art. As the head of an academy he used the position to promote Qi Baishi, an older and self-taught painter, into the national canon, an act of advocacy that changed which kind of artist could count as a master. His own subjects ranged widely, from the drawing studies of 1924 and the 1930 portrait of Sun Duoci to Put Down Your Whip of 1939 and The Buffalo Demon and the Snake Spirit of 1943. He died in 1953, remembered as much for what he built and championed as for what he painted.

liuhaisu.blurb: Shanghai's educator who defended Pan Yuliang.
liuhaisu.bio: Liu Haisu, born in 1896, was a prominent Chinese painter of the twentieth century and one of its most consequential art educators, equally at home in Chinese painting and in oils. He is counted among the four pioneers of modern Chinese art known as the Four Great Academy Presidents, a title that names exactly where his influence lay: in the running of schools, and in deciding who was allowed inside them. The clearest instance is Pan Yuliang. Liu admitted her to the Shanghai Art School and then stood by her publicly through the scandal that followed. Careers turn on decisions like that, and hers did. Liu himself went on working for decades after it, teaching and painting in both of the traditions he had mastered, and he died in 1994.

panyuliang.blurb: China's first woman painter in oils.
panyuliang.bio: Pan Yuliang, born Chen Xiuqing in 1895, was the first Chinese woman to paint in the Western manner, and one of the earliest to be formally trained in oils and life drawing. Liu Haisu admitted her to the Shanghai Art School and defended her through the scandal that followed. She went on to study in Lyon, Paris and Rome, and later taught at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts. Out of that double training came a distinctive hybrid, European modernist technique carrying a Chinese pictorial sensibility, as in her self-portrait of 1951. She was a sculptor and an educator as well as a painter, and held French as well as Chinese nationality. She died in 1977. Recent scholarship reads her as one of the most important modern Chinese women artists, and reads the work through the tensions she lived.

gaojianfu.blurb: Led the Lingnan school's new national art.
gaojianfu.bio: Gao Jianfu, born in 1879, led the Lingnan School's effort to modernise Chinese traditional painting into what its members called a new national art. A Cantonese artist by origin, he worked with his brother Gao Qifeng and his friend Chen Shuren to bring the Japanese nihonga manner into Chinese practice, a transfusion intended to renew brush painting rather than to replace it with something imported wholesale. He was active before and during the Second World War, and among his best-known works are The Sickly Tiger of 1935 and The Destruction of Civilization. That pairing of inherited means with contemporary argument is the Lingnan position condensed into a single artist. Gao died in 1951, having established one of the few routes by which Chinese brush painting entered the twentieth century on its own terms.

likeran.blurb: Guohua's teacher at the Central Academy.
likeran.bio: Li Keran, born in 1907 and known by the art name Sanqi, was a guohua painter and art educator regarded as one of the most important Chinese artists of the second half of the twentieth century. He was trained in Western oil painting, but the work he became known for is literati painting in the traditional manner, shaped by the example of two renowned masters of that tradition, Qi Baishi and Huang Binhong. The double training is the point: he could measure the old practice against the new one and choose deliberately between them. As a professor at the Central Academy of Fine Arts he was equally influential, teaching a generation of Chinese artists and passing on a way of working that neither abandoned the brush tradition nor treated it as untouchable. He died in 1989.

jacksonpollock.blurb: Put the canvas on the floor.
jacksonpollock.bio: Jackson Pollock, born in 1912, made the most conspicuous break in twentieth-century American painting by laying the canvas flat and pouring or splashing liquid household paint across it, working from every side and using the force of his whole body. Critics called it all-over painting and action painting, and split over it: some praised the immediacy, others derided the randomness. The route there was long. He studied under Thomas Hart Benton at the Art Students League from 1930, later calling him the thing he had to react against, and in 1936 he worked in David Alfaro Siqueiros's Experimental Workshop in New York, pouring and spraying enamel. John Graham chose him for the 1942 show that got him noticed, Peggy Guggenheim gave him a first solo show in 1943, and Clement Greenberg declared him the greatest painter in America in 1947. He died in 1956.

willemdekooning.blurb: Never stopped arguing with the figure.
willemdekooning.bio: Willem de Kooning, born in Rotterdam in 1904, moved to the United States in 1926 and became an American citizen in 1962. From 1933 he shared a studio with Arshile Gorky, and the decade of daily argument that followed did as much to form both painters as any teacher could have. In 1943 he married Elaine Fried, who had been his student and who became, as Elaine de Kooning, a painter and critic of real consequence in her own right. He was central to Abstract Expressionism without ever fully surrendering the human figure, and he worked as a sculptor too, making pieces such as Seated Woman and Standing Figure in 1969. The dealer Sidney Janis took on the New York School after Parsons, and de Kooning with it. He died in 1997.

franzkline.blurb: An action painter with his own accent.
franzkline.bio: Franz Kline, born in 1910, is one of the central painters of the Abstract Expressionist movement of the 1940s and 1950s. He belonged to the loose company that came to be called the New York School, alongside action painters including Willem de Kooning, Lee Krasner, Robert Motherwell, John Ferren and Jackson Pollock, together with the local poets, dancers and musicians who shared their arguments and their bars. It was never a movement with a manifesto so much as a group of people who happened to be in one city at one moment. Kline explored the same innovations to painting as the others, but his work has always been recognised as distinct from theirs, and it has been revered continuously since the 1950s. He taught as well as painted, and died in 1962 with his reputation already secure.

leekrasner.blurb: Hofmann's student, Pollock's editor, her own painter.
leekrasner.bio: Lee Krasner, born Lenore Krasner in 1908, was an American painter whose work sits at the centre of Abstract Expressionism and whose life has too often been told as somebody else's. From 1937 she studied at the Hofmann School in New York under Hans Hofmann, and she was already a serious abstract painter when she married Jackson Pollock in 1945. Through the marriage she edited and promoted his work, and afterwards she managed what he left behind, outliving him by twenty-eight years and continuing, through all of it, to paint her own pictures. She worked in New York for most of her life, as a printmaker and illustrator as well as a painter. Krasner died in 1984, and the account of the New York School has been quietly rewritten around her ever since.

joanmitchell.bio: Joan Mitchell, born in Chicago in 1925, took an active part in the New York School through the 1950s and was one of the strongest painters it produced. She enrolled briefly with Hans Hofmann in New York and left almost at once, which says something about her appetite for instruction. She worked mainly in painting and printmaking, and also in pastel and other media on paper. From 1955 until 1979 she was with the painter Jean-Paul Riopelle, living in Paris and then at Vetheuil, and she remained in France for much of her career, an American abstract expressionist at a permanent distance from the scene that formed her. That distance seems to have suited the work rather than thinned it. She died in 1992, after four decades of painting at a consistently high pitch.

elainedekooning.blurb: Painter and critic, in equal measure.
elainedekooning.bio: Elaine Marie Catherine de Kooning, born in 1918, was an American painter and art critic, and unusually good at both. She was a key contributor to Abstract Expressionism and to Figurative Expressionism, and she wrote extensively about the art of the period as it happened, working as an editorial associate at ARTnews, which means a great deal of what later historians know about those years passed through her hands first. She began as Willem de Kooning's student and married him in 1943; they stayed married until she died in 1989, though much of that time was spent apart. She worked as an illustrator and sculptor as well. Her double role, making the art and describing it, kept her at the centre of the New York School while complicating her position within it.

gracehartigan.blurb: New York School painter, then teacher.
gracehartigan.bio: Grace Hartigan, born in 1922, was a significant member of the New York School during its most vivid decades, the 1950s and the 1960s. Her circle was effectively her working method: Frank O'Hara, Larry Rivers, Jackson Pollock, Helen Frankenthaler and Willem and Elaine de Kooning all belonged to it, and the group inspired one another's work continually, so that the writing and the painting of those years are hard to hold apart. Her paintings entered major collections, the Museum of Modern Art in New York among them. The second half of her life went largely to teaching: as director of the Hoffberger School of Painting at the Maryland Institute College of Art she influenced a great many younger artists, well away from the scene that had made her. She died in 2008.

normanlewis.blurb: Abstraction that never left Harlem behind.
normanlewis.bio: Norman Lewis, born in 1909 and of Bermudian descent, was an American painter, scholar and teacher who worked inside Abstract Expressionism while asking it to carry more than pure abstraction usually allows. He studied at the Harlem Community Art Center with Augusta Savage, and Harlem stayed with him: he used representational strategies within an abstract language to focus on Black urban life and the struggles of his own community. Alabama, painted in 1960, is among his best-known works. In 1963 he co-founded the New York group Spiral with Romare Bearden, one of the few settings in which artists of his generation could take up such questions together. He was a draughtsman as well as a painter, and taught throughout his life. Lewis died in 1979, a full member of the New York School whose subject was never only paint.

philipguston.blurb: Went from abstraction back to figures.
philipguston.bio: Philip Guston, born in 1913, moved between artistic modes more radically than almost any painter of his generation, from Renaissance-inspired figuration to formally accomplished abstraction and then, late on, to a cartoonish and mocking figuration that scandalised many of his admirers. He met Jackson Pollock at Manual Arts High School in Los Angeles, where the two were expelled together over a satirical pamphlet, an early indication of where his instincts lay. He worked as a muralist in the 1930s, including a study for the post office at Commerce, Georgia, in 1938. Racism, antisemitism, fascism, American identity and, in the last work, the banality of evil are his recurring subjects. He died in 1980. In 2013 his To Fellini fetched 25.8 million dollars at Christie's, an auction record.

arshilegorky.blurb: The bridge from Surrealism to abstraction.
arshilegorky.bio: Arshile Gorky, born in 1904 in the Ottoman Empire, survived the Armenian genocide, and that experience had a crucial influence on everything he painted, most directly in The Artist and His Mother of 1931. He moved from Impressionism and Post-Impressionism towards something entirely his own, and from 1933 he shared a studio with Willem de Kooning, the two of them arguing daily for a decade. Roberto Matta taught him and the other New York painters Surrealist automatism between 1941 and 1944, the method that shaped his late work. John Graham championed him, and Graham's 1942 American and French Paintings show put Pollock, de Kooning and Krasner in one room. Gorky died in 1948, having presaged Abstract Expressionism rather than joined it, and is now ranked among the most powerful American painters of the century.

hanshofmann.blurb: Taught half the New York School.
hanshofmann.bio: Hans Hofmann, born near Munich in 1880, belonged to the European avant-garde of the early twentieth century before emigrating to the United States in 1932, bringing with him a working synthesis of Symbolism, Neo-Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism that almost no American painter then possessed. His own painting is built on pictorial structure and unity, spatial illusionism and bold expressive colour, and Clement Greenberg treated his 1944 debut at Peggy Guggenheim's Art of This Century, the first solo show he had in New York, as the breakthrough that heralded Abstract Expressionism. His largest effect, though, was as a teacher. Louise Nevelson studied with him in Munich in 1931 and again in New York; Lee Krasner joined his school in 1937; Helen Frankenthaler came to Provincetown in 1950; Allan Kaprow studied with him in 1947 and 1948; Joan Mitchell enrolled and left almost at once. He died in 1966.

robertmotherwell.bio: Robert Motherwell, born in 1915, ranked among the youngest of the New York School painters and was the most literary of them: he edited The Dada Painters and Poets, the anthology that gave American artists their working knowledge of Dada. In 1941 he travelled to Mexico with Roberto Matta and came back with Surrealist automatism, the method that loosened a great deal of American painting over the decade that followed. At Black Mountain College in 1951 he taught Cy Twombly, then wrote the catalogue for Twombly's first show, an act of sponsorship as consequential as anything he painted that year. He married Helen Frankenthaler in 1958 and they were together until 1971. A printmaker and lithographer as well as a painter, Motherwell worked until his death in 1991.

markrothko.blurb: Latvian-born master of the colour field.
markrothko.bio: Mark Rothko, born in Latvia in 1903, gave the last two decades of his life to a single problem: irregular, painterly rectangles of colour, worked and reworked from 1949 until 1970. He arrived there slowly, through the 1930s and under the informal mentorship of Milton Avery, for whom he later gave the eulogy. In 1935 he and Adolph Gottlieb founded The Ten, and the two of them together wrote the 1943 letter to the New York Times that set out what the new painting was for. Betty Parsons handled him in the late 1940s, alongside Newman, Still and Pollock. His alliances with Barnett Newman and Clyfford Still were close and then bitter; both branded him a sell-out in the mid-1950s and the friendships ended. He died in 1970, and the Rothko Chapel opened the following year.

barnettnewman.blurb: Simplest forms, charged with sheer presence.
barnettnewman.bio: Barnett Newman, born in 1905, counts as a major figure of Abstract Expressionism and stands among the foremost of the colour field painters. His paintings use the simplest available forms, and their real subject is less what you are looking at than where you are standing: the sense of place a viewer experiences before the work is the thing being made. The Stations begun in 1958 and Black Fire I of 1961 belong to that pursuit, and in 1967 he extended it into sculpture with Broken Obelisk. Through the 1940s he was closely allied with Mark Rothko, but after 1955 he and Clyfford Still branded Rothko a sell-out and the friendship ended, a reminder of how much these painters believed was at stake in questions of purity. Newman died in 1970.

clyffordstill.blurb: Reached abstraction before the others did.
clyffordstill.bio: Clyfford Still, born in 1904, was one of the leading figures of the first generation of Abstract Expressionists, and he arrived first: his shift from representational to abstract painting happened between 1938 and 1942, while colleagues such as Pollock and Rothko went on working in figurative-Surrealist modes well into the decade. The powerful approach he developed in the years immediately after the war was unlike anyone else's. He taught at the California School of Fine Arts, where Richard Diebenkorn was his student in 1946 and then a faculty colleague until 1950, and where Elmer Bischoff joined the faculty in the same year, making the school a second centre for the new painting. He was close to Mark Rothko in the late 1940s and cut him off entirely by the mid-1950s. Still died in 1980.

adreinhardt.blurb: Painter and theorist of radical reduction.
adreinhardt.bio: Ad Reinhardt, born Adolph Friedrich Reinhardt in 1913, spent more than three decades working in New York City as an abstract painter and, just as importantly, as an art theorist. He wrote and lectured extensively on what painting was and on what it ought to refuse, and the arguments were built as carefully as the pictures. He belongs to the New York School by chronology and association, but his direction ran against the gestural current around him, towards a steady reduction and the monochrome. That position made him a major influence on what came next: conceptual art, minimal art and monochrome painting all draw on ground he established. He taught at university level and worked as a printmaker and collagist as well. Reinhardt died in 1967, having narrowed painting down to what he believed could not be given up.

helenfrankenthaler.blurb: One studio visit changed American painting.
helenfrankenthaler.bio: Helen Frankenthaler, born in Manhattan in 1928, began exhibiting large-scale abstract expressionist paintings in the early 1950s and went on showing for more than six decades, spanning several generations of abstract painting while the work kept changing. She studied with Hans Hofmann at Provincetown in the summer of 1950, and was influenced by Pollock's painting and by the critic Clement Greenberg, with whom she was involved from 1950 to 1955. The decisive moment came in 1953, when Morris Louis and Noland saw Mountains and Sea in her studio and changed course that same week. Greenberg later included her in the 1964 Post-Painterly Abstraction exhibition that introduced the colour field generation. She married Robert Motherwell in 1958 and they separated in 1971. The Museum of Modern Art gave her a retrospective in 1989. She died in 2011.

davidsmith.bio: David Smith, born in 1906, was the sculptor of Abstract Expressionism, making large abstract geometric works in welded steel at a time when American sculpture had no such tradition of its own to draw on. The direction came from John Graham, who showed him welded European sculpture and effectively set his course. He married Dorothy Dehner in 1927 and the marriage lasted until 1952; both of them had trained at the Art Students League. The Cubi series, including Cubi VI of 1963, is his best-known achievement. He painted, designed and photographed as well, and the sculpture keeps a painter's attention to surface throughout. Smith died in 1965, having built out of industrial material a vocabulary that a great deal of later abstract sculpture simply took as given.

louisebourgeois.bio: Louise Bourgeois, born in France in 1911, spent a very long career making art out of a small number of hard subjects: domesticity and the family, sexuality and the body, death and the unconscious. She connected all of it to events in her own childhood, and described the making as a therapeutic process rather than a metaphor for one. She is best known for large-scale sculpture and installation, the several versions of Maman dated 1999 and 2001 among them, but she was also a prolific painter and printmaker. She showed alongside the Abstract Expressionists, and the work shares a great deal with Surrealism and with feminist art, yet she was never formally affiliated with any movement, which is part of why so many of them have since claimed her. She died in 2010.

louisenevelson.bio: Louise Nevelson, born in the Russian Empire in 1899, came with her family to the United States in 1905, learning English at school while Yiddish remained the language of home. She became the sculptor of monumental wall pieces: wooden constructions, each finished in a single colour, assembled into structures that read as architecture as much as sculpture, along with outdoor works at a similar scale. She studied under Hans Hofmann in Munich in 1931 and again in New York, which placed her inside the same argument about structure and space that shaped the painters around her. Night Wall I of 1972 and the two works of 1976, Bicentennial Dawn and Sun Disk/Moon Shadow V, come from her most ambitious years. She painted, printed and drew as well. Nevelson died in 1988.

isamunoguchi.blurb: Sculpture, stage sets, lamps, whole gardens.
isamunoguchi.bio: Isamu Noguchi, born in 1904, worked across six decades from the 1920s onward and refused throughout to keep sculpture separate from everything else. He is known for sculpture and public artworks, among them The Cry of 1959, Khmer of 1962 and the Cullen Sculpture Garden of 1986, but he also designed stage sets for various Martha Graham productions, made the Akari light sculptures, and produced furniture pieces that are still manufactured and sold. Landscape architecture was as much his medium as stone. That range was not restlessness but a position, that one sensibility should shape the object you hold, the room you sit in and the ground you walk across. New York's Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum holds his work, as do many museums elsewhere. He died in 1988.

clementgreenberg.blurb: The critic who made Abstract Expressionism.
clementgreenberg.bio: Clement Greenberg, born in 1909, was the essayist and art critic most closely bound to American modern art at mid-century, and the most formidable formalist aesthetician of his generation. He occasionally wrote under the pseudonym K. Hardesh. In 1947 he declared Jackson Pollock the greatest painter in America, a judgment that did as much as any exhibition to establish Abstract Expressionism; critics rarely get to build a movement, and he did. He was involved with Helen Frankenthaler between 1950 and 1955, and it was Greenberg who took Louis and Noland to see her studio, an introduction that redirected a good deal of postwar American abstraction. He worked as an art historian and collector as well. Greenberg died in 1994, his authority long contested by then but the shape he gave the period still visible in most accounts of it.

haroldrosenberg.bio: Harold Rosenberg, born in 1906, was an American writer, educator, philosopher and art critic, and the man who gave Abstract Expressionism its other name. In 1952 he coined the term Action Painting for what the New York painters were doing, a phrase that put the emphasis on the act of painting rather than on the finished image, and that has shaped how the work is described ever since. His account stood in permanent tension with the formalist criticism of the period, which is part of the reason both survived. He held the art critic's chair at The New Yorker from 1962 until he died, writing for a general readership about art that most of it found baffling. Rosenberg died in 1978, best remembered for the criticism as a body of work rather than for any single argument within it.

jeanfautrier.bio: Jean Fautrier, born in France in 1898, was a painter, illustrator, printmaker and sculptor, and one of the most important practitioners of Tachisme. That movement, and the wider currents of Art Informel and Art Brut around it, belong to the years after the war when painters in Paris were looking for a way to make marks that had not been agreed in advance, and for whom the matter of paint itself became the argument. Fautrier is central to that story. He worked across several media without settling in any one of them, which was itself characteristic of a generation suspicious of finish and of inherited categories. He died in 1964. His name recurs whenever the postwar Paris school is discussed, usually at the point where the discussion begins.

wols.bio: Wols was the pseudonym of Alfred Otto Wolfgang Schulze, born in Germany in 1913 and predominantly active in France. He painted and he photographed, and he went broadly unrecognised in his lifetime; the recognition came afterwards, when he was read as a pioneer of lyrical abstraction and as among the Tachisme movement's most influential figures. He also wrote on art theory, in a book of aphorisms published under his adopted name. He died in 1951, young, and before the movements he had helped make possible reached their full run. What makes him unusual in this part of the story is the size of the gap between the life and the influence: almost no career at all while it was happening, and a decisive one in retrospect.

jeandubuffet.blurb: Founded Art Brut, distrusted good taste.
jeandubuffet.bio: Jean Dubuffet, born in France in 1901, built a career against the idea of good taste. A painter and sculptor of the Ecole de Paris, he embraced what the art world dismissed as low art and rejected traditional standards of beauty in favour of something he believed more authentic and more humanistic. In 1948 he founded the Compagnie de l'Art Brut with Andre Breton, a partnership that collapsed within three years, though the art brut movement and the Collection de l'art brut that grew from it long outlasted the quarrel. His own work became increasingly monumental and public: Arbre biplan of 1969, the Jardin d'email of 1974, Monument with Standing Beast in 1984 and Tour aux figures in 1985. He exhibited prolifically in France and America, and died in 1985.

hanshartung.bio: Hans Hartung, born in 1904, was a German-French painter whose gestural abstraction is what he is known for, a way of working he arrived at early and returned to across an entire career. He was a draughtsman, photographer and calligrapher as well as a painter, and the calligraphic side of that training is legible in the paintings, where the mark carries the whole weight of the picture. His life was not confined to the studio: he served in the Second World War and was a decorated veteran of the Legion d'honneur. He belongs to the Paris circle of Art Informel and Tachisme, the postwar generation that put the unpremeditated mark at the centre of European abstraction. He worked in France, and died in 1989, the most disciplined gesture in a movement built on release.

pierresoulages.blurb: Honoured, at last, in his lifetime.
pierresoulages.bio: Pierre Soulages, born in France in 1919, worked as a painter, printmaker, copper engraver, illustrator and sculptor across a career of exceptional length. He belongs to the postwar Paris generation of Art Informel and Tachisme, the painters who answered the war with an abstraction built out of the physical act of marking a surface rather than out of geometry. Recognition arrived in full while he was alive, which is unusual in this story: his works are held by leading museums around the world, and a museum devoted entirely to his art opened in his hometown of Rodez. In 2014 France's president, Francois Hollande, called him the greatest living artist in the world. Soulages died in 2022, having stayed with the same single problem for longer than most painters get to work at all.

georgesmathieu.bio: Georges Mathieu, born in France in 1921, was a painter and art theorist who became one of the founding figures of European lyrical abstraction, the strand of informalism that cut abstraction loose from geometry and handed it over to speed. Working alongside the Tachiste and Art Informel painters of the postwar decades, he treated the canvas as a field for improvisation rather than a composition worked out in advance. He was a draughtsman as well, and a medallist and a designer of postage stamps, carrying his abstract handwriting into public and everyday forms in a way few of his contemporaries attempted. Election to the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Paris confirmed his standing within the French establishment, an unusual place for an artist so committed to spontaneity. He wrote as much as he painted, arguing the theoretical case for his own practice. Mathieu died in 2012.

nicolasdestael.blurb: Between abstraction and figuration, always moving.
nicolasdestael.bio: Nicolas de Staël was born Baron Nikolai Vladimirovich Staël von Holstein in 1914 and became a French painter of Russian origin, counted among the artists who mattered most in Europe after the war. His working life lasted barely fifteen years, yet in that span he produced over a thousand paintings, moving constantly between abstraction and figuration rather than settling into either camp. Colour was his instrument, used with a richness that gives the pictures a physical weight photographs never quite carry, and his handling of light and texture is as distinctive as the colour itself. Alongside painting he worked in lithography, engraving, collage and drawing, testing the same problems in different registers. He belonged to the Art Informel generation of postwar Europe, though his restlessness kept him at its edges rather than at its centre. He died in 1955, his short career leaving an outsized mark on European painting.

mariahelenavieiradasilva.blurb: Painter of cities folding into space.
mariahelenavieiradasilva.bio: Maria Helena Vieira da Silva, born in 1908, was a Portuguese abstract painter who made her career largely in France and held both nationalities. She is counted a leading member of Art Informel, the European abstract movement of the postwar years, though her pictures are unmistakably her own: intricate interiors and views of cities, assembled from ranks of small marks that pull space open and then fold it shut again. Perspective, in her hands, is something to be tested rather than obeyed, and the eye is never allowed to settle. She worked well beyond easel painting, making tapestry, stained glass and graphic work, and the discipline of those crafts feeds back into the lattice structures of her canvases. She died in 1992, leaving one of the most distinctive bodies of abstract painting produced anywhere in postwar Europe.

jeanpaulriopelle.bio: Jean-Paul Riopelle, born in Quebec in 1923, was a Canadian painter and sculptor whose international career ran longer, and counted for more, than almost any other among the sixteen signatories of the Refus Global, the 1948 manifesto in which Quebec's artists refused clericalism and provincialism. He is best known for the mosaic paintings of the 1950s, made after he abandoned the brush entirely and applied paint with a palette knife alone, giving the surfaces a dense, sculptural quality. A leading artist of French lyrical abstraction, he won an international standing no Canadian painter had held since James Wilson Morrice. He worked as a sculptor, printmaker and installation artist too, producing La Joute and Owl Shovel in 1969. From 1955 to 1979 his life was bound up with the painter Joan Mitchell, in Paris and at Vétheuil. He died in 2002.

antonitapies.blurb: Catalan painter, sculptor and art theorist.
antonitapies.bio: Antoni Tàpies i Puig, born in 1923, was a Catalan painter, sculptor and art theorist and one of the defining Spanish artists of the postwar decades. He belongs to the Art Informel generation, the European painters who turned away from image-making and toward the raw behaviour of materials themselves. Alongside painting he worked as a sculptor, illustrator and graphic artist, and he wrote extensively about art, thinking through in prose what his surfaces argued in matter. His long career carried him well past the informal moment that formed him: Mitjó and Les quatre cròniques sit alongside later works such as Rinzen of 1993. He held the title of Marquess of Tàpies, a rare civil honour for a painter. He died in 2012, having spent a lifetime making Catalan art legible to the rest of the world.

antoniosaura.blurb: A major voice of postwar Spanish painting.
antoniosaura.bio: Antonio Saura Atarés, born in 1930, was one of the major postwar painters to emerge in Spain during the fifties, and his work left its mark on several generations of artists who came after him. He belongs to the Art Informel and Tachiste current of postwar Europe, the tendency that put gesture, accident and raw handling ahead of composed design. Painting was only part of what he did: he was a writer, an illustrator and a draughtsman as well, and his critical voice is remembered as often as his canvases are looked at. That double practice, making the work and arguing about it in print, was characteristic of a Spanish avant-garde that had to build its own intellectual ground before it could stand on it. He died in 1998, his influence on Spanish painting long since acknowledged.

asgerjorn.bio: Asger Oluf Jorn, born in Denmark in 1914, worked as a painter, sculptor, ceramic artist and author, and was one of the great connectors of the postwar European avant-garde. In November 1948, at the Café Notre-Dame in Paris, he signed CoBrA into existence with Karel Appel, Constant, Corneille and Christian Dotremont, who coined the group's name from Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam. Constant wrote its manifesto, and the young Pierre Alechinsky joined the following year as its youngest member. Jorn's restlessness did not stop there. In 1957 he helped found the Situationist International with Guy Debord, bankrolling the group before leaving it in 1961, so that he ended up shaping two movements rather than one. He worked as a printmaker and graphic designer alongside all of this. He died in 1973.

karelappel.bio: Christiaan Karel Appel, born in the Netherlands in 1921, began painting at fourteen and trained at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam during the 1940s. In November 1948, at the Café Notre-Dame in Paris, he became one of the founders of CoBrA alongside Asger Jorn, the avant-garde group that set raw colour and unschooled mark-making against the polish of prewar abstraction. He was a poet and an avid sculptor as well as a painter, and he worked as a printmaker and muralist, taking his imagery onto walls and into public buildings in the Netherlands from 1949 onward. Later pieces such as Frog with Umbrella of 1993 kept the same cheerful violence running into his old age. His work entered MoMA and museums worldwide. He died in 2006, still one of the most recognisable painters his country produced.

constantnieuwenhuys.blurb: Painter, sculptor, author, musician and resistance fighter.
constantnieuwenhuys.bio: Constant Anton Nieuwenhuys, known simply as Constant, was born in the Netherlands in 1920 and worked as a painter, sculptor, graphic artist, author and musician, a range unusual even among the postwar avant-garde and one he never treated as a set of sidelines. His work belongs to CoBrA, the movement that set spontaneous, unschooled making against the polish of prewar geometric abstraction. He is also recorded as a resistance fighter, and that formation helps explain the political edge he brought to art after the war. Alongside painting he made sculpture and prints, and he worked at public scale: Constant's Gate, of 1963, carries his forms out of the gallery and into shared space. Writing and music ran beside the studio work rather than after it. He died in 2005, having spent his life refusing to be only one kind of artist.

corneille.blurb: Dutch co-founder of the CoBrA group.
corneille.bio: Corneille was born Guillaume Cornelis van Beverloo in 1922 and spent his working life under the single name he took as a painter; the pseudonym stuck so completely that the birth name became the footnote. He was a co-founder of CoBrA, the postwar group he helped establish alongside Asger Jorn, and that early alliance set the terms for everything that came after. Though he is remembered first as a painter, he moved easily between media, making prints, sculpture and ceramics with the same appetite; the range was part of the work, not a sideline to it. His career stretched from the postwar years until his death in 2010, and across all those decades CoBrA stayed the reference point audiences reached for whenever the Dutch artist's name came up.

pierrealechinsky.blurb: The youngest of the CoBrA painters.
pierrealechinsky.bio: Pierre Alechinsky, born in 1927, is a Belgian artist who has been based in France since 1951 and holds both Belgian and French nationality. He joined CoBrA in 1949 as its youngest member, arriving after Asger Jorn and the others had founded the group. His work sits at the meeting point of tachisme, abstract expressionism and lyrical abstraction, driven by a calligraphic line that owes as much to writing as it does to drawing. Alongside painting he is a draughtsman, a printmaker and a writer, and printmaking has been central to his practice rather than incidental to it: Sept Écritures, from 1976, belongs to that side of the work. Long after that beginning, Alechinsky has gone on working in the free, gestural idiom the group set loose.

christiandotremont.bio: Christian Dotremont, born in Tervuren, Belgium in 1922, was a painter and poet who founded CoBrA together with the Danish artist Asger Jorn, and it was Dotremont who supplied the name, compressing Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam into a single word. He had already been a founding member of the Revolutionary Surrealist Group in 1946, and he brought Henri Lefebvre's Critique de la vie quotidienne of 1946 to the group's attention, giving it a theoretical spine. His own lasting contribution came later, in the painted poems he called logograms, where handwriting is pushed until it becomes drawing and meaning survives as gesture. Writer and draughtsman by turns, he never settled the question of which craft he was practising, and Sept Écritures, from 1976, belongs to that unsettled territory. He died in 1979, poet and painter to the end.

luciofontana.bio: Lucio Fontana, born in 1899, was an Argentine-Italian sculptor, painter and theorist, and the founder of Spatialism, the movement he set out in the Manifiesto blanco. He is best known for the slashed and punctured canvases in which the picture surface is opened rather than painted upon, turning a painting into a question about the space behind it. The same thinking took him to neon, most famously in his piece for the Milan Triennale, and into design, including jewellery. Concetto spaziale Natura of 1959 belongs to that long inquiry. In Milan he became the crucial older figure for Piero Manzoni, who took the punctured canvas as licence for everything that followed in his own short and radical career. Fontana died in 1968, having handed the next generation a way out of the picture plane.

albertoburri.blurb: He made painting out of raw matter.
albertoburri.bio: Alberto Burri, born in 1915, was an Italian painter and sculptor, trained also as a physician, who worked out of Città di Castello. His painting belongs to the matterist wing of European informal art, the tendency that made the material itself the subject, and he described his own approach as polymaterialist: whatever came to hand was handled the way pigment is handled. The word was his own, and it describes a career in which the choice of substance came before the choice of image. His practice ran close to Lucio Fontana's Spatialism, and together with Antoni Tàpies he did much to revive the art of assembly in postwar Europe and the United States. Late in his career he worked as a land artist at landscape scale, most notably in the Cretto di Burri of 1984. He died in 1995, one of the defining figures of postwar Italian art.

pieromanzoni.blurb: Avant-garde irony taken to its limit.
pieromanzoni.bio: Piero Manzoni di Chiosca e Poggiolo, born in 1933, was an Italian artist whose ironic assault on the art object directly prefigured Conceptual Art. In Milan he found in Lucio Fontana the older figure who mattered most, taking the punctured canvas as licence for everything that followed, and he replaced normal artist's materials with rabbit fur, human excrement and anything else that might, as he argued, reach mythological sources and authentic universal values. Artist's Shit, of 1961, remains the sharpest of those gestures. He met Yves Klein at Klein's monochrome show in Milan in 1957, and in 1959 he founded the Azimut gallery and journal there with Enrico Castellani. His work fed straight into the generation the critic Germano Celant gathered for the first Arte Povera exhibition in Genoa in 1967. He died in 1963.

yoshiharajiro.bio: Jirō Yoshihara, born in 1905, was a Japanese painter who worked as well as an art educator, a curator and a businessman, and who became the founder and financier of Gutai. He set the group up in 1954 with Shōzō Shimamoto, who gave the association its name, and his standing instruction to the members was famously severe: do what no one has done before. Under that rule he taught and drove a remarkable generation, among them Kazuo Shiraga, Atsuko Tanaka, who joined in 1955, Saburō Murakami, Sadamasa Motonaga and Akira Kanayama. His business background paid for the group's activities, so that Gutai answered to an artist rather than to a dealer or a ministry. From 1957 the French critic Michel Tapié carried Gutai to Europe and America, and the group found an audience far beyond Japan. He died in 1972.

shiragakazuo.bio: Kazuo Shiraga, born in 1924, was a Japanese abstract painter and performance artist and a first-generation member of the Gutai Art Association. He was among the most prolific and inventive of the group's experimentalists, ranging across painting, performance art, three-dimensional objects, conceptual work and installation; much of that output survives only in documentary photographs and film. His teacher was Gutai's founder Jirō Yoshihara, whose single rule for the group, to do what no one had done before, Shiraga answered as directly as any member. He was a sculptor as well as a painter, and the physical charge of his surfaces is the mark of a practice in which the making was itself the action rather than a means to an image. He died in 2008, long since recognised as a central figure of postwar Japanese art.

tanakaatsuko.bio: Atsuko Tanaka, born in 1932, was a Japanese avant-garde artist and a central figure of the Gutai Art Association between 1955 and 1965, taught within the group by its founder Jirō Yoshihara. Gutai's insistence that material should be allowed to speak for itself suited her: she worked across painting, sculpture, performance and drawing, and is remembered above all for work that put the body into direct contact with its materials. Her reputation grew markedly from the early 2000s, when a retrospective at Ashiya was followed by the first shows of her work abroad, in New York and Vancouver, and her paintings entered international exhibitions and collections. Tanaka died in 2005, and is now read as one of the most inventive artists of the postwar Japanese avant-garde.

murakamisaburo.blurb: He burst through stretched kraft paper.
murakamisaburo.bio: Saburō Murakami, born in 1925, was a Japanese visual and performance artist and a member of the Gutai Art Association, taught by Jirō Yoshihara. He is best known for the paper-breaking performances, or kami-yaburi, in which he threw himself bodily through kraft paper stretched over large wooden frames, a work now canonical both in the history of postwar Japanese art and in the history of performance art generally. His practice extended well beyond that single gesture, taking in painting, three-dimensional objects and installation, and it is consistently conceptual in temper, refusing the dualisms that Western categories assumed. Time, chance and intuition are its recurring subjects, and its forms are playful and made to be handled. He was a draughtsman as well as a painter. He died in 1996.

motonagasadamasa.bio: Sadamasa Motonaga, born in 1922, was a Japanese visual artist who also illustrated books, and a first-generation member of the Gutai Art Association, the postwar Japanese group whose name has become shorthand for experiment. Within it he was taught by Jirō Yoshihara.
