Motonaga was a printmaker and illustrator as well as a painter, and the two lives ran together rather than in sequence: the books were not a sideline from the art but another place to put the same invention. Belonging to Gutai's first generation meant working before anyone had settled what the group's art should look like, and his own answer to that openness kept a lighter and more buoyant temper than much of what surrounded it. He died in 2011, having stayed with the work for the whole of a long career.

kanayamaakira.bio: Akira Kanayama, born in 1929, was a Japanese avant-garde artist who joined the Gutai Art Association early, taught within the group by Jirō Yoshihara. He was one of its pivotal figures and a constant presence in its exhibitions and performance events. His own contribution came through witty experiments in unconventional materials, among them toy cars and the signal lights used at railway level crossings, letting a mechanism make the marks he would otherwise have made himself. That deadpan, delegated approach gave the work a temper of its own inside the group, and it pointed toward questions about authorship that later artists would take up at length. He and Atsuko Tanaka left Gutai in 1965, and the two married later that year. He died in 2006.

shimamotoshozo.blurb: He named Gutai and threw the bottles.
shimamotoshozo.bio: Shōzō Shimamoto, born in 1928, studied from 1947 with Jirō Yoshihara, the future leader of Gutai, and in August 1954 became a key founding member of the group alongside Yoshihara and fifteen others. It was Shimamoto who gave the association its name. Close to the leader, he was deeply involved in the early activities and in the group's administration, and his own work ranged from holes poked through layered newspaper to bottles of paint hurled at canvas, from film and stage work to sound. His performance pieces were the most innovative part of it. When Yoshihara turned toward painting after meeting the French critic Michel Tapié, Shimamoto kept urging him back toward performance, wanting to work with figures such as Allan Kaprow. He was a calligrapher too. He died in 2013.

francisbacon.blurb: Painted the human figure at its rawest.
francisbacon.bio: Francis Bacon, born in Ireland in 1909 and later a British painter, made figurative art feel dangerous again. He worked almost entirely on the human body, returning to crucifixions, popes, self-portraits and portraits of the friends closest to him, and now and then shutting an abstracted figure inside a bare geometric frame. From 1945 he was inseparable from Lucian Freud; the two painted each other and kept constant company for three decades before falling out in the mid-1970s and never speaking again. George Dyer, his partner since 1963, died in 1971 on the eve of Bacon's Grand Palais retrospective. Bacon died in 1992, leaving postwar art some of its most raw and unsettling images of what a person can look like.

germainerichier.blurb: French sculptor of the postwar figure.
germainerichier.bio: Germaine Richier, born in 1902, was a French sculptor whose work belongs to the existential figuration of the postwar years, when the human figure returned to art scarred rather than whole. She held French and Swiss nationality and worked as a designer as well as a sculptor. Her hybrid figures treat the body as something caught between species, De Mantis of 1946 taking its form from the praying mantis; in the same year she made work for the church of Notre-Dame de Toute Grâce on the Plateau d'Assy, carrying her figures into a religious setting that had rarely admitted anything so unsettled. Le grand homme de la nuit followed in 1954. She died in 1959, her career cut short at the point when postwar sculpture was finally catching up with what she had already done.

balthus.bio: Balthasar Klossowski, who worked as Balthus, was born in 1908 and held Polish and French nationality. He is known for erotically charged pictures of young girls and for a dreamlike, arrested atmosphere that hangs over the whole body of work, which is argued over as fiercely as it is admired. His entry into art was unusually early: the poet Rainer Maria Rilke, his mother's lover, published the boy's Mitsou drawings when Balthus was thirteen, so that he was a published artist before he was out of childhood. He worked as a scenographer, draughtsman and illustrator alongside his painting. Against the grain of a century moving steadily toward abstraction, he held to the figure and to the deliberate, staged interior. He died in 2001, one of the most singular figures in modern art.

lucianfreud.bio: Lucian Michael Freud, born in 1922, was a British painter and draughtsman who worked in figurative art throughout his career and is counted among the foremost English portraitists of the twentieth century. He held British and German nationality, and he worked as an illustrator and printmaker alongside the painting. His subject was almost always the person in front of him, studied over long sittings until the paint itself began to behave like flesh. From 1945 until the mid-1970s he and Francis Bacon were inseparable; each painted the other, and then the friendship broke and the two never spoke again. Freud kept working in the same unhurried, unsparing way for decades after that, treating each sitting as a fresh problem rather than a repetition of the last. He died in 2011.

leonkossoff.blurb: London built up in thick paint.
leonkossoff.bio: Leon Kossoff, born in 1926, was a British figurative painter whose subjects were portraits, life drawings and the cityscapes of London. He studied under David Bomberg at the Borough Polytechnic, alongside Frank Auerbach, and that teaching shaped him permanently. Kossoff worked slowly and returned constantly to the same subjects, the same sitters and the same corners of his city, laying the paint on until the surface has real physical depth and the image seems to have been dug out of it rather than described onto it. He was a draughtsman and graphic artist as well as a painter, and drawing stayed the foundation of everything he made: the cityscapes begin on paper and keep the marks of that beginning. He died in 2019, having painted one city for the better part of his life.

frankauerbach.blurb: Portraits reworked until the paint holds.
frankauerbach.bio: Frank Helmut Auerbach, born in Germany in 1931 to Jewish parents, became a naturalised British subject in 1947. From 1947 to 1953 he attended David Bomberg's evening classes at the Borough Polytechnic in London, and those classes were the making of him as a painter. He counts among the leading names of the School of London, alongside Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud, who were both early supporters of his work at a point when little else was going his way. His practice was famously narrow and famously deep, the same subjects returned to and reworked over long stretches of time until the paint finally settled into an image. He worked as a draughtsman and graphic designer too. He died in 2024, after a career of almost unbroken concentration.

maxbill.bio: Max Bill, born in Switzerland in 1908, was an architect, painter, sculptor, typeface designer, industrial designer and graphic designer, and that range reads as an argument in itself: art, design and building answering to the same rules. He was a leading figure of concrete art, the strand of abstraction that treats a work as a constructed object obeying mathematics rather than a depiction of anything outside itself. Sculptures such as Rhythm in Space of 1967, Kontinuität of 1986, the Bildsäulen-Dreiergruppe of 1989 and the Endlose Treppe, his 1991 monument to Ernst Bloch, turn geometric progressions into public objects. He also taught at university level. His prize at the 1951 São Paulo Bienal catalysed Brazilian Concretism, drawing Waldemar Cordeiro and a whole generation into the concrete project. He died in 1994.

richardpaullohse.blurb: Colour ordered by system, not feeling.
richardpaullohse.bio: Richard Paul Lohse, born in Switzerland in 1902, was a painter and graphic artist who stood among the leading representatives of concrete and constructive art. Where the gestural painters of the same decades trusted the accident, concrete art as Lohse practised it built the picture from rules settled in advance, so that the finished work is the visible result of a method rather than the record of a mood. Colour was distributed by system, and the system was the subject. He worked as a printmaker and lithographer as well, and his parallel career in graphic design carried the same discipline onto the printed page, the two practices running as one. He died in 1988, having spent a long career arguing that rigour and colour are not opposites.

waldemarcordeiro.blurb: Brazil's concrete theorist, later a computer artist.
waldemarcordeiro.bio: Waldemar Cordeiro, born in 1925, was an Italian-born Brazilian artist and art critic who became Latin America's pioneer of concrete art. Born in Italy, he made his career in Brazil, building the intellectual case for a non-figurative art of pure construction. Max Bill's prize at the 1951 São Paulo Bienal was the spark, and Cordeiro was the figure who turned that moment into a Brazilian movement with a programme behind it. He worked as a painter, designer, printmaker and journalist, arguing in the press as vigorously as he argued on canvas. He was also, in the early days of computer art, one of the first artists anywhere to work with the machine, using it as a tool for making images when very few had access to one at all. He died in 1973.

lygiaclark.blurb: She handed the artwork to the viewer.
lygiaclark.bio: Lygia Pimentel Lins, known as Lygia Clark, was born in Brazil in 1920 and trained with two remarkable teachers: Roberto Burle Marx in Rio de Janeiro in 1947, and Fernand Léger in his Paris studio between 1950 and 1952. Back in Brazil she became central to the country's constructivist currents, co-founding Grupo Frente and then, in 1959, the Neo-Concrete movement with Hélio Oiticica, Lygia Pape, Amilcar de Castro, Franz Weissmann and the poet Ferreira Gullar, who wrote its manifesto. From 1960 onward she found ways for viewers to complete her works by handling them, moving her practice away from the object and toward the body. What she was finally after was the passage between inside and outside, and between a self and the world it sits in. She also taught. She died in 1988.

heliooiticica.blurb: He turned art into something you enter.
heliooiticica.bio: Hélio Oiticica, born in Brazil in 1937, was a visual artist, sculptor, painter, performance artist and theorist, and also a filmmaker and writer. He came up through the Neo-Concrete Movement, which he co-founded in Rio in 1959 with Lygia Clark out of the Grupo Frente circle, signing the Neoconcrete Manifesto that broke geometric abstraction open toward the body and the senses. His innovative use of colour ran through everything he made, but his lasting invention was what he later called environmental art: the Parangolés, begun in 1960, and the Penetrables, structures a visitor goes into rather than looks at. The most famous of the Penetrables was Tropicália. He kept writing and filming alongside the objects, treating theory as part of the work rather than commentary on it. He died in 1980.

lygiapape.blurb: Geometry pushed toward politics and touch.
lygiapape.bio: Lygia Pape, born in Brazil in 1927, worked as a visual artist, sculptor, engraver and filmmaker, and was central to the Concrete movement before helping to found the Neo-Concrete Movement in the Brazil of the 1950s and 1960s. With Lygia Clark and Hélio Oiticica she belongs to the trio who pushed Brazilian geometric art past the limits of pure composition, opening it up to interaction and to ethical and political themes at a moment when neither was an obvious move for an abstract artist. Her range was unusually wide, taking in engraving, sculpture, drawing and film, and she moved between them without treating any one as secondary to the others. Their combined work is much of the reason contemporary art in Brazil expanded when and how it did. She died in 2004.

amilcardecastro.bio: Amílcar Augusto Pereira de Castro, born in Brazil in 1920, was an artist, sculptor and graphic designer and one of the Neoconcrete signatories, alongside Ferreira Gullar. His sculpture puts the Neoconcrete argument into three dimensions, insisting that a work be a thing in its own right rather than a picture of one, and that a viewer meet it as an object standing in shared space. Abertura, of 1979, and Carranca belong to that long, patient line, as do the untitled works catalogued only by the places that hold them. His parallel career in graphic design applied the same clarity to the printed page, and the two practices are better read as one thing than as two. He died in 2002, his work by then a fixed point in Brazilian sculpture.

ferreiragullar.blurb: The poet who wrote Neoconcretism's manifesto.
ferreiragullar.bio: José Ribamar Ferreira, who wrote under the name Ferreira Gullar, was born in Brazil in 1930 and worked as a poet, playwright, essayist, art critic, translator and television writer. He was instrumental, in 1959, in bringing the Neo-Concrete Movement into being, and it was Gullar who wrote its manifesto, the document that gave the group its argument. Lygia Clark and Amilcar de Castro were among the signatories, and Gullar's presence among them is the point: Neoconcretism was a movement in which a poet set the theoretical terms for painters and sculptors. He kept both vocations going for the rest of his life, moving between poetry and criticism without subordinating one to the other, and the essays are as carefully made as the poems. He died in 2016.

gyulakosice.blurb: He made sculpture out of water.
gyulakosice.bio: Gyula Kosice, born Ferdinand Fallik in 1924, was a Czechoslovak-born sculptor, plastic artist, theorist and poet who became a naturalised Argentine and was pivotal in giving his adopted country its concrete and non-figurative movements their shape. He stood among the precursors of kinetic, luminal and hydrokinetic art, and his contribution was genuinely first: he was the earliest artist on the international scene to use water and neon gas as materials in their own right rather than as light or subject. That insistence on movement put him at the far edge of the concrete project, where a work is not merely constructed but alive in time. He wrote as well as made objects, publishing poetry and theory alongside the sculpture. He died in 2016.

carmeloardenquin.bio: Carmelo Arden Quin, born in Uruguay in 1913, was a painter, sculptor and theorist whose primary focuses were painting and poetry, two occupations he treated as versions of the same activity rather than as separate careers. Ambitious and idealistic from a young age, he is best remembered today as a co-founder of Madí, a movement that started in Argentina and ended up international. Madí's programme was invention over replication or representation: a work should bring something genuinely new into the world instead of reporting on what is already there. Arden Quin pursued that principle relentlessly across decades, chasing new forms and new ideas long after the group's first moment had passed. He died in 2010, still committed to the position he had staked out as a young man.

tomasmaldonado.bio: Tomás Maldonado, born in Argentina in 1922, was a painter, designer and thinker who worked in the concrete art tradition before becoming one of the principal theorists of twentieth-century design. From 1954 to 1967 he taught at the Ulm School of Design in Germany, and the philosophy developed during that tenure, the Ulm Model, remains a reference point in how design education is argued about. He was a philosopher and industrial designer as well as a painter and teacher, and the move from canvas to curriculum was continuous rather than a change of direction: concrete art's belief that form should be constructed from rational principles is precisely what the Ulm programme applied to manufactured objects. He died in 2018, his influence larger in design than in painting.

raullozza.bio: Elbio Raúl Lozza, born in Argentina in 1911, worked as a painter, draughtsman, designer, journalist and theorist, and belonged to the concrete art movement through the Asociación Arte Concreto-Invención. He went on to found the Perceptivist group, pushing the concrete programme toward a theory of perception itself, concerned less with the arrangement of shapes than with how colour and shape act on the eye that meets them. He wrote as much as he painted, and his journalism kept the argument in public rather than confined to studios. In 1992 Argentina awarded him the Platinum Konex Award in Visual Arts, a late recognition of a career spent at the theoretical end of abstraction. He died in 2008, having spent that career insisting abstraction was a discipline rather than a style.

jesusrafaelsoto.blurb: Vibrating grids you can walk into.
jesusrafaelsoto.bio: Jesús Rafael Soto, born in Venezuela in 1923, was a kinetic and op artist, sculptor and painter who held Venezuelan and French nationality. He studied at the Escuela de Artes Plásticas in Caracas in the 1940s alongside Carlos Cruz-Diez, and the two of them, both later based in Paris, became the twin poles of Venezuelan kinetic art. With Alejandro Otero he co-founded Los Disidentes. Soto's own contribution was the optically unstable surface, works such as Double progression vert et blanc of 1969, where line laid against line makes the picture shimmer and shift as the viewer moves past it. From that he developed the Penetrable, work the visitor enters bodily rather than observes from a distance. He died in 2005.

carloscruzdiez.blurb: Colour as an event in time.
carloscruzdiez.bio: Carlos Cruz-Diez, born in Venezuela in 1923, was a Franco-Venezuelan artist counted within the kinetic art movement; from 1960 until his death he lived and worked in Paris. He studied at the Escuela de Artes Plásticas in Caracas in the 1940s alongside Jesús Rafael Soto, and the two later shared the Parisian base from which Venezuelan kinetic art reached Europe. His proposal was radical and simple: colour is an autonomous reality unfolding in time and space, needing neither form nor a support to carry it. He organised his life's work into eight lines of investigation, among them Additive Colour, Physichromie, Chromatic Induction, Chromointerference, Transchromie, Chromosaturation, Chromoscope and Colour in Space. Fisicromía para Madrid of 1991 belongs to that programme. He worked as a sculptor, painter and serigrapher. He died in 2019.

alejandrootero.blurb: Los Disidentes co-founder and public sculptor.
alejandrootero.bio: Alejandro Otero, born in Venezuela in 1921, worked as a painter of geometric abstraction, and also as a sculptor, a writer and a cultural promoter, that last role belonging in the list rather than as a footnote to it. He was a founding member of Los Disidentes, the group he formed with Jesús Rafael Soto, and the two of them anchored a generation of Venezuelan artists who were remaking what abstraction could be asked to do. Later he worked at large scale in sculpture, carrying the same geometry out of the picture and into three dimensions; Delta Solar, made in 1977, is the best known of these. Painting, writing and organising ran in parallel throughout his career rather than succeeding one another. He died in 1990, his work by then a fixed point in Venezuelan art.

gego.blurb: Drawings without paper, built in space.
gego.bio: Gertrud Louise Goldschmidt, known as Gego, was born in 1912 and became a German-Venezuelan visual artist working in sculpture, lithography and drawing. She is best known for the geometric and kinetic sculptures of the 1960s and 1970s, open structures of line that she herself described as drawings without paper, a phrase that catches exactly what they do: they occupy space and are read as drawing rather than as mass. Her work sits alongside the Venezuelan kinetic and concrete artists of her generation but keeps its own temper, closer to the hand than to the system. She taught as well, and drawing remained the foundation of everything she built, the discipline that all the rest of it rested on. She died in 1994, her reputation still growing.

faeqhassan.blurb: The father of Iraqi modern art.
faeqhassan.bio: Faeq Hassan, born in 1914, was an Iraqi painter, sculptor and visual artist noted above all for founding a series of twentieth-century art groups which together bridged the gap between Iraqi heritage and traditional art on one side and modern art on the other. The title often given him is father of Iraqi modern art, and it is organisational as much as stylistic: he built the structures within which other artists could work, and he kept building them when each one had served its purpose. His group al-Ruwwad, founded in 1950, was the body from which Jewad Selim's circle broke away, and that split was less a quarrel than a sign of a scene fertile enough to divide. He died in 1992, having given Iraqi modernism its institutions as well as its pictures.

hafidhaldroubi.blurb: Cubism and the schooling of Iraqi art.
hafidhaldroubi.bio: Hafidh al-Droubi, also known as Hafez al-Droubi, was born in Iraq in 1914 and worked as a painter and draughtsman, noted both for Cubist canvases and for the effort to professionalise the teaching of art in Iraq through the early and middle decades of the twentieth century. He belonged to the Pioneer generation, the first Iraqi artists to work in a recognisably modern idiom, and he painted prolifically across a long career. His significance is double, and the two halves are hard to separate: he mattered to the development of modernism in Iraq, and he mattered to the development of its early art education. In a country building its artistic institutions from very little, the teaching counted for as much as the painting. He died in 1991.

jewadselim.bio: Jewad Selim, born in Ankara in the Ottoman Empire, was an Iraqi painter and sculptor and is considered one of Iraq's greatest twentieth-century sculptors. His influence ran through the Baghdad Modern Art Group, which he founded in 1951 with Shakir Hassan Al Said and which encouraged artists to explore techniques holding Arab heritage and modern form together rather than choosing between them. Selim's circle had broken away from al-Ruwwad, the group Faeq Hassan founded in 1950, and that separation set the direction of Iraqi art for a generation afterward. He worked as a painter as well as a sculptor, and the two practices informed each other throughout. He died in 1961, his career short but his programme carried forward by the artists he had gathered around him.

shakirhassanalsaid.blurb: He charted a new Arabic aesthetic.
shakirhassanalsaid.bio: Shakir Hassan Al Said, born in Iraq in 1925, was a painter, sculptor and writer, and also a philosopher, art critic and art historian, considered one of the most innovative and influential artists his country produced. He was actively involved in forming two art groups that shaped the direction of post-colonial art in Iraq, among them the Baghdad Modern Art Group, founded in 1951 with Jewad Selim. Through those groups and through his own writing he worked to close the distance between modernity and heritage. His theories mapped out a new Arabic aesthetic, one that let regional art be judged by uniquely Arabic standards rather than Western ones, which at the time was a genuinely radical proposition. He died in 2004, having argued the case for it across a long working life.

abdelhadielgazzar.blurb: Egyptian painter of modernisation's human cost.
abdelhadielgazzar.bio: Abdel Hadi El-Gazzar, born in Egypt in 1925, holds a position unlike anyone else's among the painters who came up beside him. Joining the Contemporary Art Group lifted his standing as an artist: where that group pursued a rooted, traditional Egyptian identity, El-Gazzar added a layer of social commentary that looked hard at the country in front of him. The instinct shows most clearly in The High Dam, a painting in which he weighed the Egyptian government's drive toward modernisation against the way of life it was reshaping. He died in 1966, and the work has never settled quietly into history since. It goes on unsettling painters, intellectuals and critics alike, at home and well beyond Egypt, and his name remains a fixed reference for the Arab modernisms that treated social reality as their subject rather than their setting.

hamednada.bio: Hamed Nada, born in Cairo in 1924, grew up in a popular neighbourhood in the Citadel, one of the oldest districts of the city, and much of his early art draws directly on memories of that communal home and the streets around it. The mosque of Sayeda Zeinab, named for a member of the Prophet Muhammad's family, stood in that neighbourhood, and Nada's father held a large role in its administration. His painting turned toward symbolism and spirituality, including a stylised way of depicting the djinn and the Muslim spirit world. Introduced to Egyptian culture through mentors and his own curiosity from an early age, he joined various art groups and institutions and shaped much of Egypt's post-colonial modern art. He worked as a draughtsman as well. He died in 1990.

injiefflatoun.blurb: Painter and feminist voice of Egypt.
injiefflatoun.bio: Inji Aflatoun, born in Egypt in 1924, was a painter and an activist in the women's movement, described as a leading spokeswoman for the Marxist, progressive, nationalist and feminist current of the late 1940s and 1950s. She counts as a pioneer of Egypt's modern art and among its important visual artists, and in her case the two roles are inseparable: the politics were not a sideline to the painting but the condition of it. She belongs to the generation of Arab modernists who were making a modern art and a modern politics at the same moment, and in her case neither project waited on the other. Painting and organising ran together across her whole working life. She died in 1989.

mahmoudmokhtar.blurb: The father of modern Egyptian sculpture.
mahmoudmokhtar.bio: Mahmoud Mukhtar, born in 1891, was an Egyptian sculptor and one of the original Pioneers of Egyptian art. He entered the College of Fine Arts in Cairo in 1908, the year Prince Yusuf Kamal opened it, and so was among the first Egyptians to receive a formal modern art training in his own country. His sculpture is credited with marking the start of Egyptian modernism: Renascence of Egypt, completed in 1928, is the monument by which he is best known, and The Secret Keeper belongs to the same sculptural language. He died in 1934, and although the career was short it greatly shaped the realisation and formation of contemporary Egyptian art. He is often called the father of modern Egyptian sculpture.

madihaumar.blurb: The first to make calligraphy abstract.
madihaumar.bio: Madiha Omar, born in 1908, was an Iraqi artist and calligrapher generally seen as the first Arab artist to bring calligraphy together with abstract art, treating the Arabic letter as plastic form rather than as a carrier of text. That move made her the precursor to the Hurufiyya movement, which took the letter as the basis for a modern Arab art in the decades that followed. She was also the Iraqi government's first female scholarship holder to study in Europe, and that training abroad, rare for an Arab woman of her generation, gave her a working knowledge of Western modernism to set against her own inherited tradition. She died in 2005, her innovation by then absorbed into a movement much larger than her own work.

ismailfattah.bio: Ismail Fattah, born in Basra in 1934, was an Iraqi painter and sculptor whose work ran from the intimate to the monumental. He is remembered for his abstraction and, above all, for public sculpture, and he belonged to the Baghdad Modern Art Group, a circle that set out to foster a sense of national identity in Iraqi art rather than borrow one wholesale from elsewhere. That double commitment, to modern form and to a specifically Iraqi imagination, shaped a career spent largely in the service of public space. His al-Shaheed Monument stands as the best known piece of public sculpture in Baghdad, a shape so widely recognised that it now works as shorthand for the city itself. Fattah died in 2004, leaving behind a body of work in which abstraction is civic rather than private.

njamahdaoui.bio: Nja Mahdaoui, born in 1937 in Tunisia, then under French protectorate, is a painter and visual artist who turned calligraphy into a graphic art of its own. Rather than treating the Arabic letter as a vehicle for a message, he releases it from legibility, massing strokes, curves and dots into rhythmic fields that ask to be read as pure form. The phrase that has followed him for decades, choreographer of letters, catches the movement in the work: the surface becomes a stage across which letterforms turn, gather and disperse. That approach places him among the Arab modernists who looked to their own written heritage rather than to imported European abstraction for a modern visual language, and who found in the alphabet a way of being contemporary and rooted at once.

hassanmassoudy.bio: Hassan Massoudy, born in Iraq in 1944, is a painter and calligrapher who has long lived and worked in Paris. He came up through the discipline of Arabic calligraphy and carried it into painting, where the letter becomes gesture and image rather than only text. The French writer Michel Tournier called him the greatest living calligrapher, a description that has trailed him ever since and that says as much about the reach of his reputation in France as about the work itself. His influence has run well past the gallery: a whole generation of calligraffiti artists, who took Arabic letterforms onto walls and into street practice, look back to his example. Holding Iraqi and French nationality both, Massoudy belongs to the modernist current that treated the alphabet as living material.

diaalazzawi.blurb: An Iraqi modernist, long based in London.
diaalazzawi.bio: Dia al-Azzawi, born in 1939, is an Iraqi painter and sculptor who has spent much of his working life in London. He trained at the College of Arts in Baghdad, emerging from the postwar Iraqi scene in which artists were rethinking abstraction, inherited heritage and the Arabic letter as living material rather than ornament. Working across painting, sculpture and works on paper, he became one of the most visible Iraqi artists based abroad, and his long residence in Britain, where he now holds nationality, made him a bridge figure between Baghdad and the European art world. In exhibitions outside the region he has stood for a strand of Arab modernism that grew from its own sources rather than from borrowed models, and that asks to be read as part of the same century of experiment.

charleshosseinzenderoudi.blurb: Saqqakhaneh's pioneer of the Persian letter.
charleshosseinzenderoudi.bio: Charles Hossein Zenderoudi, born in 1937, is an Iranian painter, calligrapher, printmaker and sculptor, and one of the founding figures of Iranian modern art. He was among the earliest artists anywhere to build Persian calligraphy into modern picture-making, treating the written character as a compositional unit rather than a caption. He helped pioneer the Saqqakhaneh School, the neo-traditional movement that grew in Iran from the visual world of Persian coffee-house painting and Shia devotional imagery, and that found a way to be modern without severing itself from that inheritance. Out of that current came a language later Iranian artists could argue with or extend, rooted in a local visual history rather than borrowed from Europe. He now divides his life between Paris and New York, still identified with the school he helped begin.

parviztanavoli.bio: Parviz Tanavoli, born in 1937, is an Iranian sculptor and painter who is also an educator and art historian, and a pioneer of the Saqqakhaneh movement, the neo-traditionalist current that drew modern Iranian art out of its own devotional and vernacular imagery. His long-running Heech series is his best-known work, held by the British Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Aga Khan Museum and Hamline University, and installed as public art in Vancouver. Alongside the sculpture he has written extensively on the history of Persian art and craftsmanship, work that treats craftsmanship as an ancestry for the sculpture rather than as folklore. He has been among the highest-selling Iranian artists in the market. A dual citizen of Iran and Canada since 1989, he has lived and worked in both Tehran and Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver.

faramarzpilaram.blurb: From figures to letters to abstraction.
faramarzpilaram.bio: Faramarz Pilaram, born in 1937, was an Iranian painter, calligrapher and educator, and one of the pioneers of the Saqqakhaneh school, the neo-traditionalist movement that gave modern Iranian art a vocabulary drawn from its own visual inheritance. His career moved through three clear phases, figurative, then decorative, then calligraphic, and it is the last of these that he is remembered for: abstract paintings built out of letterforms, where the written character carries the composition instead of a message. Within that Saqqakhaneh current he helped make calligraphy a modern pictorial resource rather than a heritage craft kept alive out of duty, and as a teacher he passed that conviction on to his students. He died in 1983, his work standing as one of the movement's most concentrated statements of the calligraphic idea.

monirshahroudyfarmanfarmaian.bio: Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian, born in 1924, was an Iranian painter and mosaicist who was also a serious collector of traditional folk art, and she became one of the most prominent Iranian artists working in the contemporary period. Her achievement was a genuine fusion rather than a quotation: she was the first artist to marry the geometric patterning and cut-glass mosaic technique of Iranian aina-kari to the rhythms of modern Western geometric abstraction, so that a craft practised for centuries on palace walls became a contemporary sculptural language. The collecting and the making fed each other, the folk objects supplying the vocabulary the abstractions were built from. She died in 2019, at the end of a long life, having established a body of work that neither tradition nor modernism can claim on its own.

salouaraoudachoucair.blurb: Lebanon's painter who thought in sculpture.
salouaraoudachoucair.bio: Saloua Raouda Choucair, born in 1916, was a Lebanese painter and sculptor whose life spanned almost the whole of the century her art belongs to. She worked in both two and three dimensions and is counted among the Arab modernists of the postwar decades, the generation that built a modern art in the region on its own terms rather than as an echo of anywhere else. Her practice bridged the flat surface and the object, and it is the traffic between the two, painting thought through as sculpture and back again, that the work is built on. She lived to 2017, long enough to see the recognition of Arab modernism widen considerably beyond the region, and long enough for her own work to be read afresh by audiences who had not encountered it when it was made.

eteladnan.blurb: Poet, novelist and painter at once.
eteladnan.bio: Etel Adnan, born in 1925, was a Lebanese-American poet, essayist, novelist and visual artist who refused to rank her mediums. She is the author of Sitt Marie Rose, the novel that carried her name furthest, and the academic journal MELUS, writing in 2003, judged her arguably the most celebrated Arab author then at work. Alongside the writing ran a lifetime of painting and drawing, pursued with the same directness, so that the two practices read as one sensibility working in different materials rather than a writer's hobby. Holding both Lebanese and American nationality, she belonged to the Arab modernist generation while living much of her life outside the region. She died in 2021, by which point her paintings had found an audience as wide as the one her books had built.

benenwonwu.blurb: Nigeria's pioneer, acclaimed as Africa's greatest.
benenwonwu.bio: Ben Enwonwu, born Odinigwe Benedict Chukwukadibia Enwonwu in 1921, was a Nigerian painter and sculptor, by many accounts the twentieth century's most influential artist from the African continent. He was one of the first artists from the continent to win sustained critical acclaim abroad, exhibiting in major European and American spaces and appearing in international directories of contemporary art at a time when that was almost unheard of for an African artist. From 1950 the international press was calling him Africa's Greatest Artist, and his fame was enlisted in support of Black Nationalist movements around the world. His career opened the way for the postcolonial expansion and visibility of modern African art that followed in the decades after independence. He died in 1994; the Enwonwu crater on Mercury carries his name.

ucheokeke.bio: Uche Okeke, born Christopher Uchefuna Okeke in 1933, was a Nigerian painter, illustrator, sculptor and teacher, and the art theorist most seminal to Nigerian modernism. In 1958, as a student at the Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology, he co-founded the Zaria Art Society with Bruce Onobrakpeya, Demas Nwoko and Yusuf Grillo, the group that argued for an art rooted in indigenous form rather than colonial academic training. His influence ran even further as a teacher. From 1970 at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, he taught Obiora Udechukwu, and in 1975 he brought El Anatsui onto the Nsukka faculty, a single appointment that reshaped African sculpture. Okeke died in 2016, having built not only a body of work but the institution and the argument that carried a generation.

bruceonobrakpeya.blurb: The Zaria founder who became printmaking's elder.
bruceonobrakpeya.bio: Bruce Obomeyoma Onobrakpeya, born in 1932, is a Nigerian printmaker, painter and sculptor, and one of the founding members of the Zaria Art Society, which he started in 1958 with Uche Okeke and their fellow students at the Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology. That group's argument, that a Nigerian modern art should draw on indigenous form rather than imported academic convention, has run through his work ever since. He is named first of all as a printmaker, and colourful abstract canvases of his hang at the National Gallery of Modern Art in Lagos. His work has been shown at Tate Modern in London, at the Smithsonian's National Museum of African Art in Washington and at Malmo Konsthall in Sweden, and gathered in the Virtual Museum of Modern Nigerian Art.

demasnwoko.bio: Demas Nwoko, born in 1935, is a Nigerian artist, designer, architect and master builder whose career refuses the usual boundaries between art and building. He was a founding member of the Zaria Art Society alongside Uche Okeke, the student group that set the terms for a Nigerian modernism drawn from indigenous rather than colonial sources, and he carried that argument out of painting and into structures people live and work in. In the 1960s he belonged to the Mbari club of Ibadan, a gathering of emerging Nigerian and foreign artists that was one of the liveliest cultural engines of the independence years, and he lectured at the University of Ibadan. His publishing venture came next: New Culture magazine, now defunct, which extended the same case for a self-made modern Nigerian aesthetic through the 1970s.

yusufgrillo.blurb: A Zaria founder, painter and muralist.
yusufgrillo.bio: Yusuf Grillo, born in 1934, was a Nigerian painter, sculptor and muralist, and one of the founding members of the Zaria Art Society, the student group he formed with Uche Okeke and their contemporaries. That society's case, that a modern Nigerian art should grow from indigenous form rather than from the conventions of colonial art schooling, shaped everything that followed for its members. Grillo worked across easel painting, sculpture and mural work, the last of which put his art into public buildings rather than private collections, and he spent much of his life as an academic, teaching the generations that came after the independence moment. He died in 2021, by which time the group he had helped found was long since taken as the starting point of modern Nigerian painting.

elanatsui.blurb: Bottle tops sewn into monumental cloth.
elanatsui.bio: El Anatsui, born in Ghana in 1944, is a sculptor who has worked for most of his career in Nigeria. In 1975 Uche Okeke brought him onto the faculty at Nsukka, where he spent two decades alongside Obiora Udechukwu, and it was from that base that his work developed. He is known internationally for his bottle-top installations: thousands of aluminium fragments taken from alcohol recycling stations and joined with copper wire into vast metallic hangings that behave like cloth. Materials that look stiff and industrial turn out to be free and flexible, which is what lets each installation be draped differently every time it is hung. Man's Cloth of 2001 is among the best known. Okwui Enwezor championed his work through the 1990s and 2000s, carrying it onto the largest international stages.

obioraudechukwu.blurb: A painter and poet out of Nsukka.
obioraudechukwu.bio: Obiora Udechukwu, born in 1946, is a Nigerian painter and poet who came up inside one of the most consequential teaching relationships in modern Nigerian art. From 1970 he studied under Uche Okeke at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, absorbing a theory of modern Nigerian art at first hand rather than at second, and he then spent two decades at Nsukka as a colleague of El Anatsui, the two of them working in close proximity year after year. Poetry and painting run together in his practice rather than sitting in separate compartments, each feeding the other's economy of means. His importance in this story is partly as a link: the student who received the Nsukka idea directly from its author and carried it forward into the generation that came next.

skunderboghossian.bio: Alexander Boghossian, known as Skunder, was an Ethiopian painter and professor born in 1937 who spent his working life largely in the United States. He was among the first Black artists of the modern era from the African continent to win international attention, and by a distance the most acclaimed of that early group, which made him a reference point for artists who followed the same route outward. Teaching was a substantial part of his life rather than a sideline, and his years as a professor in America put him in front of students at the moment when African and African American art histories were being connected in earnest. He died in 2003. His significance lies in that double position: an Ethiopian modernist abroad, whose recognition abroad helped make room for others.

gerardsekoto.blurb: Urban black realism, painted from exile.
gerardsekoto.bio: Gerard Sekoto, born in 1913, was a South African painter and musician, and a recognised pioneer of urban black art and of social realism. He painted black urban life at a time when it was largely absent from the country's official picture of itself, and the directness of the work is what has kept it central. He spent years in Paris, where he and Ernest Mancoba, fellow South Africans, were friends in exile, two men making modern art far from the country their subject matter came from. Exhibitions took the paintings to Stockholm, Venice, Washington, Senegal and Paris, as well as to audiences in South Africa itself. He died in 1993. The music and the painting ran in parallel throughout, two sides of the same displaced sensibility.

ernestmancoba.blurb: The only African artist in CoBrA's orbit.
ernestmancoba.bio: Ernest Methuen Mancoba, born in the Transvaal Colony in 1904, was in all probability the first professional Black modern artist South Africa produced, exhibiting from the late 1920s onward and spending most of his long life in Europe. In 1942 he married Sonja Ferlov Mancoba, and through that partnership he became the only African artist in the orbit of CoBrA, a fact that has taken decades to be properly registered in the histories of that group. In Paris he and Gerard Sekoto, fellow South Africans, were friends in exile, each pursuing modernism at a distance from home. Mancoba worked as a painter, sculptor and teacher, and died in 2002, by which time the recognition that had eluded him for much of his career was finally arriving.

malangatanangwenya.blurb: Mozambique's painter-poet, known by one name.
malangatanangwenya.bio: Malangatana Valente Ngwenya, born in 1936, was a Mozambican painter, sculptor and poet who frequently exhibited under his first name alone, as Malangatana, and it is as Malangatana that he is known. He belonged to the generation of African artists whose careers ran alongside the independence struggles of their countries, and he was a politician as well as an artist, which gives some measure of how far the work reached outside the studio. Poetry and painting were parallel practices for him rather than competing ones. His imagery became closely identified with Mozambique itself, to the point where his name functions as a national cultural shorthand. His death came on 5 January 2011, in Matosinhos in Portugal, at the end of a life that had carried Mozambican art onto an international footing.

ibrahimelsalahi.bio: Ibrahim El-Salahi, born in 1930, is a Sudanese painter who was also a public servant and diplomat, and one of the foremost artists of the Khartoum School. From 1960, after both had returned from studying in London, he and Ahmed Shibrain founded that school, which sits at the meeting point of African modernism and the pan-Arab Hurufiyya movement, the current that took traditional Islamic calligraphy into contemporary art. When Tate Modern gave him a retrospective in 2013, the first the gallery had given any contemporary artist from Africa, his achievement was characterised as a new Sudanese visual vocabulary, one built on the pioneering integration he made of Islamic, African, Arab and Western traditions in art. That formulation still stands as the clearest account of what he made and why it mattered.

ahmedshibrain.bio: Ahmed Shibrain, also known as Ahmad Mohammad Shibrain, born in 1931, was a Sudanese modernist painter and, from 1960, a founder of the Khartoum School with Ibrahim El-Salahi, the two of them setting it going after both returned from study in London. That school gave Sudanese art a modern idiom built from Islamic calligraphy, African form and Western picture-making rather than one imported wholesale. Shibrain's other role was institutional and arguably as consequential: as Dean of the College of Fine and Applied Art in Khartoum, and as a university teacher, he shaped the training of the artists who came after, turning a founding argument into a curriculum. He died in 2017, remembered as much for what he built for others as for his own painting.

osmanwaqialla.blurb: Arabic letters as modern graphic form.
osmanwaqialla.bio: Osman Waqialla, born in 1925, was a Sudanese painter and calligrapher known for the inventive use of Arabic letterforms in his work. What he did was subtle but decisive: he took calligraphy out of its religious setting and treated it as a modern, secular graphic form, which is precisely the move that defines the Hurufiyya movement he belongs to. In doing so he brought African and Islamic cultural traditions together inside the contemporary art of Sudan, at a moment when the country was working out what its modern art would look like. He stands here among the Khartoum School figures, and his handling of the letter as pure form still reads as one of the origins of much that came after it. He died in 2007.

affandi.bio: Affandi, born in Cirebon in West Java in 1907, was the son of R. Koesoema, a surveyor at a local sugar factory. He finished upper secondary school in Jakarta and then gave up his studies altogether to pursue the one thing he wanted to do, and from 1934 he taught himself how to paint, without the academy training that shaped most of his contemporaries. That self-schooling is the key to him: the work came out of direct looking and constant practice rather than inherited method. Maryati, a fellow artist, became his wife, and one of their children, Kartika, became an artist in turn, so the household was itself a small studio. Affandi died in 1990, one of Indonesian modernism's central figures and a demonstration of what a self-taught painter could reach.

hendragunawan.blurb: The revolution's painter, taught by his peers.
hendragunawan.bio: Raden Hendra Gunawan Prawiradilaga, born in Bandung in 1918 to a family of Sundanese gentry, left home as a young man to become an artist. After spells as a healer and a freelance painter he met Affandi, and from then on painting took over. He learned from his contemporaries rather than from a school, Affandi, Wahdi Sumanta and S. Sudjojono among them, and honed his work under the Japanese occupation. He joined the Pelukis Front during the Indonesian National Revolution, painting the realities of the battlefield, which brought him to the attention of President Sukarno, who sponsored his first solo exhibition in 1946. A short spell with the Young Artists of Indonesia followed, and then he co-established the artist collective Pelukis Rakjat. He died in 1983, a sculptor and politician as well as a painter.

victorioedades.blurb: The father of modern Philippine art.
victorioedades.bio: Victorio Candido Edades, born in 1895, is named in the histories as the father of modern Philippine art. He was schooled in the United States and came home with an entirely new way of thinking about what art was for, and he led the revolutionary Thirteen Moderns, the group that took on their classical compatriots in a long and heated public argument about the nature and function of art. His case was that a painting need not be a faithful record of the world: it could be reality as it passes through the mind and the emotions of the artist. That was a direct challenge to the reigning taste of the day, and it was made in public rather than in private. National Artist status came to him in 1976, and he died in 1985, the argument long since won.

fernandoamorsolo.blurb: The Grand Old Man of Philippine art.
fernandoamorsolo.bio: Fernando Amorsolo y Cueto, born in 1892, made his name as a portraitist and as a painter of the rural Philippine landscape, and the nickname that stuck was the Grand Old Man of Philippine Art. Recognition followed: he was the first person ever named a National Artist of the Philippines, honoured for a pioneering use of impressionistic technique and for a command of lighting, particularly backlighting, that gave his countryside scenes their distinctive glow. His importance is not only art-historical: those images shaped Filipino notions of self and identity, supplying the country with a picture of itself that persisted for generations. That very success made him the figure the modernist generation that followed had to argue with, since to make something new they first had to displace him. Amorsolo died in 1972, his standing undiminished by the quarrel.

anitamagsaysayho.bio: Anita Magsaysay-Ho, born in 1914, was a Filipina painter who worked in social realism and a post-Cubist idiom, and who took as her enduring subject the women of Filipino culture. The only woman among the Thirteen Moderns, she belonged to that group of Filipino modernists who fought the public argument for modern art in the country, and in 1958 a panel of experts named her one of the six major painters in Philippine history. Her paintings characteristically show Filipino women at ordinary work and ordinary difficulty, handled through abstracted design rather than realist description, which is where her modernism lies. Museums across the Philippines hold her work. She died in 2012, having spent a long career making the everyday labour of women the central subject of a national art.

nguyengiatri.blurb: Vietnamese lacquer raised to modern art.
nguyengiatri.bio: Nguyen Gia Tri, born in 1908, was a Vietnamese painter whose reputation rests above all on his work in lacquer, the medium he is credited with carrying furthest. Lacquer was a material more usually associated with decoration, and his achievement was to work it at the scale and ambition of modern painting, so that a traditional craft became the vehicle for a modern art. Standing Screen of 1939 and North Central South Spring Garden of 1969 are among his known works, three decades apart and spanning the transformation of the country in between. He drew cartoons too, on political and social subjects, many of them attacking French colonial rule, so the same hand that produced the lacquer panels was also making public arguments in print. He died in 1993.

lepho.blurb: Hanoi's painter, absorbed into the School of Paris.
lepho.bio: Le Pho, born in 1907, was a Vietnamese painter later counted within the School of Paris, and his training placed him at the exact junction of two art worlds. From 1925 to 1930 he was a student at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts of Hanoi, then won a scholarship that took him to the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he spent two years under Victor Tardieu, described in the record as a friend and companion of Henri Matisse. Back in Vietnam he joined the teaching staff of the Ecole Superieure des Beaux Arts de l'Indochine in Hanoi, passing that French academic training on to the next generation of Vietnamese painters. He held French as well as Vietnamese nationality. A watercolourist above all, he died in 2001, having spent most of a long century between Hanoi and Paris.

tongocvan.blurb: A painter and teacher lost at Dien Bien Phu.
tongocvan.bio: To Ngoc Van, also known as To Tu, born in 1906, was a Vietnamese painter and art critic whose work is held by the Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts. Young Woman with Lilly of 1943 and Two women and a child of 1944 come from the period he is most identified with. During the war with the French he ran a resistance art class in the north, carrying art training into the conditions of a war rather than suspending it, and he died in 1954 from injuries received at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu. That ending fixed him in Vietnamese memory as both artist and participant. In 1996, four decades after his death, he was in the first group to receive the Ho Chi Minh Prize.

robertrauschenberg.bio: Robert Rauschenberg, born in 1925, was an American painter and maker of multi-media work that touches nearly every mid-century movement, from the New York School to Neo-Dada, Pop and conceptual art. He studied under Josef Albers at Black Mountain College in 1948 and 1949 and called him the most important teacher he ever had. At Black Mountain in 1952 he took part in John Cage's Theatre Piece No. 1, and his White Paintings gave Cage the idea for 4'33". He travelled Europe and North Africa with Cy Twombly in 1952 and 1953, and from 1954 to 1961 he and Jasper Johns were partners in adjoining Pearl Street lofts. Leo Castelli represented him from 1958. The Combines of 1954 to 1964 put everyday objects into art and dissolved the line between painting and sculpture.

jasperjohns.blurb: The flag, painted as an object.
jasperjohns.bio: Jasper Johns, born in 1930, is an American painter and sculptor who has also worked as a draftsman and printmaker, and one of the central figures in the development of American postwar art. His work has been claimed in turn by abstract expressionism, Neo-Dada and Pop, which says something about how squarely it sits at the hinge between them. Three Flags of 1958 is the emblematic case: an image so familiar that painting it turned the picture into an object rather than a depiction. From 1954 to 1961 he and Robert Rauschenberg were partners, working in adjoining lofts on Pearl Street, an arrangement that is one of the most consequential proximities in postwar art. It was in Rauschenberg's loft that Leo Castelli saw Johns's work and gave him a show in 1958.

cytwombly.blurb: A painter formed at Black Mountain.
cytwombly.bio: Edwin Parker Twombly Jr, known as Cy Twombly, born in 1928, was an American painter who also worked as a sculptor and photographer. He studied at Black Mountain College in 1951 with Robert Motherwell, who thought enough of the work to write the catalogue for Twombly's first show, an endorsement that arrived unusually early in a career. In 1952 and 1953 he travelled through Europe and North Africa with Robert Rauschenberg, the two of them partners at the time, a journey that took both of them out of the American orbit at the precise moment their generation was defining itself against it. He died in 2011, his work standing somewhat apart from the movements around it while remaining bound to those Black Mountain origins, where painting, drawing and friendship were never separate things.

allankaprow.blurb: The man who invented the Happening.
allankaprow.bio: Allan Kaprow, born in 1927, was an American performance and installation artist, painter and assemblagist who helped develop both the Environment and the Happening in the late 1950s and 1960s, and wrote the theory for them. He studied with Hans Hofmann in 1947 and 1948, then took John Cage's experimental composition class at the New School for Social Research from 1957 to 1959, the class out of which the Happenings came. He made some two hundred of them before shifting into what he named Activities: intimately scaled works for one player or a few, devoted to studying ordinary human behaviour on its own terms. Fluxus, performance and installation art all follow from that work. At Rutgers he was a colleague of Roy Lichtenstein, and his comic-strip challenge is the origin story of the Pop paintings.

jimdine.blurb: A painter working across every medium.
jimdine.bio: Jim Dine, born in 1935, is an American visual artist whose practice has never settled into a single medium: painting, drawing, printmaking, sculpture and photography have run alongside each other throughout his career, and the drawing in particular underlies the rest. He belongs to the Neo-Dada and proto-Pop generation, the American artists who in the late 1950s and early 1960s turned away from the heroics of abstract expressionism towards ordinary objects and the stuff of daily life, without yet arriving at the cool commercial surfaces of Pop proper. Walking to Boras is among his known works. What holds the different mediums together is a persistent attachment to particular objects and images returned to over decades, treated less as subjects than as personal vocabulary, which gives the work its unusual continuity.

claesoldenburg.bio: Claes Oldenburg, born in Sweden in 1929, was an American sculptor best known for public installations that take an ordinary object and blow it up to the scale of civic monument. Running alongside those was his other great theme, soft sculpture: the same everyday things rendered in yielding materials, so that objects designed to be rigid slump and sag. Between them the two strategies made the familiar unfamiliar without ever leaving the familiar behind. Many of the pieces were made together with his wife Coosje van Bruggen, to whom he was married for thirty-two years and who died in 2009; the public works in particular were a genuinely shared authorship. La Bicyclette ensevelie, Inverted Collar and Tie, Houseball and Flying Pins are among them. He lived and worked in New York City and died in 2022.

pierrerestany.blurb: The critic who named Nouveau Realisme.
pierrerestany.bio: Pierre Restany, born in 1930, was a French art critic and cultural philosopher with an international reputation, and the man who gave Nouveau Realisme its name and its founding document. He wrote the movement's manifesto and it was signed in Yves Klein's flat in 1960, the moment that turned a loose group of artists working with objects, posters and machines into a movement with a programme. His role is a reminder that the critic can be a constitutive figure rather than a commentator: the artists were already at work, but it took Restany's formulation to make them legible as a collective proposition. He continued writing on art and culture for the rest of his life, well beyond the group he had convened, and died in 2003.

yvesklein.blurb: He made a blue his own.
yvesklein.bio: Yves Klein, born in 1928, was a French artist and one of the decisive figures in postwar European art. As a teenager in Nice he took judo classes with Arman and Claude Pascal, a friendship that later fed straight into the movement they helped make. He developed International Klein Blue, the pigment that became inseparable from his name, and pioneered performance as an artistic medium, which places him behind much of what minimal and Pop art went on to do. In 1957 Piero Manzoni met him in Milan at his monochrome show. He collaborated with Jean Tinguely on the Excavatrice de l'espace in 1958, and in 1960 Pierre Restany wrote the Nouveau Realisme manifesto and signed it in Klein's flat. He married Rotraut Klein-Moquay in 1962, five months before his death, becoming Gunther Uecker's brother-in-law.

arman.blurb: Accumulations of objects, gathered and broken.
arman.bio: Arman, born Armand Fernandez in Nice in 1928, was a French and American artist who began as a painter and ended up dispensing with paint. His decisive move was to stop using objects for the traces of ink or paint they could leave on a surface and start using the objects themselves as the artwork, a shift that produced his Accumulations, massed groupings of identical or related things, and his destruction and recomposition pieces, in which an object is broken apart and reassembled as art. As a teenager he took judo classes in Nice with Yves Klein and Claude Pascal, and that friendship put him at the centre of Nouveau Realisme when it formed. He later settled in the United States and held both nationalities. He died in 2005, best known for those two bodies of work.

jeantinguely.blurb: Machines built to mock the machine age.
jeantinguely.bio: Jean Tinguely, born in Switzerland in 1924, was a sculptor best known for kinetic machines that carried the Dada tradition into the later twentieth century. His constructions clatter, spin and rattle, and their target is clear enough: the automation and technological overproduction of goods that defined the postwar decades, satirised by building machines that produce nothing. In 1958 he made the Excavatrice de l'espace with Yves Klein, and he was part of the Nouveau Realisme circle that formed around them. From 1960 he was with Niki de Saint Phalle, whom he married in 1971, and the two collaborated on the Stravinsky Fountain and on her Tarot Garden, one of the most productive partnerships in postwar European art. Heureka, Le Cyclop and the Carnival Fountain are among his works. He died in 1991.

nikidesaintphalle.blurb: Nanas, monuments and a tarot garden.
nikidesaintphalle.bio: Niki de Saint Phalle, born in 1930, was a French American sculptor and painter who also made films and wrote colourful hand-illustrated books, and one of the very few women to work at monumental scale in twentieth-century sculpture. Her Nanas, the exuberant female figures she is most identified with, put a kind of joy into public sculpture that had few precedents. From 1960 she was with Jean Tinguely, whom she married in 1971, and their collaboration produced the Stravinsky Fountain as well as her Tarot Garden of 1979, the sculpture park that became her life's largest undertaking. The Golem of 1972 belongs to the same expansive project of art that people can walk into and around. Her social commitment ran through the work rather than beside it. She died in 2002.

cesar.blurb: Placed here among the Nouveau Realistes.
cesar.bio: Cesar appears in this constellation among the Nouveau Realistes, the French circle of the 1960s turn that took the objects and detritus of consumer society as its raw material rather than treating paint as the only proper medium of art. That is the position this entry occupies, and the movement it is filed under. The biographical record supplied for it does not correspond to that identity, so nothing is claimed here about his birth, his nationality, his training, his exhibitions or his individual works: to repeat those details would be to describe somebody else entirely. What remains is the placement, which is the reason the name sits in this section at all, alongside the other artists who worked out of objects, posters and machines in postwar Europe.

danielspoerri.bio: Daniel Spoerri, born in Romania in 1930, was a Swiss visual artist and writer whose route into art ran through the theatre: he worked as a choreographer, and he taught at university level as well, so that performance and teaching bracket the object-making he is best known for. He is generally counted an important figure among the artists of what has been called the second wave of Pop, and he belongs to the Nouveau Realisme grouping, where the everyday object is taken as material rather than as subject matter. Der Tropfler is among his known works. Writing stayed part of the practice throughout rather than serving as commentary on it, and the two activities are hard to separate in his output. He died in 2024, at the far end of a very long working life.

jacquesvillegle.blurb: Torn street posters, taken as art.
jacquesvillegle.bio: Jacques Villegle, born Jacques Mahe de la Villegle in 1926, worked in mixed media as a French affichiste, which is to say an artist of the poster wall. His method was decollage: he took ripped and lacerated posters from the street, already torn by other hands, and presented them as they were, so the authorship belonged partly to the city. He also developed an alphabet of symbolic letters, and STAR is among his known works. What interested him throughout was the anonymous and the marginal, the discarded remains of a civilisation rather than its monuments. He was a member of the Nouveau Realisme group from 1960 to 1970. The sociologist Zygmunt Bauman, in Liquid Life, named him among the outstanding exponents of what he called liquid art. He died in 2022.

raymondhains.blurb: A founding signer of Nouveau Realisme.
raymondhains.bio: Raymond Hains, born in 1926, was a French visual artist and one of the founders of Nouveau Realisme. In 1960 he signed the Manifesto of New Realism alongside Arman, Francois Dufrene, Yves Klein, Jean Tinguely, Jacques Villegle and Pierre Restany, the document that turned a set of shared instincts about objects and the street into a movement. He worked as a photographer, sculptor, painter and printmaker, moving between them with a wit that also shaped how he presented himself. In 1976 Daniel Abadie organised his first retrospective at the Centre National d'Art et de Culture in Paris, the last exhibition ever shown there; Hains named it La Chasse au C.N.A.C., and Daniel Spoerri answered with a dinner called La faim au C.N.A.C. He died in 2005.

christo.blurb: Wrapped landmarks, made by two people.
christo.bio: Christo Vladimirov Javacheff and Jeanne-Claude Denat de Guillebon, known simply as Christo and Jeanne-Claude, were born on the same day in 1935, married, and worked as a single artist. Their subject was scale and site: large environmental installations that wrapped landmarks and landscape features in fabric, so that a structure everybody already knew was made strange for as long as the piece stood. The Wrapped Reichstag, Running Fence in California, The Pont Neuf Wrapped and The Gates in New York's Central Park are the works most people know, along with Valley Curtain, The Umbrellas and The Floating Piers. Jeanne-Claude died in 2009. Their insistence on shared authorship, on one artist made of two people, reset how partnership in art could be credited, and it is how the pair are recorded here.

richardhamilton.blurb: Pop art's first collage, and its thinker.
richardhamilton.bio: Richard William Hamilton, born in 1922, was an English painter and collage artist whose small collage of 1956, Just what is it that makes today's homes so different, so appealing?, is generally counted among the earliest works of Pop art. He made it for the This Is Tomorrow exhibition mounted by the Independent Group, which he had co-founded with Eduardo Paolozzi at the ICA in London between 1952 and 1955, a discussion circle as much as an artists' group and the place where British Pop was thought through before it was painted. His 1955 exhibition Man, Machine and Motion belongs to the same enquiry. He was also Marcel Duchamp's most rigorous interpreter, reconstructing the Large Glass in 1965 and 1966 and editing the Green Box in English. He died in 2011; Tate Modern gave him a major retrospective in 2014.

eduardopaolozzi.blurb: Scottish sculptor, Pop art's other founder.
eduardopaolozzi.bio: Sir Eduardo Luigi Paolozzi, born in 1924, was a Scottish artist known for sculpture and graphic work, and one of the pioneers of Pop art. With Richard Hamilton he co-founded the Independent Group at the ICA in London, which met between 1952 and 1955 and worked out the case for taking mass culture seriously as material for art, several years before Pop became a movement with a name. The sculpture and the graphic work ran alongside each other for the rest of his career, and pieces such as Piscator, Ventilation Shaft Cover, For Leonardo and The Artist as Hephaestus are among the works his name is attached to. He taught at university level for much of his life. He died in 2005, his reputation resting equally on the sculpture and on the founding argument.

peterblake.blurb: The man who built Sgt. Pepper's cover.
peterblake.bio: Sir Peter Thomas Blake, born in 1932, is an English Pop artist whose work reached an audience most painters never touch, because so much of it arrived on record sleeves rather than gallery walls. He co-created the cover of the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band in 1967, the sleeve design his name is most attached to. He also made covers for two of the Who's albums and for the Band Aid single Do They Know It's Christmas?, designed the Live Aid concert poster, and in 2012 designed the Brit Award statuette. Working as a painter, draughtsman, photographer and graphic artist, he took the same interest in popular imagery that drove British Pop and put it straight back into the popular culture it had come from, which is where most people have met it since.

davidhockney.blurb: Pop's champion of vivid figurative painting.
davidhockney.bio: David Hockney, born in 1937, was a British painter, printmaker, photographer and stage designer, and one of the most influential British artists of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. He arrived at the Royal College of Art in 1959, where he met the American painter R. B. Kitaj; Kitaj's advice, to paint the things he actually cared about, pushed Hockney towards the openly personal subjects that became his signature. As an important contributor to the Pop art of the 1960s, he made his name with a vivid, stylised kind of realism, and he kept faith with figurative painting through a period when abstraction held the upper hand. His work ranged across painting, printmaking, photography and design for the stage, and he moved between those media all his life. He died in 2026.

allenjones.blurb: A Pop painter turned Royal Academician.
allenjones.bio: Allen Jones, born in 1937, is a British artist who came up with the Pop generation and has worked across painting, sculpture, design and graphic art. He is best known for his paintings, his sculpture and his lithography, three strands that have run in parallel for most of his career. Recognition arrived early: the 1963 Paris Biennale gave him its Prix des Jeunes Artistes while he was still in his twenties. Over the following decades he became a fixture of the British art establishment rather than an outsider to it, and he holds the rank of Senior Academician at the Royal Academy of Arts. The Honorary Doctorate of Arts awarded to him by Southampton Solent University in 2017 took him back to the town he came from, more than half a century after the paintings that first made his name.

paulineboty.bio: Pauline Boty, born in 1938, was a British painter and actor, and a co-founder of the British Pop art movement of the 1960s, the only woman in it whose membership was acknowledged at the time. Her paintings and collages take an unembarrassed pleasure in femininity and in female sexuality, and they are equally clear-eyed about the man's world she was working inside; the criticism and the joy arrive together. That combination, together with the free-spirited life she led alongside the work, has since made her read as a herald of the feminism of the 1970s. She worked as an actor as well as a painter. Boty died in 1966, leaving a body of work made almost entirely within a single, crowded decade, and a reputation that has grown steadily since.

rbkitaj.blurb: Told Hockney to paint what mattered.
rbkitaj.bio: R. B. Kitaj, born Ronald Brooks Kitaj in 1932, was an American artist who spent most of his working life in England, and who is grouped with the British Pop art of the 1960s despite arriving at it from outside. He met David Hockney at the Royal College of Art in 1959, when both were students, and the friendship that followed mattered to the shape of post-war British painting: it was Kitaj who told Hockney to paint what he actually cared about. They were studio-mates at the moment British Pop was forming around them, and Kitaj's outsider's eye on English subjects gave the group part of its character. He worked as a painter, illustrator and photographer, and remained in England for the greater part of his career. He died in 2007.

andywarhol.blurb: Turned mass production into high art.
andywarhol.bio: Andy Warhol, born in 1928, was an American artist and filmmaker whose practice ran through painting, film, photography, publishing and performance, and whose subject was the traffic between advertising, consumerism, mass media and celebrity. Ivan Karp, Leo Castelli's gallery director, was the first dealer to visit his studio, in 1961; Castelli himself turned him down at first and then represented him from 1964. At the Factory he worked with Gerard Malanga, his assistant and silkscreen partner from 1963 to 1970, and Billy Name, who silvered the place and lived in its darkroom. Edie Sedgwick co-starred in a dozen films in 1965; Brigid Berlin tape-recorded the scene for two decades; Valerie Solanas, a fringe figure there, shot him in June 1968. In 1984 and 1985 he made some 150 canvases with Jean-Michel Basquiat. Warhol died in 1987.

roylichtenstein.blurb: Comic-strip panels blown up as painting.
roylichtenstein.bio: Roy Lichtenstein, born in 1923, was an American painter and sculptor who became one of the defining figures of Pop art with large canvases drawn from comic books, advertisements and other mass-produced imagery. The turn came while he was teaching at Rutgers alongside Allan Kaprow, whose challenge about comic strips is the origin story of the Pop paintings; Leo Castelli signed him in 1961, and the years that followed produced pictures such as Whaam! in 1963. He worked in the same idiom for decades, including public pieces such as The Face of Barcelona in 1992, the Times Square Mural of 1994 and the Brushstrokes of 1996. Alongside the painting he taught at university level and designed for the stage, and his work is held in major museum collections worldwide. Lichtenstein died in 1997.

jamesrosenquist.bio: James Rosenquist, born in 1933, came to Pop art from the sign-painting trade, and the training never left him: he built his pictures with the techniques and the scale of commercial billboard work. His subject was advertising itself and the consumer culture around it, but where Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein took mass imagery more or less whole, Rosenquist cut it up. He fitted fragments of adverts and cultural icons against one another in ways closer to Surrealism, so that the effect is of being overwhelmed by images rather than shown one. He worked as a photographer, a designer and a sculptor as well as a painter, carrying the same appetite for scale across all of it. He was inducted into the Florida Artists Hall of Fame in 2001 and died in 2017.

tomwesselmann.blurb: Pop in painting, collage and sculpture.
tomwesselmann.bio: Tom Wesselmann, born in 1931, was an American artist associated with the Pop art of the 1960s. He worked in three media in parallel, painting, collage and sculpture, and also as a draughtsman and lithographer, moving between the flat image and the constructed object as the work required. Collage sits at the centre of that list, and the habit of assembling a picture out of separate found parts is the thread that runs through the paintings and the free-standing pieces alike. Like the other American artists gathered under the Pop label, he treated the imagery of advertising and mass production as material fit for serious large-scale art, at a moment when that argument still had to be won. He stayed with that territory for the rest of his working life, and died in 2004.

edruscha.blurb: California's Pop painter of artist's books.
edruscha.bio: Ed Ruscha, born Edward Joseph Ruscha IV in 1937, is an American artist associated with Pop art. He has worked across painting, printmaking, drawing, photography and film, and is noted in particular for his artist's books, a form he did much to establish as a category of serious work rather than a by-product of it. Twentysix Gasoline Stations, whose title states its contents exactly, is the best known of them, and that flat, declarative manner is characteristic of him: the subject is named and the naming is a large part of the work. He has also directed films and worked as a designer. Ruscha lives and works in Culver City, California, and his career has been made on the West Coast rather than in New York.

marisolescobar.bio: Marisol Escobar, known to everyone as Marisol, was a sculptor of Venezuelan and American nationality, born in Paris in 1930, and she made her working life in New York City. Fame arrived in the mid-1960s, when her sculpture sat close to Pop art; within a decade she had slipped back into relative obscurity. She went on making work through those years regardless, and returned to the limelight in the early twenty-first century, capped by a major retrospective organised by the Memphis Brooks Museum of Art in 2014. Marisol died in 2016 and left her artwork and archival material to the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, which drew on that bequest for Marisol: A Retrospective, the largest survey of her career, curated by Cathleen Chaffee and shown in Montreal, Toledo, Buffalo and Dallas. She painted and designed as well as sculpting.

rosalyndrexler.blurb: Pop painter, playwright and professional wrestler.
rosalyndrexler.bio: Rosalyn Drexler, born in 1926, was an American visual artist, novelist, playwright, screenwriter and, for a time, a professional wrestler. Hers was a genuinely polymathic career, and the awards came in more than one field: an Obie for her plays and an Emmy for her screenwriting. She is best known, though, for two things, her Pop art paintings, made in New York, and the novelisation of the film Rocky, which she wrote under the pseudonym Julia Sorel.
