Painting, fiction, theatre and film each took her attention in turn, and she appears to have given none of them up for the others. Drexler lived and worked in New York City and died in 2025. Her paintings are counted among the American Pop art of the 1960s, and among the least categorisable of it.

ushioshinohara.bio: Ushio Shinohara, born in 1932 and nicknamed Gyu-chan, is a Japanese painter, sculptor, printmaker and performance artist based in New York City. He is best known for the Boxing Painting series, large-scale canvases made with the gestures of boxing, in which the picture is the record of a physical action carried out at speed. That use of the whole body as the instrument of painting runs through the rest of his work as well, alongside appropriation and assemblage, a magpie use of both mass-culture imagery and the iconographies of traditional art, and consistently vivid, high-key colour. He is grouped with Pop, though his practice is more multidisciplinary than that label suggests, moving between painting, sculpture, printmaking and live performance, and the work has stayed vigorous and various rather than settling into a manner.

tadanoriyokoo.bio: Tadanori Yokoo, born in 1936, is a Japanese graphic designer, illustrator, printmaker and painter, and one of the artists who made graphic design a fully expressive medium rather than a service trade. His signature manner mixes psychedelia with pastiche, drawing on a wide span of modern visual and cultural material from Japan and from the rest of the world and setting the borrowings against one another at full intensity. He has also directed films and acted in them. His work includes designs for the National Bunraku Theatre in 1984 and the Teshima Yokoo House, and it moves freely between the printed image and painting, a crossing he made in the middle of an already established design career. He continues to be one of the defining figures of Japanese post-war visual culture.

georgemaciunas.bio: George Maciunas, born in Lithuania in 1931, was the founding member and central coordinator of Fluxus, the international community of artists, architects, composers and designers that formed around him in the early 1960s. Trained in part as an architect and working also as an art dealer and art historian, he organised and performed in the early Fluxus Happenings and festivals, designed the movement's graphic material, and assembled the series of highly influential Fluxus artists' multiples that carried its ideas about cheaply. He showed Yoko Ono at his AG Gallery in 1961, designed La Monte Young's An Anthology, and drew in Nam June Paik, Wolf Vostell and Dick Higgins, the last from the Wiesbaden festival of 1962 onwards. Fluxus never had a single style; what it had was Maciunas, coordinating it. He died in 1978.

yokoono.bio: Yoko Ono, born in 1933, is a Japanese artist, musician and peace activist whose work takes in performance and filmmaking as readily as objects. Her first husband, the composer Toshi Ichiyanagi, had studied with John Cage, and together they ran the Chambers Street loft series in 1960 and 1961, one of the seedbeds of the New York avant-garde. George Maciunas showed her at his AG Gallery in 1961, and she became one of the artists who made Fluxus what it was, working in the instruction-based, participatory vein the group opened up. In 1969 she married John Lennon; the two collaborated on films, records and the Bed-Ins, turning their private life into a public campaign. That campaigning has continued through works such as the Imagine Peace Tower of 2007. She is based in the United States.

namjunepaik.bio: Nam June Paik, born in 1932, was a Korean-born artist generally credited as the founder of video art. He met George Maciunas and the Fluxus circle in the early 1960s and never lost the movement's habit of treating any material as available; in his case the material was television. From 1967 he worked with the cellist Charlotte Moorman on pieces including TV Bra for Living Sculpture and TV Cello, and she was arrested performing his Opera Sextronique. He met Joseph Beuys at the Dusseldorf Fluxus events of 1962, and the two performed together for thirty years. Bill Viola, then a technician at the Everson Museum in Syracuse, installed his early video shows. In 1974 Paik coined the phrase electronic super highway to describe the future of telecommunications. He died in 2006.

dickhiggins.bio: Dick Higgins, born in 1938, was an American artist, composer, poet, publisher, printmaker and theorist, and a co-founder of Fluxus. He came to it through John Cage's class at the New School, and from 1962, beginning at the Wiesbaden festival, he was one of the artists gathered by George Maciunas. In 1965 he coined the word intermedia to name the work that falls between established forms, defining it in an essay of that title in the first issue of his Something Else Newsletter; the term has outlived the movement that produced it. His Danger Music scores are the best known of his compositions, and he was an early pioneer of electronic correspondence. He married Alison Knowles in 1960, and both were core to Fluxus. Higgins died in 1998.

alisonknowles.blurb: Fluxus founding member of tactile performance.
alisonknowles.bio: Alison Knowles, born in 1933, was an American artist known for installations, performances, soundworks and publications, and a founding member of Fluxus, the international network that set out to merge separate artistic media and disciplines. Three things distinguish her work: performance as its arena, the indeterminacy of her event scores, which leave a great deal for the performer to decide, and an insistence on tactile participation, so that an audience handles things rather than watching from a distance. She took an honours degree in fine art at Pratt Institute in New York, and Pratt awarded her an honorary doctorate in May 2015. She married Dick Higgins in 1960, and the two of them remained at the centre of Fluxus. Knowles died in 2025.

wolfvostell.bio: Wolf Vostell, born in 1932, was a German painter and sculptor and one of the pioneers of Happenings and of Fluxus, which he joined in the circle around George Maciunas. He was among the earliest artists to work with video, with street art and with installation. Two techniques define his output: blurring, and the de-coll/age that took images apart rather than assembling them. He painted pictures drawn from graffiti, embedded objects in concrete, and built television sets into his works long before that was an ordinary thing to do. Ruhender Verkehr dates from 1969, and Cadillacs in Form der Nackten Maja and The Turtle both from 1987. He was married to the Spanish writer Mercedes Vostell, with whom he had two sons, David and Rafael. Vostell died in 1998.

lamonteyoung.blurb: Minimalism's first composer of sustained tones.
lamonteyoung.bio: La Monte Young, born in 1935, is an American composer, musician and performance artist, among the first American minimalist composers and a central presence in the post-war avant-garde. His subject, from Trio for Strings in 1958 onwards, has been the sustained tone: sound held long enough that the ear begins to hear inside it. The text scores collected as Compositions 1960 push further, calling into question what counts as music at all, and it was that temper that connected him to Fluxus and to George Maciunas, who designed An Anthology. Few of his recordings have stayed in print, which has not stopped his influence spreading well beyond the concert avant-garde into rock and ambient music. He remains one of the defining figures of American minimalism.

charlottemoorman.bio: Charlotte Moorman, born in 1933, was an American cellist, performance artist and tireless advocate for avant-garde music, called in her lifetime the Jeanne d'Arc of new music. She founded the Annual Avant Garde Festival of New York, which put experimental work in front of general audiences year after year, and she was Nam June Paik's most frequent collaborator. From 1967 she performed his TV Bra for Living Sculpture and his TV Cello, playing instruments that were also sculptures and television sets, and she was arrested for performing his Opera Sextronique, a case that turned the limits placed on performance into a public argument. She was a composer as well as a player, and much of the early history of video art reached its first audiences through her. Moorman died in 1991.

josephbeuys.blurb: The Dusseldorf teacher who taught everyone.
josephbeuys.bio: Joseph Beuys, born in 1921, was a German artist, teacher and art theorist whose work bent art towards humanism and social organisation. A member of Fluxus, he was singularly important to the development of performance art, in the form he called Kunst Aktionen, and he met Nam June Paik at the Dusseldorf Fluxus events of 1962; the two performed together for thirty years. His teaching is the other half of the story. Jorg Immendorff came to him from 1963, Blinky Palermo from 1964 to 1967, and Imi Knoebel and Katharina Sieverding passed through the same Dusseldorf classes, while Anselm Kiefer visited regularly from 1970 and treated him as a teacher without ever enrolling. Harald Szeemann championed him at When Attitudes Become Form in 1969 and at documenta 5 in 1972. He planted 7000 Oaks in 1982 and died in 1986.

shigekokubota.bio: Shigeko Kubota, born in 1937, was a Japanese video artist, sculptor and performance artist who spent most of her working life in New York. She saw John Cage perform in Tokyo in 1962, moved to New York in 1964, and became a key member of Fluxus, the group centred on George Maciunas, who named her its Vice Chairman. In 1970 she was among the first artists to take up the portable Sony Portapak camera, which she likened to a new kind of paintbrush. From that came the work she is best known for: sculptural installations with a strong do-it-yourself aesthetic, monitors embedded in constructed forms and playing videos she had shot herself. Her closest working associations were with John Cage, George Brecht, Jackson Mac Low, Joe Jones, Ay-O and Nam June Paik. Kubota died in 2015.

donaldjudd.bio: Donald Judd, born in 1928, was an American artist generally considered the leading international exponent of minimalism, a label he was unhappy with. What he wanted from a work was autonomy and clarity: the constructed object, the space it creates around itself, and a rigorously democratic presentation in which no part is subordinated to another. He argued the case in print as much as in the studio, above all in his 1964 essay Specific Objects, which remains the movement's central text. In Arts Yearbook 8 he denied that the new three-dimensional work amounted to a movement, school or style at all, holding that the differences between its makers were greater than the similarities. He worked as a sculptor, painter, draughtsman and architect, and titled work after work simply Untitled. Judd died in 1994.

frankstella.bio: Frank Stella, born in 1936, was an American painter, sculptor and printmaker whose early work catalysed the minimalist movement in the late 1950s. He arrived in New York at the end of that decade with paintings that insisted on the picture as an object rather than a window, a position he reached partly by working through the abstract expressionism of Franz Kline and Jackson Pollock rather than around it. Carl Andre had been his schoolfriend at Phillips Academy; between 1958 and 1960 Andre worked in Stella's studio and cut his first sculptures there. Leo Castelli gave Stella his first show in 1960. New York City held him for most of his career, until he moved the studio out to Rock Tavern, and he kept up sculpture and printmaking alongside the painting. He died in 2024.

carlandre.blurb: Sculpture laid flat on the floor.
carlandre.bio: Carl Andre, born in 1935, was an American minimalist artist recognised for ordered linear and grid-format sculptures, work that ranges from large public pieces to floor-level arrangements laid out flat inside a gallery and small, intimate objects. He was a writer and a poet as well as a sculptor, and is counted among the land artists of his generation. He and Frank Stella were schoolfriends at Phillips Academy, and from 1958 to 1960 Andre worked in Stella's studio, where he cut his first sculptures. Konrad Fischer's Dusseldorf gallery gave him and the other American Minimalists their European debut from 1967. In January 1985 he married the artist Ana Mendieta; that September she fell from the window of their thirty-fourth-floor apartment. Andre died in 2024.

danflavin.bio: Dan Flavin, born in 1933, was an American minimalist who made sculptural objects and whole installations out of commercially available fluorescent light fixtures, standard tubes bought rather than fabricated and arranged so that the light itself becomes the material of the work. In the early 1960s he and Sol LeWitt were both on the Museum of Modern Art staff in New York, minding the collection at the moment they were working out what might come after it. Untitled (To Bob and Pat Rohm), from 1970, carries a dedication in its title, as some of his work does. He worked as a draughtsman, an architect and an installation artist as well as a sculptor, and his pieces are made for particular rooms rather than for anywhere. Flavin died in 1996.

sollewitt.blurb: Conceptual art's man of wall drawings.
sollewitt.bio: Sol LeWitt, born in 1928, was an American artist whose work sits across conceptual art and minimalism. In the early 1960s he was on the Museum of Modern Art payroll in New York, at the book counter and the night desk, while Robert Ryman and Dan Flavin worked there as guards, an unglamorous shared apprenticeship for three artists who each went on to rethink what a work of art needed to be. He met the critic Lucy Lippard at the same museum, and in 1976 the two co-founded Printed Matter. Konrad Fischer showed his first European wall drawing in Dusseldorf in 1968. Eva Hesse was a close friend from 1960, and the letter he wrote her in 1965, telling her simply to do, is a document of that friendship. LeWitt died in 2007.

robertmorris.bio: Robert Morris, born in 1931, was an American sculptor, conceptual artist and writer, regarded alongside Donald Judd as one of the most prominent theorists of minimalism. He did not stay inside it. His work made important contributions to the development of performance art, to land art, to the process art that treated making itself as the subject, and to installation, so that the career reads as a series of departures from a position he had helped to define. He lived and worked in New York. Observatory dates from 1977. In 2013 MIT Press devoted a volume of its October Files series to him, edited by Julia Bryan-Wilson, examining his work and his influence on the artists who followed. Morris died in 2018.

annetruitt.bio: Anne Truitt, born in 1921, was an American sculptor who became widely known in the late 1960s for large-scale minimalist works. Two exhibitions did much to establish that reputation: her solo show at the Andre Emmerich Gallery in 1963, which proved influential well beyond its immediate audience, and the group show at the Jewish Museum in Manhattan in 1966 that placed her among the artists then being gathered under the minimalist heading. She painted and drew as well as sculpting, and she wrote, the writing standing alongside the objects rather than explaining them. Her sculpture belongs to the same moment as the rest of American minimalism, though she reached its scale and its reticence by a route entirely of her own. Truitt died in 2004.

agnesmartin.bio: Agnes Martin, born in 1912, was an abstract painter, Canadian by birth and later American, whose work has been described as an essay in discretion, inwardness and silence. She is usually filed with the minimalists, but she rejected the label: she thought of herself instead as an abstract expressionist, and is counted among that movement's leading practitioners of the twentieth century. In New York she had a loft on Coenties Slip in Lower Manhattan, where her neighbours included Ellsworth Kelly, Robert Indiana, James Rosenquist and Lenore Tawney, a working community that produced a great deal of the period's most durable art. She drew and made prints as well as painting. Martin was given the National Medal of Arts by the National Endowment for the Arts in 1998, and the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts elected her in 2004, the year she died.

larrybell.bio: Larry Bell, born in 1939, is an American artist and sculptor best known for his glass boxes and for large-scale illusionistic sculptures, work in which the material is less the glass than what happens to light as it meets a surface and passes through it. He also paints and makes assemblage. Grants have supported the work, among them awards from the Guggenheim Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts, and examples of it are held by many major cultural institutions. His base is Taos, New Mexico, with a second studio kept in Venice, California. Bell belongs to the generation that took the reduced forms of minimalism and made perception itself the subject, so that the viewer's position in the room is part of what the sculpture is doing.

robertsmithson.blurb: Land art's maker of Spiral Jetty.
robertsmithson.bio: Robert Smithson, born in 1938, was an American sculptor whose work belongs to land art, a movement he helped to found. He used drawing and photography in close relation to the spatial arts, so that a work often exists as much in its documents as at its site. Spiral Jetty, made in 1970 and funded by the dealer Virginia Dwan, is the best known of them; Broken Circle and Spiral Hill followed in 1971 and Amarillo Ramp in 1973. He married Nancy Holt in 1963, and after his death in 1973 she completed the unfinished work and spent the following decades preserving it. His pieces have been exhibited internationally and are held in public collections, though the largest of them can only be visited where they stand.

morrislouis.bio: Morris Louis, born Morris Louis Bernstein in 1912, was an American painter and one of the earliest exponents of colour field painting, the tendency that followed abstract expressionism and put flat, saturated colour in place of the gestural mark. Working in Washington, D.C., he formed with Kenneth Noland and other painters there the loose cohort now known as the Washington Color School, and he and Noland worked in close exchange throughout the 1950s. The decisive moment came in 1953, when the two of them saw Helen Frankenthaler's Mountains and Sea in her studio and changed course within the week; almost everything he is remembered for came afterwards. Louis died in 1962, with only a short span of mature work behind him, and his reputation has grown steadily since.

kennethnoland.bio: Kenneth Noland, born in 1924, was one of the best-known American colour field painters, though the labels moved around him: an abstract expressionist in the 1950s, a minimalist painter in the early 1960s. He studied under Josef Albers at Black Mountain College between 1946 and 1948, an education in colour as a subject in its own right. In Washington he worked in close exchange with Morris Louis through the 1950s, and helped establish the Washington Color School, the loose cohort of Washington-area painters with whom both men are identified. The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum gave him a major retrospective in 1977, which travelled on to the Hirshhorn and to the Toledo Museum of Art in 1978, and his Stripe Paintings were shown at Tate in London in 2006. Noland died in 2010.

julesolitski.bio: Jules Olitski was born Jevel Demikovski in 1922 and worked in the United States as a painter, printmaker and sculptor, using the professional name by which he is now known. He is grouped with the post-painterly abstraction that followed abstract expressionism, the tendency that set aside gestural drama in favour of open fields of colour and surfaces that carry little trace of the hand. Painters of that group were less interested in the mark than in what colour does across a large canvas, and the criticism of the period made them its central case. Olitski moved between painting, printmaking and sculpture throughout his career rather than settling into any one of them. He held both Soviet and American nationality. He died in 2007.

samgilliam.bio: Sam Gilliam, born in 1933, was an American painter of abstraction who also made sculpture and taught. Born in Mississippi, raised in Kentucky, he spent the whole of his adult life in Washington, D.C., where he came to be described as the dean of the city's arts community. He began within the Washington Color School, the group of Washington-area artists who developed a form of abstraction out of colour field painting through the 1950s and 1960s, but by the middle of that decade he had moved beyond its core aesthetic of flat fields of colour by introducing process and sculptural elements into the paintings themselves, so that the painting became something handled and shaped rather than simply looked at. He also made public work, including Solar Canopy in 1986, and worked as a printmaker. Gilliam died in 2022.

ellsworthkelly.bio: Ellsworth Kelly, born in 1923, was an American painter, sculptor and printmaker whose work is placed with hard-edge painting, colour field and minimalism. His techniques were unassuming and his means few: line, colour and form, with bright colour used unapologetically, an approach with something in common with the work of John McLaughlin and Kenneth Noland. He met Jack Youngerman in Paris, and back in New York the two took lofts on Coenties Slip in Lower Manhattan, where Agnes Martin, Robert Indiana, James Rosenquist and Lenore Tawney were neighbours. Red Yellow Blue White and Black dates from 1953, and Totem from 1987. He also worked as a designer and graphic artist. Kelly lived and worked in Spencertown, New York, and died in 2015.

alheld.bio: Al Held, born in 1928, was an American abstract expressionist painter, particularly well known for hard-edge pictures made on a very large scale. His style changed repeatedly across his career, but never at the same time as a popular emerging style and never simply against one: an abstract expressionist tone in the 1950s, a geometric manner in the 1960s, and from the 1980s a painting of bright geometric space whose depth reaches towards infinity. That independence from fashion is the through-line of the work. He taught as a professor of art at Yale University from 1963 to 1980, seventeen years of it, and he worked as an illustrator as well as a painter. Passing Through, from 2004, is among his late pictures. Held died in 2005.

leonpolksmith.bio: Leon Polk Smith, born in 1906, was an American painter whose geometrically oriented abstraction took its bearings from Piet Mondrian, and who is counted among the followers of the hard-edge school. His best-known paintings are reduced about as far as a painting can be: two colours on a canvas, meeting along a single sharply delineated edge, often on an unframed support cut to an unusual shape, so that the outline of the object and the division inside it do the same work. He drew as well as painted. His pictures are held in museums across the United States, Europe and South America, and the Brooklyn Museum owns a substantial group of them thanks to a generous bequest from the artist. Smith died in 1996.

victorvasarely.bio: Victor Vasarely, born in Hungary in 1906, was a Hungarian-French artist widely accepted as the grandfather and leader of the Op art movement. Op art made the picture surface act directly on the eye: precisely ruled patterns of colour and tone that appear to vibrate, swell or recede while the canvas itself stays perfectly still. Vasarely worked as a painter, printmaker, sculptor and designer, and treated the visual unit, a shape with its colour and its variations, as something to be recombined systematically rather than composed by feel. That method suited reproduction and design as readily as it suited painting, which is part of why the style travelled so far beyond galleries in the 1960s. He held both Hungarian and French nationality, and died in 1997.

bridgetriley.blurb: The English painter of op art.
bridgetriley.bio: Bridget Riley, born in 1931, is an English painter known above all for her op art paintings. The work makes patterns that act physically on the eye: ruled and repeated forms that appear to shift, flicker or swell while the surface itself does nothing at all, painting understood as an event that takes place in the viewer rather than on the canvas. She has worked as a draughtswoman, a printmaker and a sculptor as well as a painter, and Sea Cloud dates from 1981. Riley divides her time between London, Cornwall and the Vaucluse in France. Her paintings are among the most widely reproduced British pictures of the 1960s, and she is the figure most often named when op art is discussed in Britain.

julioleparcandgrav.blurb: Kinetic art made by a group.
julioleparcandgrav.bio: Julio Le Parc, born in Argentina in 1928, was an artist who worked at the meeting point of op and kinetic art. He attended the School of Fine Arts in Argentina and later held French as well as Argentine nationality. He was among the founders of the Groupe de Recherche d'Art Visuel, known as GRAV, a collective that pursued art as shared visual research rather than as individual authorship, working with light, movement and the participation of the viewer, so that a piece only completes itself when somebody stands in front of it. His own award-winning work belongs to that programme and outlasted the group. He is one of the significant figures in the history of modern Argentine art, and received the Konex Award in Argentina in 1982 and again in 2022, forty years apart. Le Parc died in 2026.

yaacovagam.blurb: Kinetic art that changes as you move.
yaacovagam.bio: Yaacov Agam, born in 1928, was an Israeli sculptor and experimental artist whose name is bound up with optical and kinetic art. His work changes as the viewer moves, so that no single position gives the whole of it and the act of looking becomes part of the piece. He worked as a sculptor, painter and serigrapher, and he held French as well as Israeli nationality. Among his works are Roots - Menora from 1985 and Wheels from 2002. He belongs to the generation of post-war artists who set movement and optical effect at the centre of art in place of composition and gesture, an approach that took his work out of the gallery and into public settings. The Israel Prize for Visual Arts came to him in 2026, the year he died.

takis.blurb: Self-taught Greek master of kinetic sculpture.
takis.bio: Panayiotis Vassilakis, who worked under the single name Takis, was born in Greece in 1925 and was entirely self-taught. He became known for kinetic sculpture, objects that move, or that hold movement in reserve, rather than standing still to be looked at. He exhibited widely across Europe and the United States and found his warmest audience in France, where his pieces still occupy public sites in and around Paris. He also worked as a draftsman and designed jewellery, so the scale of his output ran from the hand-held to the civic. Further works are held at the Athens-based Takis Foundation Research Center for the Arts and Sciences, a centre carrying his name that pairs artistic enquiry with scientific enquiry. He died in 2019, his reputation resting on work that made movement itself a sculptural material.

ottopiene.bio: Otto Piene, born in 1928, was a German-American artist specialising in kinetic and technology-based art, and one who preferred to work collaboratively. In 1957 he founded Zero in Dusseldorf with Heinz Mack; the two shared a studio and held evening exhibitions in it, and Zero became one of the defining European groups of light and kinetic art. Gunther Uecker joined them in 1961. Piene divided his later life between Germany and the United States, living and working in Dusseldorf, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in Groton. His works include Licht und Bewegung of 1966, Silberne Frequenz of 1971, Star Pit of 1992 and Feuerwerk fur Celle of 2005, and he worked as a sculptor, painter, draughtsman and graphic artist across those decades. He died in 2014.

heinzmack.bio: Heinz Mack, born in 1931, is a German artist who founded the ZERO movement with Otto Piene in Dusseldorf in 1957; the two shared a studio and held evening exhibitions in it, which is how the group began. His reputation rests on op art, light art and kinetic art, work in which reflective surface, movement and the behaviour of light take the place of painted incident. Mack exhibited at documenta in 1964 and again in 1977, and represented Germany at the Venice Biennale in 1970. Among his sculptures are Wasserplastik of 1976, Columne pro Caelo of 1984, and the Zigzag Stele and Obelisk of 1987, pieces made for open air and daylight as much as for a gallery floor. He works as a printmaker and photographer as well as a sculptor and painter.

guntheruecker.bio: Gunther Uecker, born in 1930, was a German painter and sculptor who worked in op art and installation, known primarily for his nail reliefs, made from nails driven into a surface in dense fields so that the object registers as much through light and shadow as through form. He joined the ZERO group in 1961, taking his place there alongside Otto Piene, and shared its concern with light and movement rather than painted incident. He was Yves Klein's brother-in-law: Klein married Uecker's sister Rotraut in 1962. His works include Tisch der Austreibung of 1977, Light Column of 1981 and a sculpture made for Gotz Friedrich in 2008. He taught at university level alongside his own practice, and also worked as an illustrator and a painter. Uecker died in 2025.

janschoonhoven.bio: Jan Schoonhoven is placed here with the hard-edge, op and kinetic strand of post-war abstraction, within the 1960s turn the surrounding entries map, and the record attached to his name lists his occupation simply as painter. Beyond that, the entry cannot be trusted. The biographical text supplied with it, along with the dates and the account of a career spent on large public murals, belongs to a different artist who happens to share the surname, and even those dates contradict one another. None of that material can safely be attributed to Schoonhoven, so no birth or death year, no titles of works, no exhibitions and no relationships are given here. The gap is left open deliberately: an accurate blank is worth more in a reference of this kind than a plausible sentence built on somebody else's life.

josephkosuth.blurb: Conceptual art as language and definition.
josephkosuth.bio: Joseph Kosuth, born in 1945, is an American conceptual artist whose work treats language, definition and the conditions under which something counts as art as the material of the work itself. One and Three Chairs dates from 1965, when he was twenty, and it remains the piece he is most often shown by. In 1969 he joined Art & Language as its American editor, bringing a New York voice into the collaboration Terry Atkinson had started in England, and the same year Seth Siegelaub included him in The Xerox Book and in the exhibition known as January 5-31, 1969, the shows that gave conceptual art its first public shape. Later works include Axioms from Spinoza's Ethics of 2011. He lives in New York and Venice, having earlier worked in London, Ghent and Rome.

lawrenceweiner.blurb: Language used as a sculptural medium.
lawrenceweiner.bio: Lawrence Weiner, born in New York City in 1942, was among the handful of artists at the centre of conceptual art as it formed in the 1960s, and he spent his career exploring the potential of language as a sculptural medium. A work of his might be installed as text on a wall, printed in a book or a catalogue, spoken in a film or in ordinary conversation, or simply remembered. The format stayed open because, as he put it in 1970, there is no correct way to construct a piece and no incorrect one; building it shows only how it could look. Seth Siegelaub organised the shows and catalogues that constituted conceptual art as a movement between 1968 and 1971, with Weiner among the artists in them. His works include IRON & GOLD IN THE AIR DUST & SMOKE ON THE GROUND of 1995. He died in 2021.

artandlanguage.bio: Art & Language began around 1967 as a collaboration among English conceptual artists. Its name is taken from the journal Art-Language, which grew out of what Terry Atkinson and Michael Baldwin were doing together with Harold Hurrell and David Bainbridge; the four of them were its first editors. The shared name was adopted to reflect the conversational basis of the activity, so that the joint and several works of the group are credited to the conversation rather than to individuals. By late 1969 the conversation had taken in contributions from New York by Ian Burn, Mel Ramsden and Joseph Kosuth. By the end of 1976 the line of the work ran through Michael Baldwin and Mel Ramsden alone, and it has stayed with them since. Its works include Mirror Piece of 1965, Secret Painting of 1967, Index 01 of 1972 and Index: Incident in a Museum of 1985.

onkawara.bio: On Kawara, born in 1933, was a Japanese conceptual artist who lived in SoHo, in New York City, from 1965 until his death. He arrived as conceptual art was taking shape, in the years when artists on both sides of the Atlantic were setting aside the handmade object in favour of language, system and procedure, and he is placed with the conceptual artists of that generation. He worked as a painter, printmaker and draughtsman as well, and the disciplines of those trades stayed in what he made. He took part in many solo and group exhibitions over the following decades, among them the Venice Biennale in 1976. Kawara died in 2014, having spent almost fifty years working in the same few streets of the same city.

hannedarboven.blurb: Numbers written out by hand, endlessly.
hannedarboven.bio: Hanne Darboven, born in Germany in 1941, was a conceptual artist who made writing itself her medium. She is best known for large-scale minimalist installations built from handwritten tables of numbers, sheet after sheet of them, hung until a room becomes something closer to a calendar than an exhibition. Trained as a painter and draftsperson, and working with photography as well, she belonged to the generation of the 1960s that let the idea outrank the object; her version of that shift was unusually physical, since the labour of the hand is visible on every page. The work is systematic without being cold, a private discipline carried out at public scale. Darboven died in 2009, leaving one of the most single-minded bodies of work in postwar conceptual art.

douglashuebler.blurb: A conceptualist who worked in documents.
douglashuebler.bio: Douglas Huebler, born in the United States in 1924, was one of the artists who made conceptual art a matter of documents rather than objects. A photographer, illustrator and long-serving university teacher, he worked in the register of the record: statements, photographs and descriptions standing in for the thing itself. In 1968 Seth Siegelaub gathered him with a small circle of like-minded artists in the Xerox Book, a publication that functioned as an exhibition and put conceptual work in the hands of anyone who could hold a page. That project remains the clearest picture of the moment Huebler helped shape, when the gallery wall stopped being the only place art could happen. He died in 1997, his influence carried more by ideas and printed matter than by objects.

robertbarry.blurb: Art made from what cannot be seen.
robertbarry.bio: Robert Barry, born in the United States in 1936, began as a painter and then, from 1967, turned to work made from things that cannot quite be seen. Since then he has produced non-material pieces, installations and performances using otherwise invisible media, leaving the viewer with a proposition rather than an object. In 1968 he remarked that nothing seemed to him the most potent thing in the world, a line that has followed his work ever since and reads less like provocation than like method. That same year Seth Siegelaub included him in the Xerox Book, the printed exhibition that gathered the emerging conceptual circle and carried their ideas beyond the gallery. Barry has kept working in that vein for decades, an artist whose materials are attention, language and empty space.

melbochner.blurb: Made the working drawings the art.
melbochner.bio: Mel Bochner, born in the United States in 1940, is counted among the founders of conceptual art and is credited with reshaping what the field considered admissible. In 1966 he mounted 'Working Drawings And Other Visible Things On Paper Not Necessarily Meant To Be Viewed As Art', an exhibition often cited as one of the first conceptual shows anywhere; the title doubles as the argument, since what went on display was the kind of paper a studio usually throws away. A painter, photographer and illustrator by training, Bochner spent the following decades pressing at measurement, number and language as subjects in their own right. He died in 2025, after a career that began by putting the studio's discarded thinking on the wall and never stopped taking ideas at their word.

adrianpiper.blurb: Philosopher and artist, confronting the viewer.
adrianpiper.bio: Adrian Piper, born in the United States in 1948, is a conceptual artist and Kantian philosopher who has never treated those two careers as separate. Her work examines what happens to people who belong to more than one discipline or category: otherness, racial passing, racism and professional ostracism, approached through traditional and non-traditional media designed to push a viewer into self-analysis. She often uses her own career as the case study, which gives the work its particular edge, since the argument is being tested on the person making it. The critic and curator Lucy Lippard included her in the numbers shows that defined dematerialised art, placing Piper inside the conceptual canon at the moment it was forming. She remains one of the movement's most rigorous voices, and one of its most uncomfortable.

lucylippard.bio: Lucy Lippard, born in the United States in 1937, is a writer, art critic, activist and curator who gave conceptual art much of its vocabulary. She argued earlier than almost anyone that the new art of the 1960s was dematerialising, and she championed feminist art when few critics were paying attention; her numbers shows, which brought Adrian Piper and others together, remain a defining record of the period. She met Sol LeWitt at the Museum of Modern Art, and in 1976 the two co-founded Printed Matter. Thirty books and around fifty exhibitions across Europe, the United States and Latin America later, she lives and works in Galisteo, New Mexico, an activist as much as a critic and still one of the field's essential voices.

cildomeireles.blurb: Brazilian installations that resist by immersion.
cildomeireles.bio: Cildo Meireles, born in Brazil in 1948, is a conceptual artist, sculptor and installation-maker whose work turns political pressure into physical experience. Many of his installations register resistance to political oppression in Brazil, and they tend to be large and dense: rooms you enter rather than pictures you inspect, built so that the meaning arrives through the body. Trained also as a painter and printmaker, he has consistently favoured environments that put the viewer inside the problem, where scale and accumulation do most of the arguing. That phenomenological approach makes him one of the most physically ambitious conceptualists of his generation, working far from New York while asking the same questions about what art is for. He remains among the most influential artists to have come out of Brazil.

luiscamnitzer.blurb: Printmaker, teacher, conscience of Latin American conceptualism.
luiscamnitzer.bio: Luis Camnitzer, born in Germany in 1937 and Uruguayan by formation, was at the forefront of conceptual art in the 1960s and has spent the decades since arguing about what it meant. He works mainly in sculpture, printmaking and installation, taking up repression, institutional critique and social justice as his recurring subjects. He is also a curator, art critic and university teacher, which makes him unusual among his peers: he helped build the account of the period as well as the work inside it. Coming to conceptualism from outside its New York and European centres, he has insisted that the Latin American version carried its own political urgency rather than arriving as an import. That double role, artist and historian, has shaped how the whole movement is read today.

martaminujin.bio: Marta Minujín, born in Argentina in 1943, is a conceptual and performance artist who has been one of the defining figures of the Argentine avant-garde since the 1960s. Trained as a painter, sculptor and printmaker, she moved early towards work that happened in time and in public, and the piece that has carried her name furthest is La Menesunda of 1965. Her practice belongs to the moment when the object began to loosen its hold on art and the event took its place, a shift she pursued from Argentina rather than from the northern art capitals. That location matters: it made her the local proof that the new art was not something arriving from elsewhere. She remains among the best-known living artists in Latin America.

alfredojaar.blurb: Images, ethics, and the Rwanda Project.
alfredojaar.bio: Alfredo Jaar, born in Chile in 1956, is a visual artist, architect, photographer and film director based in Lisbon. He is best known as an installation artist, often incorporating photography and addressing socio-political subjects and war with unusual care about what an image can and cannot carry. The Rwanda Project, made over six years, is his sustained response to the 1994 genocide and remains the work most closely identified with him. He has also made numerous public interventions: The Skoghall Konsthall, a paper museum in Sweden that existed for a single day; A Logo For America, an early electronic billboard piece; and The Cloud, staged on both sides of the Mexico-United States border. Park of Laments dates from 2010. He has been featured on Art:21 and won the Hasselblad Award for 2020.

danielburen.blurb: Co-founder of BMPT, painter of place.
danielburen.bio: Daniel Buren, born in France in 1938, is a conceptual artist, painter and sculptor whose work is inseparable from the places it occupies. In 1966 he and Olivier Mosset, with Parmentier and Toroni, formed the Paris group BMPT, an alliance that lasted barely a year and set the terms for everything he did afterwards. Buren carried that discipline outdoors and into institutions: Les Deux Plateaux, in the Cour d'honneur of the Palais-Royal, is his best-known permanent work, and the Observatory of the Light at the Fondation Louis Vuitton is another that made his name worldwide. Awards have followed steadily: the 1986 Venice Biennale's Golden Lion for best pavilion, the International Award for best artist in Stuttgart in 1991, and the Praemium Imperiale for painting in Tokyo in 2007. Few living artists are so widely installed.

hanshaacke.bio: Hans Haacke, born in Germany in 1936, has lived and worked in New York for most of his career and counts as one of the leading exponents of institutional critique. Among the Euro-American artists of his generation he has been the most consistent and the most severe critic of museums, treating the institution itself, its funding and its blind spots, as the material of the work rather than the frame around it. A printmaker and conceptual artist who taught for many years, he has kept that line of enquiry going for over half a century. Der Bevölkerung, installed in 2000, and Gift Horse, from 2015, are among his best-known public works. His art has shown that a museum can be described accurately from the inside, and that doing so is rarely welcome.

marcelbroodthaers.bio: Marcel Broodthaers, born in Belgium in 1924, was a poet before he was an artist. The turn came in 1964, when René Magritte gave him a copy of Mallarmé; that book prompted him to move from writing into art, at the age of forty. What followed was brief and extraordinarily influential: sculpture, photography, film and painting, made by someone who never stopped thinking like a poet and who treated the museum as a form that could be written in rather than merely shown in. He became one of the central figures of institutional critique, the tendency that takes galleries and museums as its subject rather than its setting. Broodthaers died in 1976, twelve years after starting, leaving work that later artists are still unpacking.

michaelasher.blurb: Rearranged the museum instead of filling it.
michaelasher.bio: Michael Asher, born in the United States in 1943, was described by The New York Times as one of the patron saints of institutional critique, the strand of conceptual art that picks apart the assumptions behind how we perceive art. Instead of making new objects, he worked with what was already there: repositioning or removing artworks, taking down walls, altering facades, letting the changed room become the piece. The results could be nearly invisible to a casual visitor and unforgettable to anyone who understood what had shifted. He taught as well, and his influence on younger artists travelled through the classroom as much as through exhibitions. Untitled of 1991 is among his documented works. Asher died in 2012, having spent a career making the container visible.

andreafraserandfredwilson.blurb: Two artists who question the museum.
andreafraserandfredwilson.bio: Andrea Fraser and Fred Wilson share a card here because they share a project. Institutional critique means asking, systematically, how art institutions actually work: how a gallery or a museum decides what is shown, whose story gets told, and what its display conventions quietly assert. Both artists are named among those most associated with it, alongside Michael Asher, Marcel Broodthaers, Daniel Buren, John Knight, Adrian Piper and Hans Haacke. It is a tendency with its own body of scholarship, from Alexander Alberro and Benjamin H. D. Buchloh to Birgit Pelzer and Anne Rorimer, which is itself telling: the critique was absorbed by the academy it examined. Where the conceptual artists of the 1960s asked what a work of art could be, this group asked who decides.

germanocelant.blurb: The critic who named Arte Povera.
germanocelant.bio: Germano Celant, born in Italy in 1940, was the art historian, critic and curator who gave Arte Povera its name. He coined the term in a 1967 piece for Flash Art, 'Appunti Per Una Guerriglia', which became the manifesto of the artistic and political movement that followed, and he set the argument out again the same year in a Genoa exhibition that gathered the artists into a visible group. Mario Merz, Michelangelo Pistoletto and Jannis Kounellis were among those he championed, and the label he invented gave their disparate work a shared address in the international art world. He kept writing about it for the rest of his life, in articles and books, and curated widely beyond it. Celant died in 2020, his term still standard usage.

mariomerz.blurb: Igloos, neon and the Fibonacci sequence.
mariomerz.bio: Mario Merz, born in Italy in 1925, was a painter, sculptor and installation artist and one of the central figures of Arte Povera. He married Marisa Merz in 1950, and she became the only woman associated with the group; theirs was a working partnership as much as a marriage. Merz is best known for two motifs he returned to for decades: the igloo, a shelter built from whatever material was to hand, as in Igloo di pietra of 1982, and the Fibonacci sequence rendered in neon, which appears in works such as Acceleration=Dream, Fibonacci Numbers in Neon and Motorcycle Phantom. Germano Celant named the movement he belonged to; Harald Szeemann carried it into the international circuit. Merz died in 2003, having made mathematics look like a natural process.

marisamerz.blurb: The only woman in Arte Povera.
marisamerz.bio: Marisa Merz, born in Italy in 1931, was the only female protagonist associated with Arte Povera, the radical Italian tendency of the 1960s. She married Mario Merz in 1950 and worked alongside him in Turin, though she pursued her own line in painting, sculpture and installation throughout, and the two practices should not be read as one. Recognition came slowly and then unmistakably: in 2013 the Venice Biennale gave her its Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, the honour that fixed her place at the centre of the story rather than at its margin. She lived and worked in Turin until her death in 2019. Her reputation has grown steadily since, as the movement's history has been rewritten with her contribution given its proper weight.

janniskounellis.blurb: A Greek at the heart of Arte Povera.
janniskounellis.bio: Jannis Kounellis, born in Greece in 1936, moved to Rome as a young man and studied at the Accademia di Belle Arti there, basing himself in the city for the rest of his life. He became one of the key figures of Arte Povera, the Italian movement named by the critic Germano Celant, who championed him from the start. Kounellis worked as a painter and sculptor, and the movement's turn towards installation suited him: it let the gallery be treated as a space with a history rather than as a neutral container. A Greek in Italy, he kept a sense of displacement in the work that never quite resolves. He taught for many years and died in 2017, an artist claimed by two countries at once.

michelangelopistoletto.blurb: Reflection, and art folded into life.
michelangelopistoletto.bio: Michelangelo Pistoletto, born in Italy in 1933, is a painter, an artist of actions and objects, and an art theorist, and one of the main representatives of Arte Povera. Reflection is his enduring subject, and with it the unification of art and everyday life into a single total work, a Gesamtkunstwerk in which the viewer is never quite outside the picture. He was part of the Turin nucleus of the movement, which he co-founded with Alighiero Boetti, who later split from the group over its politics. The critic Germano Celant championed him under the Arte Povera banner. Now in his nineties, Pistoletto has kept the theoretical side of the practice as active as the studio side, and the early work still reads as entirely current.

giovannianselmo.blurb: Sculpture that keeps time with nature.
giovannianselmo.bio: Giovanni Anselmo, born in Italy in 1934, emerged after the Second World War as one of the artists of Arte Povera, and with Gilberto Zorio he formed part of the movement's Turin nucleus. He worked as a sculptor, draftsperson and conceptual artist, and his most famous piece, Untitled of 1968, is a work about time and nature: a proposition rather than a monument, in which natural process is left to do its work in front of the viewer. Verkürzter Himmel of 1987 is among his later works. Anselmo's sculpture is characteristically quiet and physically exact, closer to a demonstration than a display, and it holds its own within a movement not short of larger gestures. He died in 2023, after six decades of that steady enquiry.

alighieroboetti.blurb: Alighiero e Boetti: one man, doubled.
alighieroboetti.bio: Alighiero Boetti, born in Italy in 1940, was a painter, sculptor, photographer and conceptual artist, and a member of Arte Povera from its Turin beginnings. He co-founded that circle with Michelangelo Pistoletto, though he later split from the group over its politics and went his own way. He is known as Alighiero e Boetti, Alighiero and Boetti, as though the artist were two people rather than one: a small and permanent joke about authorship, and a fitting signature for someone so interested in what it means to be the maker of a work. Boetti died in 1994, and his reputation has grown steadily since, in part because the questions he raised about who actually makes an artwork have become central to contemporary art.

giuseppepenone.blurb: Sculptor of trees and human contact.
giuseppepenone.bio: Giuseppe Penone, born in Italy in 1947, is a sculptor best known for large-scale works involving trees, and for an art built around the link between people and the world that grows around them. The early work is associated with Arte Povera, the Italian movement that stripped materials back to the elemental, and he has stayed with those questions rather than moving past them: growth, contact and the slow work of time on matter. L'Arbre des voyelles of 1999, Faggio di Otterlo of 1987, Elevazione of 2001 and Idee di pietra – 1891 Kg di luce of 2010 are among the works that have carried his name furthest. He received the Praemium Imperiale in 2014, and lives and works in Turin.

gilbertozorio.bio: Gilberto Zorio, born in Italy in 1944, is a sculptor and painter associated with Arte Povera, and with Giovanni Anselmo he formed part of the movement's Turin nucleus. His work is fascinated by natural process, by alchemical transformation, and by energy let loose: incandescent light tubes, steel, pitch, and processes such as evaporation and oxidation, materials chosen because they are still doing something while the viewer looks. Sculptures, paintings and performances alike have been read as metaphors for revolutionary action, for transformation and for creativity itself, which places him at the political end of a movement that never separated the two. He also builds precarious installations from fragile materials, among them Stella di Bronzo and Acidi. Zorio has sustained that vocabulary of instability for six decades.

pinopascali.blurb: Sculptor and set designer, gone by 1968.
pinopascali.bio: Pino Pascali, born in Italy in 1935, was a sculptor, set designer and performer whose career lasted only a few years and still left a mark on Arte Povera. He worked across scenography and sculpture at a moment when the boundary between the two was becoming productive, and his objects keep something of the constructed, staged quality of things made for an audience. Trap, from 1968, is among the works most often cited; he was a photographer as well. Pascali died in 1968, while the movement was still forming, which has left his output small, concentrated and permanently associated with a beginning rather than a development. He is remembered in Italy as one of the great unfinished careers of the postwar avant-garde.

lucianofabro.blurb: Sculptor and writer of Arte Povera.
lucianofabro.bio: Luciano Fabro, born in Italy in 1936, was a sculptor, writer and conceptual artist who belonged to Arte Povera. He was part of the generation that made Italian art of the late 1960s an argument about materials, and he was among its most articulate members, writing as seriously as he sculpted. His objects and performances share a preoccupation with weight, surface and the way a thing meets the space around it, which kept his work legible even as the movement's label became a convenience for critics. La doppia faccia del cielo of 1986, Badenden of 1994 and The Ball of 2004 are among his later works. Fabro died in 2007, leaving a practice that ran from the movement's first years into the twenty-first century without settling into a signature style.

leeufan.bio: Lee Ufan, born in South Korea in 1936, is a minimalist painter, sculptor and academic whose work insists on process, materials and the experiential encounter between viewer and site rather than on the image alone. Based in Tokyo, he became the writer who gave Mono-ha its terms: his account of Sekine Nobuo's Phase—Mother Earth of 1968 defined what the group was doing and turned a set of gestures into a position, one that argued against European phenomenology as much as from it. That same Tokyo base made him the theorist and broker for Dansaekhwa abroad, carrying Park Seo-Bo and his colleagues into international view. A museum bearing his name opened in 2010, and his spare, deliberate paintings are among the most recognisable in postwar Asian art.

sekinenobuo.blurb: Made the earth into a sculpture.
sekinenobuo.bio: Sekine Nobuo, born in Japan in 1942, was a sculptor and land artist who divided his later life between Tokyo and Los Angeles. He studied at Tama Art University in Tokyo under Saitō Yoshishige, the teacher behind much of the generation that became Mono-ha. In 1968 he made Phase—Mother Earth, the work that gave the group its founding image; Lee Ufan's writing about it defined Mono-ha as a movement and turned Sekine's gesture into a principle, that material be encountered as itself rather than shaped into representation. He went on working in sculpture and in the landscape for decades afterwards, on a scale that kept him closer to land art than to the gallery. Sekine died in 2019, remembered above all for the work that changed the terms.

sugakishio.blurb: Arranges materials and lets them be.
sugakishio.bio: Suga Kishio, born in Japan in 1944, is a sculptor and installation artist and one of the central figures of Mono-ha. Like several of the group he studied at Tama Art University under Saitō Yoshishige, the teacher whose students went on to reset the terms of Japanese sculpture in the late 1960s. Mono-ha, the school of things, worked by placing materials in relation to one another and to the space they occupy, leaving them as far as possible unaltered, and Suga has pursued that idea longer and more consistently than almost anyone else associated with it. He lives and works in Itō, in Shizuoka, and continues to make installations that ask a viewer to attend to arrangement rather than to form.

koshimizususumu.bio: Koshimizu Susumu, born in Japan in 1944, is a sculptor and installation artist who belongs to the Mono-ha group. He studied at Tama Art University under Saitō Yoshishige, alongside the other artists who would form the core of the movement in the late 1960s. Mono-ha's premise was that materials should be presented as they are, arranged in relation to a site rather than carved into images, and Koshimizu's contribution has been among its most methodical: work concerned with how a substance behaves when it is handled, opened or simply set down. He has worked as a painter as well as a sculptor. Long after the group dispersed he has continued to make work from that same starting point, which has kept the Mono-ha argument alive in the present tense.

enokurakoji.blurb: Painter and installation artist of Mono-ha.
enokurakoji.bio: Enokura Kōji, born in Japan in 1942, was a painter and installation artist associated with Mono-ha, the group that emerged at the end of the 1960s and refused the idea that art should be carved or modelled into an image. His position within it was unusual because he came at the group's questions from painting: surface and mark rather than mass and arrangement, with the material itself left to register what had happened to it. That gave his installations a different temperature from the placements of stone, steel and timber more commonly associated with the movement. Enokura died in 1995, before the international interest in Mono-ha that arrived later and carried the group's reputation, and his own, well beyond Japan.

akasegawagenpei.blurb: Novelist, artist, co-founder of Hi-Red Center.
akasegawagenpei.bio: Akasegawa Genpei, born Akasegawa Katsuhiko in Japan in 1937, was an artist and writer who published his literary work under a second pseudonym, Otsuji Katsuhiko. He belonged to two of the most influential Japanese artist groups of the period: the Neo-Dada Organizers and, from 1963, Hi-Red Center, which he founded in Tokyo with Nakanishi Natsuyuki and Takamatsu Jirō. The group's name is built from the first characters of all three surnames. Afterwards he maintained a deliberately multi-disciplinary practice, moving between art, photography and writing for the rest of his career. Retrospectives followed at the Chiba City Museum, the Oita City Museum and the Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art, and his work entered the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Nam June Paik called him an unexportable genius.

nakanishinatsuyuki.blurb: From happenings to subdued abstract painting.
nakanishinatsuyuki.bio: Nakanishi Natsuyuki, born in Japan in 1935, was a visual and conceptual artist at the centre of the Japanese avant-garde of the 1960s. He co-founded Hi-Red Center with Takamatsu Jirō and Akasegawa Genpei in 1963, and his work of those years ran from Neo-Dadaist object pieces to happenings and performance art staged in public. Later he turned to painting, developing a practice of subdued palettes and idiosyncratic marks that occupied him for decades and made him, to a younger generation, primarily a painter. He was also an influential teacher, involved with the experimental Bigakko school and later a professor at Tokyo University of the Arts. Nakanishi died in 2016, having spanned both halves of postwar Japanese art: the street actions of the 1960s and the studio that followed them.

takamatsujiro.blurb: Shadows, tautologies and the zero dimension.
takamatsujiro.bio: Takamatsu Jirō, born in Japan in 1936, was among the most important postwar Japanese artists, using photography, sculpture, painting, drawing and performance to test the philosophical and material conditions under which art exists. He co-founded Hi-Red Center with Akasegawa Genpei; the group's name is assembled from the first characters of the three surnames. His practice was dedicated to a critique of cognition and perception, pursued through devices he returned to repeatedly, among them shadow, tautology, appropriation and distortions of perspective and representation. He described what he called the Zero Dimension, in which an object is reduced to its fundamental geometrical components; the smallest of these, he argued, is at once the ultimate division and emptiness itself, and reality is produced from them. Takamatsu died in 1998.

hermannnitsch.blurb: Vienna Actionism's ritual master of ceremonies.
hermannnitsch.bio: Hermann Nitsch, born in Austria in 1938, was an artist and composer and a leading figure of Viennese Actionism. From 1962 he built the group with Otto Muehl, and around them formed the circle that included Günter Brus and Rudolf Schwarzkogler. His art took the form of wide-scale performances combining theatre, multimedia, ritual and acted violence, with music he composed himself as an integral part rather than an accompaniment. Trained as a painter, he treated the performance as an event that left a painted residue behind, so that the aftermath could hang on a wall. The work drew controversy from the beginning and never stopped drawing it, which was plainly part of the proposition. Nitsch died in 2022, after six decades spent on essentially one continuous project.

gunterbrus.blurb: Fled Vienna after Art and Revolution.
gunterbrus.bio: Günter Brus, born in Austria in 1938, was a painter, graphic artist, experimental film-maker, writer and performance artist, and one of the founders of Viennese Actionism with Hermann Nitsch. Where Nitsch worked through ritual and ceremony, Brus worked directly with his own body, in performances that pushed hard against the conventions of Austrian public life. In 1968 the Art and Revolution event brought that confrontation to a head, and Brus left for Berlin. He continued afterwards in drawing, writing and film, and the graphic work of his later decades is substantial in its own right, a second career rather than a coda. Brus died in 2024, having outlived the other founders of the group and long since turned the violence of the early actions into something drawn and written down.

ottomuehl.blurb: Actionist co-founder, later a convicted criminal.
ottomuehl.bio: Otto Muehl, born in Austria in 1925, was one of the co-founders of Viennese Actionism and among its main participants, working with Hermann Nitsch from 1962 in the performances that made the group notorious. He was a painter and a film director as well as a performance artist, and the action was for him a way of taking those disciplines off the wall and into the room. He later founded the Friedrichshof Commune, an attempt to extend the group's programme into a whole way of living. He was also a convicted sex criminal, a fact that is inseparable from any account of his life and work. Muehl died in 2013, leaving a body of work that cannot now be looked at apart from the conviction.

rudolfschwarzkogler.blurb: An Actionist whose work ended in 1969.
rudolfschwarzkogler.bio: Rudolf Schwarzkogler, born in Austria in 1940, was a performance artist who kept close company with the Viennese Actionists, a circle that also took in Günter Brus, Otto Muehl and Hermann Nitsch. He came to it as a photographer, film-maker, choreographer and draftsperson, and those disciplines shaped work that was composed and precisely staged rather than improvised in front of a crowd, which sets him apart from the group's more confrontational public performances. His involvement was short. Schwarzkogler died in 1969, while the group was at its most active, leaving a small and exacting body of work behind. It has been returned to repeatedly by later generations of performance artists, for whom the staged photograph became a medium in its own right.

marinaabramovicandulay.blurb: Two artists, one shared performance practice.
marinaabramovicandulay.bio: This card pairs Marina Abramović with Ulay, the German artist born Frank Uwe Laysiepen in 1943, who worked from Amsterdam and Ljubljana. Ulay first made his name with Polaroid art, an intensely personal use of instant photography, before the collaboration that came to define both careers: a long partnership with Abramović in which the two made performance together rather than separately, so that the relationship itself became the material of the work. That joint practice brought international recognition and remains one of the defining models for collaborative performance, the point at which body art became a question of what passes between two people rather than what one person can endure alone. Ulay died in 2020. What they made together is now inseparable from either name.

vitoacconci.bio: Vito Acconci, born in the United States in 1940, started out as a poet and ended as a designer of buildings and landscapes, with performance and video in between. That middle period made his name: work characterised by existential unease, exhibitionism, discomfort, transgression and provocation, and also by wit and audacity, crossing the boundaries between public and private, consensual and non-consensual, the real world and the art world. Kathy Dillon was his partner and co-performer in the pieces of the early 1970s, and much of their tension comes from a relationship being conducted in front of an audience. He later moved into sculpture, architectural and landscape design; Wavewall dates from 2005. His influence runs through Bruce Nauman, Laurie Anderson, Karen Finley and Tracey Emin, among others. Acconci died in 2017.

chrisburden.bio: Chris Burden, born in the United States in 1946, became known in the 1970s for performances in which he put his own body at genuine risk. Shoot, of 1971, in which a friend, at his request, shot him in the arm with a small-calibre rifle, is the work that fixed his reputation and is still the first thing said about him. It was not the whole story. He went on to become an exceptionally prolific maker of installations, public artworks and sculpture, trading danger for engineering and scale: Urban Light, from 2008, and Beam Drop, from 2009, are among the best known. The distance travelled between the first work and the last is one of the more remarkable arcs in American art. Burden died in 2015.

caroleeschneemann.blurb: A painter who moved off the canvas.
caroleeschneemann.bio: Carolee Schneemann, born in the United States in 1939, read poetry and philosophy at Bard College before taking a Master of Fine Arts at the University of Illinois, and began as a painter in the Abstract Expressionist tradition. She had no interest in the masculine heroism of the New York painters around her and turned instead to performance-based work, making multi-media pieces about the body, narrative, sexuality and gender, and about taboo and the individual body's relation to social bodies. She never accepted that this was a change of profession: she called herself a painter to the end, describing everything she developed as an extension of visual principles off the canvas. The composer James Tenney was her partner and performed in Fuses and Meat Joy. Schneemann died in 2019.

valieexport.blurb: Took cinema out into the street.
valieexport.bio: VALIE EXPORT, born Waltraud Lehner in Austria in 1940, took a professional name of her own devising and built one of the most confrontational bodies of work in European art. Expanded cinema made her name: film pushed out of the auditorium and into space, objects and the body, alongside provocative public performances aimed at people who had not come looking for art. The practice also took in video installation, computer animation, photography, sculpture and a substantial amount of writing on contemporary art, and she taught for many years. Working in Austria in the same years as the Viennese Actionists, she came at the body from a different position entirely. She died in 2026, by then the senior figure of Austrian media art.

ginapane.blurb: A member of France's Art corporel.
ginapane.bio: Gina Pane, born in France in 1939 to an Italian family, trained at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris between 1960 and 1965, and belonged to Art corporel, the French body art movement of the 1970s. Her performances made her own body the site of the work, in actions that put the viewer in the uncomfortable position of witness rather than spectator. She also worked as a draftsperson and as a teacher, and drawing remained part of the practice throughout, not merely a preparation for it. Pane died in 1990. Her work is now read as a foundational reference for the performance artists who followed her in France and beyond, and as the point at which body art acquired a French vocabulary.

anamendieta.blurb: Earth-body works, and a life cut short.
anamendieta.bio: Ana Mendieta, born in Havana in 1948, left Cuba for the United States in 1961 as a child and spent her career working across the gap that opened up. She is best known for her earth-body works, in which the outline of her own body meets the landscape directly, and she worked as a sculptor, painter and video artist as well as a performance artist. Her influence on Cuban-American art after the Second World War is hard to overstate, and her example has shaped generations of artists who followed her. In January 1985 she married Carl Andre. That September she fell from the window of their thirty-fourth-floor apartment and died, a loss that still shadows the reception of her work and of his.

tehchinghsieh.bio: Tehching Hsieh, born in Taiwan in 1950 and long resident in New York, is a painter and performance artist known above all for durational art, work in which the passage of time is not the setting but the material. His pieces are conceived on a scale that makes them closer to a way of living than to an event, which is why they resist both documentation and summary; what is on offer is the fact of having done it at all. Marina Abramović, no stranger to endurance herself, has called him a master, and the description has stuck. Hsieh has become a reference point for artists who take seriously the idea that a work might be measured in duration rather than in objects, and that the artist pays for it in life.

michaelheizer.blurb: Moved the desert to make sculpture.
michaelheizer.bio: Michael Heizer, born in the United States in 1944, is the land artist who reset what sculpture could be in matters of size, mass, gesture and process. From 1967 he began making work in the American West with earth-moving equipment, largely outside the traditional spaces of galleries and museums because nothing inside them was big enough. Double Negative, from 1969, was funded by Virginia Dwan, whose backing made several of the founding earthworks possible; without patrons of that kind the movement would have stayed on paper. Levitated Mass followed much later, in 2012, carrying the same logic of enormous displaced material. Heizer lives and works in Hiko, Nevada, and in New York, and his practice remains among the most physically ambitious anyone has attempted in American art.

walterdemaria.bio: Walter De Maria, born in the United States in 1935, was a sculptor, illustrator and composer whose practice sits at the meeting point of minimal art, conceptual art and the land art of the 1960s. He lived and worked in New York and made his largest pieces far from it. The Lightning Field, of 1977, was funded by Virginia Dwan together with the Dia Art Foundation, the kind of patronage arrangement that made American land art possible at all; The Vertical Earth Kilometer dates from the same year. Later works include Sphere of Human Rights of 1989 and Large Red Sphere of 2010, in which extreme simplicity of form is carried by extreme precision of making. His background as a composer is audible in the sense of interval throughout. De Maria died in 2013.

nancyholt.blurb: Framed the landscape through Sun Tunnels.
nancyholt.bio: Nancy Holt, born in the United States in 1938, was best known for land art, public sculpture, installation and concrete poetry, though she worked in film and photography throughout her career as well. Sun Tunnels, made in 1976, is her defining work and one of the landmarks of the movement. She married Robert Smithson in 1963 and the two worked in close proximity for a decade; from 1973 she completed the work he left unfinished and took on the long task of preserving and presenting it, a role that for years overshadowed recognition of her own art. Amarillo Ramp, from 1973, is listed among her works. Holt died in 2014, and since 2018 the Holt/Smithson Foundation has cared for both legacies.

richardlong.blurb: One of Britain's best-known land artists.
richardlong.bio: Sir Richard Julian Long, born in the United Kingdom in 1945, is a sculptor, painter and photographer, and one of the best known of the British land artists. He belongs to the generation that, at the end of the 1960s, decided the landscape itself was a place to make sculpture rather than a backdrop to set sculpture against; a work of his dated 1969 stands near the start of that shift. Where the American earthworks of the same years were cut into the western desert with earth-moving machinery, the British side of the movement worked at a smaller and more portable scale, and photography carries much of it back to a viewer who will never stand on the site. The knighthood is unusual recognition for an art made largely outside the museum.

hamishfulton.blurb: Only makes work about his walks.
hamishfulton.bio: Hamish Fulton, born in the United Kingdom in 1946, calls himself a walking artist, and he means it literally: since 1972 he has made works based only on the experience of walks. The walk is the art, and what appears in a gallery, whether photographs, illustrations or wall texts, is the translation of something that already happened elsewhere and cannot be brought back. He argues that walking is an art form in its own right and has campaigned for wider acknowledgement of walking art. Since 1994 he has created group walks for the public, turning a solitary discipline into a shared one. His work is held by major museums including Tate Britain and the Museum of Modern Art. Half a century on, the rule has held.

christoandjeanneclaude.bio: Christo and Jeanne-Claude were a husband-and-wife team whose large-scale, site-specific environmental installations worked at the scale of landmarks and landscapes. Their method held steady across decades: take something already familiar, a building, a bridge, a stretch of coast, a park, and change how it is seen, usually by wrapping it in fabric or running fabric across it. Running Fence in California, The Pont Neuf Wrapped, the Wrapped Reichstag and The Gates in New York's Central Park are the works most often named; The Umbrellas dates from 1991 and The Floating Piers, realised after her death, from 2016. Jeanne-Claude Denat de Guillebon was born in 1935 and died in 2009; the projects belong to both names. Every piece was temporary by design, which is much of the point.

aliceaycock.bio: Alice Aycock, born in the United States in 1946, was among the first artists in the land art movement of the 1970s and has since become known for large-scale metal sculptures installed around the world. Her drawings and sculptures propose architectural and mechanical fantasies, structures that look engineered for a purpose nobody can quite name, and they hold logic, imagination, magical thinking and science in the same frame without deciding between them. Leonardo Swirl of 1982, Another Twister (João) of 2014 and Devil Whirls of 2017 give a sense of the range, and of the recurring sense of motion in the later work. Aycock's career traces how the earthwork generation moved out of the desert and into the public spaces of cities.

andygoldsworthy.blurb: Sculpture made from ice, leaves and stone.
andygoldsworthy.bio: Andy Goldsworthy, born in 1956, works as a sculptor, photographer, land artist and environmentalist, and his practice belongs to the land art tradition that came out of the conceptual turn of the 1960s. The sculptures are site-specific: made for a particular place and situated in natural or urban settings rather than delivered to a gallery. Photography sits alongside the sculpture rather than behind it, and he is listed as a photographer as readily as a sculptor, the camera being part of how the work reaches anyone who never stood at the site. Stone River, completed in 2001, and Refuge d'art: Vieil Esclangon, from 2005, are among the named works. The environmentalism is not a separate commitment. It follows from choosing to build in the landscape itself, where the ground and the setting decide what a piece can be.

chuckclose.blurb: Massive-scale portraits of himself and others.
chuckclose.bio: Charles Thomas Close, born in 1940 and died in 2021, was an American painter, photographer and draughtsman who made portraits at massive scale, of himself and of the people around him. He worked from photographs, translating a face into marks that resolve into a likeness at a distance and come apart again as the viewer steps close. The early portraits were photorealist; later ones grew openly abstract, and he made photographic portraits as well, using a very large format camera. In 1988 an occlusion of the anterior spinal artery left him paralysed. Rather than stopping, he rebuilt his painting style and his working methods around what his body could still do, and the work went on for decades afterwards. The Subway Portraits, from 2017, carried his approach into public space.

richardestes.blurb: Photorealism's master of glass and reflection.
richardestes.bio: Richard Estes, born in 1932, is an American painter, printmaker and photographer, counted among those who founded the international photo-realist movement as it took hold in the late 1960s. His pictures are typically city views, clean and geometric and almost entirely emptied of people, so that the real subject becomes the layered reflections bouncing between shopfronts, chrome and glass.
