He belongs to a loose group of painters who arrived at the approach at the same moment, among them Chuck Close, Audrey Flack, Duane Hanson, Ralph Goings, Robert Cottingham and John Baeder. Critics have also called the tendency super-realism or hyper-realism. Its success in the late 1960s and early 1970s marked the point at which photography was absorbed into the art world, with painters using photographic stills to make pictures that at a glance pass for photographs.

audreyflack.bio: Audrey Lenora Flack, born in 1931 and died in 2024, was an American painter, printmaker, lithographer and sculptor whose work pioneered the genre of photorealism. Her practice was unusually wide for that tendency. It took in painting and printmaking, sculpture and photography, so that the same artist is filed under flat, meticulously rendered surfaces and under work made in three dimensions. That range matters to how the movement is understood, since photorealism is often remembered as a narrow technical exercise, and a practice spread across four mediums complicates the picture. Her work is credited with pioneering the genre rather than following it, which places her at the start of the story instead of somewhere along its edge, and the sculpture stands as evidence that she never treated photorealism as the whole of what she had to say.

duanehanson.bio: Duane Hanson, born in Minnesota in 1925 and died in 1996, was an American sculptor, painter and installation artist who spent the greater part of his career in South Florida. He is known for life-sized realistic figures of ordinary people, cast from human models and finished in polyester resin, fiberglass, Bondo and bronze. The realism was never an end in itself: the figures carry political and social commentary, and a streak of satire aimed at the everyday American life they reproduce so exactly. Working in the same current as the photorealist painters, he pushed their question into three dimensions, asking what happens when a made object becomes hard to tell apart from the thing it copies. The materials were industrial and unglamorous, well matched to the unheroic people he chose to cast.

malcolmmorley.blurb: The restless painter who won the first Turner.
malcolmmorley.bio: Malcolm A. Morley, born in 1931 and died in 2018, was a British-American painter and draughtsman who refused to stay in one style. He is remembered first as a pioneer of photorealism, working from photographic sources, but he moved on through expressionism and a long string of other manners, treating each as something to be used and then abandoned. That restlessness is the through-line of the work rather than any single look. He won the inaugural Turner Prize in 1984, and went on painting for another three decades after it. Wall Jumpers, from 2002, comes from the later part of that career. Among the photorealists he is the awkward case, the artist who helped invent the position and then walked away from it, which is why no one picture stands for him.

alexkatz.blurb: Flat, cool portraits that anticipated Pop.
alexkatz.bio: Alex Katz, born in 1927, is an American figurative artist working in painting, sculpture and prints. Since 1951 his work has appeared in more than two hundred solo exhibitions and nearly five hundred group shows, in the United States and internationally. The pictures are large, flat and coolly simplified, faces and figures reduced to clean shapes and heightened colour, and that bold simplicity is widely read as a precursor to Pop Art, arriving before the movement it anticipated. Paul Taylor Dance Company, from 1963, is among the works listed under his name. Grouped here with the new figuration of the 1960s, Katz sits slightly apart from the photorealists: where they worked from photographs toward ever more detail, he pared the portrait down until only the essentials were left standing.

fernandobotero.blurb: Colombia's painter of inflated, voluminous figures.
fernandobotero.bio: Fernando Botero Angulo, born in Colombia in 1932 and died in 2023, was a painter and sculptor whose figures are swollen to an exaggerated volume, a manner so distinctive that it acquired its own name, Boterismo. The inflation is not simply comic. Depending on the piece it carries humour, tenderness or sharp political criticism, and the same rounded bodies serve satire and monument alike. He worked as a draughtsman, illustrator and sculptor as well as a painter, and held both Colombian and French nationality. In his lifetime he was the most recognised and most quoted artist from Latin America, and his work stood in some of the most visible places in the world, including Park Avenue in New York and the Champs-Elysees in Paris. Among his pieces are Monument to Roman Gladiator, The Raval Cat and La Maternidad.

antoniolopezgarcia.blurb: Called the greatest realist artist alive.
antoniolopezgarcia.bio: Antonio Lopez Garcia, born in Spain in 1936, is a painter, sculptor and draughtsman known for a realism so exacting that it is often described as hyperrealistic, and he has taught at university level alongside the studio work. Leading art critics have praised him for decades. Robert Hughes, writing in 1986, called him the greatest realist artist alive, which is about as far as that sort of judgement can be pushed. His painting became the subject of a film, El Sol del Membrillo, made by Victor Erice in 1992 and still the best-known account of him at work. Later pieces such as Dia y Noche, from 2008, and La Mujer de Coslada, from 2010, carry the same exactness into sculpture, where realism registers as stillness rather than as description. He is grouped here with photorealism and the new figuration of the 1960s.

jeffdonaldson.blurb: AfriCOBRA co-founder, painter and art historian.
jeffdonaldson.bio: Jeff Donaldson, born in 1932 and died in 2004, was an American painter, printmaker and art historian who did as much as anyone to shape the Black Arts Movement across the 1960s and 1970s. In Chicago in 1968 he co-founded AfriCOBRA with Wadsworth Jarrell, Barbara Jones-Hogu and Gerald Williams, giving the movement a collective and a shared set of principles rather than a loose affiliation of individuals. He also contributed to the momentous Wall of Respect, and his was a pioneering career in African-American academic and personal achievement alike. His aim was an alternative Black iconography, rooted in struggle and tied to Africa, able to displace the demeaning stereotypes carried by mainstream white culture. As artist and as scholar alike he pursued that project, in painting and in writing.

barbarajoneshogu.blurb: AfriCOBRA co-founder from Chicago's Black arts scene.
barbarajoneshogu.bio: Barbara Jones-Hogu, born in 1938 and died in 2017, was an African-American artist and designer, best known for co-founding the Chicago collective AfriCOBRA alongside Jeff Donaldson, and for her earlier involvement with the Organization of Black American Culture. That older body supplied much of the ground from which AfriCOBRA grew, and her passage from the one to the other traces how the Black Arts Movement in Chicago built itself: through community organisations first, then through collectives with a stated programme. Her work belongs to that larger effort to make a visual language of its own, bright and legible and addressed directly to a Black audience rather than to the museum. She worked as painter and as designer, a combination well suited to a movement that wanted its images to circulate rather than simply hang.

wadsworthjarrell.blurb: AfriCOBRA co-founder who painted jazz's colour.
wadsworthjarrell.bio: Wadsworth Aikens Jarrell, born in Albany, Georgia in 1929, is an American painter, sculptor and printmaker who moved to Chicago and studied at the Art Institute there. His early work took up the working life of African Americans in the city and drew heavily on the sights and sounds of jazz, a debt that stayed audible in the rhythm and colour of everything that followed. He opened WJ Studio and Gallery with his wife, Jae, in the late 1960s, and the space became a gathering point for regional artists and musicians. Out of that circle came AfriCOBRA, which he co-founded in Chicago in 1968 with Jeff Donaldson. The collective gave a shared name and a programme to work he was already making, and he has carried it on in painting, sculpture and print.

geraldwilliams.bio: Gerald Williams, born in 1941, is an American painter and visual artist, and a founding member of AfriCOBRA, the Chicago collective he helped start with Jeff Donaldson. His work has carried real weight inside the Black Arts Movement, an aesthetic phenomenon transnational from the start, which surfaced in the 1960s and evolves still. His paintings have been shown at some of the most significant museums anywhere: the Studio Museum in Harlem, Tate Modern, the Institute of Contemporary Art in Philadelphia, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago. Colour, legibility and an audience reached outside the gallery run straight through the work, which extends the collective's founding programme rather than departing from it. He remains one of the living links back to AfriCOBRA's beginnings, and a working artist besides.

jaejarrell.blurb: AfriCOBRA co-founder who made clothes art.
jaejarrell.bio: Elaine Jarrell, known as Jae Jarrell, born in 1935, is an American artist, fashion designer and textile artist who worked within the Black Arts Movement as it took shape through the 1960s, and a co-founder of the AfriCOBRA collective. Her chosen medium set her apart from the painters around her. She worked in cloth and in clothing, garments made to be worn rather than hung, which put the movement's imagery directly onto the body and into the street, where it could be met by people who would never walk into a gallery. Founding AfriCOBRA placed her at the centre of a group committed to a Black visual language of its own, and her contribution was to carry that language into design, textile and dress rather than onto canvas.

faithringgold.bio: Faith Ringgold, born in 1930 and died in 2024, was an American painter, author, illustrator, mixed-media sculptor, textile artist, performance artist and intersectional activist. She is best known for her narrative quilts, works that combine painted image with pieced fabric and written text so that a single hanging tells a story. That choice of material carried an argument with it, since quilting sat outside the categories the art world took seriously, and using it insisted on a lineage of Black women's making as legitimate ground for painting. Her activism and her art were never separable; she campaigned as well as painted, and the two ran together across a long career. Working within the Black Arts Movement's wider effort to build images on its own terms, she also wrote and illustrated books.

betyesaar.bio: Betye Irene Saar, born in 1926 and died in 2026, was an American artist known above all for assemblage, the practice of building a work from found objects and images rather than painting one. She was also an accomplished printmaker and graphic artist, and a visual storyteller by instinct, arranging her materials so that they narrate. Part of the 1970s Black Arts Movement, she took up the myths and stereotypes attached to race and femininity and turned them around, so that a racist object pulled out of circulation and rebuilt inside a work of art is aimed back at the culture that made it. Her work is openly political. Across her career she kept challenging the negative ideas about African Americans that American visual culture had been repeating, and that critique is what she is best known for.

davidhammons.blurb: The elusive conceptualist of New York streets.
davidhammons.bio: David Hammons, born in 1943, is an American artist working across performance, sculpture, installation and drawing, best known for what he made in and around Los Angeles and New York City through the 1970s and 1980s. The phrase in and around matters. His reputation rests on work tied to those two cities rather than to a single institution or a signature format, and performance and installation are as central to it as any object he made. That is one reason the practice resists being reduced to a list of things. African-American Flag, dated 1990, is the work that has travelled furthest beyond it. He is grouped here with the Black Arts Movement, alongside whose insistence on art addressed to Black audiences on its own terms his career sits.

romarebearden.blurb: Collage as a chronicle of Black life.
romarebearden.bio: Romare Howard Bearden, born in Charlotte, North Carolina in 1911 and died in 1988, was an American artist, author and songwriter who worked in cartoons, oils and, most famously, collage. He was raised between New York City and Pittsburgh, and took his degree from New York University in 1935. His cousin Charles Alston ran the Harlem workshop where Bearden started, a family connection that placed him inside the city's Black artistic life from the beginning. In 1963 he co-founded Spiral with Norman Lewis, Hale Woodruff and Alston himself, the group gathering in Bearden's own Canal Street studio. The question of what Black artists owed the moment they were working in runs through the collages, which assemble cut fragments into scenes of Black life with something of the rhythm of the music he also wrote.

carlosalmaraz.blurb: A pioneer of Chicano painting in Los Angeles.
carlosalmaraz.bio: Carlos D. Almaraz, born in 1941 and died in 1989, was a Mexican-American painter, one of the pioneers of the Chicano art movement. Between 1977 and 1979 he was among the founders of the Centro de Arte Publico in Highland Park, Los Angeles, an organisation built to give Chicano and Chicana artists a place of their own rather than a waiting room at somebody else's institution. That combination of studio practice with the unglamorous work of building infrastructure was characteristic of the movement, which grew out of political organising as much as out of art schools. His career was short, ending with his death in 1989, but it ran alongside the years in which Chicano art in Los Angeles established itself as a permanent public presence rather than a temporary campaign.

frankromero.blurb: Los Angeles in palm trees and hot colour.
frankromero.bio: Frank Edward Romero, born in 1941, is an American painter and muralist considered a pioneer of the Chicano art movement. His paintings and murals work through Chicano and Los Angeles iconography, palm trees and bright saturated colour among the recurring elements, and the city itself is never far from the subject. Murals matter in his practice for the same reason they mattered to the movement generally: a wall is public, free to look at, and belongs to the neighbourhood in a way that a canvas in a gallery does not. Working alongside the other founding figures of Chicano art in Los Angeles, he helped establish an imagery recognisably of that city and that community rather than borrowed from elsewhere, and he has continued to paint and to make murals since.

judybaca.blurb: Director of the Great Wall of Los Angeles.
judybaca.bio: Judith Francisca Baca, born in 1946, is an American artist, activist and muralist, and a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, teaching Chicano studies, world arts and cultures. She co-founded the Social and Public Art Resource Center in Venice, California, where she is artistic director, and she directed the mural project that produced the Great Wall of Los Angeles, as of 2018 the largest communal mural project known anywhere. The word communal is the point. A wall on that scale is painted by many hands, so that making the mural becomes a form of organising in itself. Her works include the Arch of Dignity, Equality, and Justice. Teaching, organising and painting have run together throughout, which is largely how Chicano muralism got built.

yolandalopez.blurb: She remade the Virgen de Guadalupe.
yolandalopez.bio: Yolanda Margarita Lopez, born in 1942 and died in 2021, was an American painter and printmaker, an educator and a film producer, whose work centred on the experience of Mexican-American women. Her Chicana feminist pieces set out to challenge the ethnic stereotypes attached to those women, and she is best known for a series of paintings that took the image of the Virgen de Guadalupe and re-imagined it, taking the most familiar devotional figure in Mexican culture and giving her the body and the labour of ordinary contemporary women. Printmaking and teaching carried the same argument to audiences well beyond the gallery. Museums holding her work include the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

esterhernandez.blurb: Prints for farm workers and Chicana rights.
esterhernandez.bio: Ester Hernandez, born in 1944, is an American Chicana visual artist based in San Francisco, recognised for prints and pastels dealing with farm worker rights and with cultural, political and Chicana feminist issues. She was an activist in the Chicano art movement of the 1960s, and the activism and the art were never separate strands: the pieces take up civil rights, women's rights, social justice and the Farm Worker Movement directly, as arguments rather than as illustrations. Printmaking suited that purpose, since a print can be reproduced, posted and passed along in ways a unique painting cannot. Working in California through the decades in which Chicano art established itself, she has kept the farm workers' cause and the position of Chicana women at the centre of the work.

gronk.bio: Gronk, born Glugio Nicandro in 1954, is a Chicano painter, printmaker and performance artist, and a co-founder of Asco, the collective formed in East Los Angeles in 1972 with Willie Herrón, Harry Gamboa Jr. and Patssi Valdez. Asco worked where galleries were not: on the street, in processions and staged tableaux, making art out of a city that had little room for Chicano artists inside its museums. Gronk's own work moved between painting, printmaking and performance without settling, and he has since worked in glass. His paintings are held by museums across the United States, among them the Smithsonian American Art Museum. He remains one of the defining figures of the Chicano art movement, and of a generation that treated the boundary between performance and painting as something to be crossed rather than respected.

willieherron.bio: Willie F. Herron III, born in 1951, is an American Chicano muralist and performance artist, a commercial artist too, and a founding member of Asco, the Chicano collective based in East Los Angeles and formed in 1972 with Gronk and the others. Murals and performance sat side by side in his practice, the wall painting rooted in the neighbourhood, the performance work refusing the neighbourhood's given limits. Asco emerged from a Chicano art movement in which the mural was the dominant form, and pushed it somewhere else, toward performance and the conceptual turn this entry groups it with. Herron is the figure who held both halves of that argument at once, working as a muralist while helping to invent a collective that treated the city itself as material rather than as a surface to be painted.

harrygamboajr.blurb: Asco's photographer, essayist and founding member.
harrygamboajr.bio: Harry Gamboa Jr., born in 1951, is an American Chicano photographer, essayist, illustrator, director and performance artist, and a founding member of Asco, the influential Chicano performance collective, which he helped start with Gronk. His camera did much of the group's historical work: Asco was a performance collective, and photographs and essays are how performance reaches anyone who was not in the room. He has worked in television production and new media as well as still photography, and the essays have been as central as the images, both doing the job of putting the collective and its city on record in its own terms. Asco's contribution was to insist that Chicano art did not have to mean a mural, and Gamboa's documentation is a large part of why that claim can still be demonstrated.

patssivaldez.bio: Patssi Valdez, born in 1951, is an American Chicana artist and a founder of the Asco collective, which she helped start with Gronk. Her work sits within a Chicana avant-garde expressionism and moves freely across mediums, taking in painting, sculpture and fashion design, so that studio practice and staged public performance draw on the same instincts. The collective's method of performance, costume and the constructed image mapped closely onto that range of skills, and being one of its founders put a Chicana artist at the centre of a scene that rarely made room for one. She lives and works in Los Angeles, where she continues to paint, and the later work carries forward the collective's refusal of any single medium in favour of whatever the idea requires.

cliffordpossumtjapaltjarri.bio: Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri, born in 1932 and died in 2002, was an Australian Aboriginal painter and among the most collected and renowned artists of the Western Desert movement. His work is held by the Kelton Foundation and the Royal Collection, and by the National Gallery of Australia and the Art Gallery of New South Wales. He was one of the Papunya painters championed by the schoolteacher Geoffrey Bardon, and he was working there in Papunya Tula's founding year. What emerged from Papunya was the Western Desert movement itself, and his standing inside it is measured by how far the paintings travelled: into galleries and collections in Australia and elsewhere, a long way from the settlement where the painting started. The letters AO after his name record his appointment as an Officer of the Order of Australia.

johnnywarangkulatjupurrula.blurb: The Western Desert painter of water.
johnnywarangkulatjupurrula.bio: Johnny Warangkula Tjupurrula, born in 1925 and died in 2001, was an Australian painter whose pictures have been sought out and admired since the late 1960s. He was among the Papunya artists championed by the schoolteacher Geoffrey Bardon, and out of that encouragement came Papunya Tula. What distinguishes the work is water: the transitory beauty of it in desert country, and the way it transforms the landscape a painting describes. It is a quality long said to set his pictures apart from those of other Aboriginal Australian artists of the period. His paintings are held by the Art Gallery of Western Australia, the National Gallery of Victoria, the National Museum of Australia and the National Gallery of Australia, and he remains one of the founding figures of Western Desert painting.

kaapatjampitjinpa.bio: Kaapa Mbitjana Tjampitjinpa, born around 1925 and died in 1989, was an artist of Anmatyerre, Warlpiri and Arrernte heritage, and one of the earliest and most significant painters to emerge at Papunya, in Australia's Northern Territory, during the early 1970s. He helped found the Papunya Tula artists company and served as its first chairman, the structure that turned a group of painters into an enterprise they ran themselves. In 1971 the schoolteacher Geoffrey Bardon supplied boards and paint at Papunya and the Honey Ant Mural followed, the moment usually taken as the start of modern Indigenous Australian painting. Kaapa was pivotal to that beginning, both as a painter and as the man who held the new company's chair, and much of what the movement became grew from those first boards.

geoffreybardon.blurb: The teacher who supplied the first boards.
geoffreybardon.bio: Geoffrey Robert Bardon, born in 1940 and died in 2003, was an Australian school teacher and artist whose part in the beginning of the Western Desert Aboriginal art movement was decisive. At Papunya in 1971 he supplied boards and paint to men whose designs were far older than European Australia, and the Honey Ant Mural followed. From that came Papunya Tula, and with it the painters he championed: Kaapa Tjampitjinpa, Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri, who was working there in the company's founding year, and Johnny Warangkula Tjupurrula. Bardon's role was not to teach the imagery, which belonged to the painters and to their country, but to provide the materials and the recognition that let it travel beyond the settlement. The letters AM after his name record his appointment as a Member of the Order of Australia.

emilykamekngwarreye.blurb: The Utopia painter who redefined Aboriginal art.
emilykamekngwarreye.bio: Emily Kame Kngwarreye, whose name is also written Emily Kam Kngwarray, was an Anmatyerr artist whose country was Alhalker, in the Northern Territory's Sandover region, and she died in 1996. She worked as a painter and as a textile artist, and what is claimed for her is unusually direct: a unique style and a creative vision powerful enough to redefine contemporary Aboriginal art and to draw worldwide attention to it. She is grouped here with the Western Desert movement, though the grouping holds at the level of the movement rather than of the manner, since the language she arrived at was entirely her own. Redefinition is a large word for what a painter is usually credited with, and it is the one the record uses of her. Her standing has not slipped since.

roverthomas.blurb: Warmun's painter, whose example started others.
roverthomas.bio: Rover Thomas Joolama, known simply as Rover Thomas, born in 1926 and died in 1998, was an Aboriginal Australian artist of Wangkajunga and Kukatja descent, and one of the central figures of painting at Warmun in Western Australia. He worked as a cattle rancher before he was a painter, and the record lists him as a dreamer as well, a role that sits at the source of the imagery rather than beside it. At Warmun his painting had an effect well beyond his own canvases: Queenie McKenzie took up painting after seeing his work, and the community became a centre in its own right, distinct from the Western Desert schools to the south. His work belongs to the broader Aboriginal Australian movement that reshaped what Australian art was taken to be.

queeniemckenzie.blurb: Warmun's painter of East Kimberley country.
queeniemckenzie.bio: Queenie McKenzie, also known as Nakarra and formerly as Oakes or Mingmarriya, was an Aboriginal Australian artist born at Old Texas Station on the Ord River's western bank, in the East Kimberley, and she died in 1998. She came to painting through the example of Rover Thomas. Working alongside him at Warmun in Western Australia, she took it up after seeing what he was doing, and became one of the leading artists of that community. It is among the clearest lines of influence in Australian art: not a teacher and a student in any formal sense, but one painter watching another and recognising that the thing could be done. Warmun's standing as a centre of Aboriginal painting rests substantially on the two of them working there together.

ilyakabakov.blurb: Moscow conceptualist who resettled on Long Island.
ilyakabakov.bio: Ilya Iosifovich Kabakov, born in 1933 in Dnipropetrovsk, at that time part of the Ukrainian SSR, and died in 2023, was a Soviet and American conceptual artist. For thirty years he worked in Moscow, from the 1950s to the late 1980s, before emigrating to the United States and settling on Long Island. In Moscow he shared an attic studio with Erik Bulatov, and the same illustration jobs, the official work that paid for the unofficial art. With Andrei Monastyrski he belonged to the Moscow Conceptualist circle and its Collective Actions group, the network in which unofficial Soviet art built its own audience and vocabulary. From 1992, when he married his second cousin Emilia Kabakov, every work was co-authored with her. Looking Up. Reading the Words, from 1997, belongs to that joint output.

erikbulatov.blurb: Russian nonconformist, mentored outside the academy.
erikbulatov.bio: Erik Vladimirovich Bulatov, born in 1933 and died in 2025, was a Russian artist brought up in Moscow. His father, a communist party official, died at Pskov during the Second World War; his mother had left Bialystok in Poland at the age of fifteen, in 1922. Through the 1950s he was mentored privately by Vladimir Favorsky, alongside Robert Falk, an education conducted entirely outside the official academy, which is where much of the real teaching of Soviet nonconformist artists took place. He shared an attic studio with Ilya Kabakov and the same illustration jobs, the day work that supported unofficial painting. His work entered the major collections, public and private, of Europe, Russia and the United States. In 2008 the Russian Academy of Arts made him an honorary member, and in 2015 he was made Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres.

oscarrabin.bio: Oscar Rabin, born in 1928, was a Russian painter and activist who stood at the centre of Soviet Nonconformist Art, the unofficial current that worked outside the state academies, exhibition halls and artists' unions. He was as much an organiser as a painter, and his activism shaped the careers of many painters and sculptors of that era and the decades that followed. Working without official sanction meant working without the institutions that made a career possible, and the risks of that position were real. He later lived in France. Rabin died in 2018, by which time the unofficial art he had helped define was recognised as one of the significant currents of the postwar Soviet decades, and the group around him — Ilya Kabakov, Erik Bulatov, Ernst Neizvestny — had become the recognised face of it.

ernstneizvestny.blurb: Sculptor of monuments, exile in New York.
ernstneizvestny.bio: Ernst Iosifovich Neizvestny, born in 1925 and died in 2016, was a Russian sculptor, graphic artist, painter and philosopher of art. He worked in the Soviet Union as part of the nonconformist current, the artists whose work fell outside what the state was prepared to exhibit, and in 1976 he emigrated to the United States, living and working in New York City. Sculpture at scale was his central form, and two of his best-known pieces stand at that scale: a Prometheus, and the Mask of Sorrow. He was a philosopher as well as a maker of objects, and the thinking and the sculpture pursued the same questions, about suffering, endurance and what a form can be made to carry. His career spans both sides of the emigration, and a long working life abroad.

vitalykomar.blurb: One half of Komar and Melamid.
vitalykomar.bio: Vitaly Komar is a Russian-American conceptualist and one half of Komar and Melamid, the tandem at the centre of Sots Art. He met Alexander Melamid at the Stroganov Institute in Moscow, and from 1972 the pair worked as a single author. In an artists' statement they explained that even where only one of them made a project, they would usually sign it together, on the grounds that what they amounted to was less a single artist than a movement. Both were born in Moscow; both emigrated to Israel in 1977 and then to New York in 1978. Their Stalin Monument dates from 1986. The co-authorship ended in 2003 and 2004, after which each of them worked alone, closing one of the most complete surrenders of the individual signature in twentieth-century art.

alexandermelamid.blurb: The other half of Komar and Melamid.
alexandermelamid.bio: Alexander Melamid, born in 1945, is a Russian-born conceptualist and performance artist who has also worked in painting and in installation. He met Vitaly Komar at the Stroganov Institute in Moscow, and from 1972 the two of them worked as a single author, so that the pair's joint name, rather than either man's own, became the unit under which the work was made. That arrangement is inseparable from Sots Art, the movement he is grouped with here, and from the era of Pop, Minimal and Conceptual practice in which it took shape. The collaboration is unusual in twentieth-century art for how completely it set aside the individual signature, and it is the reason his name is rarely spoken without the other half of it attached to the end.

guydebord.blurb: Theorist of the society of the spectacle.
guydebord.bio: Guy-Ernest Debord, born in 1931 and died in 1994, was a French Marxist theorist, philosopher, filmmaker and critic of work. He was a member of the Letterist International and founded a Letterist faction before becoming a founding member of the Situationist International in 1957, alongside Asger Jorn, who bankrolled the group and left it in 1961. He was also briefly involved with Socialisme ou Barbarie. His best-known work is The Society of the Spectacle, published in 1967, which gave the group its most durable idea and its most quoted title. Alongside the writing he directed films and steered the Letterist and Situationist magazines, treating publication as a form of action rather than as commentary on one. His influence on the decades that followed was out of all proportion to the size of the group.

constant.blurb: The Dutch painter who wrote CoBrA's manifesto.
constant.bio: Constant Anton Nieuwenhuys, known simply as Constant, born in 1920 and died in 2005, was a Dutch painter and sculptor, and also a graphic artist, author and musician, who had been a resistance fighter before any of that. He co-founded CoBrA with Asger Jorn and wrote the group's manifesto, which put him at the theoretical centre of one of postwar Europe's key experimental circles. The same instinct, art as a programme rather than a product, carried him toward the Situationist International, the movement he is grouped with here, where the argument moved from painting to the shape of the city and of everyday life. Constant's Gate dates from 1963. Few artists of his generation travelled so completely from making pictures to imagining how people might live, and the writing counts as much as the paintings.

raoulvaneigem.blurb: The Situationist who theorised everyday life.
raoulvaneigem.bio: Raoul Vaneigem, born in 1934 and died in 2026, was a Belgian writer, journalist and philosopher of culture, and a scholar of French literature. He is known above all for The Revolution of Everyday Life, published in 1967, the book that carried Situationist thinking to readers far outside the movement's very small membership. Where much radical writing of the period took institutions and structures as its subject, his took the texture of ordinary days: what work does to a life, what pleasure and refusal might be worth, how much of a person is spent simply getting through the week. He is grouped here with the Situationist International, the current that treated theory, publication and provocation as continuous with art rather than as commentary upon it, and his writing continued long afterwards.

judychicago.blurb: Founder of America's first feminist art program.
judychicago.bio: Judy Chicago, born in 1939, is an American feminist artist, writer and art educator, known for large collaborative installations that take up birth and creation and examine what role women have been given in history and in culture. In the 1970s she founded the country's first feminist art program, at California State University, Fresno, and the programme became a catalyst for a decade of feminist art and feminist art education. With Miriam Schapiro she went on to co-direct the Feminist Art Program at CalArts from 1971, and in 1972 the two of them staged Womanhouse. The Dinner Party, completed in 1979, is her best-known work, and its Heritage Floor carries the names of the women it honours. The collaborative method is as much the argument as the imagery, which is what the teaching was for.

miriamschapiro.blurb: She made the fan and kimono heroic.
miriamschapiro.bio: Miriam Schapiro, known as Mimi, born in 1923 and died in 2015, was born in Canada and worked in the United States as a painter, sculptor, printmaker and quiltmaker, and as a pioneer of feminist art. With Judy Chicago she co-directed the Feminist Art Program at CalArts from 1971 and staged Womanhouse in 1972. Her own work deliberately blurred the line between fine art and craft, importing hearts, floral decoration, geometric pattern and the colour pink precisely because they were associated with women. In the 1970s she painted the hand fan, a small woman's object, at six feet by twelve, making it heroic, and from that fan-shaped canvas came the textured, opulent surface that formed her mature style. From 1975 she co-founded Pattern and Decoration with Robert Kushner and Joyce Kozloff, and led that movement too.

marykelly.blurb: Feminism made conceptual, rigorous and written.
marykelly.bio: Mary Kelly, born in 1941, is an American artist who works conceptually, and a feminist, an educator and a writer besides. Four descriptions, and not one of them is decorative. The conceptual artist and the writer are the same person, so the essays and the objects belong to a single body of work rather than to a practice and a commentary upon it, and the teaching is not a sideline either. Her generation of feminist artists built programmes, courses and institutions as deliberately as they built individual works, on the reasoning that an art world which had excluded them was unlikely to correct itself unprompted. She is grouped here with feminist art in the era of pluralism, identity and postmodernism, the decades in which that argument was pressed hardest and the terms on which women artists were shown began to shift.

martharosler.blurb: Video, photo-text and the public sphere.
martharosler.bio: Martha Rosler, born in 1943, is an American conceptual artist whose mediums run from video, installation, sculpture and performance to site-specific projects, photography and photo text, and who writes about art and culture as part of the same practice. Her subject is everyday life and the public sphere, usually approached with an eye to women's experience, so that the household and the roles assigned inside it become political territory. War and the media are a recurring concern, as is architecture and the built environment: housing, homelessness, transport systems, and the places people merely pass through. She is a university teacher and a television producer as well as an artist, and the writing has carried as much weight as the video work. The connection her work keeps making is between the domestic interior and the state outside it.

nancyspero.blurb: Political, feminist painting and hand-pulled prints.
nancyspero.bio: Nancy Spero, born in 1926 and died in 2009, was an American visual artist known for political and feminist paintings and for hand-pulled art prints. She was a draughtsperson and a women's rights activist as well, and the activism was never a separate career from the art. The work took its subjects from politics, from power and from the treatment of women, and printmaking put those subjects into a form that could be repeated and circulated rather than sold once. Hand-pulling the prints kept the making slow and physical, and gave the images a route out of the gallery. Her career ran through the decades in which feminist art established itself as a movement with institutions of its own, and she belongs among the artists who insisted that political content and formal seriousness were not alternatives.

barbarakruger.blurb: Red, white and black, text over image.
barbarakruger.bio: Barbara Kruger, born in 1945, is an American conceptual artist and collagist, one of the Pictures Generation. Her best-known works are black-and-white photographs overlaid with flat declarative captions, set in Helvetica Ultra Condensed or in Futura Bold Oblique, white on red. The phrases turn on pronouns: you, your, I, we, they. That grammar is the mechanism, because it forces the viewer into the sentence and makes them take a position on the questions the work raises about power, identity, consumerism and sexuality. She has worked in photography, sculpture, graphic design and architecture as well as video and audio installation, and the work scales easily from a printed page to the side of a building. Another, from 2008, is among the later pieces, and the address has not softened with time.

cindysherman.blurb: Every character in her photographs is her.
cindysherman.bio: Cynthia Morris Sherman, born in 1954, is an American artist who works almost entirely in photographic self-portraiture, appearing in her pictures as a succession of imagined characters, in contexts she builds herself, acting as director, stylist, subject and photographer at once. The result is a body of work full of women who do not exist, assembled out of the visual conventions through which women are usually pictured. In Buffalo in the 1970s she was together with Robert Longo, and with him and Charles Clough she co-founded Hallwalls in 1974, an artist-run space of the kind that produced much important American work of that decade outside the gallery system. Her photographs became one of feminist art's central cases: the self-portrait that steadily refuses to disclose a self.

jennyholzer.blurb: Words in public, delivered in light.
jennyholzer.bio: Jenny Holzer, born in 1950, is an American neo-conceptual artist who lives in Hoosick, New York, and whose subject is the delivery of words and ideas into public space. She has used large-scale installations, advertising billboards, projections thrown across the faces of buildings and other structures, and electronic displays lit at civic scale, taking over the formats of commerce and announcement for language that is not selling anything. That choice puts the work in front of people who did not decide to look at art, which is largely the point of it. She is credited as a painter, sculptor and draughtsperson too, but the medium that defines her is text at civic scale. Green Table dates from 1992. Grouped here with feminist art, she turns public messaging against itself.

guerrillagirls.blurb: Anonymous feminists auditing the art world.
guerrillagirls.bio: The Guerrilla Girls formed in New York City in 1985, an anonymous collective of feminist women artists set against sexism and racism in the art world. The group came directly out of a picket mounted the year before at the Museum of Modern Art, a protest rather than a manifesto, and the pattern held. Anonymity is method as much as protection: with no individual names attached, the argument cannot be shrunk to one woman's grievance or one career's disappointment. The core of the work has been to bring gender and racial inequality into focus, first inside the greater arts community and then across society at large, holding institutions to their own numbers. They have kept at it for decades, and the questions they put to museums have proved harder to retire than to answer.

robertkushner.blurb: A founder of Pattern and Decoration.
robertkushner.bio: Robert Kushner, born in 1949, is an American contemporary painter and printmaker known above all for his part in Pattern and Decoration, and he has been called a founder of it. From 1975 he built it with Miriam Schapiro and the artists who argued that ornament, textile pattern and decorative beauty had been wrongly ruled out of serious painting, a position taken directly against the austerity of the minimal and conceptual work that dominated the preceding decade. His own practice runs from large-scale public mosaics to delicate paintings made on the pages of antique books, and he makes installations across a variety of mediums alongside the canvases. 4 Seasons Seasoned dates from 2004. Pattern and Decoration overlapped closely with feminist art, since the crafts it rehabilitated were largely those historically assigned to women.

joycekozloff.bio: Joyce Kozloff, born in 1942, is an American painter and printmaker whose work runs from easel-scale pattern painting to murals and public art installations. She belonged to the founding circle of Pattern and Decoration, the movement she helped establish alongside Miriam Schapiro, which set ornament and the decorative against the austerity of late modernism. Kozloff was also an early figure in the 1970s feminist art movement: she helped start the Heresies collective, and she joined the Guerrilla Girls under the pseudonym Liubov Popova. Works such as New England Decorative Arts, completed in 1985, show her characteristic weaving of decorative traditions into architectural settings. Her career makes the case that the decorative was never a lesser category, only an undervalued one, and that public space is a proper place for a painter to work.

valeriejaudon.blurb: Between pattern, abstraction and public space.
valeriejaudon.bio: Valerie Jaudon, born in 1945, is an American painter and printmaker whose work sits at the meeting point of several postminimal tendencies. She emerged with Pattern and Decoration, the 1970s grouping of artists who put ornament, repetition and the decorative back into serious painting at a moment when American abstraction had grown severe. Jaudon has also worked extensively in site-specific public art, making pieces conceived for particular buildings and spaces rather than for the neutral gallery wall, and her painting has continued to track new tendencies in abstraction rather than settling into a single manner. Commentators tend to describe her practice through that range of associations rather than through any one label, which is perhaps the most accurate summary of it: a body of work that has kept its structural rigour while refusing the idea that pattern and seriousness are opposites.

kimmacconnel.bio: Kim MacConnel, born in 1946, is an American artist who works across painting, sculpture and mixed-media collage, often using fabric as both surface and subject. He studied at the University of California, San Diego, taking a BA with honours in 1969 and an MFA, also with honours, in 1972. Through the seventies he was a central figure in Pattern and Decoration, the movement that answered minimalism's restraint with bright colour, repeated motifs and the visual habits of furnishing and textile design. Cut and reassembled cloth, painted surfaces and constructed objects all belong to his vocabulary. His work has since ranged well beyond the movement it is usually filed under, to the point where the category has stopped being a useful description of it, though the appetite for pattern, colour and the decorative object has stayed constant throughout.

parkseobo.bio: Park Seo-bo, born in 1931 and died in 2023, was a South Korean painter and the central organising figure of Dansaekhwa, Korea's monochrome painting tendency. He came up through the Korean Art Informel movement of the postwar years before arriving at the Écriture series, the long sequence of works on which his reputation rests and in which drawing, mark and surface are treated as one continuous act. From 1975 he organised the exhibitions that grouped a set of independent painters — among them Ha Chong-hyun and Chung Sang-hwa — under a shared banner, which is how Dansaekhwa came to be legible as a movement at all. Lee Ufan, based in Tokyo, became its theorist and broker abroad, carrying the work to audiences outside Korea. Park's formal concerns have led critics and historians to place him at the head of that generation.

hachonghyun.bio: Ha Chong-hyun, born in 1935, is a South Korean painter best known for Conjunction, the series he began in 1974 and has continued ever since, and which established him as a leading practitioner of Dansaekhwa, the Korean monochrome tendency. That reputation slightly undersells him: from the 1960s onward his real subject has been materiality itself, and the arc of his practice is a long sequence of experiments in what a painting can be made of and how far the conventions of art making will bend. He was grouped with Park Seo-bo, who from 1975 organised the exhibitions that gave Dansaekhwa its shape as a movement, and the two are usually named together as its founding figures. The restraint of the finished surfaces conceals an unusually stubborn appetite for testing the physical limits of the medium.

yunhyongkeun.blurb: Umber and ultramarine soaked into linen.
yunhyongkeun.bio: Yun Hyong-keun, born in 1928 and died in 2007, was a South Korean painter who graduated from Hongik University and became associated with Dansaekhwa, the Korean monochrome movement. His signature works are made by letting burnt umber and ultramarine blue bleed into raw canvas or linen, the pigment smearing and soaking rather than sitting on the surface, in a way critics have read as a Korean temper of reflection and meditation. His closest tie within the movement was familial: Kim Whanki was his father-in-law, a relationship that gave Dansaekhwa something as near to a direct lineage as it had. The restraint of the work is deceptive — the staining is a slow, physical process, and the paintings register the time and the absorbency of the cloth as much as any decision about composition.

chungsanghwa.bio: Chung Sang-hwa is a painter placed within Dansaekhwa, the Korean monochrome tendency, and named among its founding figures alongside Park Seo-bo. That affiliation is the whole of what the material assembled for this entry will honestly support. The biographical record filed under the name belongs to a different person working in another field altogether, and its dates, occupations and credits have therefore been set aside in full rather than laundered into a plausible-sounding life story. No birth year, no training, no exhibitions and no individual paintings are claimed here. What remains is the placement itself, which is not nothing: it puts him inside the group of Korean painters who made surface, repetition and process the substance of the picture rather than its background. A proper account waits on a source that actually describes the painter.

kwonyoungwoo.blurb: A painter of the Dansaekhwa generation.
kwonyoungwoo.bio: Kwon Young-woo is a painter placed within Dansaekhwa, the Korean monochrome tendency, and that placement is the only claim this entry can support. The reference material gathered under the name describes someone else entirely, in a field with no connection to painting, so none of its dates, training or achievements have been carried across. What is left is the affiliation: a painter working among the Korean artists who treated the handling of the support — its surface, its absorbency, the repetition of a single act across it — as the substance of the work rather than a means to an image. Any account of his life, his materials or his individual paintings must wait for a source that documents them. Leaving the gap visible is better than filling it with invention that would read as fact.

ohyoon.blurb: Grouped with Korea's postwar painting movements.
ohyoon.bio: Oh Yoon is a Korean painter filed here under the heading that gathers Dansaekhwa and Minjung art, the two poles of Korean painting after the war: one turned toward monochrome surface and material, the other toward politics, history and the people. Which of them his work belongs to is not something the material assembled for this entry can settle. The record filed under the name describes a different person in another field, so its dates, credits and affiliations have been set aside in full, and no birth year, training, exhibitions or individual works are claimed here. The placement is the claim, and deliberately the only one. It is worth stating even so, because the argument between those two positions is the argument Korean painting of the period was having with itself.

shinhakchul.bio: Shin Hak-chul is a South Korean painter and one of the representative figures of Minjung art, the people's art of Korea that turned painting toward politics and history. He trained in oil painting and spent the 1970s applying modernist technique to realist subject matter, an unusual combination at the time, and out of it he built, from the 1980s onward, a distinctive kind of history painting. His best-known works are photo collages and montages that assemble images of Korea's modern and contemporary past into compositions addressing social injustice directly rather than by allusion. Where the Dansaekhwa painters of the same decades pursued the monochrome surface and the material of painting itself, Shin's side of Korean art insisted that a picture could carry an argument about the country it was made in. His work remains one of the clearest statements of that position.

minjoungki.bio: Min Joung-ki is a Korean painter grouped here under the heading that covers Dansaekhwa and Minjung art — the monochrome and the politically engaged sides of Korean painting. Beyond that grouping, the material collected for this entry identifies the wrong person: the dates, nationality and career it carries belong to a performer rather than a painter, and none of it has been used. That leaves no birth year, no training, no exhibitions and no titled works that can honestly be set down here. What can be said is the placement, and why it matters — Korean painting of the period is usually told as an argument between abstraction and engagement, and Min's name appears inside that argument. A proper account of the work waits on a source that actually describes it.

georgbaselitz.bio: Georg Baselitz, born in 1938 and died in 2026, was a German-Austrian artist: painter, sculptor, and graphic artist. He became widely known in the 1960s for figurative paintings of raw expressive force, and then in 1969 made the decision that defined everything after: he began painting his subjects upside down, a device meant to break the hold of content and subject matter and force attention onto the artifice of the picture itself. He drew on an unlikely range of sources — Socialist Realism, Mannerism, African sculpture — and fused them into a language recognisably his own. The inversion was never a joke or a trademark but a working method, kept for decades because it made the surface rather than the story the thing being looked at. Folk Thing Zero, dated 2009, is among his later works.

anselmkiefer.blurb: Straw, ash and lead against history.
anselmkiefer.bio: Anselm Kiefer, born in 1945, is a German painter and sculptor who trained under Peter Dreher and Horst Antes as the 1960s closed. From 1970 he visited Joseph Beuys regularly and treated him as his teacher, though he never formally enrolled — an informal apprenticeship that shows in his willingness to load a painting with matter. Straw, ash, clay, lead and shellac enter the work directly, so that the surface behaves less like a picture than like a scorched field or a ruined wall. The poems of Paul Celan gave him a way into his central subjects, German history and the horrors of the Holocaust, and the spiritual concepts of Kabbalah supplied another; The Seven Heavenly Palaces is among the works listed under his name. Few artists of his generation have insisted so stubbornly that painting is obliged to remember.

jorgimmendorff.blurb: Painted Germany's division as his subject.
jorgimmendorff.bio: Jörg Immendorff, born in 1945 and died in 2007, was a German painter and sculptor who also designed for the stage and held an art professorship, and a member of the Neue Wilde. He entered the Düsseldorf Academy in 1963 and studied under Joseph Beuys. From 1976 he worked with A. R. Penck across the Berlin Wall, the two of them collaborating between East and West at a time when that was neither simple nor safe; Georg Baselitz and the dealer Michael Werner helped move the resulting work westward. Immendorff's own career took in stage design and teaching as well as painting, and his listed works include a 1999 piece titled Hans Albers. The divided Germany was not a backdrop to his painting but its subject, and the Penck collaboration turned that division into a working method rather than a lament.

markuslupertz.bio: Markus Lüpertz, born in 1941, is a German painter and sculptor who is also a graphic artist and writer, runs a magazine and plays jazz piano. His subjects carry a suggestive power and an archaic monumentality: he insists on seizing the thing represented with an archetypal statement of its existence rather than a description of its appearance. That approach places his work within neo-expressionism, alongside the other German painters who forced the figure back into serious art. A long line of named works runs through the career, from Der gestürzte Krieger of 1987 to Mercury of 2007, Apoll of 2009 and Wilhelm Busch of 2016. Known for his eccentricity as much as for the work, he has been styled by the German press as a painter prince, and he remains among the best-known German artists of his generation.

arpenck.blurb: Sign-like figures smuggled out of the GDR.
arpenck.bio: A. R. Penck, born Ralf Winkler in 1939 and died in 2017, was a German painter and printmaker who also made sculpture and played jazz drums, and who worked for years inside the German Democratic Republic under an assumed name. His flat, sign-like figures, often described as reminiscent of so-called primitive art, became one of the recognisable marks of neo-expressionism. The Cologne dealer Michael Werner showed him in the West and got his paintings physically out of East Germany, and from 1976 he collaborated with Jörg Immendorff across the Wall, with Georg Baselitz and Werner moving the work westward. He later taught at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, where Yoshitomo Nara was among his students between 1988 and 1993. The pictures look immediate, almost offhand, but they were made under conditions that gave every mark a political weight it would not otherwise carry.

sigmarpolkeandgerhardrichter.bio: This pairing joins two German painters; the record gathered here covers Gerhard Richter, born in 1932. Richter is a visual artist who has moved between apparently incompatible modes — photorealist canvases derived from photographs on one side, large abstractions on the other — along with photographs and works in glass, including the Cathedral Window of 2007. He has taught as well as painted, and the refusal to settle into a single signature style has itself become his signature. He counts among the most important German artists working today, and his work has repeatedly set auction records, at one point making him the most expensive living painter. Sigmar Polke is named alongside him here as the other half of the pairing, though no further verified detail about Polke is carried in this entry, and none has been invented to fill the space.

salome.blurb: Neue Wilde painter and punk singer.
salome.bio: Salomé, born in 1954, is a German artist known as one of the Junge Wilde, the group of young painters also called the Neue Wilde. He works as a painter, sculptor and performance artist, and he is equally recognised as a punk singer — a double life entirely typical of a scene that moved freely between studio and stage. Museums and collections around the world hold his paintings, and his listed works include the rainbow stele of 2000. Salomé's reputation rests on the combination rather than on any single strand of it: the same energy runs through the canvases, the objects and the performances, and pulling them apart misses what the work was for. Among the German painters of that generation, he is one of the few whose practice never settled inside the frame.

rainerfetting.bio: Rainer Fetting, born in 1949, is a German painter and sculptor who has also worked as an illustrator and photographer. He is placed within neo-expressionism, the return to bold, gestural figuration in German art that set itself against the cooler conceptual and minimal work preceding it. The range of media attached to his name suggests an artist who never treated painting as a closed practice, and his listed works include Der Steiger, dated 2000. Beyond that outline, the documented record gathered for this entry is unusually thin: the biographical detail that surrounds better-catalogued members of his generation has not been assembled here. Rather than fill the gap with plausible-sounding invention, this account keeps to what can be stated with confidence — the medium, the moment, and the fact of a long working life.

helmutmiddendorf.bio: Helmut Middendorf is a German painter placed with the neo-expressionists, the generation that pushed bold, gestural figuration back to the centre of German art against the cooler conceptual and minimal work preceding it. That placement is as far as this entry can honestly go. The reference material filed under his name reproduces another painter's record — another German artist of the same milieu, with his dates, his listed occupations and his titled works — so none of it has been carried across, and no birth year, exhibitions or individual pieces are claimed here. The mix-up illustrates a real hazard for painters of a crowded movement: shown in the same rooms and printed in the same catalogues, they get filed together and then confused. A source describing Middendorf's own work would settle it.

elvirabach.bio: Elvira Bach, born in 1951, is a German painter known for vivid, high-colour images of women, painted again and again with an assurance that turns the female figure into a recurring emblem rather than a passive subject. She was a member of the Junge Wilde, the young German painters who pushed figuration back to the centre in a deliberately raw, saturated register, and she has continued to live and work in Berlin. Alongside painting she has worked as a sculptor and serigrapher. Her two children include the basketball player Maodo Lô. Bach's presence in the Junge Wilde matters to the history of the group, which is usually told through its men; her insistence on the female figure, painted by a woman, gives that history a strand it is rarely credited with.

lucianocastelli.bio: Luciano Castelli, born in 1951, is a Swiss artist who paints, makes graphic work, photographs, sculpts and plays music, and who is placed here among the neo-expressionists — the loose international generation that brought figuration, colour and performance back into painting. The range of media in his listing is the most telling thing the record holds: someone who moves between canvas, camera, printed image, sculpture and music is unlikely to have treated any one of them as the main event. Sources also describe him as a conceptual and visual artist, which suggests a practice sitting closer to idea-driven work than the neo-expressionist label alone would imply. Beyond that outline the documented detail assembled for this entry is thin, and rather than fill it with plausible-sounding invention, this account stops where the evidence does.

achillebonitooliva.bio: Achille Bonito Oliva, born in 1939, is an Italian critic and historian of contemporary art who has taught at La Sapienza in Rome since 1968. He is the man who named the Transavanguardia, coining the term in 1979 for the direction taken by a set of Italian painters at the end of that decade — Mimmo Paladino, Nicola De Maria, Enzo Cucchi, Francesco Clemente and Sandro Chia — and then promoting them relentlessly through his writing. It is one of the clearest cases in late twentieth-century art of a critic supplying the frame that made a group legible and saleable. He has organised and curated a long list of exhibitions and events, and in 1993 served as artistic director of the Venice Biennale. His prolific writing on contemporary artists has kept him at the centre of Italian art debate for decades.

francescoclemente.blurb: Transavanguardia's traveller between Italy and India.
francescoclemente.bio: Francesco Clemente, born in 1952, is an Italian artist who has lived at different times in Italy, India and New York, and whose work carries the traces of all three; the traditional art and culture of India in particular runs through it. He has worked in drawing, fresco, mosaic, graphics, oils and sculpture, moving between them with unusual ease. In the 1980s he was one of the principal figures of the Transavanguardia, the Italian tendency named and promoted from 1979 by the critic Achille Bonito Oliva, which rejected formalism and conceptual art in favour of a return to figuration and symbolism. In 1984 he made three-way paintings with Jean-Michel Basquiat and Andy Warhol, a collaboration that set the Italian revival of the figure directly alongside the New York downtown scene. He remains one of the most widely travelled imaginations of his generation.

sandrochia.bio: Sandro Chia, born in 1946, is an Italian painter and sculptor who also works as a printmaker and illustrator. He was one of the principal members of the Italian neo-expressionist group that the critic Achille Bonito Oliva baptised the Transavanguardia in the late 1970s and early 1980s, together with Mimmo Paladino, Nicola De Maria, Enzo Cucchi and Francesco Clemente. The name mattered as much as the painting: Bonito Oliva's championing gave five independent artists a shared identity and an international audience at the moment they most needed one. What the label gathered was a shared return to the figure, the common ground of the neo-expressionism his work is filed under. Chia has kept sculpture and printmaking running alongside the canvases, and he remains one of the most visible survivors of the Italian eighties, a decade whose reputation has swung more sharply than most.

enzocucchi.bio: Enzo Cucchi, born in 1949, is an Italian painter who also works as a sculptor, printmaker and installation artist. He was among the artists gathered under the Transavanguardia, the label supplied by the critic Achille Bonito Oliva, who championed him and in doing so made the tendency legible as a movement — one of the clearest cases in recent Italian art of a critic providing a frame that a set of independent painters then occupied. Cucchi's range across painting, sculpture, print and installation is characteristic of that grouping, which treated the boundaries between media as no more binding than the one it had already crossed in turning back toward the figure. The documented record collected for this entry is otherwise slight: beyond his birth year, no exhibitions and no individual titles can be set down here with confidence.

mimmopaladino.blurb: Transavanguardia's sculptor of horses and doors.
mimmopaladino.bio: Mimmo Paladino, born in 1948, is an Italian sculptor, painter and printmaker, and a leading name in the Transavanguardia, the Italian group named by the critic Achille Bonito Oliva, who championed his work. He belongs to the wider set of European artists who revived Expressionism in the 1980s, and unlike some of his contemporaries he pushed that revival firmly into three dimensions. Hortus Conclusus of 1992 and the Door of Europe of 2008 are among his major works, and the horse recurs across his output in pieces including Cavallo blu. He has also designed jewellery, a range of activity that fits the group's indifference to hierarchies of medium. His commissions have given that Italian revival a physical presence in civic space which the painting alone could never have supplied.

julianschnabel.bio: Julian Schnabel, born in 1951, is an American painter who became a filmmaker. In the 1980s he drew international attention for his plate paintings, in which broken ceramic is set into large-scale canvases so that the surface itself becomes an obstacle. His reputation was made by the dealer Mary Boone, whose shows in 1979 and 1981 established him almost overnight, and by Charles Saatchi, who bought his work in bulk in the early 1980s and then sold it in bulk — a lesson in how quickly a market can be made and unmade. From the 1990s onward he has argued for independent arthouse cinema. He directed Before Night Falls, which gave Javier Bardem his Academy Award-nominated breakthrough, and The Diving Bell and the Butterfly, which received four Academy Award nominations and won him Best Director at Cannes and a Golden Globe.

davidsalle.bio: David Salle, born in Norman, Oklahoma in 1952, is an American painter, printmaker, photographer and stage designer usually placed among the postmodernists. He took both a BFA and an MFA at the California Institute of the Arts, where he studied with John Baldessari in the Post-Studio class — a course built on the premise that an artist's job was to think about existing images rather than simply make new ones. Salle's own work came to public attention in New York in the early 1980s, and the dealer Mary Boone represented him from 1979, which placed him early inside the New York gallery system. Stage design has run alongside the painting, and East Hampton, New York, is where he lives and works. His generation's argument about whether a picture could still be sincere runs directly through his canvases.

ericfischl.bio: Eric Fischl, born in 1948, is an American painter and sculptor who also works as a printmaker and draughtsman and is listed as an educator. He is known above all for the paintings of American suburbia he made in the 1970s and 1980s, work that took the ordinary middle-class world as a subject worth the full attention of a serious realist. That choice set him slightly apart from the neo-expressionists he is usually grouped with, whose material was history, myth and the wreckage of Europe rather than the domestic interior. His contribution to American painting of the period was to insist that the suburb was not a backdrop but the place where the country's private life actually happened, and that it could be painted without either mockery or sentiment.

jeanmichelbasquiat.blurb: From SAMO tags to Neo-Expressionist stardom.
jeanmichelbasquiat.bio: Jean-Michel Basquiat, born in 1960 and died in 1988, was an American painter whose success arrived in the 1980s with neo-expressionism. He began on the street: between 1977 and 1979 he and Al Diaz wrote the tag SAMO© across SoHo. He met Keith Haring through the Club 57 and Mudd Club scene, and the two remained close enough that Haring wrote his obituary. The dealer Annina Nosei gave him a studio in the basement beneath her gallery in 1981, and Bruno Bischofberger brokered the collaboration with Andy Warhol that produced around 150 joint canvases between 1984 and 1985; a three-way set with Francesco Clemente followed in 1984. Almost every turn in that career came through a person rather than an institution, which is exactly how the downtown scene worked and why it moved so fast.

keithharing.blurb: Chalk subway drawings became a language.
keithharing.bio: Keith Allen Haring, born in 1958, was an American artist and activist whose bold graphic imagery hardened into a visual language recognised almost everywhere. He came up through the downtown art and graffiti scenes of New York in the early 1980s, and the chalk drawings he made in the subway turned into a career celebrated far beyond the city — one that held street art and Pop art together. In 1978 he shared rooms at the School of Visual Arts with Kenny Scharf, and through the Club 57 and Mudd Club scene he met Jean-Michel Basquiat, for whom he later wrote an obituary. Tseng Kwong Chi photographed the subway drawings as they were made, which is why work meant to be temporary survives at all. Tuttomondo and Together We Can Stop AIDS, both from 1989, and The Boxers of 1987 carried that language into public space and activism.

paularego.blurb: Portuguese folk tales, painted in pastel.
paularego.bio: Dame Paula Rego, born in 1935 and died in 2022, was a British-Portuguese visual artist and printmaker, widely held to be the outstanding woman artist of the late twentieth century and the early twenty-first. Her style travelled the opposite way from most of her generation's, moving from abstraction toward representation rather than away from it, and for much of her career she favoured pastel over oil — a medium that let her draw and paint in the same stroke and gave the figures their dry, chalky physicality. Much of the work is built on storybooks and the folk themes of her native Portugal, retold with a feminist edge that turns familiar narratives against themselves. She made her career in Britain while keeping Portugal as her subject, and the combination gave figurative painting one of its most unsettling and most durable bodies of work.

miquelbarcelo.bio: Miquel Barceló Artigues, born in 1957, is a Spanish painter and sculptor who also works as a ceramicist and printmaker. He is grouped here with the neo-expressionists, the international generation that brought the figure, heavy materials and a physical approach to the surface back into painting. The ceramics matter to that placement: an artist who works in clay as well as oil tends to treat a painting as a substance to be handled rather than an image to be composed. Among his listed works is Gran Elefant dret, dated 2009. Beyond that outline the documented detail assembled for this entry is thin, and rather than fill the gaps with plausible-sounding invention this account stops where the evidence does — a painter and sculptor whose practice has never sat still in a single material.

christopherlebrun.blurb: Painter who led the Royal Academy.
christopherlebrun.bio: Sir Christopher Mark Le Brun, born in 1951, is a British artist known primarily as a painter, though sculpture and printmaking have run alongside the painting throughout. He served as President of the Royal Academy of Arts from 2011 until December 2019, and a knighthood followed in the 2021 New Year Honours, "for services to the arts" — an institutional career pursued in parallel with the studio rather than instead of it. Works listed under his name include Union (Horse with Two Discs) of 1999 and City Wing of 2013. Le Brun belongs to the British side of the figurative revival that ran through European painting in his generation, a quieter version of the turn than the German or Italian one. Few painters have combined studio work and public office so evenly.

futura2000.bio: Leonard Hilton McGurr, born in 1955 and known first as Futura 2000 and later simply as Futura, is an American artist who came up through graffiti. He is listed as a graffiti artist, painter and graphic designer, and that combination describes the path a number of writers of his generation took: from the street into the studio and then into commercial design, without treating any of those moves as a betrayal of the others. His work belongs to the moment when graffiti stopped being purely an illicit practice and started to be shown, sold and argued about as art. The record gathered for this entry is otherwise thin — exhibitions, collaborations and individual works are not securely documented here — so this account keeps to what can be said with confidence about a career spanning all three roles.

ladypink.blurb: Ecuadorian-born pioneer of New York graffiti.
ladypink.bio: Lady Pink, born in 1964, is an American graffiti and mural artist, born in Ecuador and working in New York. Her reputation rests on her involvement in the New York City graffiti movement that ran through the late 1970s and the 1980s, the period the practice is still dated from. The record names her twice over, as a graffiti artist and as a muralist, and the pairing is the point rather than a change of career: one vocabulary, carried from illicit surfaces onto commissioned walls, with nothing disowned on the way. Painting is the medium listed against her name, and it covers both halves of that work equally well. Accounts of the period keep returning to her involvement, which is the clearest claim the evidence assembled here will actually support.

leequinones.bio: George Lee Quiñones, born in 1960, is a Puerto Rican artist and actor who rose to prominence painting New York City subway cars on a massive scale, whole carriages carrying his moniker LEE. The work is rooted in popular culture and often carries a political message, which set it apart from writing that was primarily about the letterform and the signature. He has also worked as an actor, one of several figures from the graffiti scene who crossed into film as wider attention arrived. Quiñones belongs to the generation that turned an illegal practice into an acknowledged art form, and his trains are among the reasons that case could be argued at all: at that size and that level of finish, the work asked to be judged as painting rather than as vandalism.

rammellzee.bio: Rammellzee, born in 1960 and died in 2010, was a New York visual artist, graffiti writer, painter, sculptor, performance artist, art theoretician and hip-hop musician. He worked under the banner of Gothic Futurism, and treated theory as part of the practice rather than as commentary on it — the writing, the objects and the records were versions of a single argument. He has been credited with carrying elements of the avant-garde into hip-hop culture, which is an unusual thing to be able to say about anyone: he worked on both sides of a divide that most people at the time treated as impassable. The graffiti came first, but the career that followed refused every category it was offered, including the ones invented for artists who refuse categories.

sherrielevine.bio: Sherrie Levine, born in 1947, is an American photographer, painter and conceptual artist. A strand of her work consists of exact photographic reproductions of photographs by other people — Walker Evans, Eliot Porter, Edward Weston — presented as her own, a manoeuvre that raises questions about originality, authorship and who owns an image, and answers none of them politely. She was among the artists gathered by the critic Douglas Crimp for Pictures at Artists Space in 1977, the exhibition that named the tendency and gave a loose set of practices a shared identity. Levine's version of appropriation is the most literal and therefore the hardest to argue with: nothing has been added, nothing transformed, and the entire content of the work is the act of taking. She paints and draws as well, and the logic stays the same.

richardprince.bio: Richard Prince, born in 1949, is an American artist who came to prominence in the East Village in the 1980s, working across conceptual and pop registers. His method is rephotography and appropriation: he takes existing commercial images — models, living room furniture, watches, pens, jewellery — and re-presents them, so that the subject of the work becomes American popular culture's own way of picturing desire. The approach has made him one of the most argued-over artists of his generation and, according to The New York Times, one of the most revered. Major survey exhibitions have followed at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1992, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam in 1993, the Museum für Gegenwartskunst in Basel, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, and the Serpentine Gallery in London in 2008.

robertlongo.blurb: Men in the Cities, writhing figures.
robertlongo.bio: Robert Longo, born in 1953, is an American artist, filmmaker, photographer and musician who became widely known in the 1980s for Men in the Cities, the series of drawings and prints in which figures in sharp office dress twist and buckle in contorted emotion. Before that he was in Buffalo, where in 1974 he co-founded the artist-run space Hallwalls with Charles Clough; Cindy Sherman, then his partner, was part of the same circle, and the two of them were together in Buffalo through the 1970s. Douglas Crimp included him in Pictures in 1977, the show that gave his generation's work a name and a frame. Longo has since worked in film and music as well as on paper, and lives between New York and East Hampton. Hallwalls remains one of the more consequential things a group of students ever founded.
