jackgoldstein.bio: Jack Goldstein, born in Canada in 1945 and died in 2003, was a performance and conceptual artist based first in California and then in New York, who turned to painting in the 1980s. He studied with John Baldessari in the Post-Studio class at CalArts, the course that trained a generation to treat existing images as raw material rather than to make pictures from scratch. Douglas Crimp selected him for Pictures in 1977, the exhibition that named the tendency and gathered a loose set of practices under a single heading. His shift into post-conceptual painting in the following decade followed the same instinct at larger scale, and the description that has stuck to him — a conceptualist who became a painter — captures the unusual shape of a career that changed medium without changing its mind.

louiselawler.bio: Louise Lawler, born in 1947, is an American artist and photographer based in Brooklyn. Her subject is other people's art: she photographs paintings hanging on museum walls, works in the opulent homes of collectors, pieces being installed in galleries, sculptures being looked at by spectators. The attention falls on the spaces the works occupy and the methods used to place them as much as on the art itself, so what she records is the apparatus that turns an object into an artwork — the lighting, the wall, the ownership, the act of looking. That places her within the appropriation strand of her generation, though her method is quieter than most: nothing is altered or restaged, only noticed. The pictures document a system that ordinarily prefers not to be photographed.

douglascrimp.blurb: Curated the show that named Pictures.
douglascrimp.bio: John Douglas Crimp, born in 1944 and died in 2019, was an American art historian, critic and curator, and an AIDS activist. In 1977 he organised Pictures at Artists Space, the exhibition that named a tendency and gave Sherrie Levine, Robert Longo and Jack Goldstein a frame their work has been read through ever since — one of the clearest cases of a curator making a movement legible. Between 1977 and 1990 he ran the journal October as its managing editor, at the centre of the American argument about postmodern theory. His writing ranged across institutional critique, dance, film, queer theory and feminist theory, marked throughout by a conviction that politics, art and academia belonged together rather than apart. At the University of Rochester he held the Fanny Knapp Allen chair in art history and taught visual and cultural studies.

peterhalley.bio: Peter Halley, born in 1953, is an American artist who stood at the centre of the Neo-Conceptualism of the 1980s, the New York tendency also known as Neo-Geo, which put conceptual argument back inside apparently formal painting. His canvases are built from hard-edged geometry in Day-Glo colour, a palette borrowed from signage and industry rather than from the history of abstraction. Halley has written as much as he has painted, and for years published index Magazine, which gave him a platform outside the gallery system. He has taught as well, running graduate studies in painting and printmaking at the Yale School of Art between 2002 and 2011. New York City is where he lives and works, and his standing in contemporary art rests as much on the writing and the teaching as on the paintings.

jeffkoons.bio: Jeffrey Lynn Koons, born in 1955, is an American artist whose subject is popular culture and whose best-known sculptures are everyday objects rebuilt at scale — balloon animals fabricated in stainless steel with a mirror finish, so that the viewer and the room appear in the surface. He keeps studios in New York City and in York, Pennsylvania, the town he grew up in. Puppy of 1992, Kiepenkerl of 1987 and the mid-1990s pieces Balloon Flower and Tulips are among the works listed under his name. He belongs to the Neo-Geo and commodity art moment, which took the object as merchandise for its subject, though his career long outran that label. His work has repeatedly set records at auction: 58.4 million dollars for Balloon Dog (Orange) in 2013 and 91.1 million for Rabbit in 2019.

haimsteinbach.bio: Haim Steinbach, born in 1944, is an artist of Israeli and American nationality, based in New York, whose work consists of arrangements of everyday objects set out on Displays and shelves he makes himself. The shelf is not neutral furniture in his hands; it is the work, and the choice of what to put on it and how to space it does everything a composition would do in a painting. That practice made him a central figure in the commodity art and Neo-Geo moment, when a group of New York artists turned their attention to the object as merchandise rather than as sculpture. Steinbach's version is the most patient of them: nothing is altered, nothing is fabricated in the usual sense, and the entire argument rests on selection and placement. He has worked in that register for decades.

ashleybickerton.bio: Ashley Bickerton, born in Barbados in 1959 and died in 2022, was an American contemporary artist who worked in mixed media, combining photographic and painterly elements with assemblages of industrial parts and found objects. The results looked less like paintings than like packaged units — objects that acknowledged their own status as commodities to be crated, shipped and sold. That put him at the centre of Neo-Geo, the early 1980s movement he shared with Jeff Koons and Peter Halley, which took the visual languages of abstraction and commerce and refused to keep them apart. What those objects set aside was the idea of a picture as a window, and the blunt honesty of the results — art as product, with the labels attached — has aged better than much of the decade's irony.

allanmccollum.bio: Allan McCollum, born in 1944, is an American artist who has lived and worked in New York City since 1975 — the year the Whitney Biennial included his work and he moved to the city. By the late 1970s he was especially well known for the Surrogate Paintings, objects that occupy the place of a painting without being one, produced in numbers so that the individual example matters less than the system generating it. That interest in mass production and uniqueness has run through everything since, including Allégories de McCollum of 2000 and The Shapes Project of 2005. It also explains his place alongside the commodity artists: where they took existing goods, he manufactured his own and made the manufacturing visible. Few artists have looked so steadily at what happens to an artwork when there are thousands of it.

eddiechambers.bio: Eddie Chambers, born in Britain in 1960, has worked on both sides of the gallery wall, as an artist and as the curator and art historian who assembled the record of what Black British artists were making. In 1979, still a teenager, he helped found the BLK Art Group in Wolverhampton with Keith Piper; Marlene Smith and Donald Rodney belonged to the same founding circle, and between them they gave Black British art an organised centre of gravity. Chambers has also championed Rasheed Araeen, the figure behind the journal Third Text, founded in 1987, and the 1989 exhibition The Other Story. His academic post is the David Bruton, Jr. Centennial Professorship in Art History, held at the University of Texas at Austin, where the history he helped make is also the history he now teaches.

keithpiper.blurb: Artist, curator and critic of Black Britain.
keithpiper.bio: Keith Piper, born in 1960, is a British artist who also works as a curator, critic and academic. He helped found the BLK Art Group, the groundbreaking association of Black British art students formed in Wolverhampton in 1979 with Eddie Chambers and based mostly in the West Midlands — a self-organised network that gave a generation of young Black artists a platform at a time when the British art establishment offered them almost none. Piper has worked across photography, painting and sculpture, and his roles as critic and curator have meant that he helped write the history of the movement as well as make it. That double position, practitioner and commentator, is characteristic of the group, which understood from the start that being shown was not the same as being understood.

lubainahimid.blurb: Curated Black women artists into view.
lubainahimid.bio: Lubaina Himid, born in 1954, is a British artist and curator who holds the chair of contemporary art at the University of Central Lancashire. Her painting works on cultural history and on reclaiming identities the official record left out. Curating has been just as central to that project: in 1985 she organised The Thin Black Line at the ICA, the exhibition that put Sonia Boyce and Claudette Johnson in front of a national audience and made the case that Black women artists in Britain were not a footnote to anyone else's movement. Her partner Maud Sulter was also her collaborator on exhibitions and publishing, a working relationship that ran alongside the personal one. Himid's influence is best measured by how many other careers she helped make possible.

soniaboyce.bio: Sonia Boyce, born in 1962, is an educator and a British Afro-Caribbean artist who has made London her base, and who holds the professorship of Black Art and Design at University of the Arts London. She came to wider notice through Lubaina Himid's exhibition The Thin Black Line at the ICA in 1985, which put her and Claudette Johnson in front of a national audience. Since 1990 her practice has turned decisively towards collaboration, handing much of the work over to the improvisation and unplanned performance of the people she invites in. She moves freely between drawing, print, photography, video and sound, drawn to how sound and memory bear on one another, to the dynamics of a space, and to the part the spectator plays in it. Alongside all this she has taught fine art studio practice at art colleges across Britain.

marlenesmith.blurb: A founder of the BLK Art Group.
marlenesmith.bio: Marlene Smith, born in 1964, is a British artist and curator, and one of the founding members of the BLK Art Group in the 1980s. She helped start it with Eddie Chambers, and the group gave a generation of young Black British artists a platform of their own at a moment when the mainstream offered them very little. Smith has worked on both sides of that history: as a painter, and as a curator responsible for how the work of the period is shown and understood. That second role matters as much as the first, since the story of the BLK Art Group has depended on people willing to organise exhibitions, gather material and keep the record straight. Her career sits at the point where making art and framing it meet.

donaldrodney.blurb: The BLK Art Group's restless inventor.
donaldrodney.bio: Donald Rodney, born in 1961, was a British painter and multimedia artist and one of the leading figures of the BLK Art Group, which he helped found with Eddie Chambers in the 1980s. He worked by appropriation, pulling images out of the mass media, art and popular culture and recombining them so that questions of racial identity and racism surfaced inside material everyone already recognised. He moved between painting and other media with unusual freedom, and was later described as one of the most innovative and versatile artists of his generation. He died in 1998, and the body of work he left has grown steadily in influence since. Among the artists of that circle he remains the one whose formal restlessness has proved hardest for anyone else to imitate.

isaacjulien.blurb: The moving image as Black British art.
isaacjulien.bio: Isaac Julien, born in 1960, is a British installation artist and filmmaker whose work sits close to the centre of Black British art. He came to the moving image at a moment when a generation of Black artists in Britain was building its own platforms, and he took film and installation as his tools rather than painting or sculpture. Working as both artist and director, he treats the moving image as something to be built into a space, not simply projected at a seated audience, so that the viewer moves through a work instead of sitting in front of it. He was later knighted, and he teaches as a Distinguished Professor of the Arts at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Few artists of the period are so equally at home in the gallery and the cinema.

rasheedaraeen.blurb: Engineer turned sculptor, critic and champion.
rasheedaraeen.bio: Rasheed Araeen, born in Karachi in 1935, is a conceptual artist, sculptor, painter, writer and curator who has lived in London since arriving from Pakistan in 1964. He trained first as an engineer, taking a civil engineering degree at the NED University of Engineering and Technology in 1962, and a structural logic stayed with him when he turned to sculpture. Ever since, he has worked at the join between life, art and activism, refusing to keep them in separate rooms. In 1987 he founded the journal Third Text, and in 1989 he assembled The Other Story, an exhibition that pressed the case for Black British artists within the account of postwar British art. Both projects gave Eddie Chambers and his contemporaries a platform, and both changed what British art history was willing to include.

huangyongping.blurb: Xiamen's provocateur, later a French citizen.
huangyongping.bio: Huang Yong Ping, born in Xiamen in Fujian province in 1954, was one of the most influential figures of the Chinese avant-garde before making his later career in France. His work was deliberately provocative and experimental, setting Chinese and Western traditions against one another and questioning the political and cultural norms of both. Gao Minglu included him in China/Avant-Garde in Beijing in February 1989, the exhibition that gathered the generation of the 85 New Wave into a single room and into public view. Later pieces such as The Overturned Tomb of 1994, 100 Arms of Guanyin of 1997 and Serpent d'ocean of 2012 show how far he pushed scale and irreverence once he was working internationally. He died in 2019, a French citizen and a Chinese artist in every argument his work made.

xubing.blurb: The printmaker who rebuilt written language.
xubing.bio: Xu Bing, born in 1955, is a Chinese artist whose training as a printmaker underlies almost everything he has made since. He is best known for taking language apart, words, characters and text itself, and rebuilding it into installations that unsettle the way a viewer assumes meaning arrives. Gao Minglu selected his Book from the Sky for China/Avant-Garde in Beijing in 1989, placing him at the centre of the generation that came out of the 85 New Wave. He went on to serve as vice-president of the Central Academy of Fine Arts, and teaches internationally as an A.D. White Professor-at-Large at Cornell University. A MacArthur Fellowship in 1999 and the Fukuoka Prize in 2003 marked how far the work had travelled. Few artists have made the plain mechanics of reading feel so strange.

guwenda.bio: Gu Wenda, born in 1955, is a Chinese artist who has lived and worked in New York for much of his career. He belongs to the generation that came up through the 85 New Wave, and like several of his contemporaries he took the most venerable materials of Chinese culture, calligraphy and classical poetry, as things to be questioned rather than preserved. Much of his work uses human hair, massed into forms that carry the look of writing while refusing to settle into readable text. The combination is deliberately uncomfortable: script that promises meaning, made from the most personal material a body leaves behind. Working between China and the United States, he has spent decades testing how much of a tradition survives translation, and how much of it is carried in the body rather than the page.

wangguangyi.blurb: Cultural Revolution imagery meets brand logos.
wangguangyi.bio: Wang Guangyi, born in 1957, is the painter most closely identified with Political Pop, the label the critic Li Xianting attached to the Chinese art that emerged after 1989. His Great Criticism series sets the propaganda imagery of the Cultural Revolution years, 1966 to 1976, directly against the logos of Western consumer brands, so that two systems of persuasion end up sharing a canvas. The paintings are usually read as satire, though Wang has described his aim as reviving a socialist spirit rather than mocking it, which leaves the work harder to settle than it first appears. Li Xianting's championing helped make him a leader of the new art that started in China after 1989, and the Great Criticism format became one of the most recognisable images to come out of that shift.

fanglijunandyueminjun.bio: Fang Lijun and Yue Minjun are the two painters most often paired under the banner of Cynical Realism, the tendency that took shape in Chinese art in 1989. Yue Minjun, born in 1962 and based in Beijing, is known for oil paintings of himself frozen mid-laugh, a grin repeated until it stops reading as happiness at all. He has carried the same figure into sculpture, watercolour and print, and the 2009 work A-maze-ing Laughter takes it into three dimensions. He is wary of the Cynical Realist label without much minding who uses it. Fang Lijun's paintings of the same years are read alongside his, and the two names have travelled together ever since, a shorthand for a generation that answered the aftermath of 1989 with faces rather than slogans.

zhangxiaogang.blurb: Family portraits with unnerving dark eyes.
zhangxiaogang.bio: Zhang Xiaogang, born in 1958, is a Chinese painter whose work is usually described as symbolist or surrealist, though its power comes from something plainer: the family photograph. His Bloodline series, largely monochrome, stages stiffly posed portraits of Chinese sitters with large dark-pupilled eyes, deliberately recalling the studio family pictures of the 1950s and 1960s. Painted in the years after the 85 New Wave, they turn private memory into public history, and the resemblance between one face and the next becomes the point. More recently he has translated the characters of the Bloodlines Big Family paintings into sculpture, giving three dimensions to figures that had only ever existed as flat, frontal likenesses. He is among the most sought-after Chinese artists of his generation, and among the few whose signature image still unsettles.

aiweiwei.blurb: The Stars group's most defiant survivor.
aiweiwei.bio: Ai Weiwei, born in 1957, is a Chinese artist, documentarian and activist whose politics began at home: his father, the poet Ai Qing, was sent into internal exile, and the son was raised in consequence in China's far northwest, where conditions were harsh. In 1979 he was among the founders of the Stars group in Beijing, alongside Ma Desheng and Wang Keping, the first collective to push publicly against official Chinese art. Since then he has worked across sculpture, architecture, design and film, with pieces such as Sunflower Seeds of 2010 reaching enormous audiences. His investigations into government corruption, particularly the collapse of the so-called tofu-dreg schools in the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, made him a target: in April 2011 he was arrested at Beijing Capital International Airport for alleged economic crimes and held for eighty-one days without charge.

bhupenkhakhar.bio: Bhupen Khakhar, born in 1934, was an Indian painter and a member of the Baroda Group. He won international recognition as India's first Pop artist, a description that pointed at his willingness to take popular imagery and ordinary life as fit subjects for painting at a time when Indian modernism was largely looking elsewhere. From 1976 he was close friends with Howard Hodgkin, and the friendship worked in both directions: Hodgkin's visits to India and Khakhar's own exhibitions in Britain both grew out of it and kept it going. That connection helped make him one of the first Indian painters of his generation to be seen properly abroad rather than treated as an exotic guest. He died in 2003, and his standing among younger South Asian figurative painters has kept rising since.

nalinimalani.bio: Nalini Malani, born in 1946, is an Indian artist who belongs to the first generation in her country to work with video. She came to it from painting and printmaking, and that grounding shows: the moving-image work is built by someone used to thinking in layers, marks and surfaces rather than in shots. Working through the decades when Indian contemporary art was finding an international audience, she helped establish that a South Asian artist could take up new media without abandoning the traditions of drawing behind them. Her position matters as much for what it opened as for what it made, since younger Indian artists took the possibility of video for granted partly because she did not. She remains one of the defining figures of Indian contemporary art.

vivansundaram.blurb: Made his aunt's archive his subject.
vivansundaram.bio: Vivan Sundaram, born in 1943, was an Indian artist who moved through painting, sculpture, printmaking, photography, installation and video without treating any of them as home. His work was politically conscious and densely intertextual, returning to social problems, popular culture, memory and the unreliability of what we think we see. Family history ran through it too: the painter Amrita Sher-Gil was his aunt, since his mother Indira was Amrita's younger sister, and Sundaram turned the family archive into his own material, reworking its photographs rather than simply preserving them. He was married to the art historian and critic Geeta Kapur, and the pair sat at the intellectual centre of Indian contemporary art for decades. He died in 2023, having spent a career linking India's modernist past to its contemporary practice.

arpitasingh.blurb: Miniature traditions turned toward women's lives.
arpitasingh.bio: Arpita Singh, born in 1937, is an Indian painter, a figurative artist and a modernist who fills her canvases with something between a story and a crowd. Her pictures hold both a story and a crowd of figures set down in a quietly subversive order, so that what looks decorative at first glance turns out to be doing something else entirely. She draws steadily on Indian traditions, the conventions of miniature painting and of folk art, and folds them into a contemporary practice rather than quoting them from a distance. Much of her subject matter comes from her own background and from what she observes around her, particularly the pressures society places on women. Her approach has been described as an expedition without a destination, which is as good an account as any of how the paintings unfold.

rummanahussain.bio: Rummana Hussain, born in 1952, was an Indian conceptual, visual and performance artist who moved from painting into installation and multimedia at a moment when few artists in India were working that way. Her mature work concentrated on female subjectivity as it is caught inside the discourses of family, religion, nationalism and welfare, not as abstract theory but as the everyday pressure those systems exert on a life. Performance was central to it, which made the argument harder to keep at arm's length. She also worked as a television producer, and something of that medium's directness carries into the installations. Her career was short: she died in 1999, just as Indian contemporary art was finding the international audience her work had anticipated.

zarinahashmi.bio: Zarina Hashmi, who worked simply as Zarina, was born in 1937 and spent her career in New York City as an Indian American printmaker and artist. She worked across drawing, printmaking and sculpture, and is associated with minimalism, though her use of it was unusual: the abstract and geometric forms she pared her work down to were meant to produce a spiritual response rather than a purely formal one. Line, paper and the printed mark carried the weight, and the restraint was the means rather than the message. Working in New York from a South Asian background, she occupied a position for which the art world of her lifetime had few categories, and she declined to make it easier by explaining herself. She died in 2020.

davidwojnarowicz.bio: David Wojnarowicz, born in 1954, was a painter, photographer, writer, filmmaker and performer at the centre of New York's East Village art scene, and one of the fiercest artist-activists of the AIDS crisis. Peter Hujar was briefly his lover and then his closest friend; when Hujar died in 1987, Wojnarowicz photographed his death, an act of witness that set the terms for much of what followed. He worked in whatever medium was to hand, paint, film, text, performance and recorded song, and pushed his own life into all of it, so that personal narrative and political fury became inseparable. He died of AIDS-related illness in 1992. His images and his writing remain the most unguarded first-person record the epidemic produced in American art.

felixgonzaleztorres.blurb: Grief built from candy and clocks.
felixgonzaleztorres.bio: Felix Gonzalez-Torres, born in Cuba in 1957, studied in Puerto Rico and worked in New York from 1979. He built a body of conceptual art out of ordinary things, strings of light bulbs, paired clocks hung side by side, stacks of paper and individually wrapped candies, arranged with a minimalist's restraint and loaded with everything minimalism kept out. He joined Julie Ault's collective Group Material in 1987 and stayed until 1991, and he worked through the same New York activist graphics culture as Avram Finkelstein and ACT UP. Ross Laycock was his partner from 1983 to 1991, and the candy spills visitors are invited to deplete and the clocks that drift out of step are about his death. His dealer Andrea Rosen later became the executor administering the certificates that let the work exist at all. He died in Miami in 1996.

granfury.bio: Gran Fury was an AIDS activist artist collective that emerged from ACT UP in New York in 1988, borrowing the hard, plain graphic language of a public campaign and turning it on a government that was letting people die. Its eleven members, among them Avram Finkelstein, Tom Kalin, Marlene McCarty, Donald Moffett, Loring McAlpin, John Lindell, Richard Elovich, Amy Heard, Michael Nesline, Mark Simpson and Robert Vazquez-Pacheco, worked collectively and largely without individual credit, so that the message rather than the authorship carried the work. Pieces such as Let Them Die in the Streets of 1990 were made to be read at a glance and to make silence hard to maintain. The decision to work as a collective was itself political, refusing the artistic signature the 1980s art market prized above all else.

actup.blurb: The AIDS activism behind the art.
actup.bio: ACT UP is the AIDS activist movement from which much of the queer art in this part of the map came. It appears here not as a studio but as a context: the organising, the protests and the graphics culture that shaped a generation of American artists working through the epidemic.

robertmapplethorpe.blurb: Classical form applied to forbidden subjects.
robertmapplethorpe.bio: Robert Mapplethorpe, born in 1946, was an American photographer whose black-and-white pictures brought an almost classical sense of form to whatever he pointed the camera at: celebrity portraits, male and female nudes, still lifes, and himself. His most contested images documented the gay male BDSM subculture of New York in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and it was the collision of that content with such controlled, formal photography that his critics found hardest to answer. Patti Smith was first his lover and then his lifelong friend, and she later told the story of their years together in Just Kids. The curator and collector Sam Wagstaff was his partner and the financier of his career, buying him the time and the standing to make the work. He died in 1989.

damienhirst.blurb: Organised Freeze; ran the YBA decade.
damienhirst.bio: Damien Hirst, born in 1965, studied at Goldsmiths from 1986 to 1989 under Michael Craig-Martin, and in August 1988, while still a student, organised Freeze in an empty Port of London Authority building at Surrey Docks. Mounted with Angus Fairhurst, Mat Collishaw, Anya Gallaccio, Michael Landy and Fiona Rae, the exhibition is where the Young British Artists effectively begin. With Fairhurst and Sarah Lucas he formed the trio at the social centre of that scene. Charles Saatchi funded The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living in 1991 and staged Sensation in 1997, and the alliance carried Hirst through the decade until frictions ended it in 2003. Later works range from Verity of 2012 to Hydra and Kali of 2016. He is reportedly Britain's richest living artist.

traceyemin.blurb: Confession as material: neon, thread, bed.
traceyemin.bio: Tracey Emin, born in 1963, makes work out of her own life without apology, moving between neon text, sewn applique, sculpture, film, photography, painting and drawing depending on what a given confession needs. In 1993 she and Sarah Lucas ran The Shop in Bethnal Green together, selling things they had made themselves and turning a retail unit into the social hub of a scene. Jay Jopling's White Cube took her on, and in 2000 Charles Saatchi bought My Bed, the work that made her famous well beyond the art world. Cast as the enfant terrible of the Young British Artists, she has long outlasted the label: she was elected a Royal Academician in 2016 and continues to make large-scale work such as The more of you the more I love you of 2017.

sarahlucas.blurb: Bawdy puns built from found objects.
sarahlucas.bio: Sarah Lucas, born in 1962, came out of Goldsmiths, where Michael Craig-Martin taught her, and emerged with the Young British Artists in 1988. Her work runs on visual puns and bawdy humour, assembled from photography, collage, sculpture and found objects, with whatever household thing can be made to stand in for a body. The jokes are exact rather than loose: a substitution that looks crude at first turns out to be precisely the right one. With Damien Hirst and Angus Fairhurst she formed the trio at the social centre of the YBA world, and in 1993 she and Tracey Emin ran The Shop in Bethnal Green, an operation that was half business and half artwork. Few artists of her generation have got so much out of so little material.

rachelwhiteread.blurb: Casts the space things leave behind.
rachelwhiteread.bio: Rachel Whiteread, born in 1963, is an English sculptor who works almost entirely by casting, taking the space inside and around ordinary things and making it solid. The method turns absence into mass: what you look at is the shape of what is no longer there. In 1993 she became the first woman to win the Turner Prize, at a moment when the Young British Artists were reshaping what British sculpture could look like, though her work has always been quieter and more architectural than most of that company. Her Judenplatz Holocaust Memorial, completed in 2000, applies the same logic at civic scale, where an inverted interior becomes a public monument. She has since been made a Dame, and her casts remain among the most immediately legible sculptures of her generation.

garyhume.bio: Gary Hume, born in 1962, studied at Goldsmiths under Michael Craig-Martin and came to prominence with the Young British Artists in the early 1990s. He was the painter in a generation better known for vitrines, neon and found objects, and he held that position without apology, keeping colour and surface at the centre of his practice while the scene around him chased shock. He has worked in sculpture as well, as in Liberty Grip of 2008. He divides his time between London and Accord, New York, and the distance from the London art world appears to suit work that has stayed deliberately unhurried. Among the artists Craig-Martin taught at Goldsmiths, Hume is the one who kept faith with painting throughout.

chrisofili.bio: Chris Ofili, born in 1968, is a British painter who builds his pictures out of materials that have no business sharing a surface: oil paint, resin, glitter, beads, cut-outs from pornographic magazines and lumps of elephant dung. The results have been called punk art, though the craft involved is closer to devotional painting than to anything thrown together in a hurry. He won the Turner Prize in 1998, at the height of the Young British Artists' visibility, and his work sat awkwardly and productively inside that moment, decorative where the scene was blunt and layered where it was literal. He now lives and works in Trinidad. Among the painters of his generation he is the one who made ornament carry an argument.

jakeanddinoschapman.bio: Jake and Dinos Chapman are British artists and brothers who worked for years as the Chapman Brothers, making sculpture and painting designed to be difficult to look at and harder to dismiss. Their work went into the Young British Artists showcases Brilliant! and Sensation in the mid-1990s, placing them squarely inside the decade's appetite for provocation, and in 2003 they were nominated for the Turner Prize, losing to Grayson Perry. Their tactics have often been appropriative: in 2008 they produced a series built on original watercolours by Adolf Hitler, altering the objects themselves rather than merely quoting them. Their painting One Day You Will No Longer Be Loved III became the subject of Derren Brown's Channel 4 programme The Great Art Robbery in 2013. With the Chapmans the provocation is the argument, not the packaging.

marcquinn.blurb: Blood, marble and the human body.
marcquinn.bio: Marc Quinn, born in 1964, is a British sculptor who came up with the Young British Artists and has spent his career on the question of what being human means in the world today, working through the body, genetics, identity, the environment and the way the media handles all four. His materials swing wildly by design, from blood, bread and flowers to stainless steel and marble, and the choice of substance usually carries as much meaning as the form does. Works such as Sphinx of 2006 and 12,5% Proof show how far that range stretches. He has held solo exhibitions at Sir John Soane's Museum, Tate, the National Portrait Gallery, the Fondation Beyeler, the Fondazione Prada and the South London Gallery, a spread of venues that says something about how widely the work reads.

gillianwearing.bio: Gillian Wearing, born in 1963, is an English conceptual artist who emerged with the Young British Artists and won the Turner Prize in 1997. Where much of that generation traded in shock, her subject has been other people: how they present themselves, and who gets represented at all. Both of her best-known public commissions follow from that. A Real Birmingham Family puts an ordinary family where a civic monument would normally stand, and her statue of the suffragist Millicent Fawcett was installed in London's Parliament Square in 2018. She was elected a lifetime member of the Royal Academy of Arts in 2007 and holds a CBE. Her career traces the route from the conceptual gestures of 1990s British art to sculpture standing in the country's most political square.

nicolasbourriaud.bio: Nicolas Bourriaud, born in 1965, is a French critic and curator who has made a career of naming what artists were already doing. He began in criticism before turning to curating in 1990, and in 1996 he assembled Traffic at the CAPC in Bordeaux, the exhibition out of which the idea of relational aesthetics came. Rirkrit Tiravanija, Philippe Parreno, Pierre Huyghe, Dominique Gonzalez-Foerster and Liam Gillick were all in it, and the term he coined for their work, art whose material is human relations and social context, became one of the most argued-over ideas of the following decade. He went on to nominate other tendencies too, among them Altermodern. From 1999 to 2006 he co-founded and co-directed the Palais de Tokyo in Paris alongside Jerome Sans.

rirkrittiravanija.blurb: Cooks, and calls the room art.
rirkrittiravanija.bio: Rirkrit Tiravanija, born in Buenos Aires in 1961, is a Thai artist who divides his time between New York, Berlin and Chiang Mai. His installations tend to be rooms rather than objects: places to cook and share a meal, to read, to play music, with the gathering itself as the work. Nicolas Bourriaud put him in Traffic at the CAPC in Bordeaux in 1996, the exhibition that produced relational aesthetics, and Tiravanija became its most quoted example. From 1994 the dealer Gavin Brown was his collaborator as much as his representative, which suited an art that needed accomplices rather than a display system. In 1998 he and Kamin Lertchaiprasert founded The Land Foundation in Chiang Mai, a long-term project deliberately set outside the gallery economy.

philippeparreno.bio: Philippe Parreno, born in 1964, is a French artist based in Paris whose work spans film, installation, performance, drawing and text. He was among the artists in Nicolas Bourriaud's Traffic in 1996, the show from which relational aesthetics emerged, and his practice has always treated the exhibition as something closer to a script than a display. In 1999 he and Pierre Huyghe bought the manga character Annlee and then lent her out to other artists to use, a shared figure passed between hands until she had a body of work of her own. It remains one of the sharpest arguments about authorship any artist made in the 1990s, and it depended entirely on collaboration, which is the through-line of Parreno's career.

pierrehuyghe.bio: Pierre Huyghe, born in 1962, is a French artist who works across film, sculpture, public intervention and living systems, works that continue to grow and change after the artist has stepped away. He was in Nicolas Bourriaud's Traffic in 1996, the exhibition that gave rise to relational aesthetics, though his own practice pushed past the social encounter towards something less centred on human company. In 1999 he and Philippe Parreno bought the manga character Annlee and then lent her to other artists, turning a piece of intellectual property into a shared protagonist and a question about who owns a fiction. He is now based in Santiago de Chile. His art keeps asking what happens when a work is given its own life and left to run.

dominiquegonzalezfoerster.bio: Dominique Gonzalez-Foerster, born in 1965, is a French artist and educator who works in video projection, photography and installation, and who has also worked in landscaping, design and writing. Nicolas Bourriaud included her in Traffic in 1996, the exhibition that produced relational aesthetics, and she remains one of the artists most closely associated with that circle. What holds her varied practice together is a preference for processes she does not yet know how to carry out: she has said she looks for experimental methods, likes beginning without knowing how, and finds that exhibitions too rarely leave room for that kind of learning. The result is a body of work that resists a signature style, built instead around the pleasure of not being fluent yet.

liamgillick.bio: Liam Gillick, born in 1964, took a fine art degree at Goldsmiths and in the 1990s belonged to the loose group around the Young British Artists, though his work went in a different direction from most of theirs. He was among the artists in Traffic at the Musee d'art contemporain in Bordeaux in 1996, the exhibition where Nicolas Bourriaud first proposed his concept of relationality, and Gillick's work has been read against that idea ever since. He is a sculptor, a painter and a maker of installations, and the conceptual framing of a piece tends to matter as much as the object standing in the room. He lives in New York, at one remove from the London art school that formed him.

carstenholler.bio: Carsten Holler, born in 1961, is a Belgian-born artist who lives and works in Stockholm. He is associated with the relational tendency, in which the public became the material of a work rather than its audience, and his pieces typically ask a visitor to do something, to enter, to move, to submit to an apparatus, instead of merely looking at it. Test Site of 2006 is the best known of them, and the title is exact about the terms it sets. The framing is deliberate: an exhibition set up as an experiment, with conditions and subjects, is a very different proposition from a display. What results is work that only fully exists while somebody is using it, which makes any documentation of it faintly beside the point.

berndandhillabecher.bio: Bernd Becher and Hilla Becher, born Hilla Wobeser, worked as a single artistic unit, photographing industrial buildings and structures and arranging the results in grids so that the differences between near-identical forms became visible. They called these typologies, and the discipline behind them was absolute, each structure recorded under the same conditions as the last. Their example founded what is now called the Becher school, or the Dusseldorf School of Photography, and through it they shaped generation after generation of documentary photographers working in Germany and well beyond it. They received both the Erasmus Prize and the Hasselblad Award. Few artists have exerted so much influence by insisting on so little variation, or made a stricter case that a photograph could be a piece of systematic description rather than a personal impression.

andreasgursky.bio: Andreas Gursky, born in 1955, is a German photographer who arrived at the Kunstakademie Dusseldorf in 1981, after studying at the Folkwangschule, and entered Bernd Becher's class. He became a Meisterschuler in 1987, and the Becher training, the frontal view, the levelled discipline, the belief that a photograph could be a piece of systematic description, stayed in his work long after his subjects moved away from industrial structures. He later taught at the same academy as a professor, closing the loop between the school that formed him and the one that formed the generation after. Of all the photographers to come out of the Dusseldorf School, he is the one whose pictures have travelled furthest into the general public awareness.

thomasstruth.blurb: Left Richter's painting class for photography.
thomasstruth.bio: Thomas Struth, born in 1954, began at the Dusseldorf Academy in Gerhard Richter's painting class before switching to Bernd Becher and photography, a move that says a good deal about how porous that school was in the 1970s. His black-and-white photographs of the streets of Dusseldorf and New York, made in that decade, apply Becher rigour to the city rather than to industrial plant. He went on to the Museum Photographs, which turn the camera on people looking at art, and to a long series of family pictures. Struth lives between Berlin and New York. Of the Becher students he is the one most interested in the act of looking itself, what a viewer does in front of a picture, and how a family arranges itself for one.

thomasruff.bio: Thomas Ruff, born in 1958, studied under Bernd Becher at the Dusseldorf Academy from 1977 to 1985 and has lived and worked in Dusseldorf since. He took the Becher discipline in the least expected direction: rather than photographing the world more precisely, he began working with pictures that already existed, editing, reworking and reimagining found images until the question of what a photograph actually records becomes unanswerable. He has been described as a master of the edited and reimagined image, and the phrase fits a career that has treated each new technology as another way of interrogating the medium. Among the Dusseldorf School photographers he is the one who turned the school's objectivity into a set of questions rather than a method to be followed.

candidahofer.bio: Candida Hofer, born in 1944, studied under Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Dusseldorf Academy and became one of the most disciplined photographers to come out of that school. She began with portraiture and moved to the spaces themselves, libraries, museums, the interiors that institutions build for their own purposes, photographing them with a technical perfection that leaves nothing accidental in the frame. Her approach is strictly conceptual: the subject is not a room's beauty but the way institutional architecture shapes and directs the people who pass through it. Where the Bechers catalogued industry, Hofer catalogues culture's own housing, and the accumulated series makes an argument no single picture could. She has taught as well, carrying the Dusseldorf method into another generation.

axelhutte.bio: Axel Hutte, born in 1951, is a German photographer and one of the principal representatives of the Dusseldorf School of Photography. He studied under Bernd Becher at the Dusseldorf Academy, among the group of photographers who carried the Bechers' methods away from the industrial subject matter that had defined them. Hutte belongs to that first generation of Becher students whose work established the school as a school rather than a studio, a shared discipline of clarity, distance and seriality that could be applied to almost any subject. Less publicly visible than some of his contemporaries, he has kept to the rigour they were all taught, which is why his name still appears whenever the Dusseldorf School is described from the inside.

takashimurakami.bio: Takashi Murakami, born in 1962, is the artist at the centre of Superflat and its argument: that the traditions of Japanese painting and the visual culture of postwar Japan share a compressed, depthless space, and that the line between fine art and commercial art is not worth defending. He runs his practice as a studio operation, the Hiropon Factory, later Kaikai Kiki, and brought artists including Chiho Aoshima into it, producing their work alongside his own. That structure has let him move between gallery painting and mass-market design without changing register, from sculpture and film to album covers for Kanye West's Graduation in 2007, Kids See Ghosts in 2018 and The Party Never Ends, released after Juice Wrld's death, in 2024. Few artists have been so deliberate about occupying both economies at once.

yoshitomonara.bio: Yoshitomo Nara, born in 1959, is best known for paintings of big-headed girls whose piercing stare turns cuteness into something less comfortable, childlike expressions carrying adult emotions, kawaii with a dark streak, and cultural references tangled up with personal memory. He studied at the Kunstakademie Dusseldorf from 1988 to 1993 under A. R. Penck, and those German years sit oddly and productively behind an art usually read as entirely Japanese. He has held nearly forty solo exhibitions since 1984, and his work is held by the Museum of Modern Art and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. He lives and works in Nasushiobara in Tochigi Prefecture, at a deliberate distance from Tokyo. The pictures look simple and are not: one figure, one expression, and decades of variation inside it.

chihoaoshima.blurb: An economics graduate turned Superflat painter.
chihoaoshima.bio: Chiho Aoshima, born in 1974, studied economics: she graduated from the Department of Economics at Hosei University in Tokyo. Takashi Murakami hired her into the Hiropon Factory, which became Kaikai Kiki, and she has been a member of the collective since, one of the artists whose work made Superflat a shared idiom rather than one man's style. Her pictures belong to the Japanese pop lineage the group defined, and a residency at Artpace in San Antonio in 2006 was an early step into showing outside Japan. That a painter so identified with the group should have come to it with a degree in economics says something about how that generation of Japanese artists arrived at art, and how much the collective itself did the shaping.

marikomori.blurb: Casts herself as a future being.
marikomori.bio: Mariko Mori, born in 1967, is a Japanese multidisciplinary artist who puts herself at the centre of her own photographs and videos, appearing in a series of guises as a hybridised version of a future self. Traditional Japanese motifs run through the imagery alongside the surfaces of advanced technology, so that ritual and machinery end up sharing a frame. The recurring themes are technology, spirituality and transcendence, and she pursues them without irony. The guises are neither costume drama nor parody: the future self is offered as something to take seriously, a figure in which ritual survives its own technological upgrade. Working on a track entirely her own, she has made some of the most ambitious image-making in Japanese contemporary art.

yayoikusama.bio: Yayoi Kusama, born in 1929, works primarily in sculpture and installation but has never stayed inside a single discipline, moving through painting, performance, video, fashion, poetry and fiction as the need arises. Her art is conceptual at its base and carries traces of feminism, minimalism, surrealism, art brut, pop and abstract expressionism without belonging to any of them. What holds it together is the autobiographical, psychological and sexual material she has never disguised. Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg were among the contemporaries her work influenced, and pieces such as Shangri-La Tulips carry the same repeating vocabulary into three dimensions. She is now recognised as one of the most important artists Japan has produced, the top-selling female artist in the world, and the most commercially successful living artist of any kind.

billviola.bio: Bill Viola, born in 1951, was an American video and installation artist who used electronic image and sound technology to reach the oldest subjects available: birth, death and the workings of consciousness. He came to the medium from the inside, working as a technician at the Everson Museum in Syracuse, where he installed Nam June Paik's early video exhibitions, a practical apprenticeship in a form that barely existed yet. What he built from it was slower and more contemplative than most video art of the period, less interested in the television set than in what a moving image could do to a viewer standing in a dark room. He died in 2024, by which time video had gone from experimental oddity to standard museum medium, a shift his work did much to bring about.

garyhill.blurb: Video driven by language and philosophy.
garyhill.bio: Gary Hill, born in 1951, has been making video, installation, sculpture and performance since the late 1960s, and is one of the foundational figures in single-channel and multi-channel video and new-media art. His work touches conceptual art and minimalism but takes its direction from elsewhere: philosophical and literary texts matter more to him than the questions of representation, narrative and description that preoccupied the artists and filmmakers around him. He has used each new technology as it arrived, computer software, projection, virtual reality and CGI, to look at consciousness and its relation to the body, to perception, to time and to language, both spoken and seen. Across more than fifty years the tools have changed completely while the questions have not, which is why the earliest work still reads as current.

pipilottirist.blurb: Video made saturated, intimate and joyful.
pipilottirist.bio: Pipilotti Rist, born Elizabeth Rist in 1962, is a Swiss artist working in experimental video and installation. Her pieces are usually described as surreal, intimate and abstract, and they return again and again to the human body, filmed close, coloured up and set loose in ways documentary video never allowed. She began early: I'm Not the Girl Who Misses Much dates from 1986, Pickelporno from 1992, and Ever Is Over All, made in 1997, became one of the best-known video works of its decade. Later pieces such as Monochrome Rose of 2016 continue the same pleasure in saturated colour and enveloping projection. Rist's contribution was to make video art warm, funny and physically inviting at a moment when a great deal of it was cool and analytic.

matthewbarney.bio: Matthew Barney, born in 1967, is an American sculptor and filmmaker who works across sculpture, film, photography and drawing. His earliest pieces were sculptural installations bound up with performance and video, testing what a body can be made to do. Between 1994 and 2002 he built The Cremaster Cycle, five films threading together geography, biology, geology and mythology, which Jonathan Jones in The Guardian ranked among the most imaginative achievements in the history of avant-garde cinema. The later projects Drawing Restraint 9 in 2005, River of Fundament in 2014 and Redoubt in 2018 kept the same appetite for ritual, conflict and transformation. From 2000 to 2013 his partner was the musician Björk, who scored Drawing Restraint 9 and starred in it. Barney remains one of the most singular figures in American art.

dougaitken.blurb: Multimedia restlessness, from film to architecture.
dougaitken.bio: Doug Aitken, born in 1968, is an American multidisciplinary artist whose work refuses to settle into a single medium. Photography, print media and sculpture sit alongside architectural interventions; so do narrative film, sound, video in single and multiple channels, installation and live performance. He has also worked as a printmaker and a television producer. The through-line is not material but arrangement: images and sound placed in space so that an audience moves through the work rather than standing in front of it. He divides his time between Venice, California and New York City. Aitken belongs to the generation that carried video and installation out of the specialist gallery and into architecture, landscape and public life, and his practice is among the clearest demonstrations of how porous the borders between those forms became.

shirinneshat.blurb: Iran and the West, held together.
shirinneshat.bio: Shirin Neshat, born in 1957, is an Iranian artist based in New York who works chiefly in film, video and photography. Her art turns on contrasts, and on the ground between them: Islam set against the West, the feminine against the masculine, private life against public, antiquity against the modern. She treats the space in between less as a border than as somewhere to be inhabited. She works as a photographer, video artist, screenwriter and film director, and holds both Iranian and American nationality, a doubleness that runs through everything she chooses to look at. Within the late-century turn to video and installation, hers is among the most searching bodies of work about exile, gender and belief, made by an artist who addresses Iran from a distance and the West from inside it.

stevemcqueen.bio: Steve McQueen appears here among the artists of video, installation and new media, in the era this map calls Globalisation and the Contemporary, working with the moving image as gallery art rather than as cinema alone. Beyond that placement nothing can be stated with confidence, because the biographical record supplied for this entry belongs to somebody else. What arrived under the name is the file for Terrence Stephen McQueen, the American actor who lived from 1930 to 1980, a top box-office draw from the late 1950s to the mid-1970s, nicknamed the King of Cool, who raced under the alias Harvey Mushman. None of it describes the artist grouped here. No dates, works, exhibitions or associations are given for him, and none will be until the source material is corrected.

yinkashonibare.blurb: Batik cloth turned against the empire.
yinkashonibare.bio: Yinka Shonibare, born in 1962, is a British-Nigerian artist working as painter, sculptor and photographer on questions of cultural identity, colonialism and its aftermath within a globalised present. His hallmark is brightly coloured Ankara batik fabric, a material whose own tangled history of trade and imitation does much of the argument for him. Nelson's Ship in a Bottle, made in 2010, and Hibiscus Rising are among his best-known works. Paralysis down one side of his body means the making is carried out by assistants working under his direction, a division of labour he has never concealed. His career ran on the framework built by the curator Okwui Enwezor, whose journal Nka and whose biennial exhibitions gave artists of Africa and its diaspora a serious international stage.

ghadaamer.blurb: Embroidery as painting, desire as subject.
ghadaamer.bio: Ghada Amer, born in 1963, is an Egyptian American artist who works as a painter, embroiderer and sculptor, and whose subject is gender and sexuality. She is best known for layered embroidered paintings of women's bodies, in which pornographic imagery is redrawn in thread, so that a technique long dismissed as women's craft is made to carry pictures produced for the male eye. The tension between the two, needlework and painting, decoration and desire, is the engine of the work rather than its trim. Amer belongs to the generation of artists from Africa and its diaspora whose careers took shape as the international exhibition circuit widened, and her practice has kept feminist questions at the centre of contemporary painting rather than at its margins.

juliemehretu.blurb: Cities and histories, layered into abstraction.
juliemehretu.bio: Julie Mehretu, born in 1970, is an Ethiopian American painter and printmaker known for large, multi-layered canvases of abstracted landscape. Marks, architectural fragments and sweeping gestures accumulate in transparent layers until a surface reads like a city seen through its own history. What the paintings, drawings and prints register is the cumulative effect of urban and sociopolitical change rather than any single place. Scale is part of the argument, since the work asks to be walked along as much as looked at. She lives in New York and is married to the painter Jessica Rankin, the two of them building their careers in the same city. Mehretu sits at the centre of the contemporary conversation about what abstraction can be made to hold.

bodysisekkingelez.blurb: Cardboard cities from a Congolese visionary.
bodysisekkingelez.bio: Bodys Isek Kingelez, born in 1948 and also known as Jean Baptiste, was a Congolese sculptor who built models of fantastic cities from cardboard, paper, tape and other commonplace materials. The results are exuberant civic fantasies, an imagined architecture for a future assembled with ordinary supplies and extraordinary patience. His international career began with Magiciens de la Terre, the 1989 Paris exhibition organised by Jean-Hubert Martin, the first major show to put non-Western artists on an equal footing with their European contemporaries. From there his work travelled widely, to the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris, the Museum of Modern Art in New York and documenta XI in Kassel. He died in 2015, having made one of the most joyful bodies of work in modern sculpture.

cherisamba.blurb: Painting with the words left in.
cherisamba.bio: Chéri Samba, born in 1956 and known in full as Samba wa Mbimba N'zingo Nuni Masi Ndo Mbasi, is among the best-known contemporary painters from the Democratic Republic of Congo. His pictures almost always carry writing, in French and Lingala, that comments on African life and on the modern world; the words are part of the composition rather than a caption to it. He lives between Kinshasa and Paris. His paintings have entered the Centre Georges Pompidou and the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and a large number belong to Jean Pigozzi's Contemporary African Art Collection. He was invited to the Venice Biennale in 2007. His international career began at Magiciens de la Terre, Jean-Hubert Martin's exhibition of 1989.

seydoukeitaandmalicksidibe.blurb: Malian studio portraits in black and white.
seydoukeitaandmalicksidibe.bio: This entry pairs two Malian photographers. Malick Sidibé, born in 1935 in the Fulani village of Soloba, became the chronicler of popular culture in 1960s Bamako, working in carefully composed black and white. He had a long and fruitful career as a photographer there and was a well-known figure in his own community long before the wider art world noticed; his first exhibition outside Mali came only in 1994, and drew considerable critical praise. Honours followed: a Hasselblad Award in 2003, an International Center of Photography Infinity Award, and in 2007 a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, the first given to a photographer and the first to an African artist. He died in 2016. Seydou Keïta, his fellow Malian portraitist, is paired with him here.

williamkentridge.blurb: Charcoal drawings that move and erase.
williamkentridge.bio: William Kentridge, born in 1955, is a South African artist whose reputation rests on prints, drawings and animated films. The method he developed in the 1990s is the work itself: he films a drawing, erases and alters it, films it again, and repeats the process until a scene is finished, each change earning between a quarter-second and two seconds on screen. What survives is a palimpsest, a single sheet carrying the smudged ghosts of everything it has been, and those drawings are exhibited alongside the finished films. He also works as a theatre director and scenographer, and his long partnership with Adrian Kohler and Basil Jones of Handspring Puppet Company began with Woyzeck on the Highveld in 1992 and continued through the productions that followed.

kerryjamesmarshall.blurb: Black figures, painted into the canon.
kerryjamesmarshall.bio: Kerry James Marshall, born in Birmingham, Alabama in 1955 and moved in childhood to South Central Los Angeles, is an American painter and professor whose subject is the Black figure. He has spent much of his career in Chicago, where he held a teaching post in painting at the University of Illinois at Chicago's School of Art and Design, and he works as a draughtsman and collagist as well. In 2017 Time magazine placed him on its annual list of the hundred most influential people in the world. Marshall's insistence that Black figures belong in the great tradition, at full scale, on museum walls, has changed what a contemporary history painting can be and who is understood to be its subject.

gabrielorozco.bio: Gabriel Orozco, born in 1962, is a Mexican artist who built his reputation in the early 1990s through an exploration of drawing, photography, sculpture and installation, refusing to settle into any one of them. In 1998 the curator Francesco Bonami called him one of the most influential artists of the decade, and probably of the next one too. The influence was literal as well as critical: between 1987 and 1992 he ran the Taller de los viernes, a Friday workshop held in his Mexico City flat, where Damián Ortega, Abraham Cruzvillegas, Gabriel Kuri and Dr. Lakra worked through ideas alongside him. That informal school shaped a generation of Mexican artists, and stands as one of the clearest cases in this map of how a single room can seed a scene.

dorissalcedo.blurb: Grief given form in ordinary objects.
dorissalcedo.bio: Doris Salcedo, born in 1958, is a Colombian sculptor and installation artist who works with the most ordinary things: wooden furniture, clothing, concrete, grass, rose petals. Her subject is loss as Colombia has produced it, and it is not abstract to her, since her own relatives are among the many who have vanished in the country's political troubles. Her particular concern is the difference between a death, which can be mourned, and a disappearance, which leaves an emptiness with no shape. Common objects are given form until they hold that pain, making room for individual and collective mourning at once. Shibboleth, made in 2007, is among her best-known works. She lives and works in Bogotá, and the art stays rooted in the country whose history it carries.

vikmuniz.blurb: A Brazilian photographer with global reach.
vikmuniz.bio: Vik Muniz, born in 1961, is a Brazilian artist and photographer whose work has met with commercial success and critical acclaim alike, and has been exhibited worldwide. He works as a photographer, painter and film director, and the ease with which he moves between those roles is characteristic of him. He took part in the 24th International Biennale in São Paulo in 1998 and represented Brazil at the 49th Biennale in Venice in 2001, the pair of appearances that established him internationally; among his recent works is one titled 8 de janeiro de 2023. Muniz belongs to the group of Latin American artists gathered here whose careers were made by the biennial circuit, at the point when exhibitions outside Europe and North America began to set the terms.

ernestoneto.bio: Ernesto Saboia de Albuquerque Neto, born in 1964, is a Brazilian contemporary visual artist who works as a sculptor, painter, draughtsman and installation artist. His work belongs to the strand of Brazilian art in which sculpture is made to be entered rather than only looked at, and his titles carry the same unhurried, sensuous quality as the forms themselves: a piece of 2004 is called Celula Nave. It happens in the body of time, where truth dances. Neto came up in the generation of Latin American artists whose work reached international audiences through the biennial system, and he is among the Brazilian sculptors who made installation a language of touch and of the body rather than of statement, work that asks for a viewer's presence as much as a viewer's reading.

guillermokuitca.bio: Guillermo Kuitca, born in 1961, is an Argentine artist who still lives and works in Buenos Aires. Travel, maps, memory and migration recur throughout his painting, so that a canvas can read at once as a diagram and as an interior, a place charted rather than described. His pictures have travelled widely and belong to many important public collections, among them the Tate, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, the North Carolina Museum of Art, the Albright-Knox in Buffalo, the Daros Collection in Zürich and the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis. He represented Argentina at the 2007 Venice Biennale, and won Argentina's Konex Award in 1992 and again in 2002.

teresamargolles.blurb: Death examined as a social fact.
teresamargolles.bio: Teresa Margolles, born in 1963, is a Mexican conceptual artist who works as a photographer, videographer, performance artist and painter. Her subject is death, approached not as a private ending but as a social fact: she researches the causes that produce it and the consequences it leaves behind, following each back to the conditions that make it ordinary. The medium shifts between photograph, video and performance, but the line of enquiry does not. Margolles belongs to the generation of Latin American artists whose work travelled from local circumstance to international attention through the exhibition circuit of recent decades, and among them she is the one who has kept her attention fixed most steadily on what death does to a society over time.

ilyaandemiliakabakov.blurb: Conceptual art out of Soviet Moscow.
ilyaandemiliakabakov.bio: Ilya Kabakov, born in 1933 in Dnipropetrovsk in what was then the Ukrainian Soviet republic, was a conceptual artist who spent three decades working in Moscow, from the 1950s until the late 1980s, before emigrating to the United States and settling on Long Island. He worked as a painter, printmaker and sculptor. This map files him under the joint name Ilya & Emilia Kabakov, the form in which the work is listed here, including Looking Up. Reading the Words... of 1997. He died in 2023. A working life divided between the Soviet Union and America gives the entry its shape: three decades in Moscow, then a second career abroad, and a joint name under which the later work is now catalogued.

marinaabramovic.blurb: Endurance, presence, and the body's limits.
marinaabramovic.bio: Marina Abramović, born in 1946, is a Serbian conceptual and performance artist who has spent more than four decades using her own body as the material. The work tests endurance, what a body can be pushed to bear and what a mind can do with it, and above all the charged relationship between performer and audience. She has been described as perhaps the single most important figure in performance art, credited with reshaping the language of the form. From 1976 to 1988 she lived and worked with the artist Ulay; they ended the relationship by walking the Great Wall of China from opposite ends. Twenty-two years later the two were reunited during The Artist Is Present at MoMA in 2010, the piece becoming the occasion of their meeting again.

mirceacantor.blurb: Duchamp's readymade, picked up in Romania.
mirceacantor.bio: Mircea Cantor, born in 1977, is a Romanian-born artist who works with readymade objects, taking up the line that runs from Marcel Duchamp. His media are deliberately unsettled: video, animation, sculpture, drawing, painting and installation all appear in his work, each chosen for the idea at hand rather than out of loyalty to a discipline. He is placed here among the artists of post-Soviet and Eastern European art, the generation whose formative years coincided with the end of the old order and whose work often turns on objects, gestures and images that will carry more than one reading. Cantor's use of the found object sets him in a long avant-garde lineage while keeping the work anchored in his own moment.

anrisala.blurb: Albanian art with video at its centre.
anrisala.bio: Anri Sala, born in 1974, is an Albanian artist working chiefly in video, and holding both Albanian and French nationality. He works as a printmaker and visual artist besides, and has produced for television. He belongs to the group gathered here as post-Soviet and Eastern European: artists who came of age as the region's political order dissolved, and who found in video a form flexible enough to hold that shift. Sala's movement between Albania and France is typical of the generation, whose careers were built on the international exhibition circuit rather than within any single national art world. The record of his work is best read through the medium he settled on, which registers duration and change as painting cannot.

sanjaivekovic.blurb: Yugoslavia's feminist eye on the media.
sanjaivekovic.bio: Sanja Iveković, born in 1949, is a Croatian artist who photographs, performs, sculpts and makes installations, and who works as a designer and an activist besides; the activism has never been separable from the art. Her work tackles female identity, the media, consumerism and political strife, examining how images of women are manufactured and circulated and what that does to public life. She is considered one of the leading artists to have come out of the former Yugoslavia, and she continues to inspire many younger artists working on the same questions. Within this map's grouping of post-Soviet and Eastern European art, hers is the clearest case of a feminist practice built inside a socialist state and carried on well beyond it, in a country that changed its name around her.

caiguoqiang.blurb: Gunpowder and fireworks as artist's materials.
caiguoqiang.bio: Cai Guo-Qiang, born in 1957, is a Chinese artist based in the United States who works primarily with pyrotechnics, with gunpowder and fireworks at the centre of many of his pieces. The material dictates the terms: the work happens once, in the open, and then is gone, leaving photographs, residue and memory behind it. He also works as a painter, sculptor and installation artist, though it is the explosive work that has carried his name furthest. His most notable involvement came in 2008, with the fireworks for the Beijing Olympics, a spectacle watched by an audience far larger than any gallery could hold. Cai is among the Chinese artists of his generation whose work moved between a national stage and an international art world without ever settling wholly in either.

zhanghuan.blurb: From painting to performance and back.
zhanghuan.bio: Zhang Huan, born in 1965, is a Chinese artist who divides his time between Shanghai and New York City. He started out as a painter, moved across into performance art, and later came back to painting, a loop that gives his career an unusual shape: the performance work made his name, but the studio brackets it on both sides. He is primarily known for the performances, and also makes photographs and sculpture; among his later works are Three Heads Six Arms of 2008 and Hehe Xiexie of 2010, and he has worked as a theatre director. Within the Chinese contemporary grouping here, Zhang stands for the generation that made the body its first material before turning back to more traditional means, and to the studio it had started in.

songdong.blurb: Family, city and the impermanence of change.
songdong.bio: Song Dong, born in 1966, is a Chinese contemporary artist who moves between sculpture, installation, performance, photography and video. Two subjects run through the work. The first is his own family and what modern China has been like for them to live through, a private history running alongside the national one. The second is the transformation of China's urban environment, the demolition and rebuilding that has remade whole cities within a single lifetime. Behind both lies the impermanence of change itself, which he treats as a condition to be handled rather than lamented. He has taken part in many solo and group exhibitions around the world, and belongs to the Chinese contemporary generation whose art emerged while the country's cities and daily life were being reconstructed around them.

gustavemoreau.bio: Gustave Moreau, born in 1826, was called by Jean Cassou the Symbolist painter par excellence: an influential forerunner of the movement in the 1860s and, at its height in the 1890s, among its most significant figures. He painted the allegories and the biblical and mythological subjects the academies favoured and made them strange again, producing more than fifteen thousand paintings, watercolours and drawings, among them Oedipus and the Sphinx of 1864 and Hercules and the Lernaean Hydra of 1876. His deeper influence was as a teacher at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he told his students to go and paint in the street. Henri Matisse studied with him from 1892 to 1898, alongside Albert Marquet, Charles Camoin and Georges Rouault, his favourite pupil. He died in 1898.

georgesrouault.blurb: Moreau's favourite pupil, later his curator.
georgesrouault.bio: Georges-Henri Rouault, born in 1871, painted, drew and made prints, and the results are usually filed between Fauvism and Expressionism without sitting comfortably in either. He was Gustave Moreau's favourite pupil, and after his teacher's death he became curator of the Musée Moreau, a post that kept him inside the older painter's world while his own art moved elsewhere. A plate from his Miserere series is dated 1922 and the illustrations for Réincarnations du Père Ubu date from 1919, which give a measure of his graphic work; The Abandoned of 1937 is among the paintings; and in 1946 he contributed to the church of Notre-Dame de Toute Grâce at Plateau d'Assy. He worked as an illustrator and graphic artist throughout, and died in 1958.

eugenecarriere.blurb: Brown mists, and Derain's first teacher.
eugenecarriere.bio: Eugène Anatole Carrière, born in 1849, was a French Symbolist of the fin de siècle whose paintings are unmistakable: a near-monochrome brown palette, figures emerging from an ethereal haze, an atmosphere closer to memory than to observation. Women Sewing at a Table of 1894 and The First Communion of 1896 are characteristic, as is his Self-Portrait of 1893. Auguste Rodin was a close friend; he moved among writers including Verlaine, Mallarmé and Charles Morice, and his work is thought to have fed Picasso's Blue Period. He also taught. At the Académie Carrière between 1898 and 1900 André Derain was his pupil, and it was there that Derain met Henri Matisse, an introduction from which Fauvism followed. Carrière died in 1906.

ilyarepin.blurb: Russia's great realist, and a teacher.
ilyarepin.bio: Ilya Yefimovich Repin, born in 1844 in Ukraine and working within the Russian Empire, rose to become the most renowned painter of his generation in nineteenth-century Russia. Barge Haulers on the Volga of 1873, Religious Procession in Kursk Province of 1880 to 1883, Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan of 1885 and Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, painted between 1880 and 1891, are the major works. His portraits record a whole culture: Mikhail Glinka, Modest Mussorgsky, the collector Pavel Tretyakov, and above all Leo Tolstoy, his friend over many years. He taught in St Petersburg in the 1890s, where his students included Alexej von Jawlensky and Marianne von Werefkin, whom he called the Russian Rembrandt. He worked as a sculptor, an essayist and a graphic artist as well as a painter, and died in 1930.

augusterodin.blurb: The big tree nothing grows under.
augusterodin.bio: Auguste Rodin, born in 1840, is usually named as the founder of modern sculpture, though he was schooled traditionally and kept a craftsman's approach to the work all his life. What set him apart was his hand in clay: a rare ability to model a surface that is complex, turbulent and deeply pocketed, so that light travels across a figure the way it travels across a body. The Thinker, The Kiss, Monument to Balzac, The Burghers of Calais of 1888 and The Gates of Hell, begun in 1880, are the works by which he is known. In 1907 the young Constantin Brâncuși worked in his studio for a month and then left, explaining that nothing grows under big trees. Rodin died in 1917.

arnoldschoenberg.blurb: The composer who learned to paint.
arnoldschoenberg.bio: Arnold Schoenberg, born in 1874, was a modernist composer, theorist and teacher, Austrian by birth and American by the end, whose name attaches to developing variation, to the emancipation of the dissonance and to twelve-tone composition. He taught in Vienna and then at the Prussian Academy of Arts from 1925 to 1933, resigning in anticipation of Nazi Germany's restrictions on civil servants, then reaffirmed his Judaism in defiance and left for America, where a post at the University of California, Los Angeles occupied him from 1936 to 1944. He belongs in a map of painting because he painted, and because of who taught him: Richard Gerstl showed him how, between 1906 and 1908. The canvases that followed, among them Thinking of 1910, sit inside Austrian Expressionism rather than beside it. He died in 1951.

edwardhopper.bio: Edward Hopper, born in 1882, was an American painter and printmaker working in the realist line, and remains one of the country's most renowned artists. He studied under Robert Henri at the New York School of Art between 1900 and 1906, and this map places him with the Ashcan School and the Stieglitz Circle. What he made of that grounding was entirely his own: Automat of 1927, Night Windows of 1928, Early Sunday Morning of 1930 and Nighthawks of 1942 are the pictures through which modern America has come to picture itself, streets and rooms rendered with a clarity that leaves the people inside them alone. He worked as a draughtsman, illustrator and graphic artist as well as a painter. Hopper died in 1967.

percyvaltudorhart.blurb: The Paris studio where Synchromism began.
percyvaltudorhart.bio: Percyval Tudor-Hart, born in 1873, was a Canadian painter and sculptor who also taught and restored pictures, and whose own canvases, among them Farm Buildings at Kervao, France of 1905 and Evening in Huntingdonshire, are little known today.
