His importance to this map lies in his teaching. In his Paris studio, Stanton Macdonald-Wright and Morgan Russell both studied with him, and it was there, in 1911, that the two met. That meeting is the point from which Synchromism, the movement this map files him under, is traced. Tudor-Hart is a reminder that a movement can turn on a teacher whose own pictures have since slipped from view, and that the decisive event in a studio is sometimes not a lesson but an introduction. He died in 1954.

lyonelfeininger.bio: Lyonel Feininger, born in New York in 1871, came to art late and by an unusual road. He travelled to Europe in 1887 and studied in Hamburg, Berlin and Paris, then made his living from 1894 as a cartoonist and comic strip artist, working as a commercial caricaturist for twenty years; he was thirty-six before he began work as a fine artist. The mature painting is unmistakable, its prismatically broken and overlapping forms held in translucent colour, returning again and again to architecture and the sea, as in Gelmeroda IV of 1915 and The Cathedral in Halle of 1931. Walter Gropius made him the first master appointed to the Bauhaus, and he cut the woodcut for its 1919 manifesto. In 1924 he formed Die Blaue Vier with Kandinsky, Klee and Jawlensky. He died in 1956.

ezrapound.bio: Ezra Weston Loomis Pound, born in 1885, was an American poet and critic and a major figure in early modernist poetry, with Ripostes of 1912, Hugh Selwyn Mauberley of 1920 and The Cantos to his name. He belongs in a map of art rather than only of literature because of 1914: with Wyndham Lewis he co-founded the magazine BLAST and gave Vorticism its name, supplying the English avant-garde with a word and a platform at the moment it needed both, and a magazine loud enough that the word stuck. He also worked as a translator and a composer. During the Second World War he collaborated with Fascist Italy and with the Salò Republic, a record that has shadowed his reputation ever since. He died in 1972.

rogerfry.bio: Roger Eliot Fry, born in 1866, painted and wrote criticism, and belonged to the Bloomsbury Group. He established his reputation as a scholar of the Old Masters, then became an advocate for recent painting from France, and it was he who supplied the label Post-Impressionism for it. He did more than anyone else to raise public awareness of modern art in Britain, and his criticism pressed the formal properties of a picture over the associated ideas a viewer brings to it. Kenneth Clark judged him the greatest influence on taste since Ruskin. He painted too: portraits of Nina Hamnett in 1917 and Edith Sitwell in 1918, and a copy after a Cézanne self-portrait in 1925. In 1913 he co-founded the Omega Workshops with Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant; Wyndham Lewis walked out months later after a row over a commission.

vanessabell.bio: Vanessa Bell, born in 1879, painted and designed interiors, belonged to the Bloomsbury Group, and was Virginia Woolf's sister. Painting and design were never separate careers for her, and neither was ever a hobby. In 1913 she co-founded the Omega Workshops with Roger Fry and Duncan Grant, the enterprise that set Bloomsbury's painters to work on the decorated interior and made design a proper part of their output rather than a sideline. She was a photographer as well, and her images of the group form part of the record of it. Placed here alongside the Vorticists, she stands for the other half of the London avant-garde of the 1910s: decorative, domestic and collaborative, and no less consequential for being so. She died in 1961.

sophiebrzeska.bio: Sophie Suzanne Brzeska, born in 1873, was a Polish writer, remembered chiefly as the companion of the sculptor Henri Gaudier-Brzeska. He took her surname and joined it to his own, and the two lived together as brother and sister rather than as lovers. That framing, muse rather than author, is how the record has come down to us, though her own occupation was writing and little of that work is now documented. She died in 1925. Her name survives inside his, which is an unusual kind of authorship and one of the clearest cases in this map of a life made visible only through somebody else's. The Vorticist years are usually told through the sculptors and the poets; hers sat just outside that telling.

almamahler.bio: Alma Mahler-Werfel, born in 1879, was an Austrian composer and writer who also worked as an editor, and a fixture of the Viennese cultural world at the fin de siècle, musically active from her earliest years. Her friendships and relationships ran through the whole of it. The affair with Oskar Kokoschka lasted from 1912 to 1915, and after it ended he commissioned a life-size doll made in her likeness. In 1915 she married the architect Walter Gropius, a marriage that lasted until 1920 and fell between her marriages to Mahler and Werfel. She painted and wrote biography as well as composing, and the century's habit of describing her only through her husbands has obscured how much of Vienna's cultural life ran through her circle. She died in 1964.

wallyneuzil.bio: Walburga Neuzil, known as Wally, born in 1894, was an Austrian model who also worked as a nurse. Between 1911 and 1915 she was Egon Schiele's lover and muse, and his model through those years, before he left her to marry Edith Harms. She died in 1917, aged twenty-three. The record of her is thin, as it usually is for the women who sat for the painters of Austrian Expressionism, and what survives of her is largely what Schiele made of her. She is placed here as a figure in her own right rather than as a face in somebody else's pictures, because the Vienna of those years cannot honestly be described without the people who stood in front of the easel.

jacquesvillon.blurb: One of four artists named Duchamp.
jacquesvillon.bio: Jacques Villon, born Gaston Duchamp in 1875, painted as a Cubist and an abstractionist and made prints, taking a working name and building a career quite distinct from his family's. He also worked as an editorial cartoonist and illustrator, and his printmaking is as substantial a body of work as his painting. He was one of four artists in a single family: his brothers Marcel Duchamp and Raymond Duchamp-Villon and his sister Suzanne Duchamp all made art, which makes the household one of the densest concentrations of talent anywhere in this map. Villon kept steadily to painting and printmaking, out of the glare, while the family name became attached to something rather different. He died in 1963, the same year as Suzanne.

suzanneduchamp.bio: Suzanne Duchamp-Crotti, born in 1889, was a French Dadaist painter, collagist, sculptor and draughtswoman whose work mattered to how Paris Dada developed, and to modernism more widely. Her drawings and collages explore gender dynamics with a directness the movement rarely credited, and her career ran across five decades of great social upheaval, which she used the work to comment on. As a woman in a male-dominated movement she was seldom credited as an artist in her own right: she was overshadowed by her famous older brothers, Marcel Duchamp among them, or reduced to being described as the wife of her fellow artist Jean Crotti. Later reassessment has made clear how much of Paris Dada, and of women's place within it, ran through her studio.

ambroisevollard.blurb: The dealer who gave first shows.
ambroisevollard.bio: Ambroise Vollard, born in 1866, was among the most important dealers of French contemporary art at the start of the twentieth century. He was a collector and a publisher as well as a dealer, and his particular gift was for backing artists before anyone else would: Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Paul Gauguin, Vincent van Gogh, Aristide Maillol, Louis Valtat, André Derain and Georges Rouault all passed through his hands, and he supplied exposure and emotional support in roughly equal measure. In 1901 he gave Pablo Picasso his first Paris show, and in 1904 he mounted Henri Matisse's first solo exhibition, two decisions that between them launched the century's two central careers. He died in 1939, and almost every account of the period passes at some point through his gallery.

danielhenrykahnweiler.bio: Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler, born in Germany in 1884, opened his Paris gallery in 1907 and became one of the twentieth century's most notable dealers in France, as well as a collector and an art historian. He championed Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque before almost anyone else did, and Cubism with them, buying the Cubist output of both men at the moment nobody else wanted it, and from 1912 he was Picasso's exclusive dealer and had Juan Gris under contract too. His backing gave a radical movement something rare: a steady income. In 1914 his stock was seized as enemy property, scattering one of the great holdings of early Cubism. He died in 1979, long after the movement he had bankrolled passed into history.

gertrudestein.blurb: The salon where modernism met itself.
gertrudestein.bio: Gertrude Stein, born in Allegheny, Pennsylvania in 1874 and raised in Oakland, California, settled in Paris in 1903 and never left France again. She was a novelist, poet and playwright, and an art collector whose eye arrived early and stayed ahead. Her salon was where modernism introduced itself to itself: Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, Ezra Pound, Ernest Hemingway, Scott Fitzgerald, Sinclair Lewis and Sherwood Anderson all passed through her rooms. She bought Picasso when he was unknown and sat for him about ninety times for the portrait of 1906, and the Steins bought Matisse's Woman with a Hat out of the 1905 Salon d'Automne. She died in 1946, her patronage as consequential as her writing, and the two never entirely separable.

sergeishchukin.bio: Sergei Ivanovich Shchukin, born in 1854, was a Russian businessman who became one of the most consequential collectors of his age, buying French Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painting while it was still contested. In 1909 he commissioned two large panels from Henri Matisse, Dance and Music, for the staircase of his Moscow house; Matisse painted them the following year, and they remain among the most ambitious decorative commissions in modern painting. By 1914 Shchukin had assembled around fifty works by Pablo Picasso. What he bought hung in Moscow rather than Paris, and that mattered a great deal for how quickly the newest French painting travelled east. Nothing in his life as a businessman predicted the risk he was willing to take on painters whom Paris itself had not yet accepted. He died in 1936.

herwarthwalden.blurb: Der Sturm's founder and tireless promoter.
herwarthwalden.bio: Herwarth Walden, born in 1878, was a German Expressionist artist and an expert across many disciplines, widely credited as one of the great discoverers of the German avant-garde, and among its most tireless promoters, in the early twentieth century. His instrument was Der Sturm, the Expressionist magazine he founded, together with the gallery and the offshoots that grew from it. The Blaue Reiter painters, Franz Marc among them, showed under its banner; Marc Chagall was given his first solo exhibition there, in Berlin in 1914; and from 1919 Der Sturm showed Kurt Schwitters's Merz work. Walden was a writer and a composer as well as a painter, which is part of why the enterprise ranged as widely as it did. He died in 1941.

wilhelmuhde.bio: Wilhelm Uhde, born in 1874, was a German collector and dealer who wrote and criticised as well, settled in France, and bought modernist painting while it was still cheap and disputed. He was an early collector of the new work, and Henri Rousseau's career owed a great deal to him: he was among the first to take Rousseau seriously as an artist rather than as a curiosity. He was also Sonia Delaunay's dealer, and briefly her first husband: the marriage, from 1908 to 1910, was one of convenience. Uhde wrote as well as dealt, and the criticism was part of the same advocacy. Through that marriage and the dealing around it he sat close to the Paris circle from which Orphism came. He died in 1947, having spent a life on painters whose worth few others could yet see.

sarahbernhardt.blurb: The actress who made Mucha famous.
sarahbernhardt.bio: Sarah Bernhardt, born in 1844, was among the most celebrated stage actresses of her age, starring in La Dame aux Camélias, Ruy Blas, Fédora, La Tosca and L'Aiglon, and taking male roles too, including Shakespeare's Hamlet. Hugo praised her golden voice. She toured the world several times over and was among the first prominent actresses to make sound recordings and to appear in motion pictures, and she was an accomplished painter and sculptor besides. Her place in this map is as a patron: in 1894 she commissioned a poster for Gismonda from the then-unknown Alphonse Mucha and followed it with a six-year contract. The poster made his name overnight, and that commission is why an actress belongs in a map of painters. She died in 1923.

guillaumeapollinaire.bio: Guillaume Apollinaire, born in 1880, was a poet, playwright, short story writer, novelist and art critic, French by adoption and of Polish, Swiss and Italian descent. He was one of the presiding intelligences of the Paris avant-garde, and his criticism did much of the work of explaining the new painting to the people standing in front of it. His friendships did the rest. In 1907, at the Bateau-Lavoir, he introduced Georges Braque to Pablo Picasso, a meeting from which Cubism followed, and out of which two careers were rebuilt. He appears in this map among the associates of the Fauve circle, one of the writers whose company the painters kept and whose words shaped how their work was understood. He died in 1918, at thirty-eight.

georgmuche.blurb: The Bauhaus master who handed over weaving.
georgmuche.bio: Georg Muche, born in 1895, painted, made prints, built, wrote and taught, and was one of the masters of the Bauhaus. The range is characteristic of the school, which expected its masters to move between disciplines rather than to specialise, and he later held a university post as well. His place here rests on what he handed on. He led the weaving workshop until Gunta Stölzl took it over, and Stölzl went on to become the only woman to hold the rank of master at the Bauhaus. Muche also worked as a photographer, and he kept painting and writing for decades afterwards, well into old age. He died in 1987, having outlived by a very long way the experiment that made his name.

winoldreiss.blurb: He pointed Aaron Douglas toward Africa.
winoldreiss.bio: Winold Reiss, born in Karlsruhe in 1886, emigrated to the United States in 1913 and built a career there as an artist and graphic designer, working also as an illustrator, interior designer and architectural draftsman. He went West for the first time in 1920 and spent an extended stretch on the Blackfeet Reservation; he made more than 250 paintings of Native Americans, and from the 1920s to the 1950s the Great Northern Railway commissioned pictures of the Blackfeet that were reproduced as lithographs on its calendars and reached a wide public. In New York in 1925 he encouraged the young Aaron Douglas to draw on African sources, advice that helped shape the visual language of the Harlem Renaissance. Reiss died in 1953.

marceljanco.bio: Marcel Janco, born in 1895, was a Romanian and Israeli painter, architect and art theorist, and one of the co-inventors of Dada. As a young man he co-edited the art magazine Simbolul with Ion Vinea and Tristan Tzara, working his way through Art Nouveau, Futurism and Expressionism before he arrived at Dada. With Hugo Ball he helped found the Cabaret Voltaire, and the masks he made for its performances gave the movement its face; he supplied painting and stage design to Tzara's literary Dadaism as well. He parted with Dada in 1919, founding the Constructivist circle Das Neue Leben with the painter Hans Arp, and Eastern European Constructivism found in him its leading exponent. Trained as an architect, he built as well as painted, and later settled in Israel. He died in 1984.

richardhuelsenbeck.blurb: The man who took Dada to Berlin.
richardhuelsenbeck.bio: Richard Huelsenbeck, born in Frankenau in Hessen-Nassau in 1892, was a German writer and poet who helped bring Dada into being. He was one of the voices at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire, and in 1917 he carried the movement north to Berlin, where it turned harder, louder and more political. His judgements shaped it as much as his poems did: he blackballed Kurt Schwitters from Club Dada, a rejection that pushed Schwitters to invent his one-man Merz instead, alone. Trained as a physician, Huelsenbeck spent the second half of his life as a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, writing as a doctor as much as a poet, and he ended his career a long way from the noise he had helped make. He died in 1974.

katherinedreier.blurb: Founder of America's first modern-art museum.
katherinedreier.bio: Katherine Dreier, born in 1877, was an American painter, lecturer, collector and social reformer whose money and conviction went into other people's art as much as her own. Wealthy, progressive parents let her study art in the United States and Europe, often travelling with her sister Dorothea, a Post-Impressionist painter. Modern art absorbed her, and her friendship with Marcel Duchamp mattered most of all; frustrated by how badly the new work was received, she turned herself into its advocate. She co-founded the Society of Independent Artists, and in 1920, with Duchamp and Man Ray, the Société Anonyme, America's first museum of modern art, which assembled a permanent collection of more than 800 works by 175 artists. A suffragist as well as a patron, she left the collection to Yale University. She died in 1952.

emmyhennings.bio: Emmy Hennings, born in 1885, was a German poet, editor and performing artist, and a co-founder of Dada. A cabaret performer and actress by trade, she and Hugo Ball, her partner and later her second husband, opened the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in February 1916, the small noisy room where the movement began. Hennings performed there night after night, and her stage experience gave the venture its shape as a cabaret rather than a lecture hall. She wrote and edited as well, publishing poetry alongside the manifestos of the men around her, though she has often been remembered first as Ball's wife rather than as a founder in her own right. Later accounts have put her back at the centre of the story she helped start. She died in 1948.

bellarosenfeld.blurb: The woman floating through Chagall's skies.
bellarosenfeld.bio: Bella Rosenfeld, born in 1889, was a Russian Jewish writer who married Marc Chagall in 1915. She wrote as a novelist in her own right, but she is best known as the figure who floats through thirty years of her husband's paintings, from Bella au col blanc of 1917 onwards. Their marriage carried her from the Russian Empire to France, and her presence in Chagall's work is less portraiture than a private language of lovers suspended above rooftops, the same face returning through village scenes, weddings and flowers. She died in 1944, and Chagall went on painting her afterwards; she surfaces once more in Bouquet près de la fenêtre, a canvas of 1959–60. Few partners in modern art remain so continuously visible in the work itself.

luciamoholy.blurb: The Bauhaus as we picture it.
luciamoholy.bio: Lucia Moholy, born in 1894, was a photographer and publications editor whose pictures are the reason the Bauhaus looks the way it does in our heads. Working at the school alongside her husband László Moholy-Nagy, she photographed its architecture and the products of its workshops in a clear, frontal, undramatic style that made them legible as ideas rather than as merchandise. Those images carried the school's thinking to an international audience after the Second World War, decades after the pictures themselves were taken. Credit rarely followed: her photographs were routinely attributed to her husband or to Walter Gropius, so the most widely reproduced record of the Bauhaus circulated for decades under other people's names. She taught, and wrote as a journalist, and went on pressing her case. She died in 1989.

jeannehebuterne.blurb: Modigliani's model, and a painter herself.
jeannehebuterne.bio: Jeanne Hébuterne, born in 1898, was a French painter who has been remembered almost entirely as somebody else's subject. She trained and worked as an artist, leaving self-portraits from 1916 and 1917 and a canvas of red roofs, small sober pictures made in the same years she was sitting as an art model for Amedeo Modigliani, whose common-law wife she became. His portraits of her became some of the best-known images of the École de Paris, so that her face is famous and her own painting is not. Their life together was short and precarious. Two days after Modigliani died in 1920, Hébuterne took her own life, nine months pregnant, and she is buried beside him. Her last painting, made that same year, is titled The suicide.

pauleluard.blurb: Surrealism's founding poet, and Gala's first husband.
pauleluard.bio: Paul Éluard, born Eugène Émile Paul Grindel in 1895, was a French poet who helped found Surrealism. He came out of the Dada years into the circle around André Breton, sharing in the review Littérature and in the manifesto group of 1924 that gave the movement its name and its rules. His private life was as entangled as its politics: between 1922 and 1924 Max Ernst lived with Éluard and his wife Gala at Eaubonne, in an openly three-way household. Éluard was a politician as well as a poet, and a fighter in the French Resistance; he wrote love poetry and political poetry with the same plain directness, and he remained a public figure in French letters long after Surrealism fractured, still writing under the name he had chosen as a young man. He died in 1952.

kikidemontparnasse.bio: Kiki de Montparnasse, born Alice Ernestine Prin in 1901, was a French model, singer, memoirist and painter who became the presiding figure of Jazz Age Paris. She did not simply belong to the liberated culture of the années folles; she helped define it, singing in Montparnasse, painting, and eventually publishing her own memoirs, and the nickname that stuck was the Queen of Montparnasse. From 1921 to 1929 she lived and worked with Man Ray, and their partnership produced some of the most reproduced photographs of the century, including Le Violon d'Ingres, for which she was the model. Being one of the most famous models of the twentieth-century avant-garde meant being looked at constantly and credited rarely, and her own painting has only lately been taken seriously. She died in 1953.

leemiller.bio: Lee Miller, born in 1907, crossed more lines than almost any photographer of her century. She was a fashion model in New York in the 1920s before going to Paris, where she arrived at Man Ray's studio as an assistant and left as his partner and collaborator; the solarised images that became a signature of the Paris avant-garde came out of their shared darkroom between 1929 and 1932. She then built her own career as a fashion and fine-art photographer. During the Second World War she worked as a war correspondent and photojournalist, and the pictures she brought back from the front are among the hardest images made by anyone who came up through that avant-garde. She was later Lady Penrose, and she died in 1977.

wielandherzfelde.bio: Wieland Herzfelde, born in 1896, was the publisher who put German Dada into print. Where his circle made images, he made the means of circulation, producing books and journals that carried German avant-garde work and Marxist argument to a wider readership than any gallery could reach. He worked constantly with his brother, the photomontage artist John Heartfield, whose covers and montages appeared under Herzfelde's imprint; Heartfield had anglicised the family name in protest at German nationalism, while Wieland kept it. Both men were shaped by Dada's politics as much as by its jokes. Herzfelde spent his later years in the German Democratic Republic, where he taught at university, translated, and went on writing about the avant-garde he had helped publish. He died in 1988.

josevasconcelos.blurb: The minister who commissioned the murals.
josevasconcelos.bio: José Vasconcelos, born in 1881, was the Mexican writer, philosopher and politician who gave muralism its walls. Known as the cultural caudillo of the Revolution, he became Minister of Education and treated public buildings as the natural home of a national art: in 1921 he commissioned the first murals from Diego Rivera, and he handed José Clemente Orozco the cycle at the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria. The programme he built made Mexico the one country in the 1920s where the most ambitious modern painting was public, monumental and paid for by the state. His own thinking, especially his idea of the cosmic race, shaped Mexican cultural, political and economic policy for decades and remains contested. A lawyer and university teacher as well as a writer, he died in 1959.

leopoldzborowski.bio: Léopold Zborowski, born in 1889, was a Polish poet who became one of the most devoted dealers of the École de Paris. He came to Paris as a writer and drifted into dealing largely because the painters he loved had nobody else acting for them. For Amedeo Modigliani he was dealer, landlord and unpaid promoter at once, finding him rooms and buyers at a time when there were almost no buyers to find. He did the same for Chaïm Soutine, keeping him housed and painting through the 1920s, so that much of the work surviving from those years exists because Zborowski underwrote it. Poet, writer, dealer and patron by turns, he backed two of the century's most difficult painters when almost nobody else would. He died in 1932.

alainlocke.bio: Alain Locke, born in 1885, was the philosopher and teacher who gave the Harlem Renaissance its argument. In 1907 he became the first African-American Rhodes Scholar, and he returned to a career in philosophy and education in which aesthetics and race were inseparable questions. His 1925 anthology The New Negro gathered a generation of Black writers and artists between two covers and effectively announced the movement; Aaron Douglas illustrated it, and Locke's backing helped set the young painter on his way. Contemporaries called Locke the Dean of the Renaissance, its acknowledged architect rather than its performer. His standing outlasted the decade: in 1968 Martin Luther King Jr. named him, alongside W. E. B. Du Bois, among the philosophers Black children should be taught. He died in 1954.

charlotteosgoodmason.blurb: The Harlem Renaissance's demanding white patron.
charlotteosgoodmason.bio: Charlotte Osgood Mason, born Charlotte Louise Van der Veer Quick in 1854, was a wealthy white American socialite who became one of the most significant and most complicated patrons of the Harlem Renaissance. She gave more than 100,000 dollars to Black artists and writers, a sum reckoned at more than a million by later measures, and her money mattered most during the Great Depression, when foundation support fell away and young artists had nowhere else to turn. Aaron Douglas was among those she supported. The terms were controlling: she expected influence over what her artists made, and her patronage came bound up with her own ideas about what Black creativity ought to be. The result is a legacy that enabled and constrained in equal measure. She died in 1946.

paulstrand.blurb: Made photography modern, then made films.
paulstrand.bio: Paul Strand, born in 1890, was an American photographer and filmmaker who helped force photography into the company of the other modern arts. His pictures from the mid-1910s set the terms: Wall Street, Blind, Abstraction, Porch Shadows and The White Fence gave him hard-edged geometry, unposed strangers and ordinary objects seen as pure form. Alongside Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Weston he made the case that a photograph could be a work rather than a record. In 1921 he and Charles Sheeler co-directed Manhatta, a short film that carried the same Precisionist eye into motion. The Photo League, which he helped establish in 1936, banded photographers together around shared social and creative causes. His work then ran for six decades across the Americas, Europe and Africa. He died in 1976.

elizabethcatlett.blurb: Sculptor of the Black woman's experience.
elizabethcatlett.bio: Elizabeth Catlett, born in Washington, D.C., in 1915, was a sculptor and printmaker who spent a career giving form to the Black American experience, and particularly to the lives of Black women. She grew up in a family of educators and was the grandchild of formerly enslaved people; the path to a working artist's life was narrow for a Black woman of her generation, and teaching carried her through much of it. Howard University connected her with Loïs Mailou Jones, who taught there for forty-seven years. A fellowship in 1946 took her to Mexico City, where she settled, spent twenty years at the Taller de Gráfica Popular and headed sculpture at the Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas. From the 1950s her main medium shifted from print to sculpture. She died in 2012.

charlesalston.bio: Charles Alston, born in 1907 and known all his life as Spinky, was a painter, sculptor, muralist and teacher whose Harlem studio at 306 West 141st Street became one of the most productive rooms in American art. He ran the Harlem Art Workshop there, where the young Jacob Lawrence learned to paint and where his cousin Romare Bearden started out. He was the first African-American to supervise a unit of the Federal Art Project, and he designed and painted murals for Harlem Hospital and for the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Building; Magic in Medicine is among his works. Later he and Bearden helped found Spiral, which met in Bearden's Canal Street studio. His 1970 bust of Martin Luther King Jr. entered the White House in 1990, the first image of an African American displayed there. He died in 1977.

gwendolynknight.blurb: Trained with Savage, married to Lawrence.
gwendolynknight.bio: Gwendolyn Knight, born in Bridgetown, Barbados, in 1913, came from the West Indies to the United States, living in Saint Louis before New York. In Harlem she studied in Augusta Savage's studio, the workshop that trained much of the next generation of Black American artists, and Jacob Lawrence, who came up the same way under Savage, became her husband; they married in 1941. Knight drew, painted and made sculpture across a long career, though her own work stayed largely in her husband's shadow during the decades when his narrative series were making his name. Her training under Savage placed her in a lineage running from the Harlem Renaissance into the postwar years, and the recognition she is given now arrived very late. She died in 2005.

antoinebourdelle.bio: Antoine Bourdelle, born Émile Antoine Bordelles in 1861, was a French sculptor who stands exactly at the hinge between the Beaux-Arts tradition and modern sculpture. He trained under Auguste Rodin, then pulled away from Rodin's restless surfaces towards something tauter and more architectural; Hercules the Archer of 1909 is the pivot, a body drawn as tense structure rather than as flesh. He made public monuments, including the war memorial at Montauban of 1902, and portraits such as Dr. Koeberlé and Gustave Eiffel. Teaching mattered to him as much as carving. At the Académie de la Grande Chaumière in Paris he taught Alberto Giacometti between 1922 and 1927, and Henri Matisse was among his students too. He is also an important figure in Art Deco. He died in 1929.

gonzalofonseca.bio: Gonzalo Fonseca, born in Uruguay in 1922, was a sculptor who carried the discipline of architecture into art. He began as an architecture student at the University of Montevideo, and found modern art in 1942 through the Taller Torres-García, the Montevideo workshop of Joaquín Torres-García. Fonseca joined in 1943 and stayed until 1949, learning painting first and absorbing the workshop's fascination with pre-Columbian form: the grid, the sign, the compartment. He carried all of that into stone, and he went on painting as well, though it is the carving that lasts. His sculpture is usually placed within Universal Constructivism, though it became steadily more his own, dense chambered blocks that read like small architectures waiting to be inhabited. His Tower of the Winds dates from 1968. He died in 1997.

julioalpuy.blurb: The grid broken open by myth.
julioalpuy.bio: Julio Alpuy, born in Uruguay in 1919, was a painter, sculptor and muralist who came up inside the Taller Torres-García and spent a career testing what its rules could hold. His early work followed Joaquín Torres-García's Constructive Universalism closely, with its compartmented grid and each symbol set in its own box. Study and travel in Europe and Latin America widened the vocabulary, bringing him to Cubism and to myths drawn from many cultures, and gradually the grid in his work loosened and broke open until the figures spilled past their frames. He worked prolifically across painting, carving and mural-scale commissions, and his work is exhibited around the world, carrying the ideas of the Montevideo workshop far beyond it. He died in 2009.

miltonavery.bio: Milton Avery, born in Altmar, New York, in 1885, was an American modern painter who worked in flat, simplified fields of colour at a time when American painting was mostly doing something else. He moved to Connecticut as a boy and later to New York City, painting alongside his wife, the artist Sally Michel Avery; their daughter March Avery became a painter too. Avery never joined a movement, but the younger New York painters came to him. Through the 1930s he was an informal mentor to Mark Rothko, and he spent summers at Gloucester with Rothko and Adolph Gottlieb, all three painting the same stretch of coast. What they took from him was the conviction that colour alone could carry a picture. When Avery died in 1965, Rothko gave the eulogy.

adolphgottlieb.blurb: Signed the letter that announced Abstract Expressionism.
adolphgottlieb.bio: Adolph Gottlieb, born in 1903, was an American painter who helped write Abstract Expressionism's terms before the paintings had a name. In the 1930s he was close to Milton Avery, spending summers at Gloucester with Avery and Mark Rothko and making works such as Sun Deck of 1936 while the older man's colour did its slow work on all of them. In 1935 he and Rothko were among the founders of The Ten, a small exhibiting group of independents. Their most consequential collaboration came in 1943, when the two sent a letter to the New York Times setting out what the new painting was for, making a manifesto out of a letter to the editor. Gottlieb later made sculpture and prints as well. He died in 1974.

ramkinkarbaij.bio: Ramkinkar Baij, born in 1906, helped pioneer modern sculpture in India and stands as a key figure of Contextual Modernism. He trained at Kala Bhavana in Santiniketan under Nandalal Bose, in a school built on the belief that Indian art should modernise on its own terms rather than by copying Europe. Baij pushed that further than his teacher. His subjects were the Santhal people and the labourers of the surrounding countryside, and he gave them the scale usually reserved for gods and rulers: Santhal Family of 1938, still his best-known work, sets a family group on a monumental base, and Mill Call followed in 1956. He made a Seated Buddha as well, and he painted throughout his life, sculptor and painter at once. He died in 1980.

benodebeharimukherjee.blurb: Pioneer of the modern Indian mural.
benodebeharimukherjee.bio: Benode Behari Mukherjee, born in West Bengal in 1904, was one of the pioneers of modern Indian art and a central figure of Contextual Modernism. He studied at Kala Bhavana under Nandalal Bose and was among the first painters in modern India to treat the mural as a serious modern form rather than as a decorative survival. His wall paintings were made for the buildings that held them, working with their light, their corners and the way people moved through them, so that architecture and image belonged to one another. He was a university teacher and a writer as well as a painter, and his thinking about how an image sits in real space shaped the students who came after him. He died in 1980.

luciensimon.blurb: The Paris teacher who trained Sher-Gil.
luciensimon.bio: Lucien Simon, born in Paris in 1861, was a French painter, lithographer and teacher whose own reputation rested on Brittany, in pictures such as Wrestlers in Brittany of 1898 and Bretons of 1907, and on large warm family scenes like Jour d'été, a portrait of his children painted in 1905. He worked in a broad, painterly figurative manner well outside the avant-garde, and he painted mythological subjects too, among them Nausicaa of 1915. His place on this map is as a teacher. Teaching occupied much of his career, and at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris between 1930 and 1934 his students included Amrita Sher-Gil, who took a European academic training back to India and turned it into something entirely her own. He died in 1945.

zaowouki.bio: Zao Wou-Ki, born in 1920, was a Chinese-French painter who made abstraction that reads at once as landscape and as calligraphy. He entered the academy at Hangzhou in 1935, when it was led by Lin Fengmian, and studied there under the French-trained painters Fang Ganmin and Wu Dayu, in a school deliberately built to put Chinese and European practice in the same room. He graduated from what is now the China Academy of Art and later settled in France, where his canvases opened into fields of light, weather and moving marks with no fixed horizon. In time he became a member of the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Paris, one of a generation of Chinese modernists trained first at home and then in France, and a lithographer and stamp designer besides. He died in 2013.

chutehchun.blurb: Abstraction written with a calligrapher's hand.
chutehchun.bio: Chu Teh-Chun, born in 1920, was a Chinese-French painter who built an abstract language out of the techniques of traditional Chinese painting. He enrolled at the national art academy at Hangzhou, then led by Lin Fengmian, and studied under the French-trained Fang Ganmin and Wu Dayu. Chu later moved to France, where his canvases opened into storms of colour held together by brushwork that never stopped behaving like calligraphy, the gesture always legible as a stroke rather than as a stain. He was the first artist of Chinese descent to join France's Académie des Beaux-Arts. With Zao Wou-Ki and Wu Guanzhong, all of them trained in China and then in France, he was nicknamed one of the Three Musketeers of modernist Chinese art. He died in 2014.

wuguanzhong.blurb: Where Chinese ink met Western colour.
wuguanzhong.bio: Wu Guanzhong, born in 1919, is widely regarded as one of the founders of modern Chinese painting. He trained at the Hangzhou academy under Lin Fengmian, and unlike many who passed through that school he made his whole career at home. His paintings hold two traditions at once: the flat singing colour of Western Fauvism and the line of Chinese calligraphy, applied to architecture, plants, animals and people, and to the landscapes and waterscapes of the country he spent his life crossing. The results can look like early modern European painting and like ink painting within the same glance, which is precisely the point. He wrote extensively on contemporary Chinese art as well, arguing his case in print as steadily as he argued it on paper and canvas. He died in 2010.

louisaragon.blurb: Surrealist poet who chose the Party.
louisaragon.bio: Louis Aragon, born in 1897, was one of the leading voices of French Surrealism and, later, one of its most public defectors. In 1919 he founded the review Littérature with André Breton and Philippe Soupault, the magazine that carried the group from Dada into Surrealism proper. He wrote poetry and novels, edited, and worked as a journalist. His long commitment to the Communist Party eventually collided with Breton's refusal to subordinate art to politics, and in 1932 the two broke for good. Aragon stayed with the Party for the rest of his life and became a major public figure in French letters, elected to the Académie Goncourt and, after 1959, nominated again and again for the Nobel Prize in Literature. He died in 1982.

philippesoupault.bio: Philippe Soupault, born in Chaville in 1897, was a French poet, novelist and critic who was present at the exact moment Surrealism began. He came through Dada, and in 1919 he founded the review Littérature in Paris with André Breton and Louis Aragon, which for many readers marks the movement's starting line. That same year he and Breton sat down to write without deliberation or correction, and the result, Les Champs magnétiques, published in 1920, was the first book of automatic writing, the technique that would define Surrealist practice for decades afterwards. Soupault went on writing novels, criticism and journalism, and stayed politically active through a very long life. He died in 1990, having outlived nearly everyone who was in the room at the start.

georgesbataille.blurb: Surrealism's antagonist and theorist of excess.
georgesbataille.bio: Georges Bataille, born in 1897, was a French writer, librarian and theorist whose work refused to stay inside any one discipline, moving between art history and anthropology, philosophy and sociology, religious studies, political economy and literature. He wrote novels and erotic fiction, criticism, lectures, diaries and fragments, treating writing as a way of testing the limits of human experience rather than as a way of building a system. His relationship with Surrealism was antagonistic at close range: in 1929 and 1930 he and André Breton conducted a bitter public feud, and Breton's Second Manifesto attacked him by name. The quarrel mattered because Bataille stood for everything Breton wanted kept out, and his ideas went on to shape French thought well beyond it. He died in 1962.

benjaminperet.bio: Benjamin Péret, born in 1899, was a French poet who came out of Parisian Dada and became one of the founders and most constant members of the Surrealist movement. Where others drifted away, quarrelled or were expelled, Péret stayed, and he pushed automatism harder than almost anyone, writing that follows its own associations wherever they go, comic and violent by turns. From 1936 he was the partner of the painter Remedios Varo, and in 1941, with Europe closing around them, he got her out and across to Mexico, where she would eventually make the work she is now known for. Their journey was one of many that carried Surrealism out of Europe and into the Americas. He died in 1959.

peggyguggenheim.bio: Peggy Guggenheim, born in 1898, was an American collector and dealer whose taste and money redirected the course of modern art. Her father, Benjamin Guggenheim, went down with the Titanic in 1912; her uncle Solomon founded the museum foundation that carries the family name. Between 1938 and 1946 she collected across Europe and America, exhibiting the work almost as fast as she acquired it. Her marriage to Max Ernst, from 1941 to 1946, got him into the United States at a moment when Europe had become impossible for him. Her gallery, Art of This Century, gave Jackson Pollock his first solo show in 1943 and kept him on a monthly stipend, effectively underwriting American abstraction at its birth. In 1949 she settled in Venice, where her collection still sits on the Grand Canal. She died in 1979.

galadali.blurb: Muse, manager, and half a signature.
galadali.bio: Gala Dalí, born in the Russian Empire in 1894, was an artist and businesswoman who spent her life at the centre of Surrealism without ever being merely its subject. She was married first to the poet Paul Éluard, and later to Salvador Dalí, for whom she was model, manager and business brain; in the end her name became part of his signature. Gala shaped her own image with great care, largely through fashion, which she treated as the medium of her own self-expression, and the creative circle around her took her seriously as a stand-alone creator even when the histories reduced her to a muse. She inspired a long list of writers and artists, and both the men she married were central to the movement she helped hold together. She died in 1982.

federicogarcialorca.bio: Federico García Lorca, born in 1898, was a Spanish poet, playwright and theatre director, and an emblematic member of the Generation of '27, the group that brought European modernism into Spanish literature. He belongs on a map of visual art because of the Residencia de Estudiantes in Madrid, where between 1922 and 1926 he formed an intense attachment to Salvador Dalí: a friendship, an infatuation and a long argument about art that marked both men permanently. The recognition Lorca won was international, and it reached well beyond poetry into the theatre he wrote for and directed. He drew as well as wrote, and made a Portrait of Salvador Dalí in 1927. He died in 1936, and his plays and poems have outlived every quarrel of the period.

leontrotsky.blurb: The exile who stayed at the Casa Azul.
leontrotsky.bio: Leon Trotsky, born in 1879, was a Russian revolutionary and political theorist, central to the revolution of 1905, to the October Revolution of 1917 and to the civil war that followed, and, with Lenin, one of the two most prominent men of the early Soviet state. A Marxist and a Leninist, he gave his name to a whole school of Marxism. Exiled in 1929, he spent his last decade moving between the few countries that would take him. He appears in this constellation because of where that exile came to rest: from 1937 he sheltered at Frida Kahlo's Casa Azul, and he and Kahlo had an affair that year. The episode pulled the circle around Kahlo directly into the century's sharpest political fight. Trotsky was assassinated in 1940.

johnskeaping.blurb: Hepworth's first husband, and a carver.
johnskeaping.bio: John Rattenbury Skeaping, born in 1901, was an English sculptor and painter best known for animals, and above all for horses. In the late 1920s he and Barbara Hepworth, whose first husband he was, carved side by side, both working the material directly rather than modelling something for another hand to translate into stone. That shared discipline sits at the very beginning of British modern sculpture, though the two went in different directions afterwards, Skeaping towards the naturalistic animal subjects that occupied the rest of his life. Animal figures he designed were produced by Wedgwood, and his life-size statue of Secretariat stands at the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame. He was elected a Royal Academician. He died in 1980.

diegogiacometti.bio: Diego Giacometti, born in 1902, was a Swiss sculptor and designer who spent forty years inside his brother Alberto's studio. He was Alberto's studio assistant and his most constant model, sitting for him again and again across four decades while the work that made his brother's name took shape in front of him. He also made furniture, and it is that work, designed as sculpture rather than as joinery, for which he is now valued in his own right. A third brother, Bruno, was an artist too, so all three sons of the family made things for a living. The arrangement between the two elder brothers was unusually complete: one name went on the work, but both pairs of hands were in it. He died in 1985.

herbertread.blurb: The critic who made British modernism respectable.
herbertread.bio: Herbert Read, born in 1893, was the English critic, poet and philosopher who argued the case for modern art in Britain when there was almost no audience for it. From 1931 he wrote the criticism that built Henry Moore's reputation, and he championed Barbara Hepworth alongside Moore and Ben Nicholson, giving a scattered group of British artists the language that turned them into a movement. He wrote prolifically on art and on the place of art in education, and he co-founded the Institute of Contemporary Arts. A committed anarchist, he was also among the first English writers to take existentialism seriously, and he co-edited the British edition of Jung's Collected Works. His authority came from breadth: sculpture, psychoanalysis, politics and teaching all belonged in one argument. He died in 1968.

johngraham.blurb: The eye that spotted them all.
johngraham.bio: John Graham was the connector at the centre of the New York art world in the years just before Abstract Expressionism had a name. A painter himself, and a tireless promoter of other people's careers, he had the European eye that the young Americans lacked, and he used it on their behalf. He showed David Smith what welded European sculpture could do, which set the direction of Smith's entire career. He took up Arshile Gorky. And in 1942 he assembled an exhibition of American and French paintings that put Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning and Lee Krasner in one room, the show that first got Pollock noticed and, in retrospect, the moment the New York School began to recognise itself.

qibaishi.bio: Qi Baishi, born in 1864 to a peasant family in Xiangtan, Hunan, taught himself to paint, set going by the Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden. He came to art late and by an unofficial route, and the whimsy of his work, its plants and creatures and small things looked at very closely, never lost the directness of that beginning. After the age of forty he travelled widely among China's scenic sites, and from 1917 he settled in Beijing. His Twelve Landscape Screens are among the best known of his works. Xu Beihong, running the national academy, promoted the older self-taught painter into the official canon, and Qi taught in turn: Hu Jieqing, the wife of Lao She, was his student. A poet and calligrapher as well as a painter, he died in 1957.

luisbunuel.blurb: Dreamed Un Chien andalou with Dalí.
luisbunuel.bio: Luis Buñuel, born in 1900, was a Spanish and Mexican filmmaker whose career ran through France, Mexico and Spain, and who turned Surrealism into a way of making films that lasted half a century. He met Salvador Dalí as a student at the Residencia de Estudiantes in Madrid, and in January 1929, at Figueres, the two of them wrote Un Chien andalou in six days. That film fixed his method. He kept the same instincts through a long later career, aiming avant-garde absurdity squarely at the church, the state and the middle class in films including Belle de Jour and The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie. Critics and directors have counted him ever since among the most influential filmmakers of all time. He died in 1983.

aimecesaire.bio: Aimé Césaire, born in Martinique in 1913, was a poet, playwright and politician who founded the Négritude movement in French-language literature and coined the word itself. His writing gave a generation of Black writers and artists across the Francophone world a language for their own inheritance rather than a borrowed one. In 1941 he met the painter Wifredo Lam in Martinique, and the two recognised the same project being pursued in different media; Lam went on to illustrate Cahier d'un retour au pays natal. Césaire's other life was electoral: mayor of Fort-de-France for fifty-six years from 1945, a deputy in the French National Assembly until 1993, president of the Regional Council of Martinique, and founder of the Parti progressiste martiniquais in 1958. He died in 2008.

ernestbinfieldhavell.blurb: Turned Calcutta's art school back towards India.
ernestbinfieldhavell.bio: Ernest Binfield Havell, born in 1861, was an English arts administrator and historian who spent his career arguing that Indian art should be judged by Indian standards. From 1896 to 1905 he was principal of the Government School of Art in Calcutta, and there, working with Abanindranath Tagore, he turned the teaching away from European academic training towards Indian models and traditions. That reorientation produced the Bengal school of art, and it made a colonial art school into an instrument of cultural self-assertion. Havell wrote many books on Indian art and architecture, pressing the same case on British readers who had been taught to see the work as craft. He came from a family of artists and art educators. He died in 1934.

daviddriskell.bio: David Driskell, born in 1931, was an American artist, scholar and curator whose work established African-American art as a distinct field of study. He studied at Howard University under Loïs Mailou Jones, joining a teaching lineage that ran back to the Harlem Renaissance, and he kept making his own art throughout a career that also made him a historian, a collector and a curator. His exhibitions and scholarship built the framework of names, chronology and argument that later curators inherited, and by the end of his life he was named among the world's leading authorities on the subject. He was Distinguished University Professor of Art Emeritus at the University of Maryland, where the David C. Driskell Center carries his name. He died in 2020.

richarddiebenkorn.blurb: From Bay Area figures to Ocean Park.
richarddiebenkorn.bio: Richard Diebenkorn, born in 1922, was an American painter who changed direction twice and got better each time. He came into abstraction at the California School of Fine Arts, where he was Clyfford Still's student in 1946 and then, until 1950, a colleague on the same faculty, an unusually direct transmission of Abstract Expressionism to the West Coast. In the 1950s he turned back to the figure and became a central artist of the Bay Area Figurative Movement, painting figures and interiors with the same loaded brush he had used for abstraction. From the late 1960s he began the Ocean Park paintings, large lyrical grids of light and colour that brought him worldwide acclaim and occupied him for the rest of his life. He died in 1993.

ruthasawa.blurb: Looped wire into hanging, breathing forms.
ruthasawa.bio: Ruth Asawa, born in 1926, was a Japanese-American sculptor known above all for abstract looped-wire forms: transparent, nested volumes drawn from natural and organic shapes, in which line and mass turn out to be the same thing. She learned her way of working at Black Mountain College, where she studied under Josef Albers between 1946 and 1949, and the discipline of that teaching, a material understood through patient and exhaustive handling, maps directly onto a career built out of one humble technique repeated with enormous care. Alongside the sculptures she drew and made prints, figurative and abstract, influenced by nature and especially by flowers and plants. She made public work as well, including a fountain in San Francisco. She died in 2013.

robertoburlemarx.bio: Roberto Burle Marx, born in 1909, was the Brazilian landscape architect who made gardens behave like modern paintings. He introduced modernist landscape architecture to Brazil, laying out parks, plazas and private gardens as flowing fields of colour and shape, planted with the tropical flora whose use in garden design he did more than anyone to establish. A painter and botanist as well, he moved freely between graphic design, tapestry, folk art, fabric, jewellery and stage sets, treating each as another way of arranging form; water gardens run through the work as a recurring theme. His Portuguese-stone mosaic pavements turned public ground into drawing, and he worked on the setting of the Church of Saint Francis of Assisi. In 1947, in Rio de Janeiro, he taught Lygia Clark. He died in 1994.

enricocastellani.bio: Enrico Castellani, born in 1930, was an Italian artist who took the monochrome and made it move. From 1959 he worked his canvases with a nail-gun, driving nails into them so that the surface bulged and dipped in regular rhythms: paintings with no image at all, whose entire content is light falling across a distorted plane. That same year, in Milan, he and Piero Manzoni founded Azimut, a gallery and a journal that gave the new European work somewhere to appear and an argument to appear under. Castellani was close to Manzoni and to Vincenzo Agnetti, and by the early 1960s his monochromatic geometric reliefs were among the clearest statements of what painting might be once representation had been set aside. He died in 2017.

dorothydehner.blurb: Painter and sculptor beside David Smith.
dorothydehner.bio: Dorothy Dehner, born in 1901, was an American painter, draughtswoman and sculptor. She and David Smith both trained at the Art Students League in New York, and they married in 1927. For twenty-five years the two shared a life and a working practice; Smith's sculpture drew nearly all of the attention that came to the household, and Dehner's own drawing and painting went on quietly beside it. The marriage ended in 1952, and she then worked for another four decades entirely on her own terms, moving into sculpture as well as painting and building, late, the reputation that had not been available to her as a wife. Sculpture, painting and drawing all belonged to her practice by then. She died in 1994, a working artist to the end.

johncage.blurb: The composer who taught artists to let go.
johncage.bio: John Cage, born in 1912, was an American composer, artist and theorist whose ideas reorganised visual art as thoroughly as they did music. A pioneer of indeterminacy, of electroacoustic work and of instruments used in ways nobody intended, he was the pivot of the postwar avant-garde. He and Merce Cunningham were partners and collaborators for fifty years, remaking modern dance together, with Robert Rauschenberg designing for the company. Rauschenberg mattered doubly: his White Paintings gave Cage the permission to write 4'33", and in 1952 the two staged Theatre Piece No. 1 at Black Mountain College. Cage then taught experimental composition at the New School for Social Research from 1957, in a class that produced Allan Kaprow, George Brecht, Dick Higgins, Al Hansen and Jackson Mac Low. He died in 1992.

mercecunningham.bio: Merce Cunningham, born in 1919, spent more than fifty years at the front of American modern dance, working until his death in 2009. He was a dancer, choreographer and draughtsman, but his defining trait was an appetite for company: he made work with artists from every other discipline and let their contributions stand alongside his own. John Cage was his partner in life and work for fifty years, and Robert Rauschenberg designed for his company. The musicians David Tudor and Brian Eno worked with him; Jasper Johns, Bruce Nauman, Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein and Frank Stella all contributed to his productions, as did the fashion designer Rei Kawakubo. What came out of those collaborations reached far beyond dance, leaving a mark on the whole postwar avant-garde that is still being traced today.

sonjaferlovmancoba.bio: Sonja Ferlov Mancoba, born in Denmark in 1911, was a sculptor and painter and one of the avant-garde figures of her generation. In 1942 she married the artist Ernest Mancoba, the only African artist working in the orbit of CoBrA, and from then on the two names are usually spoken together: a shared life and a shared set of friendships running through the northern European postwar avant-garde. Sculpture remained her principal medium across a career that lasted until her death in 1984, with painting alongside it. She is placed here among the artists of African modernism and independence because of that marriage and the circles it opened, a reminder that the map of twentieth-century art is drawn by who lived and worked with whom at least as much as by nationality.

rotrautkleinmoquay.blurb: Yves Klein's widow, and a painter herself.
rotrautkleinmoquay.bio: Rotraut Klein-Moquay, born in 1938 and known simply as Rotraut, is a German-French painter and sculptor. In 1962 she married Yves Klein, the artist at the centre of Nouveau Réalisme; he died five months later, and she has carried his name for the six decades since. Her own work in paint and sculpture has continued throughout, made across the two countries whose nationality she holds. Hers is one of the quieter positions in this constellation, the kind the record tends to compress into a single line about a famous husband. The fuller version is an artist who married into the middle of a movement at twenty-four, survived its most famous figure, and went on making work of her own long after the moment that fixed her in everyone else's story.

georgedyer.bio: George Dyer belongs to this map through the painter Francis Bacon, his partner from 1963 onward. He died in 1971, on the eve of Bacon's retrospective at the Grand Palais. The record gathered here holds little beyond that relationship and its terrible timing, and on a project about who shaped whom it is better left thin than filled in.

elmerbischoff.blurb: From abstraction back to the figure.
elmerbischoff.bio: Elmer Bischoff, born in 1916, was a painter and teacher from the San Francisco Bay Area and one of the artists who made the postwar journey out of abstraction and back to the figure. With Richard Diebenkorn and David Park he belongs to the generation that began in the language of Abstract Expressionism and then chose, deliberately, to paint people and rooms again. From 1946 he taught at the California School of Fine Arts, where Clyfford Still was on the faculty alongside him, a small institution that concentrated an unusual amount of the era's argument about what painting was for. Bischoff kept teaching for much of his life, and the Bay Area figurative position he helped establish outlasted him when he died in 1991.

bettyparsons.blurb: The dealer who backed Abstract Expressionism first.
bettyparsons.bio: Betty Parsons, born in 1900, was an artist, dealer and collector, and the person who put Abstract Expressionism in front of the public well before the market caught up. She painted and sculpted all her life, but it is her gallery that changed American art: in the late 1940s she was the dealer for Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman, Clyfford Still and Jackson Pollock at the same time, showing work that almost nobody was buying. That roster is now the standard account of the New York School, and she assembled it while it was still an argument rather than a canon. She remained one of the most dynamic figures of the American avant-garde until her death in 1982, an artist among dealers and a dealer among artists.

sidneyjanis.blurb: Took the New York School commercial.
sidneyjanis.bio: Sidney Janis, born in 1896, made his money manufacturing clothing and spent it on pictures, opening a New York gallery in 1948 that quickly became one of the most important rooms in the city. His programme did something unusual: he showed the young Abstract Expressionists next to the European moderns he collected, among them Pierre Bonnard, Paul Klee, Joan Miró and Piet Mondrian, so that American painting was seen in the company it wanted to keep. When Betty Parsons's artists moved on, Janis took on the New York School, Willem de Kooning among them, and gave the movement its commercial footing. A collector, dealer and philanthropist, he stayed a central figure in postwar New York until his death in 1989.

leocastelli.blurb: The dealer who invented the modern gallery.
leocastelli.bio: Leo Castelli, born in Trieste in 1907, is credited with originating the contemporary gallery system: the stable of artists, the steady programme, the long-term support. Across five decades his New York gallery moved through Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism, Neo-Dada, Pop, Op, colour field, hard-edge painting, Minimalism and Conceptual art, usually early. He saw Jasper Johns's work in Robert Rauschenberg's loft and gave Johns a show in 1958, taking on Rauschenberg the same year. Frank Stella had his first show with him in 1960 and Roy Lichtenstein signed in 1961; Andy Warhol, whom Castelli had initially turned down, joined in 1964. Almost every artist in this part of the constellation passed through his rooms at some point, and he kept the gallery going until his death in 1999.

rainermariarilke.blurb: The poet who published Balthus at thirteen.
rainermariarilke.bio: Rainer Maria Rilke, born in 1875, was an Austrian poet, playwright and translator and one of the defining voices in German-language literature, a writer whose work critics read for its mysticism and its close attention to subjective experience. He appears on this map for an act of patronage rather than for verse. As the lover of Balthus's mother he was close to the family, and when the boy was thirteen he saw the Mitsou drawings into print, giving the future painter a published book before he had any career at all. It was a small thing with a long consequence. Rilke's own output, spread across poetry, a novel, early novellas and volumes of correspondence, shaped the atmosphere in which that generation of European artists grew up. He died in 1926.

micheltapie.blurb: The critic who carried Gutai west.
micheltapie.bio: Michel Tapié, born in 1909 into an aristocratic French family and a second cousin once removed of Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, was a critic, curator, collector and painter, and an early and influential theorist of tachisme, the French style of abstract painting that ran parallel to American Abstract Expressionism in the 1940s and 1950s. In 1948 he was a founder member of the Compagnie de l'Art Brut with Jean Dubuffet and André Breton, and he managed the Foyer de l'Art Brut at the Galerie René Drouin. His largest act of transmission came later: from 1957 he championed Yoshihara Jirō and carried the Gutai group out of Japan, taking the work to Europe and America at a moment when almost nobody outside Japan had seen it. He died in 1987.

rudolfvonleyden.blurb: The Progressives' Berlin-born champion in Bombay.
rudolfvonleyden.bio: Rudolf von Leyden was a Berlin-born émigré critic in Bombay and one of the earliest, most consistent supporters of the Progressive Artists' Group. He backed F. N. Souza and his circle in print at a moment when Indian modernism had almost no critical apparatus of its own, and that advocacy is why his name sits on this map at all.

walterlanghammer.blurb: The art director who found the Progressives buyers.
walterlanghammer.bio: Walter Langhammer, art director of the Times of India, was one of the figures who gave the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay its first public and its first market. He championed M. F. Husain among others, and the Progressives found their earliest buyers through him at a point when there were almost none to find.

jeanpaulsartre.bio: Jean-Paul Sartre, born in 1905, was a philosopher, playwright, novelist and critic, the leading figure of French existentialism and one of the most argued-over intellectuals of his century. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964 and tried to refuse it, on the grounds that a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution. His presence on this map is as an interpreter: his essays on Alberto Giacometti framed the sculptor for a whole generation of readers, and much of what the postwar public understood by existential in art arrived through Sartre's prose rather than through the work itself. A political activist and a Marxist of his own idiosyncratic kind, his writing went on to shape sociology, critical theory and post-colonial thought. He died in 1980.

samuelbeckett.bio: Samuel Beckett, born in Ireland in 1906, wrote in both English and French and is credited with transforming modern theatre, working in a register of bleak comedy and stripped-back staging. Waiting for Godot, from 1953, is the play everyone knows; the Nobel Prize followed in 1969, awarded for finding new forms for the novel and the drama. What places him in this constellation is a physical collaboration: for the 1961 Paris revival of Godot, Alberto Giacometti made the tree, so that two of the century's most austere imaginations met on one small stage. Beckett wrote novels and poetry as well as plays, and later worked in film, and he remained one of the major figures of Irish literature until his death in 1989.

georgebrecht.bio: George Brecht, born George Ellis MacDiarmid in 1926, ran two careers at once. He was a professional chemist who consulted for Pfizer, Johnson and Johnson and Mobil Oil, and he was one of the central figures of Fluxus, involved from the first performances in Wiesbaden in 1962 through to George Maciunas's death in 1978. The bridge between the two was John Cage's class at the New School in 1958 and 1959, which gave a scientist's habits of procedure and instruction a new field to work in. Brecht called himself a conceptual artist and composer, and worked as a painter too. His influence on what Fluxus became ran well ahead of his own public visibility, which is the usual shape of a career built on giving other people things to do. He died in 2008.

alhansen.blurb: Cage's student, Fluxus collagist and performer.
alhansen.bio: Al Hansen, born in 1927, was an American artist, performer and collagist and a member of Fluxus, the loose international movement that formed around George Maciunas. Like several others in that circle he came out of John Cage's class at the New School, where a generation of visual artists learned to treat an action, a duration or an instruction as material for art. Hansen worked across performance, painting and collage for the rest of his life; Amazone, from 1994, is among the works recorded here, made the year before he died in 1995. His significance is of the connective kind this map exists to show: not one famous object but a continuous presence in the rooms where Fluxus was being made, from its first years to its last.

jacksonmaclow.bio: Jackson Mac Low, born in 1922, was a poet, composer, playwright and performance artist who spent his career handing decisions over to systems. Chance operations and other non-intentional methods drove his writing, an approach he first encountered in the music of John Cage, Earle Brown and Christian Wolff and refined after taking Cage's class at the New School. The results are texts made to be performed as much as read, closer to scores than to lyrics, and they put him alongside the composers rather than the poets of his generation. He taught at university level and worked as a printmaker as well. He was married to the artist Iris Lezak from 1962 to 1978 and to the poet Anne Tardos from 1990 until his death in 2004.

blinkypalermo.blurb: The abstract painter in Beuys's class.
blinkypalermo.bio: Blinky Palermo was the working name of a German painter born in 1943 who died in 1977, before he was thirty-five. He studied under Joseph Beuys at the Düsseldorf Academy from 1964 to 1967, in the class that turned out a whole generation of German artists, and came out of it an abstract painter rather than a maker of actions. His models were the hard cases of abstraction, Kazimir Malevich, Barnett Newman and Ellsworth Kelly, and he worked as painter, draughtsman and sculptor across a career of little more than a decade. The brevity is part of the story: an artist formed by the most charismatic teacher of the period who found a quieter register of his own and then ran out of time.

imiknoebel.blurb: Knife-cuts in red, yellow and blue.
imiknoebel.bio: Imi Knoebel, born in Germany in 1940, studied under Joseph Beuys at the Düsseldorf Academy and then went a long way from his teacher, towards a minimal, abstract art of painting and sculpture. His signature technique is the Messerschnitt, the knife cut, and he returns constantly to the primary colours: red, yellow and blue. He has worked with photography and video installation as well, and Kinderstern, from 1988, is among the works recorded here. He still lives and works in Düsseldorf, the city where he trained, which makes him one of the long continuities in this part of the map: a Beuys student who outlasted the moment, kept to the same small set of means, and built an entire body of work from cutting, layering and colour.

katharinasieverding.bio: Katharina Sieverding, born in Germany in 1941, is a photographer known above all for self-portraiture, returning to her own face again and again as the material of the work. She studied at the Düsseldorf Academy under Joseph Beuys, among a group of students who each took his teaching somewhere he had not gone himself, and hers went into photography rather than sculpture or action. She has lived and worked between Berlin and Düsseldorf, and taught for many years at the University of the Arts in Berlin, where she is now professor emeritus. Her long career sits at the junction of performance and portraiture, and it connects the Beuys classroom to the German photographic tradition that grew up in the same city a few doors away.

saitoyoshishige.bio: Saitō Yoshishige, born in 1904, was a Japanese painter, sculptor and installation artist whose longest-running influence came through teaching. At Tama Art University in Tokyo he taught Sekine Nobuo, Suga Kishio and Koshimizu Susumu, three of the artists who would go on to define Mono-ha, and the movement is traceable in large part to that one classroom. His own practice moved between painting and three-dimensional work across a career that ran through most of the twentieth century; he was in his nineties when he died in 2001. This map is full of teachers whose names are less familiar than their students', and Saitō is among the clearest cases: an educator whose reputation rests as much on what he made possible as on what he made.

vladimirfavorsky.blurb: Woodcut master who mentored the nonconformists.
vladimirfavorsky.bio: Vladimir Favorsky, born in 1886, was a Russian draughtsman, engraver and teacher who worked in Moscow from the reign of Nicholas II through to the Khrushchev years, best known for his woodcut illustrations. He belonged to the Four Arts society, became a full member of the Soviet Academy of Arts in 1962 and was named a People's Artist of the USSR the following year, official honours arriving at the very end of a long life. The role that puts him on this map is unofficial: through the 1950s he and Robert Falk privately mentored the young Erik Bulatov in Moscow, outside the academy altogether. That quiet teaching is one of the threads by which an older Russian modernism reached the Soviet nonconformists. He died in 1964.

gerhardrichter.blurb: Painting after photography, both at once.
gerhardrichter.bio: Gerhard Richter, born in Germany in 1932, has spent more than sixty years declining to settle into a single manner: photorealistic paintings, large abstractions, photographs, and glass and window pieces such as the Cathedral Window of 2007. In 1963, with Sigmar Polke and Konrad Lueg, he declared Capitalist Realism in Düsseldorf, and that same year he and Lueg staged Living with Pop in a furniture store, using the shop floor as the gallery. Lueg would later reappear on the other side of the trade as the dealer Konrad Fischer. Richter went on to teach as well, and Thomas Struth began in his painting class before crossing over to Bernd and Hilla Becher. He is counted among the most important German artists of the contemporary period, and was at one point the most expensive living painter.

sigmarpolke.bio: Sigmar Polke, born in 1941, treated painting as an open experiment. With Gerhard Richter and Konrad Lueg he declared Capitalist Realism in Düsseldorf in 1963, and from there he moved through styles, subjects and materials with no evident intention of settling on any of them. In the 1970s he concentrated on photography, though Propellerfrau dates from 1969, and when he returned to paint in the 1980s he made abstractions whose images arose by chance, out of chemical reactions between pigment and other substances. The last twenty years of his life produced paintings built around his reading of historical events. Alongside Richter he is the central German painter of the postwar generation, and the more unruly of the two. He worked as photographer, painter, sculptor and designer until his death in 2010.

konradlueg.blurb: The painter who became dealer Konrad Fischer.
konradlueg.bio: Konrad Lueg was one of the young Düsseldorf artists who declared Capitalist Realism in 1963, and with Gerhard Richter he staged Living with Pop that year in a furniture store, using the shop floor as the exhibition. He then left his own painting for the other side of the trade, becoming the dealer Konrad Fischer.

terryatkinson.bio: Terry Atkinson, born in England in 1939, is a painter and object-maker who helped turn conceptual art into a collective enterprise. In 1968, in Coventry, he founded Art and Language with Michael Baldwin, David Bainbridge and Harold Hurrell. Joseph Kosuth joined in 1969 as the group's American editor, a title that says a good deal about how the project worked: as much a publication and a running argument as a studio, and now tied to the New York conceptualists as well. Art and Language became one of the few genuinely collaborative bodies of work in twentieth-century art, with authorship deliberately dispersed among its members. Atkinson has continued to work as a painter and maker of objects, but the Coventry years remain the point at which British conceptualism found its argument.

michaelbaldwin.blurb: Art and Language, from the first day.
michaelbaldwin.bio: Michael Baldwin, born in Britain in 1945, is a conceptual artist, writer and editor and a founding member of Art and Language. He and Terry Atkinson started the group in Coventry in 1968, and Baldwin has been associated with it ever since, across a project designed from the outset to make individual authorship difficult to locate. Writing and editing were as much his medium as painting; his own record lists artist, editor, writer and painter side by side, which is a fair description of how the group operated. He was in his early twenties when it began, and his has been a career conducted very largely under a collective name rather than under his own, which is precisely the point the work was making.

davidbainbridge.blurb: The sculptor among Art and Language's founders.
davidbainbridge.bio: David Bainbridge, born in Britain in 1941, was a sculptor and conceptual artist and one of the founding members of Art and Language, the group he started with Terry Atkinson. He came to it from sculpture, at the moment when a handful of British artists decided that the discussion about art could be the art itself. Bainbridge is recorded as a sculptor as well as a conceptual artist, and the move from making objects to making propositions is the story of his generation in miniature. Like the others he worked in a way that makes individual attribution awkward, which is exactly what the project intended: the group is credited, not the person. He died in 2013, remembered as much for the collective he helped start as for anything signed with his own name.

haroldhurrell.blurb: A founding member of Art and Language.
haroldhurrell.bio: Harold Hurrell, born in Britain in 1940, is a conceptual artist and one of the founding members of Art and Language, the group he started with Terry Atkinson. He worked in painting and installation alongside the group's collective output, and he later left it, a common ending in a project built on argument, where disagreement about what counted as the work was itself part of the work.
