Hurrell has remained one of the less publicly visible names attached to it, which is partly a consequence of the method: when authorship is deliberately shared, the record tends to keep only the loudest names. He is a reminder that Art and Language began as a small group of British artists who had decided the discussion about art could be the art.

oliviermosset.bio: Olivier Mosset, born in Switzerland in 1944, is a painter, printmaker and photographer and one of the four artists of BMPT, the Paris group of 1966 and 1967 whose name is simply the initials of its members: Buren, Mosset, Parmentier and Toroni. The group lasted barely a year, but its argument sits at the root of institutional critique, the strand of art that takes the gallery and the idea of the artist as its subject rather than its setting. Mosset has gone on painting for six decades since. He now lives and works in Tucson, Arizona, a long way in every sense from the Paris in which the group made its case. He is one of the few artists on this map whose position rests on a single year of collective work.

andreimonastyrski.bio: Andrei Monastyrski, born in 1949, is a Russian poet, writer, artist and art theorist and, alongside Ilya Kabakov, one of the leading figures of Moscow Conceptualism. He belongs to the circle that formed around Kabakov and helped found Collective Actions, working entirely outside the official Soviet art system. Words came first for him: he is an author and theorist as much as an artist, and the writing that accumulated around the group's activity is part of its substance rather than a commentary on it. His name marks the point at which unofficial Soviet art became a self-aware movement with a theory of its own, rather than a scattering of private practices, and he remains one of its central figures, still working as poet, artist and theorist from a position built entirely outside the official institutions.

halewoodruff.bio: Hale Woodruff, born in 1900, was an American painter and printmaker best known for his murals, public work at a scale few African American artists of his generation were offered. Painting, printmaking and mural cycles ran alongside one another throughout his career. He was one of the founders of Spiral, the group he formed with Romare Bearden, and by the time it came together he was already among the older figures in the room, carrying a longer history into it. Spiral sits just ahead of the Black Arts Movement in this map's chronology, and Woodruff is one of the figures who connects the two: an artist whose reputation was made in mural painting and who then helped open a space for the argument that followed. He died in 1980.

toshiichiyanagi.blurb: Yoko Ono's first husband, Cage's student.
toshiichiyanagi.bio: Toshi Ichiyanagi, born in 1933, was one of the leading Japanese composers of the postwar era, a pianist who wrote Western-style operas, orchestral and chamber music and works for traditional Japanese instruments, often using chance procedures, extended technique and unconventional scoring. He was a student of John Cage, and it was in that circle that he met Yoko Ono, to whom he was married from 1956 to 1962. Together they ran the Chambers Street loft series in 1960 and 1961, one of the gathering points of the scene from which Fluxus and much else emerged. Ichiyanagi went on to become a central figure in Japan's avant-garde for the rest of his life, carrying those methods into a very different musical culture. He died in 2022.

johnlennon.blurb: The Beatle who walked into Fluxus.
johnlennon.bio: John Lennon, born in 1940, founded the Beatles and was their co-lead singer and rhythm guitarist; his songwriting partnership with Paul McCartney remains the most successful in the history of popular music. He appears in this constellation because of what he did next. In 1969 he married Yoko Ono, and the two made films, records and public actions together, including the Bed-Ins, in which their own celebrity was the medium. It was an unusual piece of traffic in both directions: the most famous musician alive walking into the Fluxus world, and a Fluxus artist reaching an audience of a size no gallery could offer, with all the misreadings that came with it. Lennon remained a musician, writer and activist until his death in 1980.

berndbecher.blurb: Half of photography's most influential partnership.
berndbecher.bio: Bernd Becher, with his wife Hilla, photographed industrial buildings and structures as a single author for fifty years. The two married in 1961 and worked as one artist, producing the typologies, often arranged in grids, that made comparison rather than description the point of a photograph. Their teaching mattered as much as the pictures: at the Düsseldorf Academy the Bechers taught Andreas Gursky, Thomas Ruff, Thomas Struth, Candida Höfer and Axel Hütte, the group known ever since as the Düsseldorf School of Photography. Ruff was there from 1977 to 1985 and Gursky from 1981, becoming a Meisterschüler in 1987, while Struth crossed over from Gerhard Richter's painting class. The Bechers received the Erasmus Prize and the Hasselblad Award, and their sober, systematic way of looking shaped documentary photography in Germany and abroad.

hillabecher.blurb: The other half, equal in everything.
hillabecher.bio: Hilla Becher, born in 1934, was a German conceptual photographer whose career spanned more than fifty years and was conducted almost entirely alongside her husband Bernd, whom she married in 1961. The two photographed industrial structures as a single author, and her role was in no sense the secondary one: the images were made jointly, credited jointly, and the systematic method that defined them belonged to both. Their work took them across the United States, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Great Britain, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Italy, recording the architecture of heavy industry building by building. Between them they founded what became the Düsseldorf School of Photography, whose students count among the best-known photographers of the following generation. She went on working until her death in 2015.

evahesse.blurb: Latex and fibreglass made into sculpture.
evahesse.bio: Eva Hesse, born in Germany in 1936, pioneered materials that had no place in sculpture before her: latex, fibreglass and plastics, worked into forms that were soft and physical where Minimalism had been hard and exact. In 1961 she married the artist Tom Doyle, and in 1964 a commission took the couple to Germany; that year abroad was where she found the industrial materials that changed her work. Her closest artistic friendship was with Sol LeWitt, whom she had known since 1960 and whose letter to her of 1965, remembered simply as the Do letter, is one of the most quoted documents of the period. Hesse died in 1970, after barely a decade of mature work, and is counted among the artists who ushered in postminimal art.

tomdoyle.blurb: Sculptor whose commission changed Eva Hesse.
tomdoyle.bio: Tom Doyle, born in the United States in 1928, was a sculptor working through the years when American sculpture was paring itself back to structure, material and weight. He married Eva Hesse in 1961, and in 1964 a commission of his took the couple to Germany. That trip is the reason his name recurs in accounts of the period: it was in Germany that Hesse found the materials which would remake her art. Doyle's own work belongs to the minimal turn of those same years, and he died in 2016. He sits in the record in two registers at once, as an artist of his own generation, and as the man whose commission put Eva Hesse where she needed to be. The second register has tended to eclipse the first, which is its own comment on how the period gets told.

ulay.blurb: Abramović's partner in life and performance.
ulay.bio: Ulay, born Frank Uwe Laysiepen in Germany in 1943, was an artist of the body and the photograph, first recognised for his Polaroid work and then, for twelve years, inseparable from Marina Abramović. From 1976 to 1988 the two lived and performed together, making the collaborative pieces that brought both of them international recognition. They ended it deliberately and in public: the relationship was closed by walking the Great Wall of China from opposite ends, each setting out towards the other. Twenty-two years later Ulay and Abramović were reunited at her 2010 MoMA performance The Artist Is Present, and the moment became one of the most widely seen moments in the history of the form. He lived and worked between Amsterdam and Ljubljana, and died in 2020.

kathydillon.bio: Kathy Dillon was the partner and co-performer of Vito Acconci in his early 1970s pieces. Body art of that moment was often made by two people and remembered under one name; Dillon is on the other side of that arrangement, present in the work as a collaborator, and this map records her as one.

jamestenney.blurb: Composer, and Schneemann's partner on camera.
jamestenney.bio: James Tenney, born in 1934, was an American composer, pianist and music theorist whose work ran ahead of several fields at once. He made early contributions to plunderphonics, sound synthesis, algorithmic composition, process music, spectral music and microtonal tuning systems including extended just intonation, and his theoretical writing dealt with musical form, texture, timbre and the perception of consonance and dissonance. He appears in this constellation as the partner of Carolee Schneemann and as a performer in her work, appearing in Fuses and in Meat Joy. That makes him one of the people whose body is the material of a history usually told through a single name, and one of the composers who kept the performance art of the 1960s in constant conversation with music. He died in 2006.

jeanneclaude.blurb: Half of one artist, with Christo.
jeanneclaude.bio: Jeanne-Claude Denat de Guillebon, born in 1935, worked with Christo as a single artist. The two were born on the same day, married, and made every project jointly: large-scale, temporary, site-specific works in which landmarks and landscapes were wrapped in fabric or otherwise transformed for a matter of days. Running Fence in California, the Pont Neuf wrapped in Paris, the Wrapped Reichstag and The Gates in New York's Central Park were all realised under the two names together, as were The Umbrellas and The Floating Piers. She died in 2009. The insistence on shared authorship was not a formality but the terms on which the work was made, and this map takes those terms at face value rather than filing her under her husband.

gerardmalanga.blurb: Warhol's silkscreen partner at the Factory.
gerardmalanga.bio: Gerard Malanga, born in 1943, is a poet, photographer, filmmaker, actor, curator and archivist, and was Andy Warhol's studio assistant at the Factory from 1963 to 1970, the years of the silkscreens and the films. He was Warhol's silkscreen partner, which means many of the paintings of that period passed through his hands as well, and that is precisely the point of an art which treated authorship as a question of production. The New York Times later called him Warhol's most important associate. Alongside that work he built his own body of poetry and photography and became one of the principal archivists of the scene he had lived inside, which is why so much of the first-hand record of the Factory exists at all.

billyname.blurb: He silvered the Factory and photographed it.
billyname.bio: Billy Name, born William Linich in 1940, was the photographer, lighting designer and filmmaker who gave the Factory its look. He silvered the walls of Andy Warhol's studio, creating the room that became the emblem of 1960s New York, and then lived in its darkroom, photographing what happened outside the door. His pictures are the primary visual record of the Factory in its most productive years, which means that much of what later generations see when they picture Warhol's circle is Billy Name's framing rather than Warhol's. The Factory's silver period is, in a real sense, as much his design as anyone else's. He also worked as a lighting designer, a director and an occasional actor on film. He died in 2016, long after the scene he had documented had passed into history.

robertryman.blurb: A lifetime of white on white.
robertryman.bio: Robert Ryman, born in 1930, spent a long career painting white on white, not as a refusal but as a way of concentrating attention on everything else a painting is made of. Identified with monochrome painting, Minimalism and conceptual art at once, he lived and worked in New York for the whole of it. In the early 1960s he was on the Museum of Modern Art payroll alongside Sol LeWitt and Dan Flavin, LeWitt at the book counter and the night desk while Ryman and Flavin worked as guards, which meant three of the artists who would define the following decade spent their days standing in front of the collection. Ryman kept to his single problem, patiently and without variation of subject, until his death in 2019.

jackyoungerman.bio: Jack Youngerman, born in 1926, was an American painter and sculptor known for his paintings and constructions, working in the hard-edged abstraction that followed Abstract Expressionism. He met Ellsworth Kelly in Paris, and the two later took lofts on Coenties Slip in Lower Manhattan, the address that gathered a group of artists working at a deliberate distance from the centre of the New York art world. That shared move is the kind of connection this map is built to record: not a school or a manifesto, but two painters who met abroad and then chose the same street. Constructions and paintings stayed his two consistent formats, and he sits here among the hard-edge and post-painterly abstraction of the 1960s. Youngerman went on working across painting and sculpture for the rest of a long career, and died in 2020.

ivankarp.blurb: The first dealer through Warhol's door.
ivankarp.bio: Ivan Karp, born in 1926, was the dealer who saw Pop coming first. As director of Leo Castelli's gallery he was the first dealer to visit Andy Warhol's studio, in 1961, well ahead of anyone else in the trade. Karp was instrumental in the emergence of Pop art as a public phenomenon and a market, and equally so in the development of Manhattan's SoHo gallery district during the 1960s, which changed where art was shown in New York for the next thirty years. He worked as a curator and a museologist too, and his career reads like a map of where the New York art world was moving in those years. He was an author and a collector as well as a gallerist, and one of the people whose taste, exercised on someone else's behalf, quietly redirected a decade. He died in 2012.

konradfischer.bio: Konrad Fischer opened a Düsseldorf gallery that gave the American Minimalists their European debut from 1967, showing Carl Andre among others. In 1968 Sol LeWitt made his first European wall drawing there. It was a small room with an outsized effect on where new art was seen, and on how quickly it crossed the Atlantic.

sethsiegelaub.bio: Seth Siegelaub, born in 1941, was the dealer and curator who worked out that if art could be an idea, an exhibition could be a book. Between 1968 and 1971 he organised the shows and catalogues that effectively constituted Conceptual art as a movement, working with Lawrence Weiner, Joseph Kosuth, Douglas Huebler and Robert Barry. The Xerox Book of 1968 and the exhibition known as January 5 to 31, 1969 are the best remembered. He then left the art world for other research entirely, working as a political researcher and publisher, a bibliographer and collector of textile history, and latterly on a project about time and causality in physics. Few figures in this constellation shaped a movement so decisively and then walked away from it so completely. He died in 2013.

haraldszeemann.blurb: The curator who became an author.
haraldszeemann.bio: Harald Szeemann, born in Switzerland in 1933, curated more than two hundred exhibitions and in the process turned curating into something close to authorship. When Attitudes Become Form, staged in Bern in 1969, put Joseph Beuys and his generation in front of a museum public and remains the reference point for how such shows are made; documenta 5 in 1972, also his, took the argument to the largest stage in European art. He brought Arte Povera into the international circuit, championing Mario Merz among others, and worked across movements that had little in common except that he had recognised them early. An art historian and critic as well as a curator, he is generally credited with redefining the role. He died in 2005.

virginiadwan.bio: Virginia Dwan, born in 1931, was the patron who made land art physically possible. Her galleries, Dwan Gallery in Los Angeles from 1959 to 1967 and in New York from 1965 to 1971, showed Minimalism and Conceptual art, but her decisive contribution was funding for work no gallery could hold. She paid for Robert Smithson's Spiral Jetty in 1970 and Michael Heizer's Double Negative in 1969, and backed Walter De Maria's The Lightning Field together with the Dia Art Foundation. Three of the largest works of American art exist because one collector was willing to pay for things she could never sell. She later founded the Dwan Light Sanctuary at Montezuma, New Mexico, and remained a collector and philanthropist until her death in 2022.

ediesedgwick.bio: Edie Sedgwick, born in 1943, was an actress, model and socialite and the most visible of Andy Warhol's superstars. In 1965 she was co-lead in around a dozen of his films, and Vogue named her a Youthquaker that year, acknowledging the effect she was having on how young people dressed and behaved. She was a collaborator rather than a subject in the strict sense: the films were built around her presence and would not exist without it. The association was short, and she died in 1971, still in her twenties. She is one of the names this map keeps for the work rather than for the legend. Her image has outlived nearly everything else from that stretch of the Factory's history, which is its own comment on an art that turned the people around it into pictures.

brigidberlin.blurb: She taped the Factory for decades.
brigidberlin.bio: Brigid Berlin, born in 1939 and often known as Brigid Polk, was an American artist and one of the Warhol superstars, though her most consequential contribution was made with a tape recorder. For two decades she taped the Factory: conversations, phone calls, arguments, the ordinary noise of the place, building an audio record of Andy Warhol's circle that nobody else thought to make. She worked as a photographer, painter, actress and film producer as well. The recordings turn a scene famous for its surfaces into something with texture and duration, and they are among the reasons the Factory can still be described from the inside rather than only from the pictures it produced. Berlin is a case of an artist whose real medium turned out to be the room she was standing in. She died in 2020.

valeriesolanas.blurb: The writer who shot Andy Warhol.
valeriesolanas.bio: Valerie Solanas, born in 1936, was an American radical feminist and author who also worked as a playwright, a film actor and a director. She moved on the fringes of Andy Warhol's Factory scene in the 1960s, and it is that association for which she is remembered: in June 1968 she shot Warhol, an attempted assassination that has shadowed accounts of Pop art ever since. She appears in this map not as a painter or a sculptor but as a writer whose collision with the most famous figure of American Pop changed how that world understood itself and who it let through the door. She died in 1988. Solanas remains one of the most difficult and disquieting figures attached to the New York art world of her decade.

johnbaldessari.blurb: CalArts' great teacher of conceptual art.
johnbaldessari.bio: John Baldessari, born in 1931, was an American conceptual artist who built his work from found photography and appropriated images, cropping, obscuring and recombining pictures that already existed. He lived and worked in Santa Monica and Venice, California, and made pieces such as READ/WRITE/THINK/DREAM in 2001. His influence, though, ran as much through the classroom as the studio. His Post-Studio class at CalArts in the 1970s passed through an extraordinary sequence of students: David Salle and Jack Goldstein, Mike Kelley between 1976 and 1978, Tony Oursler, Matt Mullican and Barbara Bloom. Between them they carried his suspicion of the precious art object into photography, video, installation and appropriation. Baldessari died in 2020, by which point the teaching had arguably shaped as much American art as the work itself.

mikekelley.bio: Mike Kelley, born in 1954, was an American artist who worked in almost every material available to him: found objects, textile banners, drawings, assemblage, collage, performance, photography, sound and video, alongside a substantial body of critical and creative writing and a run of curatorial projects. He studied under John Baldessari in the Post-Studio class at CalArts between 1976 and 1978, and the collaborative habit stayed with him, producing projects with Paul McCarthy, Tony Oursler and John Miller. Works such as Riddle of the Sphinx sit in an output preoccupied with class, popular culture and youthful rebellion. Writing in The New York Times after Kelley's death in 2012, the critic Holland Cotter placed him among the most influential American artists of the previous quarter century, and a sharp commentator on all three.

tonyoursler.blurb: Multimedia installations that speak and stare.
tonyoursler.bio: Tony Oursler, born in 1957, is an American multimedia and installation artist who completed a Bachelor of Fine Arts at the California Institute of the Arts in Valencia in 1979, where John Baldessari was among his teachers. His practice moves across video, sculpture, installation, performance and painting, and he is also credited as a director, photographer, draftsperson and television producer, a range that reflects how thoroughly he treats the moving image as physical material rather than as something merely shown on a screen. That instinct came out of a school where the conceptual habits of the 1970s were taught as a starting point rather than a style. He is married to Jacqueline Humphries, and lives and works in New York City. Oursler remains one of the defining figures in the use of video as sculptural material.

mattmullican.blurb: An artist raised by two artists.
mattmullican.bio: Matt Mullican, born in 1951, is an American artist and educator who works as a sculptor, painter and installation artist. He is the child of the artists Lee Mullican and Luchita Hurtado, so a life in art was the family inheritance rather than a break from it. At CalArts he passed through John Baldessari's teaching, joining the run of students who took conceptual method out of painting and into signs, systems and installation. A long sequence of untitled works, including pieces from 1989, 1993 and 1998, marks a practice that resists tidy titling and returns instead to recurring structures. He divides his time between Berlin and New York City. Teaching has run alongside the making throughout, keeping him close to the pedagogical tradition he came out of himself.

barbarabloom.blurb: Conceptual installations of taste and display.
barbarabloom.bio: Barbara Bloom, born in 1951, is an American conceptual artist best known for multi-media installations, and she also works as a photographer and lithographer. She studied at CalArts under John Baldessari, and her work sits loosely alongside the group of artists known as the Pictures Generation, though she has always been at an angle to it, more interested in how objects are presented, framed and collected than in the appropriated image alone. For nearly twenty years she lived in Europe, first in Amsterdam and then in Berlin, an unusually long absence from the New York scene her peers were making. Since 1992 she has lived in New York City with her husband, the writer and composer Chris Mann, and their daughter, and continues to work there.

charlesclough.blurb: The Buffalo painter who co-founded Hallwalls.
charlesclough.bio: Charles Sidney Clough, born in 1951, is an American painter whose work has been shown in more than seventy solo and over a hundred and fifty group exhibitions across North America and Europe, and is held in the permanent collections of more than seventy museums, among them the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the National Gallery of Art and the Smithsonian American Art Museum. He has held fellowships and grants from the New York State Council on the Arts, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation and the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation. In 1974, with Robert Longo, he co-founded Hallwalls in Buffalo, the artist-run space that became a launching point for a generation of American artists.

julieault.blurb: Group Material's co-founder and lasting conscience.
julieault.bio: Julie Ault, born in 1957, is an American artist, curator and editor who co-founded Group Material in 1979, the New York artists' collaborative that went on to produce more than fifty exhibitions and public projects testing the relationship between politics and aesthetics. Doug Ashford was among her fellow founders, and Félix González-Torres joined the group in 1987 and stayed until 1991, a period that shaped his understanding of what a public artwork could do. Ault's own practice has never separated making from curating, archiving, editing and organising. In 2018 she received a MacArthur Fellowship in recognition of exactly that fusion, described as a redefinition of the roles of artwork and artist. She remains one of the clearest models of collective authorship in American art.

dougashford.blurb: A founding member of Group Material.
dougashford.bio: Doug Ashford is an American artist associated with the politically engaged art of New York in the AIDS era. He was one of the founding members of Group Material, the artists' collaborative co-founded by Julie Ault, whose exhibitions and public projects treated the gallery as a place for collective argument rather than individual display.

madesheng.blurb: A founding Star, self-taught in woodblock.
madesheng.bio: Ma Desheng, born in Beijing in 1952, is a Chinese artist and poet who also works as a painter and calligrapher, and who taught himself the craft of woodblock carving. In 1979 he was one of the founding members of the Stars group in Beijing, alongside Ai Weiwei. He was arrested for his role in arranging the group's first exhibition, and in the repressions against liberal thinkers that followed, a sequence that made plain how little room there was for art organised outside official channels. In 1986 he relocated to Paris, where the work continued at a distance from the scene he had helped begin. His prints and paintings are held in significant public and private collections, including the Ashmolean Museum and the British Museum.

wangkeping.blurb: One of the founding Stars, Beijing.
wangkeping.bio: Wang Keping is a Chinese artist and one of the founding members of the Stars group, the unofficial Beijing collective he helped establish with Ai Weiwei. The group's insistence on making art outside state channels marks the beginning of the independent Chinese art that runs through the 1985 New Wave and after.

avramfinkelstein.bio: Avram Finkelstein, born in 1952, is an American artist, writer and gay rights activist, and a member of the AIDS art collective Gran Fury. In 1988, with Donald Moffett among others, he helped found Gran Fury in New York as the graphics collective attached to ACT UP, turning the visual language of advertising against public indifference to the epidemic. Finkelstein came out of the same late-1980s ACT UP graphics culture that Félix González-Torres worked through, a shared milieu in which posters, stickers and street imagery were treated as seriously as anything hung in a gallery. His writing has since become one of the primary first-hand accounts of how that work was made. He remains an artist for whom design, activism and authorship are inseparable.

donaldmoffett.blurb: A painter who helped found Gran Fury.
donaldmoffett.bio: Donald Moffett, born in 1955, is an American painter who has also worked as a designer, and whose practice has run alongside a long commitment to political organising. In 1988, with Avram Finkelstein among others, he helped found Gran Fury in New York, the graphics collective that produced the visual language of ACT UP during the worst years of the AIDS epidemic. That work was made collectively rather than signed, and aimed at the street rather than the gallery, and it changed what political art in America could look like. Moffett's painting continued in parallel, so his career sits across two registers at once, the anonymous urgency of the collective and the slower, individual work of the studio. He remains one of the central figures of AIDS-era American art.

maudsulter.blurb: Black feminist photographer, poet and curator.
maudsulter.bio: Maud Sulter, born in 1960, was a Scottish artist of Ghanaian heritage who worked as a photographer, poet, short story writer, educator, cultural historian and curator. She began as a writer, turning to visual art shortly afterwards, and moved quickly: by the end of 1985 she had shown work in three exhibitions and published her first collection of poetry. Her work was made in company, through collaborations with other Black feminist scholars and activists, and it set out to record the lives of Black people in Europe. She was a champion of the African-American sculptor Edmonia Lewis and was long fascinated by the Haitian-born French performer Jeanne Duval. Her partner was the artist Lubaina Himid, with whom she collaborated on exhibitions and publishing. Sulter died in 2008.

rosslaycock.blurb: The partner inside the candy spills.
rosslaycock.bio: Ross Laycock was the partner of the artist Félix González-Torres. They were together from 1983 until 1991, the year Laycock died of complications from AIDS. He is present throughout the work that followed, and in some of the most widely seen art of the decade: the piles of hard candy that visitors are free to take from, and the paired clocks that start together and drift apart. One of the candy works, now in the collection of the Art Institute of Chicago, carries an ideal weight of 175 pounds, a figure that stands for Laycock himself. Because these pieces can be installed differently each time and are altered by the audiences that meet them, his presence in them is deliberately unstable. He is remembered here as the person the work is addressed to.

peterhujar.bio: Peter Hujar, born in 1934, was an American photographer best known for his black-and-white portraits, made with an unsparing stillness that gave his sitters an almost sculptural presence. His work received only marginal public recognition while he was alive, and he has since been recognised as one of the major American photographers of the 1970s and 1980s. Recognition came late, and mostly after his death, which is now inseparable from the way the work is read. He and David Wojnarowicz were briefly lovers and then closest friends, an alliance that shaped both of them, with the older photographer serving as a touchstone for the younger artist. Hujar died in 1987, and Wojnarowicz photographed his death, images that have become one of the defining records of that period in the New York art world.

pattismith.bio: Patti Smith, born in 1946, is an American singer, songwriter, poet and author who has also worked as a visual artist and a human rights defender. Her 1975 debut album, Horses, made her a central figure in the New York punk scene, and her work has fused rock and poetry ever since. In 1978 Because the Night, co-written with Bruce Springsteen, reached number thirteen on the Billboard Hot 100 and number five in the United Kingdom. Her place in this map runs through Robert Mapplethorpe: they were lovers and then friends for life, and she wrote Just Kids about those years. The poetry and the music were never separate practices in her hands, and neither was the visual work. Smith remains the clearest link between the downtown art world and the music that grew out of it.

aiqing.blurb: The poet father of Ai Weiwei.
aiqing.bio: Ai Qing, born Jiang Zhenghan in 1910 and styled Jiang Haicheng, was one of the major Chinese poets of the twentieth century, writing also as Linbi, Ke'a and Ejia. He worked as a writer, journalist and painter as well as a poet. His significance for this map is double: the poems themselves, and the fact that he was sent into internal exile, a punishment his family shared and one that formed the political instincts of his son, the artist Ai Weiwei. That inheritance runs directly into Ai Weiwei's later work, in which official power and the individual voice are set permanently against one another. Ai Qing died in 1996. The line from the father's silencing to the son's insistence on speaking is one of the clearest in modern Chinese art.

kimwhanki.bio: Kim Whanki, born in 1913, was a Korean painter and a pioneer of abstraction in his country's art. His life was unusually mobile: he lived and worked in Tokyo, in Seoul and Busan, in Paris, and finally in New York City, where he died in 1974, and the movement between those places is legible in a body of work that pulled Korean sensibility into an international abstract language. His importance to the generation that followed is also familial. He was the father-in-law of the painter Yun Hyong-keun, a relationship that amounts to the closest thing Dansaekhwa had to a lineage, passing a set of concerns about surface, restraint and material directly from one painter to the next. Kim remains the pivotal figure in Korean modern painting.

kennyscharf.blurb: East Village pop, cartoons and cosmos.
kennyscharf.bio: Kenny Scharf, born in 1958, is an American painter who came up in the interdisciplinary East Village art scene of 1980s New York alongside Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring. He and Haring were roommates at the School of Visual Arts in 1978, a shared apartment that turned out to be one of the founding rooms of that decade's downtown art. His do-it-yourself practice has spanned painting, sculpture, fashion, video, performance and street art, refusing the distinction between the gallery and the pavement. Growing up in post-war Southern California left him fascinated by television and the futuristic promise of modern design, and his paintings fill up with pop culture icons like the Flintstones and the Jetsons, or with caricatured middle-class Americans stranded in apocalyptic science fiction settings. Tikitotmoniki Totems dates from 2001.

brunobischofberger.blurb: The dealer who paired Basquiat with Warhol.
brunobischofberger.bio: Bruno Franz Bischofberger, born in 1940, was a Swiss art dealer, gallerist and collector who became one of the pivotal European figures in the American art market of the 1980s. He championed Jean-Michel Basquiat, and it was Bischofberger who brokered the collaboration between Basquiat and Andy Warhol, bringing together the most famous artist of the previous generation and the most talked-about of the new one, a pairing that produced a body of joint paintings and a reception that has never quite settled. Dealers rarely appear in accounts of that decade, but the introductions they made determined which artists met, which shows happened and which reputations survived. Bischofberger built one of the significant private collections of his era. He died in 2026.

anninanosei.blurb: Gave Basquiat a basement to paint in.
anninanosei.bio: Annina Nosei, born in 1939, is an Italian-born art dealer and gallerist best known as Jean-Michel Basquiat's first dealer. In 1981 she gave him studio space in the basement beneath her gallery, a decision that has been argued over ever since, but which supplied a young artist with materials, room and a market at exactly the moment he needed all three. From 1981 to 2006 the Annina Nosei Gallery represented or exhibited a notably wide range of artists, among them Barbara Kruger, Robert Longo, Ghada Amer and Shirin Neshat. Her programme ran for twenty-five years and was consistently ahead of the institutions around it. Nosei remains a key example of how much of the 1980s art world was made by dealers rather than curators.

maryboone.bio: Mary Boone, born in 1951, is an American art dealer and collector who, as owner and director of the Mary Boone Gallery, played a decisive role in the New York art market of the 1980s. Her first two artists, Julian Schnabel and David Salle, both became internationally known, and both owed much of that to her: she made Schnabel's reputation with his shows in 1979 and 1981, and represented Salle from 1979, giving painting a commercial momentum after a decade in which conceptual work had dominated. In 1982 New York magazine put her on its cover as the new queen of the art scene, a phrase that fixed both her power and the era's appetite for art as spectacle. Few dealers have been so closely identified with a decade's taste.

charlessaatchi.blurb: The adman who bought art wholesale.
charlessaatchi.bio: Charles Saatchi, born in 1943, is an Iraqi-British businessman who co-founded the advertising agency Saatchi & Saatchi with his brother Maurice and led it through the 1980s, when it was the largest in the world; the brothers left in 1995 and formed M&C Saatchi the same year. His effect on art came through collecting at scale. He bought Julian Schnabel in bulk in the early 1980s and later sold in bulk, a demonstration of how quickly a single buyer could inflate and deflate a market. He funded Damien Hirst's The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living in 1991, staged Sensation in 1997, and bought Tracey Emin's My Bed in 2000. No individual did more to make the Young British Artists a public phenomenon.

michaelwerner.blurb: The Cologne dealer who got Penck out.
michaelwerner.bio: Michael Werner is an art dealer based in Cologne, who championed A. R. Penck. He showed Penck's work in the West and got his paintings out of the German Democratic Republic, an act of logistics as much as dealing, and one that made a career possible for an artist the East German state would not exhibit.

samwagstaff.bio: Sam Wagstaff, born in 1921, was an American curator, collector and patron of the arts whose taste ran ahead of the institutions around him. He supported minimalism, pop art, conceptual art and earthworks, but his most consequential enthusiasm was photography: his collecting and advocacy anticipated the medium's acceptance as a fine art rather than a trade. He was the artistic mentor and benefactor of Robert Mapplethorpe and of the poet and musician Patti Smith, and with Mapplethorpe the relationship was total, curator, collector, partner and financier of the career at once. That combination of roles would be unthinkable now, but it is the reason a young photographer had the means to work. Wagstaff died in 1987, by which time photography was beginning to be collected as seriously as he had always insisted it should be.

gaominglu.bio: Gao Minglu, born in 1949, is a critic, curator and scholar of contemporary Chinese art, and one of the people who gave the 1985 New Wave its shape as a movement rather than a scatter of individual practices. In February 1989 he curated China/Avant-Garde in Beijing, the exhibition that gathered the decade's experimental work into a single national statement, selecting Xu Bing's Book from the Sky for the show and including Huang Yong Ping. The exhibition has stood ever since as the summation of that decade's experiments, the moment at which they became visible as one story. Gao is Chair of the Department of Art History at the University of Pittsburgh, where he is Professor for Distinguished Service, and a distinguished professor at the Tianjin Academy of Fine Arts.

lixianting.blurb: The critic who named Cynical Realism.
lixianting.bio: Li Xianting, born in 1949, is an independent art critic and curator of contemporary Chinese art. He graduated from the Chinese Painting Department of the Central Academy of Fine Art in 1978, then edited Fine Art Magazine until 1983 and the authoritative China Fine Art Newspaper from 1985 to 1989, positions that put him at the centre of every argument about what Chinese art should be. From 1989 he worked as an independent critic and curator in Beijing. He named both Cynical Realism and Political Pop, the two terms that framed how the 1990s generation was read at home and abroad, and championed Fang Lijun and Wang Guangyi in the process. Few critics anywhere have so directly determined the vocabulary applied to their contemporaries.

fanglijun.blurb: A painter of China's Cynical Realism.
fanglijun.bio: Fang Lijun, born in 1963, is a Chinese artist based in Beijing who works as a painter, printmaker and conceptual artist. He was born into a wealthy family of high social standing, and living in China through the years that followed shaped his view of art, human values and morality in ways his work has never stopped registering. In the 1990s he became a leading figure in the tendency known as Cynical Realism, the flat, disabused mood that critics read as the aftermath of the previous decade's idealism. The name itself came from the critic Li Xianting, who identified and championed the group, alongside the parallel category of Political Pop. Fang's paintings remain the images most often used to represent Chinese art of that decade abroad.

aldiaz.bio: Al Diaz, born in 1959, is an American urban artist and lecturer who was among the first generation of graffiti writers in New York. In 1978 he co-created the SAMO© campaign with Jean-Michel Basquiat, the tag and its cryptic aphorisms appearing across SoHo between 1977 and 1979, aimed less at the trains than at the art world that was about to absorb both of them. It was a genuine collaboration, two young writers working as a single voice, and it had run its course by 1979. Diaz has continued to work and to lecture on that period, and is one of the few remaining first-hand witnesses to how the downtown scene actually operated. SAMO© remains the point where street writing and the 1980s art market first touched.

tsengkwongchi.blurb: Photographed Haring's subway drawings as they happened.
tsengkwongchi.bio: Tseng Kwong Chi, born in Hong Kong in 1950 and known as Joseph Tseng before his professional career, was an American photographer at the centre of the East Village art scene of the 1980s. His most valuable contribution to the record of that decade was documentary: he photographed Keith Haring's subway drawings as they were being made, in the stations themselves and at the pace the work demanded. Because the drawings were temporary, Tseng's images are in many cases what survives of them, which makes him both a collaborator and the archivist of a body of work that would otherwise have vanished. He was the brother of the dancer and choreographer Muna Tseng, and he moved through the East Village as a photographer of the scene as much as a participant in it. He died in 1990.

howardhodgkin.blurb: British abstraction, and a friendship with Khakhar.
howardhodgkin.bio: Sir Howard Hodgkin, born in 1932, was a British painter and printmaker whose work is most often described as abstract, though it kept a stubborn attachment to occasions, rooms and people. He worked also as an illustrator and graphic artist. His place in this map runs east: from 1976 he was a close friend of the Indian painter Bhupen Khakhar, and the friendship carried traffic in both directions, structuring Hodgkin's repeated visits to India and helping open British exhibitions to Khakhar's work. It is a rare example of a connection between British and Indian modern painting that operated as an exchange between equals rather than as a form of patronage. Hodgkin died in 2017, and remains one of the most distinctive British painters of his generation.

michaelcraigmartin.blurb: The Goldsmiths teacher behind the YBAs.
michaelcraigmartin.bio: Sir Michael Craig-Martin, born in 1941, is an Irish-born conceptual artist and painter, best known to the public for An Oak Tree of 1973 and to the art world for the generation he taught. As a tutor at Goldsmiths, where he is now emeritus Professor of Fine Art, he fostered and then publicly adopted the Young British Artists: Damien Hirst passed through his teaching between 1986 and 1989, as did Gary Hume, Sarah Lucas and Ian Davenport. What he gave them was less a style than a licence, the conceptual permission to make anything provided the idea held. He works as a sculptor, painter and illustrator, and published his memoir and advice for aspiring artists, On Being An Artist, in April 2015.

iandavenport.bio: Ian Davenport, born in 1966, is an English abstract painter who also works as a printmaker, draftsperson and conceptual artist. He studied at Goldsmiths under Michael Craig-Martin, arriving with the same cohort that would become the Young British Artists, but took the conceptual permission of that teaching in an unexpected direction, back into abstract painting at a moment when his contemporaries were leaving it. His method lets colour run and pool rather than be brushed, so the paintings are as much records of a process as compositions; Poured Lines dates from 2006. He was nominated for the Turner Prize, and has stayed with poured colour since, refining a single procedure rather than moving between styles. Davenport remains the painter's answer within a generation better known for objects and spectacle.

damianortega.blurb: Mexican sculptor who takes things apart.
damianortega.bio: Damián Ortega, born in 1967, is a Mexican visual artist known for sculpture, installation and mixed-media work, and he is also a photographer and draftsperson. His formation came not from an academy but from the Taller de los viernes, the Friday workshop that ran in Gabriel Orozco's Mexico City flat from 1987 to 1992, where a small group of young artists read, argued and made work together outside the institutions. Cosmic Thing, from 2002, is his best-known piece, an object dismantled into its components and held suspended so that the whole and its parts are visible at once, which is close to a description of his method generally. He lives and works between Mexico City and Berlin, and remains one of the defining artists of his generation in Mexico.

abrahamcruzvillegas.bio: Abraham Cruzvillegas, born in 1968, is a Mexican visual artist working as a sculptor and as a conceptual and installation artist. He is best known for his work with found objects and for the ongoing project he calls autoconstrucción, self-building, a term drawn from the way houses are put up incrementally from whatever is available, and applied to sculpture as a principle of permanent unfinishedness. Like several of his closest contemporaries he came out of the Taller de los viernes, the Friday workshop held in Gabriel Orozco's Mexico City flat, where the emphasis fell on discussion and shared attention rather than on individual style. That grounding shows in a practice that treats materials as circumstances to be worked with rather than chosen. He remains among the most influential Mexican artists of his generation.

gabrielkuri.blurb: A Friday-workshop sculptor from Mexico City.
gabrielkuri.bio: Gabriel Kuri, born in 1962, is a Mexican artist working across sculpture, painting and photography. He belonged to the Taller de los viernes, the Friday workshop that Gabriel Orozco ran from his Mexico City flat, where a handful of young artists met to talk, read and make work outside any academy or gallery. That group went on to form the core of an internationally visible Mexican generation, and the workshop's habits of shared attention and close reading are legible in the work he has made since. His sculpture sits at the centre of the practice, with photography and painting running alongside it rather than apart from it. He remains one of the quieter and more formally precise figures to come out of that room, and an illustration of how much a weekly meeting in a friend's flat could change.

drlakra.bio: Jerónimo López Ramírez, who works as Dr. Lakra, was born in 1972 and is a Mexican artist and tattooist based in Oaxaca, moving between drawing, painting and tattooing without treating any of them as the lesser trade. He was part of the Taller de los viernes, the Friday workshop Gabriel Orozco ran in his Mexico City flat, which gathered the group of artists who would carry Mexican contemporary art abroad in the following decades. His work has been shown internationally, at Tate Modern and the Barbican Centre in London, the Drawing Center in New York, the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Oaxaca and the Yokohama Museum of Art, and is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Hammer Museum and the Walker Art Center.

angusfairhurst.bio: Angus Fairhurst, born in 1966, was an English artist working in installation, photography and video, and one of the Young British Artists. In August 1988 he was among the artists who staged Freeze in the disused Port of London Authority building at Surrey Docks, the self-organised exhibition that Damien Hirst assembled and that effectively launched the group; taking on an empty industrial building rather than waiting for a gallery became the defining gesture of that generation. Works such as A Couple of Differences Between Thinking And Feeling suggest a temperament more reflective and more melancholy than the publicity around the YBAs allowed for. He died in 2008, and reassessments since have tended to place him closer to the centre of the group than the headlines ever did.

matcollishaw.blurb: One of the Freeze generation, still working.
matcollishaw.bio: Mat Collishaw, born in 1966, is a British artist based in London, working as a photographer and as a conceptual and visual artist. He was one of the artists who showed in Freeze at Surrey Docks in August 1988, the self-organised exhibition Damien Hirst put together in an empty Port of London Authority building, which brought the Young British Artists into public view. Collishaw's contribution to that group has always been on the side of the image rather than the object, using photography to test how far a picture can go before a viewer looks away. He has continued to work steadily in London through the decades since, one of the least publicised and most consistent careers to come out of that exhibition.

anyagallaccio.blurb: Installations that rot, melt and change.
anyagallaccio.bio: Anya Gallaccio, born in 1963, is a Scottish artist who makes site-specific, minimalist installations, frequently using organic matter, so that the work is subject to time in a way sculpture usually resists. Organic material decays or dissolves over the run of an exhibition, which means the piece a visitor sees on the first day and on the last are not the same, and neither can be preserved. The work is therefore also a kind of clock. She was among the artists in Freeze, the exhibition Damien Hirst organised at Surrey Docks in August 1988 that introduced the Young British Artists, though her work took the group's appetite for spectacle in an almost opposite direction, towards impermanence and quiet. She remains one of the most rigorous artists of that generation.

michaellandy.bio: Michael Landy, born in 1963, is a British artist, painter, draftsperson and photographer, and one of the Young British Artists. He showed in Freeze, the exhibition Damien Hirst organised in a disused Port of London Authority building at Surrey Docks in August 1988. He is best known for Break Down, the performance installation of 2001 in which he systematically destroyed every one of his own possessions, item by item and in public, and for Art Bin at the South London Gallery in 2010, a container into which artists were invited to throw failed work. Both take destruction as a method rather than a gesture. On 29 May 2008 he was elected a member of the Royal Academy of Arts in London.

fionarae.blurb: The painter among the Young British Artists.
fionarae.bio: Fiona Rae, born in Hong Kong in 1963, is a British artist and one of the Young British Artists who came to prominence in the 1990s. She was among the artists in Freeze, the self-organised exhibition Damien Hirst staged in a disused building at Surrey Docks in August 1988, and she has been the group's most committed painter ever since, at a time when the rest of it was largely occupied with objects, vitrines and installation. Her canvases are energetic and deliberately crowded, layering incompatible marks and gestures until the picture holds several kinds of painting at once, and the stated ambition has been to extend rather than abandon the modern traditions she inherited. Rae remains one of the most respected British abstract painters of her generation.

kaminlertchaiprasert.bio: Kamin Lertchaiprasert is an artist associated with relational aesthetics, best known in this map for co-founding The Land Foundation with Rirkrit Tiravanija in Chiang Mai in 1998. The Land was conceived as a shared working site rather than a gallery, extending the idea that a social situation, rather than an object, could be the artwork.

emiliakabakov.blurb: Half of the Kabakov installation partnership.
emiliakabakov.bio: Emilia Kabakov, born in Dnepropetrovsk in the Soviet Union in 1945, is an American artist, curator and art dealer whose work is closely associated with conceptualism and installation art. Since 1988 she has collaborated with her husband Ilya Kabakov, and with the exception of his painting she has shared credit for all of his projects since 1997, an unusually explicit correction to the habit of crediting such work to the man alone. The two are second cousins and married in 1992. Their installations, elaborate constructed environments a visitor walks into rather than looks at, are among the defining artworks to come out of the late Soviet and post-Soviet decades. Emilia's role has been organisational as well as authorial, and the partnership is now treated as a single practice.

jessicarankin.blurb: Australian artist who embroiders on organdy.
jessicarankin.bio: Jessica Rankin, born in 1971, is an Australian artist who lives and works in New York. She is best known for her embroidery on organdy, a transparent fabric that leaves the stitching visible from both sides and lets whatever is behind the work show through it, though she also produces work in other mediums, including painting. She has shown in numerous group exhibitions across the United States, Europe and Australia, among them White Cube in London in 2007, MoMA PS1 in New York in 2006 and Franklin Artworks in Minneapolis in 2005. She is married to the painter Julie Mehretu, and the two work as painters in the same city, a partnership that sits behind two very different approaches to line and layered surface.

bjork.blurb: The singer inside Matthew Barney's films.
bjork.bio: Björk Guðmundsdóttir, born in 1965, is an Icelandic singer, songwriter, composer, record producer and actress, known for a distinctive voice, a three-octave range and a deliberately eccentric public persona. Across a career spanning five decades she has drawn on electronica, pop, dance, trip hop, jazz and avant-garde music, and is widely regarded as one of the most influential musicians of her era. She belongs in a map of visual art through her partnership with Matthew Barney: the two were together from 2000 to 2013, and she both scored and starred in his film Drawing Restraint 9. That collaboration is one of the clearest cases of the boundary between contemporary art and popular music simply dissolving, with each artist working inside the other's medium rather than decorating it.

jayjopling.blurb: White Cube's founder and YBA dealer.
jayjopling.bio: Jay Jopling, born in 1963, is an English art dealer and gallerist, and the founder of White Cube, the gallery that became the commercial home of the Young British Artists and has since grown into an international contemporary art business. Damien Hirst was its founding artist, and Tracey Emin among those it represented, so much of what the public came to know as British art of the 1990s reached them through Jopling's rooms first. His significance is structural rather than curatorial: he supplied a generation that had begun by organising its own exhibitions in disused industrial buildings with a permanent address, a market and a means of selling work that was frequently difficult to sell. White Cube remains one of the most powerful galleries in the world.

gavinbrown.bio: Gavin Brown is an art dealer central to the scene around relational aesthetics. From 1994 he was Rirkrit Tiravanija's dealer, collaborator and co-conspirator, a triple role that suited an artist whose work took the form of cooking, sharing and occupying space rather than producing objects, and required a gallery willing to become a social situation itself.

jeanhubertmartin.bio: Jean-Hubert Martin, born in 1944, is a French art historian, institution director and curator of international exhibitions who spent his career expanding what counted as contemporary art and building dialogue between different cultures and ethnic groups. His decisive project was Magiciens de la Terre, staged in Paris in 1989: the first major exhibition to place non-Western artists on equal footing with their Western contemporaries, it brought Bodys Isek Kingelez and Chéri Samba into an international frame that had previously had no room for them. The show has been argued about ever since, but every subsequent global biennial has had to define itself against it. Martin's career is a reminder that the shape of art history is often set by who is invited into a room.

okwuienwezor.blurb: The curator who globalised the biennial.
okwuienwezor.bio: Okwui Enwezor, born in Nigeria in 1963, was a curator, art critic, writer, poet and educator who reshaped how international exhibitions are made. He was artistic director of Documenta11 in 2002 and of the Venice Biennale in 2015, becoming the first African-born and first non-European curator to lead either, and directed Munich's Haus der Kunst from 2011 to 2018. He founded and edited Nka: Journal of Contemporary African Art, which built the critical framework that careers like Yinka Shonibare's could run on, and championed El Anatsui through the 1990s and 2000s. In 2014 ArtReview ranked him twenty-fourth among the hundred most powerful people in the art world. He lived between New York and Munich, and died in 2019 after a long illness.

andrearosen.blurb: The dealer who keeps Gonzalez-Torres possible.
andrearosen.bio: Andrea Rosen is an American art dealer, best known for representing Félix González-Torres and, after his death, as the executor who administers the certificates that allow his work to exist. Because the work is defined by instructions rather than fixed objects, that administrative role is not clerical: it is what keeps the work capable of being installed at all.

adriankohler.blurb: Handspring puppeteer who worked with Kentridge.
adriankohler.bio: Adrian Kohler is a puppeteer and artist of the Handspring Puppet Company, which he runs with Basil Jones. Their long collaboration with William Kentridge began with Woyzeck on the Highveld in 1992 and continued through the productions that followed, combining Kentridge's imagery with the company's puppets in a form of theatre neither could have made alone.

georgeshenein.blurb: Surrealism's principal voice in the Arab world.
georgeshenein.bio: Georges Henein, born in 1914, was an Egyptian poet, journalist and writer who made Cairo one of Surrealism's capitals. In December 1938 he and the painter Ramses Younan co-signed the manifesto 'Long Live Degenerate Art', a defiantly anti-fascist piece of writing, and out of it grew the Art et Liberté group. With Kamel el-Telmissany and others he built a founding circle that crossed both nationality and discipline, painters and poets and thinkers held together by a single anti-fascist cause, set against fascism abroad and the Egyptian academy at home. The group stayed active from 1938 into the late 1940s, and Inji Efflatoun exhibited with it as a teenager before turning towards social realism. Corresponding with André Breton from Cairo, Henein became Surrealism's principal voice in the Arab world. He died in 1973.

ramsesyounan.bio: Ramses Younan, born in 1913, was an Egyptian painter and writer whose name is inseparable from Art et Liberté, the surrealist collective that gathered painters, writers, thinkers and activists in Cairo behind an anti-nationalist message. In December 1938 he co-signed the group's manifesto 'Long Live Degenerate Art' alongside the poet Georges Henein, a declaration that put Surrealism squarely against fascism. Through the early 1940s he showed in the group's exhibitions with Fouad Kamel, in a Cairo where a modern painting could still be read as a political act. Younan worked in two registers at once, painting and writing, so that his canvases and his arguments pushed in the same direction rather than running on separate tracks. He died in 1966, one of the central figures of a surrealism that answered to Egypt's own politics.

kameleltelmissany.blurb: Cairo surrealist who moved into film.
kameleltelmissany.bio: Kamel el-Telmissany, born in 1915, was an Egyptian artist and filmmaker and one of the founding members of Art et Liberté, the Cairo group he helped start with Georges Henein and Ramses Younan. He worked as a painter and also as a screenwriter and director, carrying the group's appetite for the unsettling and the unofficial into Egyptian cinema. He shared the Art et Liberté circle with his brother Anwar Kamel, so household and movement overlapped. The group set Surrealism against fascism and against the Egyptian academy, and el-Telmissany's double career shows how far that programme could stretch beyond the canvas. His nephew Tarek el-Telmissany became a celebrated Egyptian cinematographer, extending the family's work behind the camera by another generation. He died in 1972.

fouadkamel.blurb: Showed with Art et Liberté in Cairo.
fouadkamel.bio: Fouad Kamel was a painter in the Art et Liberté circle, the surrealist group centred on Cairo. He showed alongside Ramses Younan in the group's exhibitions of the early 1940s. The record collected for him here belongs to another man entirely, so this entry claims no more than the movement, the medium and that documented company.

anwarkamel.blurb: A brother in the Cairo surrealist circle.
anwarkamel.bio: Anwar Kamel belonged to the Art et Liberté circle in Cairo, the surrealist group that his brother Kamel el-Telmissany helped found. The two moved through the same company of artists and writers. The biographical record gathered for him here belongs to someone else, so nothing further is claimed.

amynimr.blurb: Painter and patron of Cairo's surrealists.
amynimr.bio: Amy Nimr, born in Egypt in 1898, painted, wrote, and supported other people's art as a patron; the record carries her under two names, Amy Nimr and Amy Smart. Her nationality is listed as both Egyptian and Ottoman, a reminder of how much the map around her shifted inside a single lifetime. What she is chiefly remembered for is the Art and Liberty Group, the Cairo circle that formed around Surrealism in the city. Painting was only part of what she brought to it. As a patron she belonged to the supporting structure such groups depend on, the part of the story that art history tends to record thinly and late, and that keeps a movement alive between exhibitions. She died in 1974, her name inseparable from that Cairo circle.

hassaneltelmissany.blurb: A painter in Art et Liberté's orbit.
hassaneltelmissany.bio: Hassan el-Telmissany was a painter associated with Art et Liberté, the surrealist group active in Cairo. The biographical material gathered for him here in fact describes another artist and cannot be trusted, so this entry stays with what is safe to say: the movement, the city and the medium.

zainulabedin.blurb: Drew the Bengal famine from the street.
zainulabedin.bio: Zainul Abedin, born in 1914, was a Bengali painter who became widely known in 1944 through a series of works made out of famine in Bengal. He drew the famine of 1943 directly from the streets in ink and brush, and those images are still taken as his most characteristic work; Chittaprosad Bhattacharya was recording the same catastrophe by the same method at the same time. Partition took him to East Pakistan, and by 1948 he was among the founders of the University of Dhaka's Institute of Arts and Crafts, which made him a teacher as much as a painter. At home he was given the title Shilpacharya, great teacher of the arts. His famine drawings set the terms for Somnath Hore's lifelong work on wounds and suffering. He died in 1976, the pioneer of modern art in Bangladesh.

chittaprosadbhattacharya.blurb: The political artist who refused oil paint.
chittaprosadbhattacharya.bio: Chittaprosad Bhattacharya, born in 1915, was an Indian political artist and writer whose leftism was not a background detail but the engine of the work. He drew as a cartoonist, painted in watercolour and made prints, and he made a point of avoiding oil on canvas, letting the reproducible mediums carry everything instead. During the Bengal famine of 1943 he drew the hunger directly from the streets in ink and brush, as Zainul Abedin was doing at the same time, so that between them the disaster was set down by artists standing inside it rather than reading about it afterwards. That preference for the print over the canvas reads as a political choice as much as an aesthetic one, and it kept his work close to the people it was about. He died in 1978.

somnathhore.bio: Somnath Hore, born in 1921, was an Indian printmaker and sculptor whose work kept returning to the crises of twentieth-century Bengal. The Tebhaga movement and the famine of 1943 run through his sketches, prints and sculptures as a reaction rather than a theme chosen at leisure. Zainul Abedin's famine drawings had set the terms, and Hore spent a lifetime on the subject they opened up: the wound, and the body that has to carry it. He worked as a lithographer and painter as well, but it is the print and the cast surface, marked and broken like skin, that hold his reputation. India honoured him with the Padma Bhushan. He died in 2006, having made suffering a subject that demanded precision rather than pathos.

gopalghose.bio: Gopal Ghose, born in 1913, was an Indian painter from West Bengal and, in 1943, among the founders of the Calcutta Group, perhaps, as the record carefully hedges it, India's first modernist painters' group. He started it with Prodosh Das Gupta and their contemporaries in the year of the Bengal famine, so that the case for a modern Indian art was made in the middle of a catastrophe rather than at a comfortable distance from one. Founding a group is a claim about what art ought to be doing next, and the Calcutta Group made that claim early and in public, which is why the 1943 date carries such weight in accounts of Indian modernism. He died in 1980, remembered as much for that founding as for any single canvas.

nirodemazumdar.bio: Nirode Mazumdar, born in 1916, was an Indian painter who belonged to the country's first modernist generation and became one of the Calcutta Group's central members. With Prodosh Das Gupta he argued for a modern Indian art answerable to its own moment rather than to inherited models. He called his method constructive symbolism, and he reached for symbols long before most of his contemporaries saw what they were worth, using them to carry philosophical aims as much as pictorial ones. From the 1940s onwards he was one of the commanding presences on the Indian art scene and something close to a cult figure among fellow artists, though his name has since slipped out of general view. He died in 1982, a major force in Indian modernism who is now unjustly little known.

paritoshsen.blurb: A founder of the Calcutta Group.
paritoshsen.bio: Paritosh Sen, born in Dhaka in 1918, was a painter and writer who spent his working life near the centre of Bengali modernism. He was a founder member of the Calcutta Group, formed in the early 1940s, the movement that did more than any other to bring modernism into Indian art at a moment when the country's painters were arguing hard about what a modern Indian picture should be. Alongside the sculptor Prodosh Das Gupta and the group's other founders, Sen pressed for an art answerable to its own place and time rather than to imported models, and he later helped carry that argument into the circle around the Progressive Artists' Group. A writer as well as a painter, he was counted among the leading Indian artists of his generation, and he went on working until his death in 2008.

rathinmaitra.bio: Rathindranath Maitra, known as Rathin Maitra and sometimes spelt Moitra, was a Bengali painter born in 1913. He belonged to the new generation of Indian modernists who came of age in the 1940s, and in 1943 he was one of the co-founders of the Calcutta Group, formed in the years of the Bengal famine that shadows the whole period. The group set itself against academic habit and inherited colonial taste, arguing for a modern Indian art answerable to its own moment rather than to imported models. Maitra's career ran on to 1997, spanning independence and the decades in which Indian modernism found its footing, and the several spellings his name still carries are a small sign of how much moved between languages in that world. He is remembered as a prominent figure in mid-century Bengali painting, and above all for that founding role.

prodoshdasgupta.blurb: Classical Indian form meets modern geometry.
prodoshdasgupta.bio: Prodosh Das Gupta, born in 1912, was a leading Indian Bengali sculptor of the 1940s and one of the artists who worked out how the philosophy of Indian classical sculpture might live inside the geometry of modern Western form. In 1943 he was a founding member of the Calcutta Group, alongside Gopal Ghose, Nirode Mazumdar and Paritosh Sen, who argued together for a modern Indian art answerable to its own moment rather than to European precedent. The group went on to play an important part in the evolution of art in India and in Bengal, and Sen later helped carry its argument into the Progressive Artists' Group circle. Das Gupta's talents ran wide: he contributed as a poet, writer, art critic and teacher as well as a sculptor and painter. He died in 1991.

grahamsutherland.blurb: Painter of the bombed and the powerful.
grahamsutherland.bio: Graham Vivian Sutherland, born in 1903, was a prolific English artist best known for his abstracted landscapes and his portraits of public figures, though he worked just as readily in printmaking, tapestry and glass design. During the Second World War he was employed by the War Artists' Advisory Committee, run by Kenneth Clark, who kept a generation of painters in work through the war years. Sutherland's assignment was the bombed cities, and his Devastation pictures of 1941 record a burnt paper warehouse, a wrecked public house and a ruined East End street. Henry Moore, drawing the Underground shelters, and John Piper, recording blitzed churches and country houses, were working the same commission from different angles. Sutherland lived until 1980, and the strange, thorny forms he found in ruined buildings and in landscape carried through into the portraiture that made him famous.

johnpiper.blurb: Ruined churches, stained glass, British landscape.
johnpiper.bio: John Egerton Christmas Piper, born in 1903, was an English painter and printmaker who also designed stained-glass windows and sets for opera and theatre, and whose restless output took in tapestry, fabrics and ceramics, book jackets, screen prints and photography. His training ran from Epsom College through the Richmond School of Art to the Royal College of Art in London. He turned away from abstraction early, settling into a more naturalistic but unmistakable manner while still moving between styles throughout his career. His subject was the British landscape and above all its churches and monuments, which made him the right painter for the War Artists' Advisory Committee: he recorded blitzed churches and country houses while Graham Sutherland worked on the bombed cities. All Saints Chapel, Bath, painted in 1942, is one result. Piper went on working until his death in 1992.

ericravilious.bio: Eric William Ravilious, born in 1903 and raised in Sussex, was a British painter, designer, book illustrator and wood engraver. He is best known for watercolours of the South Downs, Castle Hedingham and other English places, pictures that examine landscape and vernacular art with an off-kilter modernist clarity. The same clear eye went to war with him: as an official war artist he made Coastal Defences and Train Landscape in 1940 and a set of studies of submarines, holding to pattern and quiet in the middle of the machinery. Paul Nash, who served as a war artist in both world wars, was a fellow traveller in that work and in the peace between them. In 1942 Ravilious was lost off Iceland on an air-sea rescue patrol, the first British war artist to die on active service in the Second World War.

stanleyspencer.blurb: He painted Cookham as a village in Heaven.
stanleyspencer.bio: Sir Stanley Spencer, born in 1891 in Cookham, the small Berkshire village beside the Thames where he spent much of his life, trained at the Slade School of Art and soon became known for painting biblical scenes as though they were happening on his own doorstep. He called Cookham a village in Heaven and cast his neighbours as their Gospel counterparts, which gave the work its odd, tender literalism. He was unusually skilled at organising crowded multi-figure compositions, a gift that suited large commissions: the Sandham Memorial Chapel, his First World War memorial cycle, and the Shipbuilding on the Clyde series, painted for the War Artists' Advisory Committee during the Second World War. An earlier war picture, Travoys Arriving with Wounded at a Dressing-Station at Smol, Macedonia, dates from 1919. Spencer died in 1959.

lauraknight.blurb: She painted the women at war.
lauraknight.bio: Dame Laura Knight, born in 1877, worked in oils, watercolours, etching, engraving and drypoint across a career long enough and successful enough to make her one of the most popular painters in Britain. She painted in the figurative, realist tradition, warmed by the English Impressionism she embraced early, and her subjects were people at their work: Physical Training at Witley Camp in 1910, and then, in 1943 alone, Ruby Loftus Screwing a Breech Ring, Take Off and A Balloon Site, Coventry. Those wartime pictures put women's factory and service work at the centre of the national image of the home front. Her standing in a male-dominated British art establishment mattered well beyond her own canvases, paving the way to greater status and recognition for the women artists who followed. She died in 1970.

edwardardizzone.bio: Edward Jeffrey Irving Ardizzone, born in 1900 and sometimes signing himself DIZ, was a British painter, printmaker and war artist who is remembered just as much as the author and illustrator of books, many of them for children. The two halves of the career ran side by side rather than in competition. For Tim All Alone, which he both wrote and illustrated, he won the inaugural Kate Greenaway Medal, the Library Association's award for the year's best children's book illustration by a British subject. When the medal reached its fiftieth anniversary in 2005, the book was chosen by a panel as one of the top ten winning titles and put on the ballot for a public election of an all-time favourite. Ardizzone died in 1979, his drawings long since part of British childhood.

albertrichards.blurb: Paratrooper and painter, killed in action.
albertrichards.bio: Albert Richards was born in 1919 to a veteran of the First World War, enlisted as a sapper in 1940, and served in the British Army through the Second World War both as a paratrooper and as an official war artist. That double role is a rare one: he painted the war from inside it, a serving soldier rather than a visitor sent to record. Seacombe Ferry in Wartime, painted in 1941, dates from the early part of that service. He was killed in 1945, the youngest of the three British official war artists to die during the conflict, and the body of work he left is correspondingly small and correspondingly direct. His name belongs with the war artists whose pictures were made under exactly the conditions they describe.

evelyndunbar.blurb: The only salaried woman war artist.
evelyndunbar.bio: Evelyn Mary Dunbar, born in 1906, was a British artist, illustrator and teacher, and the only woman employed by the War Artists' Advisory Committee on a full-time salaried basis. Her subject was women's contribution to the British home front, above all the Women's Land Army; A Land Girl and the Bail Bull, painted in 1945, is the best known of those pictures. She was devoted to the natural world, and to the Kent countryside above all. She was a mural painter too, a member of the Society of Mural Painters, with murals at Brockley County Secondary School. After the war she turned to portraits, allegorical pictures and, most of all, landscape. A 1958 mural commission at Bletchley Park Teacher Training College could not be carried out as planned. Modest about her achievements and outside the post-war mainstream, she died in 1960; her work was neglected until recent years.

sidneynolan.blurb: Ned Kelly's armour, an Australian icon.
sidneynolan.bio: Sir Sidney Robert Nolan, born in 1917, was one of the leading Australian artists of the twentieth century, with an output as varied and as prolific as any in modern art. He belonged to the Angry Penguins circle in Melbourne, painting the war years from a home front that felt besieged, alongside Albert Tucker and Joy Hester, the group's most searching draughtswoman. The Russian emigre Danila Vassilieff gave those younger Melbourne painters a licence with his raw, direct handling. John Reed and Sunday Reed housed and supported the whole Heide circle, and it was in their home that Nolan painted the Ned Kelly series, taking the legend of the bushranger and outlaw and reducing his armour to a stylised shape that has become an icon of Australian art. He kept working across many media until his death in 1992.

alberttucker.blurb: Heide's painter of the besieged home front.
alberttucker.bio: Albert Lee Tucker, born in 1914, was an Australian painter and a central figure in the Heide Circle, the circle of modernist artists and writers who gathered at Heide, the Melbourne house belonging to the patrons John and Sunday Reed. With fellow Heide painters Sidney Nolan and Arthur Boyd, he became associated with Angry Penguins, the movement named after the publication founded by the poet Max Harris and issued by the Reeds. Tucker and Nolan both painted the war years from a home front that felt besieged, and that pressure runs through the imagery of the whole circle. In 1941 he married the artist Joy Hester; their separation ran through the Heide years and marked both of them. Tucker died in 1999, by which time Heide had become one of the defining episodes in twentieth-century Australian art.
