arthurboyd.blurb: Biblical stories set in the Australian bush.
arthurboyd.bio: Arthur Merric Bloomfield Boyd, born in 1920, stood among Australia's leading painters from the middle of the twentieth century onward, and worked as a sculptor, ceramicist and lithographer besides. His pictures move between impressionist readings of the Australian landscape and a starkly expressionist figuration, and many canvases carry both at once. Several of the best known transplant Biblical narratives into the Australian landscape, among them The Expulsion of 1947-48, now in the Art Gallery of New South Wales; the Olympic Pylon is another work associated with him. A strong social conscience runs through everything he made, returning again and again to humanitarian questions and to the universal subjects of love, loss and shame. Boyd and John Perceval were brothers-in-law as well as lifelong colleagues in the Melbourne circle around Angry Penguins. He died in 1999.

joyhester.blurb: The Heide circle's most searching draughtswoman.
joyhester.bio: Joy St Clair Hester, born in 1920, was an Australian artist, poet and writer, a member of the Angry Penguins and of the Heide Circle, and an integral part of the development of Australian modernism. She is best known for bold, expressive ink drawings, and within the circle around Sidney Nolan she was its most searching draughtswoman. Her work carries a heightened awareness of mortality, shaped by losing her father when she was a child, by the threat of war, and by her own Hodgkin's disease. The series Face, Sleep and Love, made in 1948-49, and the later The Lovers of 1956-58 are her central achievements. She married Albert Tucker in 1941, and their separation ran through the Heide years; John Reed was among the circle's patrons throughout. Hester died in 1960.

johnperceval.blurb: The last of the Angry Penguins.
johnperceval.bio: John de Burgh Perceval, born in 1923, was an Australian painter and musician, and the last surviving member of the Angry Penguins, the group that redefined Australian art in the 1940s. Its other figures were Albert Tucker, Sidney Nolan, Arthur Boyd, Joy Hester and John Reed, and between them they pulled Australian painting towards something rawer and more urgent than the landscape tradition they had inherited. Perceval and Boyd were brothers-in-law as well as lifelong colleagues in the Melbourne circle, a family tie that kept the two of them working alongside one another for decades. He was later counted an Antipodean, and showed in that group's exhibition of 1959. Appointed an Officer of the Order of Australia, he died in 2000, having outlived every one of his Angry Penguins contemporaries.

danilavassilieff.blurb: Called the father of Australian modernism.
danilavassilieff.bio: Danila Vassilieff, born in 1897, was a painter and sculptor born in Russia who settled in Australia, where the title father of Australian modernism has often been attached to him. He came from the old Russian Empire with a way of working that owed nothing to local convention: raw, direct and quickly made. That handling mattered enormously to the younger Melbourne painters gathered around Angry Penguins. Sidney Nolan in particular took a licence from it, permission to trust an image before it had been tidied, and the same permission reached the rest of that circle. Vassilieff worked in sculpture as well as paint, and he remained something of an outsider in the country whose modern art he helped set in motion. He died in 1958, his influence carried forward less by a school than by the painters who had watched him work.

fujitatsuguharu.bio: Fujita Tsuguharu, also known as Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita, was born in 1886 and built a career at the centre of the modern Paris art world. He studied Western-style painting in Japan first, then travelled to France, where the international modern art crowd of Montparnasse took him in and he worked out an eclectic manner drawing on Japanese and European traditions at once. He worked as a printmaker, illustrator and draughtsman as well as a painter, and held both Japanese and French nationality. On this map he sits with the Japanese wartime painters, the generation whose careers ran straight through the war years. The Foujita Chapel, completed in 1966, is among the works most closely associated with his name. He died in 1968.

miyamotosaburo.blurb: A painter of Japan's war years.
miyamotosaburo.bio: Miyamoto Saburō is placed here among the Japanese wartime painters, the group whose work is identified with Japan's war years. The biographical record available to this project could not be confirmed for him, so no dates, works or affiliations are claimed here, only his medium, painting, and his place within that movement.

iharausaburo.bio: Ihara Usaburō belongs to the Japanese wartime painters gathered in this part of the map, the movement whose work is identified with Japan's war years. No verified dates, works or connections could be established for him within the sources this project draws on, so none are asserted; what stands is his medium, painting, and that affiliation.

kennethclark.blurb: The man who kept war artists working.
kennethclark.bio: Kenneth Mackenzie Clark, born in 1903, worked in Britain as an art historian, a museum director and a broadcaster. He wrote across a wide span of artists and periods, but his name attaches most firmly to Italian Renaissance art and above all to Leonardo da Vinci. He ran two art galleries during the 1930s and 1940s, and it is his wartime work that matters most here: as head of the War Artists' Advisory Committee he kept a generation of British painters employed and working through the war, Graham Sutherland among them. Clark also commissioned and championed Henry Moore's shelter drawings, an act of patronage that shaped what British art made of the home front. From the 1950s to the 1970s he reached a far wider public through television, most famously with the Civilisation series of 1969. Later made Baron Clark, he died in 1983.

johnreed.blurb: Heide's patron; Ned Kelly was painted there.
johnreed.bio: John Reed was, with Sunday Reed, the patron at the centre of the Angry Penguins. The couple housed and supported the Heide circle at their own home, and it was there that Sidney Nolan painted the Ned Kelly series. Joy Hester was among the artists they backed. Reed's role was not to paint but to make the painting possible.

ssudjojono.bio: S. Sudjojono, born in 1913, is the painter most often named as a founder of the Indonesian modern art movement. That phrase carries weight: it places him not simply among the country's early modernists but at the point where the story starts, the figure from whom later generations dated their own beginnings. His life spanned the decades that carried Indonesia from colonial rule into independence and on through the republic's first long chapter, and he died in 1985. What survives of him is less a single signature manner than an argument pressed through the work itself, that Indonesia could have a modern art of its own, made on Indonesian terms rather than borrowed wholesale. Any account of Southeast Asian modernism has to begin somewhere near him, which is a rarer kind of standing than simply being early.

riesmulder.blurb: The Dutchman who taught Bandung cubism.
riesmulder.bio: Marinus Mulder, known as Ries, was born in the Netherlands in 1909 and worked as a painter, lecturer and writer. His own canvases carried the imprint of Cubism, but it was through teaching that his influence travelled furthest. He became a leading lecturer in Modern Art in Indonesia, teaching at the Bandung Institute of Technology, and the cubist-derived formalism he brought into that studio became the school's defining accent, a constructive and built approach set against the social realism then centred on Yogyakarta. Ahmad Sadali was among his first students there. Srihadi Soedarsono was taught by him too, and both went on to carry that teaching into Indonesian modernism. Mulder died in 1973, but the argument he set going in that classroom outlasted him by a long way, and it was still being answered decades afterwards.

ahmadsadali.blurb: Bandung's abstractionist of nature and spirit.
ahmadsadali.bio: Ahmad Sadali, born in 1924, grew up in a family whose businesses spread across batik and printing, and became one of the most important artists of Indonesian modernism. He was among the earliest and most prominent students of the Dutch painter Ries Mulder at the Bandung Institute of Technology, and he came to represent what was known as the Bandung school. Working as both painter and art lecturer, he moved through abstract expressionism, cubism and colour field painting, and his signature manner, bold in structure and nuanced in surface, held elements of nature and of spirituality without ever naming them outright. He and Srihadi Soedarsono both taught at Bandung, carrying the school's abstraction into the wider currents of Indonesian modernism. He died in 1987. His paintings now rank among the highest-priced Indonesian works on the international art market.

srihadisoedarsono.bio: Srihadi Soedarsono, in full Kanjeng Raden Haryo Tumenggung H. Srihadi Soedarsono Adhikoesoemo, was born in 1931 and worked as both painter and tenured lecturer. He studied at the Bandung Institute of Technology under the Dutch painter Ries Mulder, whose cubist-derived formalism gave the school its character and set it against the social realism then centred on Yogyakarta. Ahmad Sadali came out of the same room, and the two of them later taught at Bandung themselves, carrying its abstraction into Indonesian modernism. He married Farida Srihadi, an accomplished painter in her own right, who trained at the same institute before continuing her studies overseas, in the Netherlands and in England. He died in 2022, by which time the Bandung lineage he had joined as a student ran through several generations of Indonesian art.
